docs.title: Volume 19: Vāṇijya and Samudra
docs.text:
Economy, Trade and Seafaring · Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā

Economic thought, merchants, money and credit, overland and maritime trade, ships and navigation in the Indian Ocean world

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 19 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Vāṇijya and Samudra: Economy, Trade and Seafaring. It brings together two subjects that are often treated separately: the history of economic thought and commercial institutions in South Asia (vāṇijya, trade, and vārttā, the economic arts), and the history of seafaring and maritime trade (samudra, the sea). They belong together. The merchants who formed guilds, lent money and paid tolls on the roads of the Gangetic plain were often the same people, or worked through the same networks, as those who freighted ships at Bharukaccha, Kāveripaṭṭinam or Cambay.

The book moves from ideas and institutions to networks and then to the long early modern and colonial transformation. Chapters 2 to 8 deal with economic thought (the Arthaśāstra, the dharmaśāstra, the Tirukkuṟaḷ, Indo-Persian writing on revenue and Buddhist and Jain ethics of wealth), land and the agrarian surplus, guilds and merchant associations, coinage, credit and banking, markets and their regulation, and the organisation of craft production; Chapter 9 examines the place of religious institutions — monasteries, temples, shrines and pilgrimage — in the economy. Chapter 10 follows the overland routes within South Asia, across Central Asia and over the Himalaya. Chapters 11 to 17 turn to the sea: seaborne trade from the Harappan period to the Indo-Roman trade, the Indian Ocean world between c. 600 and 1500, ships and shipbuilding, the monsoon and navigation, port cities and maritime law, the connections with Southeast Asia, and the coastal communities whose knowledge sustained all of this. Chapters 18 and 19 treat the Sultanate, Vijayanagara and Mughal economies, the arrival of the European companies, the trade in slaves, and the colonial economy, including the long-running debates over deindustrialisation and the “drain of wealth”. Chapter 20 follows Indian economic thought from Ranade to the planners of the 1950s, and Chapter 21 considers legacies and the uses of this history today.

Primary texts are quoted only where the wording and the reference could be confirmed, and figures are given only where a source can be named. This matters especially for the maritime chapters, where the textual evidence is thin. Some claims that are widely repeated are presented here as what they are, open questions or debates: whether the basin at Lothal was a dock, how much of the Yuktikalpataru’s ship lore reflects practice, what the long-run estimates of India’s share of world output can and cannot tell us, and how the economic effects of colonial rule should be measured. The Indian Ocean was never an Indian lake: Arab, Persian, Gujarati, Tamil, Chinese, Southeast Asian, Swahili, Armenian and Jewish merchants all shared it, and the chapters try to give each of them their place. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such; the treatment of the Arthaśāstra’s date in Chapter 2 is an example.

The Arthaśāstra’s theory of kingship and law is treated in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra), the travellers and the geography of the subcontinent in Volume 21 (Bhūgola), crafts and textiles in Volume 17 (Śilpa–Kāru) and metallurgy in Volume 14 (Rasāyana); this volume refers to them rather than repeating them. References to standard editions and studies are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography, and a glossary of principal terms is provided at the end. A survey of this scope cannot be exhaustive, and it is not a substitute for the specialist literature it cites. Every quotation and figure should, before scholarly use, be checked against the sources named.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Economy, Trade and the Sea in South Asian History
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter sets out the scope of the volume. It explains why economic thought, commercial institutions and seafaring are treated together; sketches the geography that shaped South Asian trade; offers an outline of the main periods from the Harappan cities to the colonial economy; reviews the kinds of evidence on which the history rests and their limits; and flags the debates that recur through the book, from the interpretation of Lothal to the measurement of colonial “drain”. It ends with a plan of the chapters.

docs.title: 1.1 Vāṇijya and Samudra
docs.text:
Two Sanskrit words give this volume its title. Vāṇijya (also vaṇijyā) is trade, the activity of the vaṇij or merchant. Samudra is the sea. The Sanskrit tradition of statecraft placed trade within a larger field it called vārttā, “livelihood” or the economic arts. The Arthaśāstra, a composite treatise that reached its present form between about 50 BCE and 300 CE and that tradition attributes to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya (Section 2.1.3), lists vārttā as one of the four bodies of knowledge a ruler must master, alongside philosophy (ānvīkṣikī), the Veda (trayī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and defines it as agriculture, animal husbandry and trade (AŚ 1.4.1) (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). The same text treats wealth (artha) as the foundation on which the other aims of life rest. These ideas, and the institutions that grew up around them, are the subject of the first group of chapters.

The second subject is the sea. For more than four thousand years the coasts of the subcontinent were linked to the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, East Africa, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China. Ships and the monsoon winds, the ports and their merchants, and the laws and customs that governed them are the subject of a second group. The two subjects are not separate in practice. The guild members whose endowments are recorded in the cave inscriptions of Nasik, the moneylenders and hundī brokers of Gujarat and the Coromandel, and the weavers whose cloth filled the holds of ships bound for the Red Sea or Melaka belonged to the same economic world as the ship-owners and pilots. The volume therefore treats commerce and seafaring as a single history.

Three cautions frame what follows. First, “Indian” economic history is the history of a very large and varied region over a very long time. No single “Indian commercial civilisation” existed with a fixed set of institutions; there were many economies, regional and changing, connected by trade. Second, South Asia never owned the Indian Ocean. Its ports were shared, and often dominated, by merchants from elsewhere: Arab, Persian, Armenian, Jewish, Chinese, Malay, Javanese and Swahili traders worked alongside Gujarati, Tamil, Malayali, Bengali and Sinhala ones, and the chapters on the sea try to give all of them their place. Third, the evidence is uneven, and some of the most widely repeated statements about Indian commerce and seafaring, such as that the basin at Lothal was the “world’s first dockyard” or that India produced a third of the world’s output, go beyond it. Where a question is debated, this book sets out the positions; the best-known claims of this kind are gathered and examined in Section 21.7.

docs.title: 1.2 Geography and the Shape of Trade
docs.text:
The subcontinent’s geography shaped its economy in lasting ways. In the north, the alluvial plains of the Indus and the Ganga supported dense agrarian populations and the surpluses on which towns and states depended. The great rivers were themselves routes of trade: river craft carried grain, salt, timber and cloth along the Ganga and its tributaries until the railway age (Deloche 1993). The north-western mountain passes linked the plains to Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia; through them came horses, which South Asia bred poorly and imported in large numbers for many centuries, and through them went cotton textiles, indigo, sugar and spices. The Deccan plateau and the peninsula, rich in minerals, cotton and forest products, were tied to the north by routes along the river valleys and across the Vindhyas, and to the sea by the ports of both coasts (Chapter 10).

The sea frames the peninsula on three sides. The west coast, from Sindh and Gujarat to Malabar, faces the Arabian Sea and, beyond it, the Gulf, the Red Sea and East Africa. The east coast, from Bengal and Odisha to the Coromandel, faces the Bay of Bengal and Southeast Asia. Sri Lanka stands at the junction of the two. Along both coasts, river mouths, estuaries and lagoons provided harbours, though many silted up and moved over the centuries, so that the great ports of one period (Bharukaccha, Tāmralipti, Kāveripaṭṭinam) were replaced by others (Cambay, Surat, Hughli, Masulipatnam) in later ones.

Above all, the Indian Ocean is governed by the monsoon. In the northern summer the winds blow from the south-west; in winter they reverse and blow from the north-east. This seasonal reversal made long voyages possible in sailing ships, but it also imposed a strict calendar: ships had to leave and return within fixed windows, the west coast was largely closed to shipping at the height of the south-west monsoon, and merchants often had to wait months in foreign ports for the wind to turn. The rhythm of the monsoon is the single most important fact in the history of Indian Ocean trade (Chaudhuri 1985; Pearson 2003); it is described in Chapter 14.

Key Insight: A Useful Simplification

For convenience this book sometimes speaks of three overlapping zones of South Asian trade, a working scheme of its own rather than a classification taken from any one historian: the northern plains, oriented by river and road towards Central Asia and Iran; the peninsula, with its own internal networks; and the coastal belts of Gujarat, Konkan and Malabar, Coromandel and Bengal, which faced the ocean. The division is a heuristic, not a description of fixed regions: goods, merchants and capital constantly crossed between the zones, and the coastal belts often had stronger links with ports across the sea than with the interior.

docs.title: 1.3 An Outline History
docs.text: The chapters that follow are arranged by theme, not by period. This section offers a short chronological frame to which they can be related. The dates are those accepted in current scholarship; traditional dates, where they differ, are noted as such in the chapters.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Harappan Civilisation
docs.text: The cities of the mature Harappan or Indus civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) used standardised weights based on a binary and then decimal progression, produced seals that probably marked ownership and identity, and specialised in crafts such as long carnelian beads, shell working and copper and bronze metallurgy (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). Harappan objects and seals found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf, and Akkadian references to the land of Meluhha (generally identified with the Indus region) and its ships, show that the Harappans traded by sea with the Gulf and Mesopotamia, probably through intermediaries in Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman) (Ratnagar 2004). The large brick basin at Lothal in Gujarat was interpreted by its excavator, S. R. Rao, as a tidal dock; other scholars have read it as a reservoir or tank, and its function remains debated (Rao 1979; Leshnik 1968). Chapter 11 sets out the evidence.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Early Historic Urbanisation
docs.text: After the decline of the Harappan cities, the second great phase of urbanisation came in the Ganga valley in the mid-first millennium BCE. Towns such as Rājagṛha, Śrāvastī, Kauśāmbī, Vārāṇasī and Ujjayinī grew within the territorial states (mahājanapadas) of which Magadha became the most powerful. This period saw the first coinage of the subcontinent (silver punch-marked coins, from perhaps the fifth or fourth century BCE), the spread of the Northern Black Polished Ware, the organisation of artisans and traders into corporate groups, and the rise of Buddhism and Jainism, both of which drew important support from merchants and householders (Thapar 2002; Chakravarti 1987). The Maurya empire (c. 321–185 BCE), whose most famous ruler Aśoka reigned c. 268–232 BCE, unified most of the subcontinent and maintained the royal highways later described by Greek observers (McCrindle 1877).

docs.title: 1.3.3 The Early Centuries CE
docs.text: The centuries around the beginning of the Common Era were a period of intense commercial activity. The Kuṣāṇa empire straddled the routes between India, Central Asia and China; the Sātavāhanas in the Deccan and the Western Kṣatrapas in Gujarat and Malwa controlled the ports and the routes behind them; and in the far south the Tamil chiefdoms of the Caṅkam age traded with Roman Egypt through ports such as Muziris and Arikamedu. Roman coins, amphorae and tableware in India, and Indian pottery, pepper and Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions in Egyptian Red Sea ports, attest to this trade (Tomber 2008; De Romanis 2020). Guilds made permanent endowments to Buddhist monasteries in the western Deccan, and their inscriptions are among the best evidence for commercial organisation in early India (Ray 1986; Thaplyal 1996).

docs.title: 1.3.4 From the Guptas to c. 1000 CE
docs.text: The Gupta period (c. 320–550 CE) is known for its gold coinage and for the guild seals of Vaiśālī. For the centuries that followed, historians disagree about the economy. R. S. Sharma argued for a decline of towns, trade and coinage and a shift to a “feudal” order, while others, notably B. D. Chattopadhyaya, see the formation of new regional states, market centres and networks rather than decline (Sharma 1987; Chattopadhyaya 1994). In the south, the period saw the growth of temple-centred economies and of powerful merchant associations, such as the Ayyāvoḷe Five Hundred and the Maṇigrāmam, whose inscriptions appear from Karnataka to Sumatra (Abraham 1988; Champakalakshmi 1996).

docs.title: 1.3.5 The Indian Ocean World, c. 600–1500
docs.text: The rise of Islam and of the Abbasid caliphate, and the expansion of Tang and Song China’s maritime trade, created a vast trading world from the Red Sea to the South China Sea. Indian ports took part in it alongside Arab and Persian ports in the Gulf, the Śrīvijaya polity in Sumatra, and Chinese ports such as Quanzhou. The Chola kings of south India sent expeditions to Sri Lanka and, in 1025, raided the ports of Śrīvijaya. Jewish merchants whose letters survive in the Cairo Geniza traded between Egypt, Aden and the Malabar coast (Goitein and Friedman 2008). These networks are the subject of Chapter 12.

docs.title: 1.3.6 Sultanate, Vijayanagara, Mughal
docs.text: From the thirteenth century the Delhi Sultanate, and from the sixteenth the Mughal empire, ruled large parts of the subcontinent and created monetised, revenue-based states with large cities, courts and workshops. Vijayanagara dominated the south from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. Gujarati, Bengali and Coromandel textiles were exported across the Indian Ocean and, from the seventeenth century, to Europe. The arrival of the Portuguese in 1498, and later of the Dutch, English and French companies, changed the political conditions of trade without, at first, displacing Asian merchants (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Das Gupta and Pearson 1987). Chapter 18 treats this period.

docs.title: 1.3.7 The Colonial Economy
docs.text:
After Plassey (1757) the English East India Company became a territorial power in Bengal and, by the mid-nineteenth century, across the subcontinent. The economic consequences of colonial rule (for manufacturing, shipping, agriculture, famine, and the transfer of resources to Britain) were debated by Indian nationalists such as Dadabhai Naoroji and R. C. Dutt, and are still debated by historians today (Kumar 1983; Roy 2000). Chapter 19 presents that debate. Table 1.1 gives a simplified chronology of the periods discussed in this volume.

Table 1.1. A simplified chronology of the periods discussed in this volume Period Main economic and commercial features c. 2600–1900 BCE Mature Harappan cities; standard weights; seals; trade with the Gulf and Mesopotamia c. 600–300 BCE Second urbanisation in the Ganga valley; first coinage; Buddhist and Jain lay supporters among merchants c. 321–185 BCE Maurya empire; royal roads; Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) c. 50 BCE–300 CE Composition of the Arthaśāstra in its present form (Olivelle); Indo-Roman trade; Kuṣāṇa and Sātavāhana states; guild endowments c. 320–550 CE Gupta gold coinage; guild seals; Mandasor silk-weavers’ inscription c. 600–1300 CE Regional states; temple economies; south Indian merchant associations; Chola expeditions (1025 raid on Śrīvijaya) c. 1200–1700 CE Delhi Sultanate; Vijayanagara; Mughal empire; Gujarati and Coromandel textile exports; Portuguese (1498) and European companies 1757–1947 CE Company and Crown rule; debates on deindustrialisation and the drain; famines; economic nationalism

docs.title: 1.4 Wealth and Its Ethics
docs.text:
Indian thought did not treat commerce with the suspicion found in some ancient traditions. The scheme of the four aims of life (puruṣārtha) places artha, material well-being and power, beside dharma, kāma and mokṣa. The Arthaśāstra makes wealth the root of the others; the dharmaśāstra literature, while ranking dharma first, regulates trade, interest, partnership and the duties of the merchant in detail (Chapters 2 and 6). The Buddhist canon is full of merchants: the banker Anāthapiṇḍika, who gave the Jetavana grove to the order, is among the most celebrated lay followers, and the Jātaka stories regularly feature caravan leaders and sea voyages (Chakravarti 1987; Chakravarti 2002). Jain merchant communities, especially in western India, combined great commercial success with an ethic of restraint and gift-giving that anthropologists have studied closely (Jaini 1979; Laidlaw 1995).

This tradition had a harsher side. The same texts that praise honest trade assume a hierarchy in which the merchant’s status, the interest he may charge, and the penalties he faces depend on his varṇa; the Arthaśāstra and the law books regulate slavery and bonded labour; and the state’s interest in trade was largely an interest in revenue. Merchants themselves were drawn from many castes and communities, and their position in society varied greatly between regions and periods (Thapar 2002). These questions are taken up where they arise, especially in Chapters 2, 4, 6 and 8.

docs.title: 1.5 The Evidence and Its Limits
docs.text:
The history in this volume rests on several kinds of evidence, each with its own strengths and problems.

Normative texts The Arthaśāstra, the Dharmasūtras and Dharmaśāstras (Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Bṛhaspati, Kātyāyana) and their commentaries describe how trade, credit and guilds should be regulated. They are invaluable for categories and concepts but are prescriptive and hard to date; they do not show how often their rules were applied (Olivelle 1999; Kane 1930). Narrative and poetic literature The Pali Jātakas and Vinaya, Jain narrative literature, Sanskrit drama and prose, and the Tamil Caṅkam poems describe markets, caravans, ports and ships. They are literary works, written for other purposes, and their details must be used with care. Inscriptions Thousands of stone and copper-plate inscriptions record gifts, endowments, tolls, guild agreements and royal grants. They are the most reliable dated evidence for institutions such as guilds and merchant associations (Salomon 1998; Lüders 1912). Coins Coin finds and hoards show the circulation of money, the reach of states and the direction of trade (Chapter 5). Archaeology Excavated sites, from Harappan towns to Arikamedu, Pattanam and the Red Sea ports of Berenike and Myos Hormos, provide physical evidence of goods and their movement (Ray 2003; Tomber 2008). Foreign accounts Greek and Roman writers (Megasthenes as quoted by later authors, the Periplus Maris Erythraei, Pliny, Ptolemy), Chinese pilgrims and officials, Arabic and Persian geographers, the Jewish merchants of the Cairo Geniza, Ma Huan, Ibn Baṭṭūṭa and the Portuguese chroniclers offer external views, often precise on goods and prices but limited by their authors’ interests and misunderstandings (Casson 1989; Goitein and Friedman 2008). The travellers themselves are treated in Volume 21, Bhūgola. Company and state archives From the seventeenth century the records of the European companies and of Mughal and successor states make quantitative economic history possible for the first time (Chaudhuri 1978; Prakash 1998).

Two kinds of evidence are conspicuously absent. No Indian merchant’s account books survive from before the early modern period, and no pre-modern Indian sea charts are known. Claims that rely on either should be treated with caution.

docs.title: 1.6 How the History Has Been Written
docs.text:
The economic history of South Asia has been written from several standpoints, and each has left its mark on the questions asked and on the claims that circulate today.

Colonial administrators and orientalists. Officials of the East India Company and the Crown compiled gazetteers, revenue reports and statistical surveys that remain essential sources, but they often assumed that pre-colonial India had been static, its villages self-sufficient and its economy shaped by caste and custom rather than by markets. The rediscovery of the Arthaśāstra in 1905 and the publication of inscriptions and coins challenged this picture by revealing an ancient literature of revenue, trade and administration (Shamasastry 1915).

Economic nationalism. From the 1870s Indian writers turned the colonial record against itself. Dadabhai Naoroji’s argument that Britain drained wealth from India, and R. C. Dutt’s history of the economy under Company and Crown, made economic history a central part of the nationalist case (Naoroji 1901; Dutt 1902; Chandra 1966). In the same period Radhakumud Mookerji’s Indian Shipping (1912) and R. C. Majumdar’s Corporate Life in Ancient India (1918) set out to show that India had possessed a great maritime tradition and sophisticated commercial institutions (Mookerji 1912; Majumdar 1918). These works were pioneering, and much of their evidence is still used; but they were also written to restore national pride, and some of their claims, for instance about ship lore or the “Greater India” of Southeast Asia, are more confident than the evidence allows.

Marxist and social history. From the 1950s D. D. Kosambi, R. S. Sharma and Irfan Habib placed the economy at the centre of Indian history, asking about modes of production, surplus extraction, the condition of peasants and artisans, and the reasons why capitalism did not develop in pre-colonial India (Kosambi 1956; Sharma 1983; Habib 1969). Their questions, and the debates they provoked, shaped the field for half a century.

Trade, merchants and the Indian Ocean. Auguste Toussaint’s History of the Indian Ocean (French 1961, English 1966) was an early attempt to write the ocean’s history as a whole (Toussaint 1966). From the 1960s historians such as Ashin Das Gupta, K. N. Chaudhuri, Om Prakash, Sanjay Subrahmanyam and Sinnappah Arasaratnam rebuilt the history of Indian merchants and of the Indian Ocean from Asian and European company archives, showing that Asian merchants remained active and powerful long after 1500 (Das Gupta 1979; Chaudhuri 1985; Prakash 1998; Subrahmanyam 1990; Arasaratnam 1986). For the ancient period, Himanshu Prabha Ray, Ranabir Chakravarti and others combined archaeology, inscriptions and texts to write a history of trade not centred on states (Ray 2003; Chakravarti 2002).

Global and comparative history. Since the 1990s the “great divergence” debate has asked why Western Europe, rather than South or East Asia, industrialised first. Historians such as Prasannan Parthasarathi and Tirthankar Roy have offered sharply different answers, and economic historians have produced new estimates of output and income (Parthasarathi 2011; Roy 2012; Broadberry et al. 2015).

This volume draws on all of these traditions. It also tries to avoid a temptation common to several of them: to read the past mainly as evidence for or against a present-day argument about India’s place in the world.

docs.title: 1.7 Recurring Debates
docs.text: Several debates run through the volume. The largest concerns the size of the pre-modern Indian economy: Angus Maddison’s long-run estimates, which put India’s share of world output at roughly a quarter around 1500–1700, are examined with their caveats in the debate box of Section 18.5.6. Other debates concern the interpretation of particular evidence: whether Lothal had a dock (Chapter 11); how far the ship lore of the Yuktikalpataru reflects real practice (Chapter 13); whether the early medieval period saw urban and commercial decline (Chapters 3, 4 and 5); how the Indic culture of Southeast Asia should be understood, as “Indianisation” or as local adoption and adaptation (Chapter 16); what the Chola expeditions of the eleventh century were for (Chapter 12); and how to measure the economic effects of colonial rule (Chapter 19). In each case the volume tries to set out the evidence and the main positions rather than to settle the question.

docs.title: 1.8 Plan of the Volume
docs.text:
The volume has twenty-one chapters. They are not divided into formal parts, but they fall into four groups, and the chapters within each group are best read in order.

Ideas and institutions (Chapters 2–9). Chapter 2 examines the Arthaśāstra and the wider tradition of economic thought, including the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ, Indo-Persian writing on revenue, and Buddhist and Jain ethics of wealth; the Arthaśāstra’s theory of the state is treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Chapter 3 turns to the agrarian base: the state’s claim on the harvest across the periods of the volume, the early medieval land grants and the debate over “Indian feudalism”. Chapter 4 turns to guilds and merchant associations, Chapter 5 to coinage and money, Chapter 6 to credit, banking and commercial law, Chapter 7 to markets, prices, weights and their regulation, and Chapter 8 to the organisation of craft production (techniques are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru, and Volume 14, Rasāyana). Chapter 9 examines religious institutions — Buddhist and Jain monasteries and temples, the south Indian temple, pilgrimage centres and fairs, Islamic endowments and Sikh gurdwārās — as holders, redistributors and investors of wealth.

Overland trade (Chapter 10). The routes within the subcontinent and the connections across Central Asia, including the Silk Roads and the Indian merchant diaspora in Iran, Central Asia and Russia, and the routes across the Himalaya and the north-east.

The sea (Chapters 11–17). Seaborne trade from the Harappans to the Indo-Roman trade; the Indian Ocean world from c. 600 to 1500; ships and shipbuilding; the monsoon and navigation; port cities, port administration and maritime law; the connections with Southeast Asia; and the fishing and seafaring communities of the coasts.

Transformation and legacy (Chapters 18–21). The early modern economy from the Sultanate to the late eighteenth century, including the arrival of the European companies and the trade in slaves; the colonial economy and the decline of Indian shipping; Indian economic thought from Ranade to the Second Five-Year Plan; and the legacies of this history, with a caution about its uses and misuses today.

docs.title: 1.9 A Note on Terms and Conventions
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST); Tamil words in a standard transliteration; Arabic and Persian words in a simplified scholarly form. Familiar modern place names (Surat, Calicut, Kolkata) are given in their ordinary English spelling. Dates are given as BCE and CE. References to the Arthaśāstra (AŚ) follow the book, chapter and sentence numbering of Kangle’s edition, as used in Olivelle’s translation. A glossary of principal terms is at the end of the volume.

A number of English words record the history told here. Calico takes its name from Calicut, chintz from the Hindi chīṇṭ, catamaran from the Tamil kaṭṭumaram (“tied logs”), and pepper, through Greek and Latin, ultimately from an Indian word related to Sanskrit pippalī (long pepper). They are reminders that South Asian goods travelled further than South Asian names for them.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For general frameworks see Thapar (2002) and Kulke and Rothermund (2004); for economic history over the long run, Roy (2012); for early trade, Chakravarti (2002) and Ray (2003); for the Indian Ocean, Chaudhuri (1985), McPherson (1993) and Pearson (2003); for the early modern and colonial periods, the two volumes of the Cambridge Economic History of India (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Kumar 1983).

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Arthaśāstra and Early Indian Economic Thought
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter introduces the Arthaśāstra, the most detailed early Indian text on the management of wealth, and places it within the wider body of Indian thinking about economic life. It describes the rediscovery of the text, its structure and the debate about its date and authorship, and then examines its economic ideas: the meaning of artha and vārttā, the revenue system and its officials, state enterprise and monopolies, and the regulation of labour, including slavery. The chapter closes with the later nīti literature, with the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ and the Indo-Persian writing on kingship and revenue, and with the economic ethics of the dharmaśāstras and of Buddhist and Jain traditions. The Arthaśāstra’s theory of kingship, diplomacy and law is treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra, and is not repeated here.

Kauṭilya’s Arthaśāstra is the indispensable starting point for any history of economic thought in South Asia. No other early Indian text describes in such detail how a state was to raise revenue, run workshops, mines and farms, supervise trade and regulate labour. It must, however, be read for what it is: a normative treatise addressed to a king, compiled over several centuries, which describes how an ideal administration should work rather than how any particular state did work. This chapter introduces the text and its economic ideas. The detailed regulation of markets, prices, weights and customs is reserved for Chapter 7, coinage and the mint for Chapter 5, interest and partnerships for Chapter 6, and guilds for Chapter 4.

docs.title: 2.1 The Text: Rediscovery, Structure and Date
2.1.1 Rediscovery
docs.text:
Although the Arthaśāstra was known by name and cited by later writers, no complete manuscript was known to modern scholarship until the beginning of the twentieth century. In 1905 a palm-leaf manuscript in Grantha script reached the Government Oriental Library at Mysore, where its librarian, R. Shamasastry, recognised its importance. He published portions in translation from 1905 onwards, an edition of the Sanskrit text in 1909 and a complete English translation in 1915 (Shamasastry 1915). Further manuscripts, including some in Malayalam script, were later found, and new editions followed, among them that of J. Jolly and R. Schmidt (1923–24) and T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī’s edition with his own Sanskrit commentary (1924–25). The standard critical edition is R. P. Kangle’s, published with an English translation and a volume of studies between 1960 and 1965 (Kangle 1960). Patrick Olivelle’s annotated translation of 2013 is now the standard English version (Olivelle 2013); L. N. Rangarajan’s rearranged translation of 1992 is widely read but reorders the text by topic (Rangarajan 1992). References in this volume follow Kangle’s numbering of book, chapter and sentence.

The discovery had an immediate effect. A treatise that discussed revenue, state workshops, customs schedules and wage contracts in a dry, technical prose overturned the then common European view that ancient Indian thought had been concerned only with religion and philosophy. That effect has sometimes produced the opposite exaggeration, in which the Arthaśāstra is presented as a complete economics far ahead of its time. Both views obscure what the text actually is.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Structure
docs.text:
The text describes itself as having fifteen books (adhikaraṇa), 150 chapters (adhyāya) and 180 topics (prakaraṇa), with an extent equivalent to 6,000 verses (AŚ 1.1). The “verse” here is a unit of length; the text is overwhelmingly prose, with verses mostly at the ends of chapters. Table 2.1 lists the books and indicates where economic material is concentrated.

Table 2.1. The fifteen books of the Arthaśāstra and their economic content (titles after Kangle and Olivelle) Book Title Subject and economic relevance 1 Vinayādhikārika Training of the king; the four sciences, including vārttā; ministers and spies 2 Adhyakṣapracāra Activities of the superintendents: revenue, treasury, mines, trade, customs, weights, agriculture, textiles, shipping. The main economic book 3 Dharmasthīya Civil law: contracts, debts, deposits, slaves and workers, partnerships, sale 4 Kaṇṭakaśodhana “Eradication of thorns”: policing artisans and traders, remedies for calamities such as famine 5 Yogavṛtta Secret conduct; emergency replenishment of the treasury; salaries of officials 6–7 Maṇḍalayoni; Ṣāḍguṇya Foreign policy; Book 7 includes a comparison of trade routes 8 Vyasanādhikārika Calamities affecting the constituents of the state, including the treasury 9–14 Military and secret practices Campaigns, war, confederacies, sieges, occult means 15 Tantrayukti Methods of composing a scientific treatise

docs.title: 2.1.3 Date and Authorship
docs.text:
The text names its author as Kauṭilya (the manuscripts also have Kauṭalya), and a verse at its close identifies him as the one who rescued the land from the Nanda kings. Later tradition, including the Kāmandakīya Nītisāra, the Purāṇas and the drama Mudrārākṣasa, identifies this Kauṭilya or Viṣṇugupta with Cāṇakya, the minister who helped Candragupta Maurya to power in the late fourth century BCE. On this traditional view the Arthaśāstra is a Mauryan work of c. 300 BCE, and Kangle, among others, defended an early date (Kangle 1960).

Modern scholarship has largely abandoned that view. Thomas Trautmann’s statistical study of word usage showed that different books of the text have different authors and that the work is a compilation (Trautmann 1971). Olivelle, building on this, distinguishes three stages: earlier treatises on particular subjects; a “Kauṭilya recension” that combined and reworked them, which he dates c. 50 BCE–125 CE; and a later “śāstric redaction”, c. 175–300 CE, which divided the work into chapters with closing verses and added material (Olivelle 2013). Mark McClish has argued that this redaction also reshaped the text to bring it into line with Brahmanical ideas of dharma (McClish 2019). The text that survives is therefore composite and, in its present form, belongs to c. 50 BCE–300 CE. It may preserve older material, and it cites by name earlier teachers whose views it often rejects (Bhāradvāja, Viśālākṣa, Parāśara, Piśuna and others), which shows that it drew on an established tradition of arthaśāstra writing. But it is not a document of the Mauryan administration, and its descriptions cannot be used, as they once were, as evidence for how the Mauryan empire was governed.

Debate: Traditional and Academic Dating

Traditional view. The Arthaśāstra was written by Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya, Viṣṇugupta), minister of Candragupta Maurya, c. 300 BCE, and describes the Mauryan state.

Academic view. The text is a composite whose present form dates from c. 50 BCE–300 CE (Olivelle 2013); it is the work of several hands (Trautmann 1971); and the identification of Kauṭilya with Cāṇakya is first attested in later sources. Points of difference between the text and Megasthenes’ account of Mauryan Pāṭaliputra, preserved in later Greek writers (McCrindle 1877), are among the arguments against using it as a Mauryan record.

Consequence for this volume. The Arthaśāstra is treated as evidence for ideas about economic administration current in the early centuries CE, not as a description of a working Mauryan economy. This dating is assumed wherever the text is cited in later chapters, and it is not restated there.

docs.title: 2.2 Artha, the Aims of Life and Vārttā
2.2.1 The Meaning of Artha
docs.text:
The word artha covers wealth, material well-being, advantage and power. The Arthaśāstra defines its subject in its last book: artha is the livelihood (vṛtti) of human beings, and also the earth inhabited by human beings; the science that is the means of acquiring and protecting that earth is the arthaśāstra (AŚ 15.1.1–2). Economic life and political control are thus one subject. The king’s wealth depends on a populated, productive territory, and the productive territory depends on the king’s protection.

Artha is one of the aims of human life (puruṣārtha). The older scheme was a triad (trivarga) of dharma, artha and kāma; the fourth aim, mokṣa (liberation), was added to make the familiar set of four. The Arthaśāstra discusses how the three should be balanced. A king should pursue pleasure without conflicting with dharma and artha, or the three equally, since they are bound to one another; but the text gives its own view in a short prose statement:

artha eva pradhāna iti kauṭilyaḥ. arthamūlau hi dharmakāmāv iti. “Wealth alone is the chief thing, says Kauṭilya, for dharma and pleasure have wealth as their root.” (AŚ 1.7.6–7)

The claim is not that wealth is the highest value but that the other aims cannot be pursued without it. The dharmaśāstras generally rank dharma first, and the ranking of the aims was a recurrent subject of debate in Sanskrit literature. A related idea is yogakṣema, “acquisition and security”: the king’s task is to secure what has not yet been obtained and to protect what has. In the training of the king the text also states that the king’s own good lies in the good of his subjects (AŚ 1.19.34). How these principles bear on kingship is the subject of Volume 18; for this chapter, their importance is that the text makes the productive economy the foundation of the state.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Four Sciences and Vārttā
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra names four sciences (vidyā) a king must study: philosophy or critical inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the three Vedas (trayī), economics (vārttā) and government or the science of punishment (daṇḍanīti) (AŚ 1.2–1.4). Vārttā consists of agriculture, animal husbandry and trade. It is useful, the text says, because it yields grain, livestock, money, forest produce and labour, and because through it the king brings under control both his own people and his enemies, by means of the treasury and the army (AŚ 1.4.1–2).

Three features of this classification deserve notice. First, vārttā is a body of practical knowledge, not a theory of markets; it covers the arts by which livelihood is produced. Second, it is listed among the sciences of the king, so economic knowledge is framed from the point of view of the ruler who taxes and protects. Third, labour (viṣṭi, unpaid service owed to the state) is listed among the products of vārttā, a reminder that the economy the text imagines rests in part on compulsion (Section 2.6).

Trade figures in the Arthaśāstra chiefly as a source of revenue and of goods the state needs. One passage, however, shows the kind of practical reasoning the text applies to it: in weighing which routes a king should develop, it sets the views of earlier teachers against its own, preferring land routes to water routes for their reliability, the coastal route to the open sea, and the southern route to the Himalayan one for the volume of its high-value goods (AŚ 7.12). The passage is discussed in Section 10.2.3.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Treasury and its Officers
docs.text:
“All undertakings depend on the treasury” (AŚ 2.8.1): the Arthaśāstra’s fiscal chapters are organised around this principle. Two senior officers stand at the head of the fiscal system, and their titles are easily confused. The samāhartṛ, usually translated “Collector” (Kangle: “administrator”), is responsible for assessing and collecting revenue from all sources and for supervising the countryside through district officers (sthānika) and village accountants (gopa) who keep records of land, households, occupations, livestock, income and expenditure (AŚ 2.6, 2.35). The sannidhātṛ, usually translated “Treasurer” (Kangle: “director of stores”), is responsible for building and stocking the state’s storehouses: the treasury, the warehouse for commodities, the granary, the store for forest produce, the armoury and the prison (AŚ 2.5). Both are civil officials, not military officers or ministers in a modern sense.

Accounts were kept in a records office (akṣapaṭala) where officials submitted their accounts at fixed times of the year (AŚ 2.7). The text is frank about the risk of embezzlement. It lists forty ways in which officials can misappropriate revenue (AŚ 2.8) and observes that it is as hard for an official handling the king’s money not to taste a little of it as it is not to taste honey or poison placed on the tongue, and that one can no more tell when an official is taking money than when a fish is drinking water (AŚ 2.9). The remedy is constant inspection, rotation and the use of informers.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Sources of Revenue
docs.text:
The text classifies revenue in two ways. The first is by source, the seven “bodies of revenue” (āyaśarīra) that the Collector must attend to (AŚ 2.6), summarised in Table 2.2. The second is by form: price received for state goods (mūlya), share (bhāga), surcharge (vyājī), fees and fixed payments, a charge for testing coins (rūpika), and fines (atyaya). Revenue is also divided into current, arrears and incidental receipts. Some of these technical terms are obscure, and translators differ on their exact meanings.

Table 2.2. The seven “bodies of revenue” (āyaśarīra) in AŚ 2.6 (simplified, after Kangle and Olivelle) Source Main items Fort (durga), i.e. the capital Customs (śulka), fines, fees for weights and measures, the city superintendent, the mint, passes, liquor, slaughterhouses, yarn, oil, ghee, goldsmiths, the market (paṇyasaṃsthā), courtesans, gambling, building sites, guilds of artisans, temples, gate and outsiders’ dues Countryside (rāṣṭra) Produce of crown land (sītā), the share of private produce (bhāga), bali, kara, dues from merchants, river, ferry and boat dues, ports, pasture, road cess (vartanī), rope and “thief-rope” dues Mines (khani) Gold, silver, diamonds, gems, pearls, coral, conch shell, metals, salt Irrigation works (setu) Gardens, orchards, vegetable plots, irrigated fields Forests (vana) Game, produce and elephant forests Herds (vraja) Cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, donkeys, camels, horses, mules Trade routes (vaṇikpatha) Land and water routes

The distinction between sītā and bhāga is basic. Sītā is the produce of land cultivated directly by the state under the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa); bhāga is the share of the crop taken from other cultivators. The later history of this claim on the harvest is surveyed in Section 3.1. The customary share was one-sixth: the Arthaśāstra relates, as a story to be spread by the king’s agents, that when people were oppressed by anarchy they made Manu their king and assigned him one-sixth of their grain and one-tenth of their merchandise, as well as money, as his share (AŚ 1.13). The dharmaśāstras give similar but varying rates: Manu allows the king one-sixth, one-eighth or one-twelfth of grain, and a fiftieth of increments in cattle and gold (Manu 7.130) (Olivelle 2004). The meanings of bali and kara are debated; both appear to be additional levies. Users of irrigation works built by the state paid a separate water rate, graded according to whether water was lifted by hand, carried, raised by mechanical devices or drawn from rivers and tanks (AŚ 2.24). Customs (śulka) and tolls are treated in Chapter 7.

The text expects the king to be restrained in ordinary times. Settlers on new land are to be given grain, cattle and money as advances, and remissions of tax, so that cultivation expands (AŚ 2.1). A verse in the chapter on emergency revenue compares the king to a gardener who should pick only ripe fruit, avoiding unripe fruit whose plucking causes resentment and damages the tree (AŚ 5.2). But the same chapter shows the other side. A king in financial difficulty may demand a larger share of grain from fertile regions, request “contributions” (praṇaya) from merchants and others, and, through secret agents, use fraudulent methods: staging miracles at shrines to attract donations, seizing the property of temples, or ruining wealthy subjects who are said to be disloyal (AŚ 5.2). The text limits such demands to once only, but it does not hide them.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Expenditure and Salaries
docs.text: On the expenditure side, the Arthaśāstra prescribes a scale of annual salaries in paṇas (AŚ 5.3). It suggests that the wage bill should be kept within a quarter of revenue. The highest rate, 48,000 paṇas, is given to the king’s priest, preceptor, counsellor, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, the queen mother and the chief queen; the lowest named rates, 60 paṇas, go to attendants and menial servants. The ratio between highest and lowest, about 800 to 1, reflects the steep hierarchy the text assumes. Whether any state ever paid such salaries is unknown; the figures are best read as a model of how a ruler might rank his servants.

docs.title: 2.4 The Superintendents
docs.text:
Book 2 describes some thirty superintendents (adhyakṣa) with charge of particular branches of the state economy. Their number and specialisation are the most striking feature of the book. They are not all of equal rank, and the text gives no organisational chart; the samāhartṛ and sannidhātṛ coordinate revenue and stores. Table 2.3 lists the main economic superintendents. The details of several belong to other chapters of this volume.

Table 2.3. Principal economic superintendents in Arthaśāstra Book 2 (chapter numbers after Kangle) Office AŚ Responsibility (and where treated in this volume) Kośādhyakṣa 2.11 Treasury; examination of gems and precious goods received Ākarādhyakṣa 2.12 Mines and ores (this chapter) Lohādhyakṣa 2.12 Metal workshops (this chapter; Volume 14 for techniques) Lakṣaṇādhyakṣa 2.12 The mint (Chapter 5) Khanyadhyakṣa, lavaṇādhyakṣa 2.12 Products of the sea (conch, pearl, coral); salt Suvarṇādhyakṣa 2.13–14 Gold and silver workshops; goldsmiths (Chapter 8) Koṣṭhāgārādhyakṣa 2.15 Storehouse and granary (Chapter 7) Paṇyādhyakṣa 2.16 Trade and state goods (Chapter 7) Kupyādhyakṣa 2.17 Forest produce Pautavādhyakṣa 2.19 Weights and measures (Chapter 7) Śulkādhyakṣa 2.21–22 Customs and tolls (Chapter 7) Sūtrādhyakṣa 2.23 Yarn and textile production (Chapter 8) Sītādhyakṣa 2.24 Crown agriculture (this chapter) Surādhyakṣa 2.25 Liquor Nāvadhyakṣa 2.28 Ferries, boats and ports (Chapter 15) Go’dhyakṣa, vivītādhyakṣa 2.29, 2.34 Herds; pastures Mudrādhyakṣa 2.34 Passes for travel

The superintendents of horses, elephants, chariots and infantry (AŚ 2.30–33), of courtesans (2.27) and of slaughterhouses (2.26) complete the book. The market superintendent (saṃsthādhyakṣa) appears in Book 4 (Chapter 7). Megasthenes’ account of the boards that supervised crafts, trade and sales at Pāṭaliputra, preserved by Strabo, shows that Greek observers too saw an administration that took a close interest in commerce, though his offices do not match the Arthaśāstra’s (McCrindle 1877).

docs.title: 2.5 State Enterprise: Crown Lands, Mines and Monopolies
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra imagines a state that is itself a major producer. It is not a description of a command economy: private cultivators, artisans and merchants are everywhere assumed, taxed and protected. But the state farms its own land, runs workshops and mines, and reserves certain trades to itself.

Crown agriculture. The superintendent of agriculture cultivates crown land using slaves, hired labourers and convicts working off their fines, supplied with ploughs, oxen and the services of smiths, carpenters and other artisans (AŚ 2.24). He is to be versed in agriculture, irrigation and the care of plants; the text records rainfall norms for different regions and refers to a rain gauge kept at the granary (AŚ 2.5, 2.24). Land that cannot be sown by the state may be given to sharecroppers. The settlement of new lands, mainly with Śūdra cultivators, in villages of a hundred to five hundred families is described in AŚ 2.1, which also forbids entertainers and pleasure halls in villages lest they distract people from work.

Mines and metals. The superintendent of mines (ākarādhyakṣa) is to be expert in the science of ores and metals and in testing gems, and to work with specialists. He identifies old and new workings from traces such as slag, charcoal and ash, and assesses ores by colour, weight and smell (AŚ 2.12). The text makes a practical distinction: mines that need heavy investment may be leased out for a share of the output or for a fixed rent, while those that can be worked cheaply should be worked by the state itself. Separate superintendents handle metal workshops, the mint, sea products and salt. A verse at the end of the chapter states that the treasury has its source in the mines, and that with treasury and army the earth is won. The archaeology of early Indian mining and metallurgy is treated in Volume 14, Rasāyana (Craddock 1995; Biswas and Biswas 1996).

Monopolies and single channels. The text repeatedly recommends that the sale of goods produced by the state, and of certain strategic goods, be concentrated in a single channel (ekamukha), and it fines unauthorised production and sale of mine products and salt (AŚ 2.12). Liquor was to be produced and sold under the superintendent of liquor, with restrictions on private manufacture and close control of drinking houses (AŚ 2.25). The state’s own goods were to be sold through its agents or through merchants at fixed prices (AŚ 2.16; Chapter 7). These are fiscal monopolies designed to secure revenue and control, not a theory of state ownership.

Textiles. The superintendent of yarn employs women without other support to spin, paying them by the quantity and quality of their yarn (AŚ 2.23). The passage is a rare, detailed glimpse of women’s paid work, and of the way dependent and marginal women were drawn into state production; it is discussed in Section 8.4.

Thomas Trautmann has argued that the Arthaśāstra’s economics should be understood as a coherent model of its own, combining a large state sector with private enterprise under close supervision, rather than as an anticipation of later European doctrines (Trautmann 2012). Whether any kingdom approached this model is a separate question that the text cannot answer.

docs.title: 2.6 Labour, Wages and Slavery
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra regulates several kinds of labour: hired workers (karmakara), slaves (dāsa), persons pledged for debt (āhitaka), convicts, and those who owed unpaid service to the state (viṣṭi). Its rules are among the most detailed in early Indian law, and they need to be described without either romanticising or ignoring their harshness (Chakravarti 1987).

docs.title: 2.6.1 Hired Workers
docs.text:
The rules on hired labour (AŚ 3.13–14) assume a contract made before witnesses. Wages are to be paid as agreed; if no wage was agreed, the text supplies defaults: a cultivator receives a tenth of the crop, a herdsman a tenth of the butter, and a trader a tenth of the goods he sells on another’s behalf. A worker who takes wages and fails to work, and an employer who fails to pay, are both fined. Joint work by guild workers and partners is treated under the heading of undertakings in partnership (saṃbhūya-samutthāna, AŚ 3.14), which deals with the division of earnings; the term means partnership, and it is discussed in Chapter 6.

These are rules of contract, not a code of labour rights. The text does not provide for minimum wages, and its default rates protected the employer as much as the worker.

docs.title: 2.6.2 Slaves and Pledged Persons
docs.text:
The chapter on slaves (AŚ 3.13) recognises several ways of becoming a slave: birth in the household, inheritance, purchase, capture in war, self-sale and pledging for debt. Its central rule is that an Ārya may not be made a slave, although he may be pledged in distress. “Ārya” here means a free person, and the category explicitly includes Śūdras who were not born slaves. Relatives who sell or pledge a free minor are fined, the fine increasing with the varṇa of the person concerned, from Śūdra to Brahmin. The text then states that there is no offence for barbarians (mleccha) in selling or pledging their own children.

Within this framework the text sets limits on the treatment of pledged persons and slaves. A pledged person may not be made to carry corpses or remove filth, and a pledged woman may not be beaten, stripped or sexually violated; if her master does so, he loses what he paid and she goes free. A slave may earn and keep property without detriment to the master’s work, may inherit from his father, and may buy his freedom by paying his price. The children of a master by his female slave, and the slave mother, are to be freed.

These provisions have sometimes been described as unusually humane. It is fairer to say that the text regulates an institution it fully accepts. Its protections are graded by status and birth: they are strongest for free persons who have fallen into bondage through debt, while those born or bought into slavery, war captives and the children of mlecchas are left largely to their owners, and the fines themselves vary with varṇa. The state itself employed slaves and convicts on crown land, and its claim to the unpaid labour of its subjects (viṣṭi) is treated as normal. The dharmaśāstras likewise regulate slavery and assume varṇa-graded rights (Olivelle 2004; Kane 1930). For the history of slavery in early India, see Chanana (1960) and Chakravarti (1985).

docs.title: 2.7 Calamities and the Economy
docs.text: Book 8 of the Arthaśāstra discusses calamities (vyasana) that may befall the constituents of the state: the king, ministers, countryside, fort, treasury, army and ally. It proceeds by debate, setting out the views of earlier teachers on which calamity is the more serious and then giving Kauṭilya’s own. Its economic interest lies in two places. In comparing a calamity of the treasury with one of the army, the text argues that the army depends on the treasury: without money, an army deserts to the enemy or turns on its own king (AŚ 8.1). And among the “divine” calamities it lists fire, flood, disease, famine and epidemic, weighing which does most damage to the productive population (AŚ 8.4). The practical measures the text prescribes against famine, including the release of stored grain and the employment of the hungry on public works paid in food, are described in Chapter 7. Book 8 is an analysis of the relative gravity of disasters for a king, not a theory of economic policy.

docs.title: 2.8 Later Traditions of Nīti
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra was the culmination of one tradition and the source of another. Later works on nīti (polity, prudent conduct) drew on it, usually reducing its economic detail. Table 2.4 summarises the main texts.

Table 2.4. Later works in the nīti and arthaśāstra tradition Text Date Character Kāmandakīya Nītisāra Probably mid-first millennium CE (estimates vary) Verse digest of polity that honours Viṣṇugupta as its source; much less economic detail than the Arthaśāstra Nītivākyāmṛta of Somadeva Sūri 10th c. CE Aphoristic prose on polity by a Jain author in the Deccan; absorbs much arthaśāstra material Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III c. 1131 CE Encyclopaedic Cālukya work on royal life, administration, revenue and the arts Śukranīti 19th c. CE (Gopal 1962) Compilation long presented as ancient; not evidence for early India

The Śukranīti requires a particular warning, because it is still often cited as an ancient source on taxation, prices and administration. It was edited by Gustav Oppert in 1882 and translated by B. K. Sarkar in 1914. In 1962 Lallanji Gopal showed, on the basis of its content and vocabulary, including its descriptions of firearms, that the text in its present form was composed in the nineteenth century (Gopal 1962). It is a document of the nineteenth century, not of ancient or medieval economic thought.

docs.title: 2.9 Beyond Sanskrit: The Tirukkuṟaḷ and Indo-Persian Thought
docs.text: The Sanskrit nīti literature was not the only body of Indian writing that reflected on wealth and the state before the colonial period. Two others deserve a place in a history of economic thought, although neither was written as economics: the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ, and the Persian literature of advice and ethics of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal court.

docs.title: 2.9.1 The Tirukkuṟaḷ’s Book of Wealth
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ attributed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar is a collection of 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters of ten. Its date is uncertain; it is usually placed around the middle of the first millennium CE, though estimates range more widely (Zvelebil 1973). Its three books treat virtue (aṟam), wealth and polity (poruḷ) and love (iṉpam), a scheme parallel to the Sanskrit triad of dharma, artha and kāma. The book of wealth (Poruṭpāl) is the longest, with seventy chapters on the king, his ministers, the army, allies and fortresses, and the conduct of the citizen and the cultivator.

Its economic ideas are stated as maxims, not as administrative rules. The ideal king is one who can create wealth, acquire it, guard it and distribute it well (Kuṟaḷ 385). A chapter on the making of wealth names the king’s lawful revenues as unclaimed property, customs and tolls (ulku), and what is taken from defeated enemies (756). A king who presses his subjects for money is compared to a robber who stands on the road with a spear and demands that travellers give (552). And the chapter on agriculture opens with the maxim that the world, however it turns, follows the plough, so that farming, for all its toil, is the first of occupations (1031) (Tiruvaḷḷuvar 1886). The Tirukkuṟaḷ thus shares the Arthaśāstra’s view that wealth is the foundation of the state, but it subordinates the pursuit of wealth more explicitly to virtue, it places the cultivator at the centre, and it does not frame its advice in terms of varṇa.

docs.title: 2.9.2 Indo-Persian Writing on Kingship and Revenue
docs.text:
The courts of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals produced a large Persian literature of political advice and ethics. It is used in this volume mainly as a source for the policies it describes, but it also contains reasoned views about revenue, prices and the household economy.

The most original of the Sultanate writers on these questions was Ẓiyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī, whose Fatāwā-yi Jahāndārī (“Rulings on world-government”, written in the 1350s) argues that a Muslim ruler must supplement the religious law with state regulations (ẓawābiṭ) made by reason and necessity. Baranī presented ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī’s price controls as an example of such regulation (Section 18.2.2), and he held strongly hierarchical views: wealth, learning and office, in his account, should be kept from the low-born (Habib and Khan 1961). The Persian ethical tradition (akhlāq), above all Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī’s Akhlāq-i Nāṣirī (1235), written in Iran and widely read in India, devoted a part of ethics to the management of the household (tadbīr-i manzil): how wealth should be acquired, preserved and spent. Ṭūsī divided society into four classes, the men of the pen, of the sword, of business and of the land, whose balance the ruler must keep. Muzaffar Alam has shown how far these akhlāq norms shaped Mughal political ideas, including those of Akbar’s minister Abū al-Faḍl (Alam 2004).

Abū al-Faḍl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī (completed in the 1590s) is chiefly an administrative description, the source of most of what is known about the Mughal revenue system (Section 18.5.1). But its order of presentation, from the imperial household and its workshops to the army, the revenue and the provinces, sets out a theory of an empire in which revenue is the due of a ruler who protects his subjects and keeps the classes of society in balance. These Sanskrit, Tamil and Persian traditions differed widely, but they shared a view of wealth from the ruler’s side, as something to be produced, protected and justly taken. None of them treated the market as a self-regulating system; that idea entered Indian debate with classical political economy in the nineteenth century (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 2.10 Dharmaśāstra on Wealth and Trade
docs.text:
The dharmaśāstras approach economic life from the standpoint of duty according to varṇa and stage of life. Trade, money-lending, agriculture and cattle-keeping are assigned to the Vaiśya (Manu 1.90), and Manu describes the knowledge a Vaiśya should have: the value of gems, pearls, coral, metals, cloth, perfumes and spices; the methods of sowing; weights and measures; the good and bad qualities of goods; the conditions of different regions; the probable profit and loss on merchandise; the wages of servants; and the languages of different peoples (Manu 9.326–333) (Olivelle 2004). In times of distress a Brahmin or Kṣatriya may live by trade, but certain goods, among them salt, sesame, liquor, meat, weapons and human beings, may not be sold by a Brahmin (Manu 10.85–94).

The law books also regulate the instruments of commerce: the rate of interest, which Manu and Yājñavalkya grade by the varṇa of the debtor; deposits and pledges; partnership; sale and its rescission; and the conventions of guilds (Chapters 4 and 6). Several of the eighteen titles of law listed by Manu concern commercial dealings, including non-delivery of goods sold, rescission of purchase and breach of agreement (Manu 8.4–7). The king is told to fix prices and inspect weights and measures at regular intervals (Manu 8.398–403; Chapter 7). Taken together, the law books show that commerce was regarded as a legitimate and necessary activity, but one placed within a hierarchy of birth that determined who might pursue it, on what terms and with what penalties (Kane 1930; Olivelle 1999).

docs.title: 2.11.1 Buddhism
docs.text:
Early Buddhism grew up in the towns of the Ganga valley, and its texts are addressed in large part to the wealthy householder (gahapati) and the merchant or financier (seṭṭhi). Uma Chakravarti has shown how these social categories appear in the Pali canon: the gahapati as the head of a propertied household, often a landowner, and the seṭṭhi as a man of great wealth, prominent in urban life and among the Buddha’s lay supporters (Chakravarti 1987). Anāthapiṇḍika, the seṭṭhi of Sāvatthī who bought the Jetavana grove for the order, is the best-known example.

The Pali texts offer an ethic of wealth for such people. The Sigālovāda Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 31), the fullest statement of this ethic, advises the householder to accumulate wealth gradually, as a bee gathers nectar, and to divide it into four parts: one to be used for his needs, two to be invested in his work, and the fourth to be kept for times of misfortune. Right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is part of the noble eightfold path, and the Aṅguttara Nikāya names five trades a lay follower should not engage in: trade in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants and in poison (AN 5.177). The moral precepts listed in the opening suttas of the Dīgha Nikāya include abstention from cheating with scales, metal and measures. In the Kūṭadanta Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 5), a king is advised to end banditry not by punishment but by giving seed and fodder to cultivators, capital to traders and food and wages to those in his service, so that people prosper and the country is at peace. These texts express an ethic of industry, thrift and generosity, directed at donors on whom the monastic order depended.

docs.title: 2.11.2 Jainism
docs.text: Jain merchants have been prominent in western and southern India for many centuries. The lay Jain takes lesser vows (aṇuvrata), among them non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing and the limitation of possessions (parigraha-parimāṇa), and Jain texts list occupations that a layman should avoid because they involve harm to living beings, such as trades in charcoal, lac, ivory and poisons and the clearing of forests (Jaini 1979). These restrictions, together with the high value placed on honesty and on generous giving, helped orient Jain communities towards trade and finance rather than agriculture. James Laidlaw’s ethnography of Jain merchants in Jaipur shows how a religion of renunciation and a life of commercial success are held together in practice, through gifting, fasting and a reputation for probity on which commercial credit itself depends (Laidlaw 1995).

docs.title: 2.12 Reading the Arthaśāstra Today
docs.text:
Since its rediscovery, the Arthaśāstra has been compared with Machiavelli, with European mercantilism, with Adam Smith and even with Keynes and modern development economics. Such comparisons can be useful as analogies. The text does recognise the importance of revenue for state power, it calculates the costs and gains of trade ventures, it regulates prices and weights, and it uses public works to relieve famine. But the analogies mislead when they become claims of priority or anticipation. The Arthaśāstra has no concept of a national economy, no theory of market equilibrium and no notion of rights against the state; its purpose is to strengthen a king, and its economic prescriptions serve that end. Roger Boesche reads it as a work of political realism (Boesche 2002); Trautmann stresses its distinct economic model (Trautmann 2012). Both approaches take the text on its own terms, which is the condition for using it well.

Cross-Reference: Related Volumes

The Arthaśāstra’s theory of kingship, the circle of states, espionage, law and punishment is treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Metallurgy and mining techniques are discussed in Volume 14, Rasāyana, and crafts and textiles in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the text, Olivelle (2013) is the standard annotated translation, with a full introduction on date and composition; Kangle (1960) remains essential for the Sanskrit and for detailed study. Trautmann (1971) established the multiple authorship of the work, and Trautmann (2012) is an accessible account of its economics. McClish (2019) traces the history of the text’s redaction. For the Tirukkuṟaḷ see Tiruvaḷḷuvar (1886) and Zvelebil (1973); for Baranī, Habib and Khan (1961); and for the Indo-Persian ethical tradition, Alam (2004). For the dharmaśāstra background see Olivelle (2004) and Kane (1930); for Buddhism and society, Chakravarti (1987); and for Jain merchant ethics, Jaini (1979) and Laidlaw (1995).

docs.title: Chapter 3: Land, Agrarian Surplus and Revenue
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Every form of production and trade described in this volume rested on agriculture. This short chapter gives the agrarian economy a place of its own. It first surveys the state’s claim on the harvest from the Arthaśāstra to the British settlements, as a guide to the fuller treatments in other chapters. It then looks at the early medieval land grants and the debate over “Indian feudalism”, at the village and locality assemblies of the Tamil country, at irrigation as an investment of the surplus, and at the ways in which the surplus entered the wider economy of exchange.

Throughout the period covered by this volume the great majority of people lived from the land, and the land was the main source of wealth and of state revenue. The agrarian surplus fed the artisans and the towns. It supplied the raw materials of the leading crafts: cotton, indigo and other dyes, sugarcane, oilseeds and hides. And the revenue taken from it paid for the courts, temples and armies that were the chief buyers of fine manufactures and imported luxuries. How crops were grown, irrigated and stored is the subject of Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna. This chapter looks only at the economy of surplus, revenue and exchange.

docs.title: 3.1 The State’s Claim on the Harvest
docs.text:
The ruler’s right to a share of the crop is the one constant in the fiscal history traced in this book. The normative texts state it as a fraction. The Arthaśāstra knows a customary sixth (bhāga) besides the produce of crown land (sītā) and further levies whose meaning is debated, and Manu allows the king a sixth, an eighth or a twelfth of grain (Section 2.3.2). In practice the fraction was a starting point rather than a rule. Rulers raised or lowered the demand, collected it in kind or in money, and shared it with the intermediaries through whom it was gathered. Table 3.1 sets out the main forms the claim took and where each is discussed.

Table 3.1. The state’s claim on the harvest: main forms and where they are treated in this volume Period Form of the claim Treated in Arthaśāstra and dharmaśāstra (early centuries CE) Customary share (bhāga) of a sixth; crown land worked by the state; water rates; further levies (bali, kara) Section 2.3.2 Early medieval kingdoms, c. 400–1300 Royal share and dues transferred by grant to brāhmaṇas, temples and monasteries Section 3.2 Chola and later Tamil country Dues assessed and collected through village and locality assemblies; temple lands Section 3.3; Chapter 9 Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1526 Revenue assigned as iqṭāʿ; under ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī, half the produce of the Doab by measurement Section 18.2.1 Vijayanagara and the nāyakas Territories held on condition of military service and dues Section 18.3 Mughal empire Zabṭ cash rates per unit of area; jāgīr assignments; zamīndārs as collectors Section 18.5 Marathas Chauth and sardeshmukhī on revenue assessed by others; saranjām assignments Section 18.5.9 British India, from 1793 Money demand on a proprietor or cultivator under the Permanent, ryotwari and mahalwari settlements; land saleable for arrears Section 19.5

Three features run through this long history. The demand was assessed on land or crop, not on income, so that it fell on cultivators in bad years as well as good, and remission depended on the ruler’s discretion. It was collected through layers of intermediaries, from village headmen and hereditary accountants (Section 6.7) to chiefs, zamīndārs, assignees and revenue farmers, whose rights formed a hierarchy of claims on the same harvest. And a growing part of it was demanded in money, which obliged cultivators to sell their crops and tied the village to the grain merchant and the moneylender (Section 3.5). The scale of the demand is harder to know than its form. The textual fractions are norms; Irfan Habib’s judgement that the Mughal demand often approached half of the produce rests on the schedules of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (Habib 1999); and colonial assessments, heavy at first, fell in real terms during the later nineteenth century as prices rose (Section 19.5).

docs.title: 3.2 Land Grants and Copper-Plate Charters
docs.text:
The best evidence for rural society in early medieval India is the land grant. The earliest epigraphic grants that transfer land together with fiscal privileges are those of the Sātavāhana kings to Buddhist monks in the western Deccan, for example at Nasik, in the early centuries CE. They free the granted field from the entry of royal officers and from the king’s right to dig for salt (Ray 1986). From the Gupta period onward such grants multiply. By the end of the first millennium thousands had been issued across the subcontinent, most of them engraved on copper plates (tāmraśāsana) that the donee kept as a title deed.

Three kinds of grant are especially common. An agrahāra was land, often a whole village, given to one or more brāhmaṇas. In Tamil inscriptions a village granted to a community of brāhmaṇas is a brahmadeya. A devadāna (Tamil tēvatāṉam) was land given to a temple, and land given to Jain and Buddhist establishments appears in Tamil inscriptions as paḷḷiccantam. Grants followed a set form. They name the donor and his genealogy, the donee, the land and its boundaries, and the officials and villagers who were informed. They list the rights transferred: the king’s share of the crop and other dues, and often exemption from the entry of royal soldiers and police (acāṭabhaṭapraveśya). They declare the gift valid “for as long as the moon and the sun endure”, and they end with conventional verses, ascribed to Vyāsa, which promise long ages in heaven to the giver of land and as many in hell to anyone who takes it back (Salomon 1998). The Damodarpur copper plates from north Bengal, which record the sale of state land for religious gifts with the approval of the district council, are discussed in Section 4.6.3.

What the grants transferred was, in most cases, a right to revenue rather than the soil itself. The cultivators stayed on the land and now paid their dues to the donee instead of the king. Some grants go further and transfer fines, the right to forced labour (viṣṭi) or the obligation of the villagers to obey the donee. Grants to brāhmaṇas and temples also carried agriculture, the written calendar, Sanskrit learning and the ritual authority of the king into areas that had been forest or the land of tribal peoples. Historians agree on these facts. They disagree sharply about what they meant.

Debate: Was there “Indian feudalism”?

R. S. Sharma, in Indian Feudalism (1965) and later work, argued that the multiplication of land grants from the Gupta period onward produced a feudal social order in India (Sharma 1965, 1983). In his account, kings paid priests, officials and vassals (sāmantas) with land rather than cash, and they gave away fiscal, administrative and judicial rights with it. This created a class of landed intermediaries between the state and the peasant and fragmented political power. Peasants were burdened with new dues and forced labour and were tied more closely to the land. Trade, towns and the use of coin declined, and villages became more self-sufficient (Sharma 1987). Sharma built on D. D. Kosambi, who had spoken of feudalism “from above”, created by royal grants, and “from below”, through the rise of landholders within the village (Kosambi 1956).

The thesis was criticised from several directions. Harbans Mukhia asked whether India had had feudalism at all. He argued that the Indian peasant kept control of the process of production, that there was no serfdom and no demesne worked by labour services on the European model, and that a category built for medieval Europe did not fit Indian agrarian relations; Sharma replied, and the debate continued for many years (Mukhia 1981). B. D. Chattopadhyaya proposed an “integrative” reading. In his view the land grants accompanied the spread of settled agriculture into new areas, the turning of tribal groups into peasants, the formation of many regional and local states, and the growth of new markets and temple centres. That is a picture of expansion, not of decline (Chattopadhyaya 1994). For the Chola country, Burton Stein described a “segmentary state” in which the king’s ritual sovereignty reached much further than his administrative control, and the real units of rural society were the peasant localities (nāṭu) (Stein 1980). Other historians of south India have pointed to the Chola land surveys and revenue records as evidence of a stronger state than Stein allowed. The coin evidence is discussed in Section 5.7, and the fate of guilds and towns in Section 4.6.5.

Most historians now accept that land grants transformed rural society and that the change varied greatly from region to region. Fewer accept the word “feudalism” or a single story of decline.

docs.title: 3.3 Village and Locality Assemblies in the South
docs.text:
In the Tamil country, inscriptions from about the eighth century onward show rural society organised through assemblies. The ūr was the assembly of the landholders of an ordinary village. The sabhā (or mahāsabhā) was the assembly of the brāhmaṇa landholders of a brahmadeya. The nagaram was the body of merchants of a market town, often one for each locality. The nāṭu, a cluster of villages, had its own assembly of leading peasant landholders (nāṭṭār). These bodies assessed and collected dues, managed common land and water, received endowments, and acted together with temples and merchant groups (Champakalakshmi 1996; Hall 1980). Kenneth Hall has argued that the nagaram served as the market of its nāṭu, linking the agrarian localities to wider trade (Section 4.7).

The best-known records of a sabhā are two inscriptions of 919 and 921 CE, in the reign of the Chola king Parāntaka I, at Uttaramērūr near Kanchipuram. They lay down how the brahmadeya’s committees (vāriyam) were to be chosen, by drawing palm-leaf tickets from a pot (kuḍavōlai). They also set qualifications for candidates: ownership of tax-paying land and a house, an age range, Vedic learning, and exclusion of men who had failed to render accounts and of their relatives. There were committees for the annual supervision of the village, for gardens and for tanks. The records are often cited in modern India as evidence of “ancient democracy”. They show a careful system of rotation and accountability, but it was confined to a landholding brāhmaṇa élite. The cultivators and labourers who worked the land had no voice in it.

docs.title: 3.4 Irrigation as Investment
docs.text:
Irrigation is the clearest case of investment of the agrarian surplus. The Junagadh rock inscription of the Śaka ruler Rudradāman (c. 150 CE), one of the earliest long inscriptions in Sanskrit, records the repair of the Sudarśana reservoir near Girnar. According to the inscription, the reservoir had been built under Candragupta Maurya by his provincial governor Puṣyagupta and provided with conduits under Aśoka. A storm had breached it. Rudradāman had it rebuilt from his own treasury, the inscription says, without oppressing the people with taxes, forced labour or “benevolences”. Three centuries later, under Skandagupta, the dam burst again in 455–456 CE and was rebuilt the following year, as recorded in another inscription on the same rock (Salomon 1998). The stone thus records more than seven centuries of public investment in a single irrigation work.

In the south the typical work was the tank (Tamil ēri, Kannada kere), an earthen embankment holding back monsoon run-off to irrigate rice fields below it. Hundreds of inscriptions record the building of tanks, the cutting of sluices and channels, and endowments of land or money for desilting and repair. The donors include kings, village assemblies, temples, merchants and individual landholders (Champakalakshmi 1996). Tanks needed regular collective labour and a body to organise it, which is one reason for the importance of the village assemblies and their tank committees. A Tamil inscription at Takuapa in peninsular Thailand even records a tank placed under the protection of a merchant association (Chapter 12). Gifts for tanks and wells as works of religious merit are discussed in Section 9.6.

docs.title: 3.5 From Surplus to Exchange
