docs.text: The agrarian surplus entered the wider economy in several ways. Revenue in grain fed the households of kings, donees and temples. Revenue in cash, and the need to pay it, pushed cultivators to sell part of their crop. Temples that received land redistributed its produce to priests, musicians, cooks, artisans and pilgrims, and they lent grain and money to village assemblies (Section 6.4.2). The weekly or periodic rural markets (haṭṭa) named in early medieval inscriptions connected villages to towns (Chapters 7 and 10). Some crops were grown above all for sale and export: pepper in Malabar, cotton in Gujarat and the Deccan, sugar and indigo in many regions, rice for the coastal trade (Chapter 12). Under the Mughals, Irfan Habib has argued, the demand for revenue in cash was one of the main forces drawing the peasant economy into the market (Habib 1999). Craft production and trade were large and sophisticated, but they always depended on this agrarian base. Bad harvests and famine, which no part of the economy escaped, were the clearest reminder of it (Section 7.7).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The feudalism debate can be followed in Sharma (1965), Mukhia (1981) and Chattopadhyaya (1994), and the south Indian agrarian order in Stein (1980), Hall (1980) and Champakalakshmi (1996). Salomon (1998) introduces the land grants as inscriptions. For the Mughal agrarian system the essential work is Habib (1999), and for the colonial settlements Kumar (1983).

docs.title: Chapter 4: Guilds and Merchant Associations
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Associations of artisans and merchants — śreṇī, pūga, gaṇa, nigama and their Pali and Prakrit equivalents — appear in Indian sources from the late centuries BCE and remain visible, under changing names, into the early modern period. This chapter sets out the vocabulary, the literary and legal evidence (Jātakas, Pāṇini, the Arthaśāstra, the dharmaśāstra), and the epigraphic record that gives the institution its firmest outline: the Nasik endowments, the Mandasor weavers, the Vaiśālī sealings, and the great south Indian merchant bodies such as the Ayyāvoḷe Five Hundred and Maṇigrāmam. It ends with the relation between guild and caste, the later history of the mahājan, and a short comparison with guilds elsewhere.

docs.title: 4.1 Terms and Categories
docs.text:
No single Sanskrit word corresponds exactly to the English “guild”, and the sources use several overlapping terms whose meaning shifted over time and between genres (Majumdar 1918; Thaplyal 1996).

Śreṇī (Pali seṇi). The commonest term: a body of people following the same craft or trade, such as weavers, potters, oil-pressers or goldsmiths. In inscriptions it is the usual word for a corporate body that could receive deposits and make gifts. Pūga. An association whose basis is less clear. Medieval commentators on Yājñavalkya explain it as a group of people of different castes and occupations living in one place, in contrast to the śreṇī of a single craft; modern scholars have read it variously as a local assembly or a looser commercial association (Kane 1930). Gaṇa and saṃgha. In Pāṇini and early Buddhist texts these words name non-monarchical polities (the “republics” of the older literature) as well as corporate groups; in the dharmaśāstra gaṇa can denote a body of families or of brāhmaṇas, and the Buddhist monastic community is the saṃgha. The terms do not by themselves indicate an economic association. Nigama and naigama. Nigama means both a market town and the body of its merchants or townsmen; naigama is a member of such a body. Inscriptions record gifts by a nigama, and Gupta-period sealings name the nigama of bankers, caravan traders and artisans (Section 4.6). Sārtha and sārthavāha. The caravan and its leader. The sārthavāha organised a temporary association of merchants for a journey; caravan law and the ethics of the caravan leader are a recurring theme of Buddhist and Jain narrative (see Chapter 10). Śreṣṭhin (Pali seṭṭhi). Literally “the foremost”: a wealthy merchant or banker, sometimes the head of a guild or of the merchants of a town. In the Pali Canon the seṭṭhi is above all a man of great wealth, like Anāthapiṇḍika of Sāvatthī, rather than a guild officer (Chakravarti 1987). Jeṭṭhaka and pamukha. Pali words for the “elder” or “chief” of an occupational group, as in the Jātaka expressions for the chief of the smiths or of the carpenters.

Later sources add many more terms: the kulika (a merchant or artisan of standing) and prathama-kulika of Gupta Bengal, the nagaram (the merchant body of a Tamil market town), and the names of the supra-local south Indian associations discussed in Section 4.7. Using “guild” for all of these is a convenience; it does not imply a uniform institution.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Vedic Background
docs.text: The Ṛgveda speaks of the paṇi, often hostile figures whom some scholars have connected with traders, and later Vedic texts use gaṇa, vrāta and śreṣṭhin. None of these passages describes an occupational association with rules and property, and attempts to trace guilds back to the Vedic period rest on the later meanings of words (Thapar 2002). The institution becomes visible only with the second urbanisation of the Ganges valley in the second half of the first millennium BCE.

docs.title: 4.2.2 The Jātakas and the Pali Canon
docs.text:
The Jātaka stories are the richest narrative source for early guilds. They speak, apparently as a conventional figure, of “the eighteen guilds” (aṭṭhārasa seṇiyo) without giving a fixed list, and they mention the chiefs (jeṭṭhaka, pamukha) of smiths, carpenters, garland-makers and other crafts, villages of carpenters or smiths, caravans under a sārthavāha, and wealthy seṭṭhis who had the ear of the king (Majumdar 1918; Chakravarti 2002).

The Jātakas must be used with care. The verses are older than the prose stories, and the prose commentary in which most of the social detail appears (the Jātakaṭṭhakathā) was compiled in Sri Lanka in about the fifth century CE. The material therefore mixes older tradition with later conditions and cannot be read as a simple picture of the sixth or fifth century BCE. The canonical suttas and the Vinaya give firmer, if thinner, evidence of urban merchants and householders (gahapati) as patrons of the early saṃgha (Chakravarti 1987).

docs.title: 4.2.3 Pāṇini
docs.text: Pāṇini’s grammar (c. 4th c. BCE) contains rules for forming words that denote members of a pūga, a vrāta (a band living by labour or arms) and a saṃgha, and it uses śreṇī in the sense of a group or row. These rules show that corporate groups were familiar enough to need their own derivational patterns; they do not tell us how such groups were organised (Majumdar 1918).

docs.title: 4.2.4 The Dharmasūtras and the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Gautama Dharmasūtra (probably 3rd–2nd c. BCE, on Olivelle’s dating) states that farmers, traders, herdsmen, moneylenders and artisans have authority over the rules of their own groups, and that the laws of regions, castes and families are authoritative where they do not conflict with the Veda (Olivelle 1999, GDh 11.20–21). This principle — that the king recognises and enforces the customary law of groups — runs through the whole later legal literature.

The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) mentions the śreṇī in many contexts (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). Among the kinds of troops a king may raise are corporation troops (śreṇībala), and the book on confederations (saṃgha, AŚ 11.1) distinguishes groups that live by trade and agriculture as well as by arms (AŚ 9.2, 11.1). The records office is to register the customary law of regions, villages, castes, families and corporate groups (AŚ 2.7). In the book on the “removal of thorns”, artisans who accept materials from clients are to be guaranteed by their guild, which is made answerable if the artisan defaults (AŚ 4.1), and traders who combine to hold back goods or to sell at an improper price are heavily fined (AŚ 4.2). The law of workers and of partnership (saṃbhūya-samutthāna, literally “undertaking together”) provides that guild workers and partners divide their earnings as agreed or equally (AŚ 3.14; see Chapter 6).

The overall stance is that of a government that values the productive and military capacity of corporate groups but is wary of their collective power. The book on saṃghas advises the king to win over or divide confederations rather than confront them. About the internal organisation of guilds the text says little.

docs.title: 4.3 Organisation and Leadership
docs.text:
What we know of internal organisation comes mostly from the later dharmaśāstra and from inscriptions, and it is fragmentary. A guild had a head — called śreṇī-mukhya, jyeṣṭhaka, pramukha or simply śreṣṭhin — and, according to the later smṛtis, a small number of executive officers. The Bṛhaspatismṛti, known only from quotations in medieval digests, recommends that two, three or five persons who speak for the welfare of the group be appointed as “executives” (kāryacintaka), and the Yājñavalkyasmṛti expects such officers to be honest, learned and free from greed (Kane 1930; Majumdar 1918).

The rules of a group are usually called samaya or saṃvid (“convention, compact”), and the texts insist that members abide by them. They say much less about how the rules were made. R. C. Majumdar and other writers of the early twentieth century described the guild as a self-governing, almost democratic body (Majumdar 1918); the sources show executive officers and a duty to obey the group’s compacts, but not how officers were chosen. Leadership was probably held by the wealthiest and most senior members, and in many crafts it passed within families.

Apprenticeship is treated in the dharmaśāstra under the title of the pupil who has undertaken to learn a craft: Nārada sets out how the apprentice lives with the master, receives food and training, and must not leave before the agreed period (Kane 1930). These are rules for an individual contract between master and pupil, not evidence of a guild-run training system, although in practice much skill must have been learnt within families and workshops that were also guild members.

Guilds could own property and hold funds. The inscriptions discussed below show them receiving permanent deposits and paying interest from them, and some show them building or repairing temples and halls. The texts do not say how the common fund was administered.

docs.title: 4.4 Recognition in Dharmaśāstra
docs.text:
The legal texts treat corporate groups in three ways: as a source of law, as a level of adjudication, and as parties to compacts whose breach the king must punish.

Manusmṛti 8.41

jātijānapadān dharmān śreṇīdharmāṃś ca dharmavit samīkṣya kuladharmāṃś ca svadharmaṃ pratipādayet

“A king who knows the law should examine the laws of castes, of regions, of guilds and of families, and then settle the law proper to each” (Olivelle 2004).

A source of law. Manu (c. 2nd c. CE) requires the king to take account of the law of guilds when deciding cases (8.41), and the same principle appears in Yājñavalkya (c. 4th–5th c. CE) and Nārada (c. 5th–6th c. CE). Yājñavalkya’s section on the breach of compacts (saṃvid-vyatikrama, 2.186–192) ends by extending its rules to guilds (śreṇī), merchant bodies (naigama), religious sects (pāṣaṇḍin) and gaṇas, and by directing the king to preserve their distinctive usages and former practice (Kane 1930).

A level of adjudication. Yājñavalkya (2.30) and Nārada list families, guilds and pūgas, together with officers appointed by the king, as bodies that hear disputes, each later one carrying more weight than the one before it. In other words, guild tribunals were recognised as courts of first resort for disputes within their competence, below the royal court (Kane 1930).

Compacts and their breach. Manu (8.219) prescribes banishment for a man who, out of greed, breaks a compact sworn with a village, a region or a corporate body. Yājñavalkya adds confiscation for one who misappropriates the common property of a group or breaks its compact, and Nārada’s title on the “non-observance of conventions” (samayasyānapākarma) directs the king to uphold the conventions of guilds, merchant bodies, pūgas and similar groups. The later smṛtis of Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana, quoted in the medieval digests, go further into the duties of executive officers, the expulsion of members and the limits of a group’s authority: rules that are contrary to the king’s interest or to morality are not to be enforced (Kane 1930).

Scholarly Note: Corporate personality?

Older writers argued that dharmaśāstra recognised the guild as a “legal person” centuries before European law. The texts do treat a group as able to own property, to make compacts and to be harmed by a member’s breach. But they do not formulate a general doctrine of corporate personality, and comparisons that make India “earlier” than Roman or medieval European law (which recognised the collegium and universitas) are not helpful. What the dharmaśāstra offers is a consistent principle of deference to group custom, within limits set by the king and by dharma (Kane 1930; Thaplyal 1996).

docs.title: 4.5 Guilds as Trustees: Permanent Endowments
docs.text: The firmest evidence that guilds handled money comes from inscriptions recording permanent endowments: a donor deposited a capital sum with a guild, which kept the principal and paid an agreed interest, from which a religious or charitable purpose was funded in perpetuity. Later sources call this an akṣaya-nīvī (“undecaying capital”) (Thaplyal 1996; Ray 1986).

docs.title: 4.5.1 The Nasik Endowments of Uṣavadāta
docs.text:
The best known record is an inscription in Cave 10 at Nasik of Uṣavadāta (Ṛṣabhadatta), son-in-law of the Kṣaharāta ruler Nahapāna. It is dated in the year 42, which most scholars take to be of the Śaka era (c. 120 CE), though this is debated. Uṣavadāta records that he invested 3,000 kārṣāpaṇas for the monks of the four quarters living in the cave: 2,000 with a guild of weavers (kolika-nikāya) at Govardhana, at interest of one per cent per month, and 1,000 with another weavers’ guild there, at three-quarters per cent per month (Lüders 1912; Ray 1986). The inscription is reproduced in Figure 4.1.

The capital was not to be repaid; only the interest was to be used. The interest on the first sum provided a robe allowance of 12 kārṣāpaṇas for each of the twenty monks who spent the rains in the cave, and that on the second sum went to a further allowance for the monks. The figures are internally consistent: one per cent a month on 2,000 gives 240 kārṣāpaṇas a year, or 12 each for 20 monks. The inscription adds that the gift was proclaimed in the town assembly (nigama-sabhā) and registered according to custom — direct evidence of a public record of such investments.

Figure 4.1. The endowment inscription of Uṣavadāta in Cave 10 at Nasik (Nasik inscription no. 12, dated in the year 42), which records his deposit of 3,000 kārṣāpaṇas with two weavers’ guilds at Govardhana for the monks of the cave. Ink impression reproduced in Epigraphia Indica, vol. 8. Image: E. Hultzsch (ed.), Epigraphia Indica vol. 8, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The annual equivalent rates of about 12 and 9 per cent are well below the rates for commercial loans in the legal texts (Chapter 6). They suggest that guilds regarded the deposits as a secure, low-cost source of capital and that donors valued the permanence of a corporate trustee more than a high return.

A later inscription at Nasik, of the reign of the Ābhīra king Īśvarasena, records a similar endowment by a lay woman with several guilds at Govardhana, including potters and oil-millers, to provide medicine for sick monks. Other inscriptions in the western Deccan caves record gifts by guild members and by nigamas (Lüders 1912; Ray 1986).

docs.title: 4.5.2 Mathura and the Gupta Period
docs.text:
An inscription of the reign of the Kuṣāṇa king Huviṣka at Mathura records an akṣaya-nīvī of purāṇa coins divided between two guilds, one of them a guild of flour-makers, the interest on which was to feed brāhmaṇas and the needy at a hall of charity (Thaplyal 1996). In the Gupta period the Indor copper plate of Skandagupta (Gupta year 146, i.e. 465 CE), from Indor in the Bulandshahr district of Uttar Pradesh (not Indore in Madhya Pradesh), records that a brāhmaṇa deposited money with the guild of oil-men of Indrapura on condition that the guild supply oil in perpetuity for a lamp in a temple of the Sun (Thaplyal 1996; Salomon 1998). Table 4.1 lists selected inscriptions of this kind.

Table 4.1. Selected inscriptions recording guild endowments and gifts Record Date Guild and purpose Nasik, Cave 10 (Uṣavadāta) Year 42, prob. c. 120 CE Two weavers’ guilds at Govardhana; 3,000 kārṣāpaṇas at 1% and 0.75% a month; robes and other needs of monks Nasik (Ābhīra Īśvarasena) c. 3rd c. CE Several guilds at Govardhana; medicine for sick monks Mathura (Huviṣka) Kuṣāṇa period Two guilds, one of flour-makers; feeding at a charity hall Indor plate (Skandagupta) 465 CE Oil-men’s guild of Indrapura; lamp for a Sun temple Mandasor (Kumāragupta I and later) 436–437 and 472–473 CE Silk-weavers’ guild from Lāṭa; built and repaired a Sun temple

These records are few compared with the number of guilds that must have existed, and they survive because they concern religious gifts. They tell us that guilds were trusted to hold funds over long periods, at modest and stated rates of interest; they do not show that guilds were general deposit banks lending to the public.

docs.title: 4.6 Seals, Coins and Guilds in Gupta India
4.6.1 The Vaiśālī Sealings
docs.text: Excavations at Basarh, ancient Vaiśālī in north Bihar, in the early twentieth century produced hundreds of clay sealings of the Gupta period. Many bear the legend śreṣṭhi-sārthavāha-kulika-nigama — the corporation of bankers (or chief merchants), caravan traders and kulikas — sometimes together with the seal of an individual member, while others name a śreṣṭhi-nigama or a kulika-nigama alone. Sealings were attached to letters and consignments, and their number suggests a busy correspondence. Whether the “corporation” was one body uniting the three groups or a formula naming several bodies is debated (Thaplyal 1996). Sealings of guilds and nigamas are also known from Bhita near Prayagraj.

docs.title: 4.6.2 Guild Coinage
docs.text: Copper coins from Taxila bearing the Brāhmī legend negama (“of the nigama”) together with a name have been interpreted as issues of local merchant bodies in the last centuries BCE (Allan 1936). The interpretation is widely accepted, but these coins are a small, local group; they do not show that guilds generally issued money (see Chapter 5).

docs.title: 4.6.3 Merchants in Local Administration
docs.text: The Damodarpur copper plates from north Bengal (5th–6th c. CE) show the head of a district (viṣayapati) acting together with the chief merchant of the town (nagara-śreṣṭhin), the chief caravan trader (sārthavāha), the chief artisan (prathama-kulika) and the chief scribe (prathama-kāyastha) in sales of land. Leading merchants were thus formally associated with local government in at least one Gupta province (Thaplyal 1996; Chakravarti 2002).

docs.title: 4.6.4 The Mandasor Silk-Weavers
docs.text:
The most famous guild inscription is the Mandasor (ancient Daśapura) inscription of the guild of silk-weavers (paṭṭavāya-śreṇī). It is a Sanskrit poem composed by Vatsabhaṭṭi. It records that the weavers migrated from Lāṭa (south Gujarat) to Daśapura, built a temple of the Sun in Mālava year 493 (436–437 CE) under Kumāragupta I and his local governor Bandhuvarman, and repaired it in year 529 (472–473 CE) (Salomon 1998; Thaplyal 1996).

The inscription is valuable for social history. It describes some members of the guild as having taken up other callings — archery, story-telling, astrology, religious life — while remaining in the group, which suggests that the guild was by then a community defined by origin and kinship as much as by craft. It is a literary text and its praise of the weavers is conventional, but the outline of migration, prosperity and diversification is clear.

docs.title: 4.6.5 After the Guptas
docs.text:
From the sixth century, inscriptions in western and central India record royal charters confirming the customary rules of merchant communities. The best known, the charter of Viṣṇuṣeṇa (592 CE), sets out a long list of customary regulations (ācāra) for a merchant settlement, covering dues, fines and procedure (Chakravarti 2002). Such documents show rulers negotiating with organised merchant groups rather than simply regulating them.

The older view that guilds and towns declined sharply after c. 600 CE, as part of a process of “feudalisation” and urban decay (Sharma 1987), has been challenged by historians who point to new market centres, regional trade networks and merchant bodies in the early medieval centuries (Chattopadhyaya 1994). The south Indian evidence in particular does not fit a picture of decline.

docs.title: 4.7 South Indian Merchant Associations
docs.text:
From the ninth century the Tamil, Kannada and Telugu inscriptions record merchant bodies on a larger scale than the craft guilds of the north. Historians have debated whether “guild” fits them at all: they look less like closed bodies of one trade than like associations or umbrella organisations of merchants, with their own armed retainers, a shared honorific language and links to particular towns (Abraham 1988; Hall 1980; Champakalakshmi 1996).

Nagaram. The merchant body of a market town in the Tamil country, attested widely under the Pallavas and Cholas, which managed the town’s trade, made gifts to temples and dealt with village assemblies and royal officers (Hall 1980). The Ayyāvoḷe Five Hundred. The “Five Hundred lords of Ayyāvoḷe” (Tamil Ainnūṟṟuvar), named after Ayyāvoḷe, modern Aihole in Karnataka, are recorded in a long series of inscriptions from about the late ninth to the fourteenth century across Karnataka, Andhra and Tamil Nadu. Their inscriptions open with a standard eulogy (praśasti) and speak of fortified merchant towns (eṟivīra-paṭṭaṇam) protected by armed men. The name is closely associated, and sometimes interchangeable, with the Nānādeśi (“of many countries”) and with the Vīra-Baḷañja (Abraham 1988; Champakalakshmi 1996). Maṇigrāmam. A merchant body first recorded in the Kollam copper plates (below) and in a ninth-century Tamil inscription at Takuapa on the Thai–Malay peninsula; it later appears in Tamil Nadu as well as Kerala (Abraham 1988). Añjuvaṇṇam. A body associated with merchants from West Asia, including Jews and probably Christians and Muslims; the name is usually derived from Persian hanjaman (“assembly”). In the Jewish copper plates of Cochin (c. 1000 CE) the Cēra king Bhāskara Ravivarman grants the Añjuvaṇṇam with other privileges to Joseph Rabban (Champakalakshmi 1996).

Historical Note: The Kollam (Quilon) copper plates, c. 849 CE

The plates were issued in the fifth regnal year of the Cēra king Sthāṇu Ravi by his governor of Veṇāṭu, Ayyaṉaṭikaḷ Tiruvaṭikaḷ, in favour of the Tarisā church of the Syrian Christian community at Kollam. They grant land and service groups to the church and place the grant under the protection of the Añjuvaṇṇam and the Maṇigrāmam, who are given rights in the town’s trade. The witnesses’ signatures are in Arabic (Kufic), Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and Judaeo-Persian (Hebrew script). The plates show the merchant bodies as guarantors of a royal grant and illustrate the cosmopolitan population of the Malabar ports (Abraham 1988; Champakalakshmi 1996).

Inscriptions of the Five Hundred and of related bodies have been found in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Sumatra (a Tamil inscription of 1088 CE from Barus), as well as in south India. Their overseas activity, and its relation to Chola policy, is treated in Chapter 12. The south Indian associations did not operate alone: they traded alongside, and sometimes in partnership with, Arab, Persian, Jewish and Chinese merchants, as the Kollam plates themselves show (Goitein and Friedman 2008).

These associations were closely tied to temples and to royal power. They endowed temples, received privileges from kings, and appear in Chola inscriptions as one of several corporate actors alongside the brāhmaṇa sabhā, the village ūr and the nagaram. They employed armed guards and their inscriptions use martial language, but they were not states: there is no evidence that they struck coinage or ruled territory (Hall 1980; Abraham 1988).

docs.title: 4.8 Guild, Caste and Exclusion
docs.text:
The relation between guild and caste (jāti) is one of the central questions of Indian social history. Several lines of evidence point to a gradual convergence. Crafts were increasingly hereditary, the dharmaśāstra assigns crafts and trade to particular varṇas and mixed castes, and many later occupational jātis (weavers, oil-pressers, potters, smiths, goldsmiths) correspond to crafts organised earlier as guilds. The Mandasor weavers kept a common identity after migration and even after some members changed occupation, which is the behaviour of a kin-based community rather than a purely professional body. And the legal texts treat the rules of jāti, śreṇī and kula side by side as sources of custom, without a sharp distinction between them.

Historians differ on the direction of causation — whether guilds hardened into castes, or caste-like groups used guild forms — and no single process will fit every region (Thapar 2002; Sharma 1983). What is clear is that guild membership was not open. Admission was controlled by members, often by birth, and the texts and inscriptions say nothing of the many labourers, servants and slaves who worked for guild members. The dharmaśāstra ranks some occupations, such as leather-working, as impure and assigns them to low castes, and the guild record is largely the record of the established. Women appear as donors in the inscriptions (as at Nasik) but not as guild officers.

docs.title: 4.9 Later History and Legacy
docs.text: Guild-like bodies remained part of Indian commercial life long after the classical sources. In Sultanate and Mughal India the merchant and artisan communities of the towns were organised in caste and community associations, generally called mahājan, which regulated trade, settled disputes, organised charity and represented their members before the authorities. The later history of merchant communities and their credit networks is taken up in Chapters 6 and 18; this section follows the associations themselves.

docs.title: 4.9.1 The Mahājan of Gujarati Towns
docs.text:
The mahājans of Gujarat are the best documented. In Ahmedabad, founded by the sultans of Gujarat in 1411 and from 1572–73 the capital of a Mughal province, each of the major trades — cloth dealers, bankers and money-changers, dealers in grain, and many crafts — had its own mahājan under a headman (śeṭh), and the merchants of the city as a whole recognised a leading figure with the title of nagarśeṭh (“town merchant”). The mahājan fixed working days and holidays, settled disputes among members, fined those who broke its rules, and could raise levies on its members’ trade for charitable purposes, notably the animal shelters (pāñjarāpoḷ) supported by Jain and Vaiṣṇava merchants (Gillion 1968; Laidlaw 1995).

The best known Ahmedabad merchant of the Mughal period is Śāntidās Jhaverī (d. 1659), a Śvetāmbara Jain jeweller and financier who supplied jewels to the courts of Jahāngīr and Shāh Jahān. He built a temple to Pārśvanātha in the Saraspur quarter of Ahmedabad; when the prince Aurangzeb, as governor of Gujarat in the mid-1640s, had it desecrated and turned into a mosque, Śāntidās appealed to the court, and Shāh Jahān ordered that the building be restored to him. He later obtained imperial orders concerning the Jain pilgrimage centre of Śatruñjaya at Palitana, and he lent money to Prince Murād Bakhsh during the war of succession of 1657–58 (Gillion 1968). His career shows how a merchant leader could use credit, court connections and imperial documents to protect his community’s religious and commercial interests. His descendants held the title of nagarśeṭh of Ahmedabad into the nineteenth century and beyond.

Merchant bodies could act collectively against officials. The most common weapon was the closing of shops (haṛtāl); another was migration. In 1669, after pressure on Hindu merchants at Surat by the city’s religious officials, many bāniyās left Surat for Bharuch and returned only after assurances from the authorities. Pearson and Das Gupta show that such action was effective because the revenue of the Mughal port depended on the merchants’ presence, but also that the merchants rarely sought political power for themselves (Pearson 1976; Das Gupta 1979).

docs.title: 4.9.2 Caste Councils and Occupational Associations
docs.text:
The early modern mahājan was usually organised by caste or religious community as well as by trade, and it is often hard to separate it from the caste council (jāti pañcāyat). The two had different starting points. A caste council governed the members of one jāti, whatever they did for a living: it dealt with marriage, commensality, ritual purity and disputes within the caste, and its ultimate sanction was exclusion from the caste. A mahājan of cloth dealers or bankers, by contrast, might include merchants of several castes, Jain and Hindu, who shared a trade and a market. Where an occupation was in the hands of a single caste, as with many groups of weavers, potters or oil-pressers, the council of the caste and the association of the craft were in effect the same body, and it regulated both social and occupational matters (Gillion 1968).

Colonial rule changed the setting of these bodies. British courts were often reluctant to intervene in questions of caste membership, which strengthened caste councils in their own sphere, while commercial disputes came increasingly before the civil courts. Colonial law also reclassified indigenous commercial practices — the joint family firm, the charitable gift, the customary rules of the bazaar — in its own categories, a process that Ritu Birla has studied in detail for the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (Birla 2009). Some merchant communities turned their caste organisation into an instrument of business: the Nattukottai Chettiars, for instance, organised credit through lineages and temples whose rules bound their members (Rudner 1994). From the late nineteenth century merchants also formed community associations and chambers of commerce on the European model (Timberg 1978); at the national level, the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry was founded in 1927.

docs.title: 4.9.3 Craft Associations in Colonial India
docs.text:
Weavers’ collective action is the best studied case. In south India, weaving castes such as the Kaikkōḷar and Sāliyar had long had their own organisation, linked to temples, and had used migration as a weapon against excessive taxation (Ramaswamy 1985). In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries artisan and merchant castes in the Tamil country were also grouped in the rival coalitions of the “right-hand” and “left-hand” castes (valaṅkai and iṭaṅkai), whose disputes over precedence and privileges repeatedly disturbed the English settlement at Madras (Arasaratnam 1986). When the English Company, in the later eighteenth century, tried to bind weavers to deliver only to its agents, weavers in the south responded with petitions, collective refusals of advances and desertion of their villages; Prasannan Parthasarathi has argued that these protests show both the strength of the weavers’ organisation and the growing power of the Company to override it (Parthasarathi 2001, 2011).

In the industrial city the word mahājan took on a new meaning. After the Ahmedabad mill strike of 1918, in which Gandhi intervened on the workers’ side, the textile workers of the city formed the Textile Labour Association in 1920, known in Gujarati as the Majūr Mahājan (“workers’ mahājan”), with Anasuya Sarabhai and Gandhi among its founders. It favoured arbitration over strikes, and it became one of the largest unions in India. The name deliberately borrowed the language of the merchant associations of the city, but the institution was new: a union of wage workers, open across castes, negotiating with millowners who were themselves often members of the old merchant mahājans (Gillion 1968).

Modern writers have linked the śreṇī to the cooperative movement and to modern trade associations. These are analogies: the cooperative movement in India grew from the Co-operative Credit Societies Act of 1904 and drew on European models, although it was adapted to Indian conditions. There is no direct institutional descent from the ancient guild.

docs.title: 4.10 Comparison with Guilds Elsewhere
docs.text:
Associations of craftsmen and merchants are found in many premodern societies, and the Indian evidence is best read alongside them rather than ranked against them.

  • In the Roman world, collegia of craftsmen and traders are attested from the late Republic and were regulated by the state; in Byzantium the tenth-century Book of the Eparch set out rules for the guilds of Constantinople.

  • In medieval and early modern Europe, merchant and craft guilds (from about the eleventh century) regulated entry, quality and prices, held property, supported members and endowed religious foundations. Sheilagh Ogilvie’s survey argues that they mainly secured advantages for their members and that their benefits for the wider economy have been overstated (Ogilvie 2019).

  • In China, merchant groupings (hang) organised by trade appear in Tang and Song cities, and native-place associations (huiguan) and trade associations (gongsuo) flourished under the Ming and Qing.

  • In the Islamic Middle East, craft and trade groups were organised under market inspectors (muḥtasib), and the question how far they formed autonomous guilds is debated.

The Indian case shares many features with these: control of entry, collective responsibility, endowments, and a negotiated relationship with rulers. Its distinctive traits lie in the legal principle of deference to group custom, the close link with caste, and the scale of some south Indian associations. The same questions that economic historians ask of European guilds — did they lower the costs of trade by enforcing contracts and quality, or did they mainly restrict competition? — can be asked of Indian ones, but the evidence is too thin to give a confident answer.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Majumdar (1918) remains a useful collection of the literary and legal evidence, and Thaplyal (1996) is the fullest study of northern India and the western Deccan. Ray (1986) places the Deccan guilds in the setting of Buddhist patronage, and Chakravarti (2002) surveys traders and trade in early India. For the legal texts see Kane (1930). For south India, Abraham (1988), Hall (1980) and Champakalakshmi (1996) are the essential works. Salomon (1998) introduces the inscriptions.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Coinage and Monetary Systems
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Coined money appears in South Asia in the second half of the first millennium BCE, after a long period in which cattle, ornaments and weighed pieces of metal served as measures of value. This chapter follows the main coin series from the silver punch-marked coins through the bilingual coins of the north-west, Kuṣāṇa and Gupta gold, the lead and potin of the Deccan, the Roman coins found in the south and the gold of the Chola and Vijayanagara kingdoms, to the tanka of the Delhi Sultanate and the rupee of Sher Shāh and the Mughals. It also looks at what the texts, above all the Arthaśāstra, say about mints, coin examiners and the value of money. Many questions remain open: who issued the earliest coins, how monetised the economy was at different times, and whether early medieval India really suffered a “coin shortage”. The chapter sets these out as debates.

Indian monetary history has three kinds of evidence, and each has its limits. The coins themselves survive in their hundreds of thousands, in hoards and in excavated layers, but most early coins carry no legend and no date. Texts such as the Pali canon, Pāṇini’s grammar, the Arthaśāstra and the Manusmṛti name coins and weights, but they are hard to date and are often normative rather than descriptive. Inscriptions record endowments, prices and fines in named currencies, but usually for religious gifts rather than for everyday trade. The account below tries to keep these three kinds of evidence apart. Weights and measures in general are treated in Chapter 7, and credit instruments such as the hundī in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Cattle, Ornaments and Weighed Gold
docs.text:
The Harappan cities (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) used a highly standardised system of cubical chert weights, but no coins. Exchange there was presumably by barter, by weighed metal or by other means we cannot now see (Kenoyer 1998). Chapter 7 discusses the Harappan weights.

In the Vedic texts, wealth is counted above all in cattle. The dānastuti (“praise of gifts”) verses of the Ṛgveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) list the cows, horses and chariots that patrons gave to poets. Among the gifts is the niṣka, a gold ornament worn at the neck. Because it was given and counted, the niṣka worked as a store and measure of value, but there is no evidence that it was a coin. In the later Vedic period (c. 1200–500 BCE), the Brāhmaṇas name the śatamāna (“of a hundred measures”), a gold piece of a hundred kṛṣṇalas (seeds used as weights), as a sacrificial fee. The well-known story of Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, in which his father Ajīgarta sells him for sacrifice, puts the price in cattle (a hundred cows). These terms survived. Pāṇini’s grammar (c. 4th century BCE) gives rules for words expressing a price in niṣkas and śatamānas. Pāṇini also teaches a derivative rūpya, “stamped” or “struck”, from rūpa (“form, mark”). Many scholars connect this word with the stamped metal of the early coins, and it is the remote ancestor of “rupee” (Sircar 1968; Kosambi 1981).

docs.title: 5.1.2 The Weight System and the Problem of Names
docs.text:
Indian coin standards were built on the rati (Sanskrit raktikā, guñjā or kṛṣṇala), the red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius. Modern estimates of the rati vary, but it is usually taken to be roughly 0.11–0.12 g. This is an approximation: seeds vary, and ancient standards were reconstructed from coins, not from seeds. The silver coin of the early historic period was nominally 32 ratis, which works out at about 3.5–3.8 g. Most surviving punch-marked coins weigh a little less, commonly around 3.3–3.5 g, partly because of wear.

Scholarly Note: Kārṣāpaṇa, purāṇa, paṇa: a note on terms

Numismatists conventionally call the silver punch-marked coin a kārṣāpaṇa (Pali kahāpaṇa), and this chapter does the same. The texts, however, do not use the names consistently. In the weight table of the Manusmṛti (8.131–137; c. 2nd century CE), the kārṣāpaṇa or paṇa is a copper unit of one karṣa. The silver unit of 32 ratis is called a dharaṇa or purāṇa, and the silver śatamāna is ten dharaṇas (Olivelle 2004). The Arthaśāstra calls its silver coin simply the paṇa. The Pali texts use kahāpaṇa for the ordinary coin of account. When a text names a sum “in kārṣāpaṇas”, the metal and the standard therefore cannot be taken for granted. This chapter does not convert such sums into modern values.

docs.title: 5.1.3 Cowries
docs.text: Cowrie shells (varāṭaka, kapardaka), most of them from the Maldives, served as small change in many parts of India for a very long time. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian, who travelled in the Gangetic plain in the early fifth century CE, reported that people there used cowries in buying and selling. Early medieval inscriptions from eastern India state prices and rents in cowries counted against coin or silver units. In Bengal and Odisha, cowries remained in use for petty payments into the colonial period. Cowries did not stand for a failure of money. They show that the small-change end of the system could be supplied by an imported commodity whose value was set by convention (Deyell 1990).

docs.title: 5.2.1 Technique and Date
docs.text:
The earliest Indian coins are the punch-marked coins. A piece of silver was cut to weight from a sheet or bar, and one or more small symbols were then hammered onto it with separate punches. The coins were not struck between a pair of dies, as Greek coins were. Most have no legend. The symbols include the sun, a “six-armed” wheel-like device, animals (elephant, bull, dog, frog, peacock), trees in railings, hills (the “arched hill”), fish and many abstract signs (Allan 1936; Gupta 1969).

The date of the first coins is debated. Firm archaeological anchors are few. The Chaman Hazouri hoard found at Kabul in 1933 contained bent silver bars and Indian punch-marked pieces together with Greek coins, and was deposited in the fourth century BCE. The Bhir Mound hoard at Taxila contained punch-marked coins together with coins of Alexander and of Philip III Arrhidaeus, and was deposited towards the end of the fourth century BCE. Most numismatists therefore place the beginnings of coinage in the north-west and the Gangetic plain in the fifth or fourth century BCE. Some argue for the sixth century BCE, chiefly on the basis of the Pali texts, whose own dates are uncertain, so that a date as early as c. 600 BCE remains a possibility rather than a finding.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Regional Series and the “Imperial” Series
docs.text:
Modern catalogues sort the punch-marked coins into regional groups. In the north-west there are heavy concave pieces and “bent bars” of about 11 g. In the Gangetic plain there are groups that numismatists attribute to the mahājanapadas, such as Kosala, Kāśī, Magadha and Avanti, and there are distinctive series from the Deccan and the south. These attributions rest on find-spots and on style, not on legends, and they are not all secure. The bent bars are sometimes linked to the Vedic śatamāna, and sometimes to the Achaemenid Persian silver standard used in the satrapies of Gandhāra and the Indus. Both links are hypotheses.

The most numerous and widely distributed group is the so-called “imperial” series. These are flat silver coins of about 32 ratis, each with a set of five obverse punches, and they are found from Afghanistan to the Deccan. Many numismatists attribute much of this series to the Mauryan state (c. 321–185 BCE). The attribution is plausible because of the coins’ uniformity and range, but no coin names a Mauryan king. The reverse often carries one or more small marks, which seem to have been added while the coins were in circulation (Figure 5.1). Copper punch-marked and cast coins became common only later, in the last centuries BCE (Gupta 1969; Allan 1936).

Figure 5.1. A silver punch-marked coin of the “imperial” series (3.4 g), attributed by its cataloguer to the Mauryan period, in the reign of Bindusāra (c. 297–272 BCE). The obverse (left) carries several separately punched symbols, among them a sun; the reverse (right) carries a single small mark. Photo: Jean-Michel Moullec, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.2.3 Kosambi’s Statistical Study
docs.text:
The most original work on these coins was done by the mathematician and historian D. D. Kosambi in the 1940s and 1950s. Kosambi weighed several thousand coins from excavated hoards, above all those from Taxila, and studied how their weights were distributed. He showed that coins lose weight at a fairly regular rate in circulation, so that the mean weight of a group of coins can indicate how long it had been in use. He also showed that coins with more reverse marks tend to be lighter. This supported his view that the reverse marks were added during circulation, perhaps by checking authorities, and it allowed him to propose a relative order for the obverse groups. Kosambi’s attributions of particular groups to particular kings have not been generally accepted. His method, which treats coins as a statistical population and not as individual specimens, was a landmark in numismatics (Kosambi 1981).

Debate: Who issued the punch-marked coins?

Older accounts often say that punch-marked coins were “minted by the state”. The evidence does not support that as a general statement. The later “imperial” series may well be a state issue. For the earlier regional coins, scholars have proposed several issuers. Some think they were issued by kings or janapada authorities. Others suggest that urban or merchant bodies, or even individual bankers and money-changers, put their marks on pieces of standard weight. Kosambi himself argued that the marks guaranteed weight and fineness, and he left open how far they were “royal”. Clearer evidence of non-royal issue comes from the following period. Inscribed cast copper coins from Taxila carry the word negama, most often read as referring to a merchant or town corporation. Other cast coins name towns such as Ujjayinī, Vidiśā, Erakaṇa (Eran), Tripurī and Kauśāmbī, apparently as issuing authorities (Allan 1936; Chakravarti 2002). It seems best to suppose that several kinds of authority issued coins in early historic India, and that the share of each changed over time.

Scholarly Note: An independent invention?

The relation of Indian coinage to the coins of Lydia, Greece and Achaemenid Persia is also debated. The Achaemenid empire held Gandhāra and the Indus region from the late sixth century BCE, and its silver siglos was known there. Some numismatists hold that coinage in the north-west began under Achaemenid influence and then spread east. Others stress how different the Indian technique of multiple punches on cut blanks is from die-striking, and argue for a largely local development out of the practice of marking weighed silver. Both positions are held by serious scholars. A middle view is that the idea of coinage may have travelled while the forms were local.

docs.title: 5.3 Cast, Die-Struck and Local Coinages
docs.text:
From about the third and second centuries BCE, a great variety of copper (and some silver) coins was issued alongside the punch-marked silver. Some were made by casting in moulds. Others were die-struck, sometimes on one face only. There were three broad kinds of issuer.

  • Cities. Cast and struck copper coins name or are attributed to towns such as Ujjayinī (with the cross-and-balls “Ujjain symbol”), Vidiśā, Eran, Tripurī, Kauśāmbī and Taxila.

  • Local kings. Dynasties at Kauśāmbī, Ayodhyā, Mathurā and Pañcāla issued copper coins with their names in Brāhmī.

  • Republican peoples (gaṇas). The Yaudheyas, Mālavas, Ārjunāyanas, Audumbaras and Kuṇindas issued coins in the name of the people itself. A well-known example is the Yaudheya coin legend yaudheya-gaṇasya jaya (“victory to the Yaudheya gaṇa”). The Kuṇinda king Amoghabhūti issued silver with both Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī legends (Allan 1936; Sircar 1968).

This copper coinage matters for economic history. It shows that coins were used for small, everyday transactions in many towns, and not only for large payments in silver.

docs.title: 5.4 The North-West: Indo-Greek, Śaka and Kuṣāṇa Coinage
5.4.1 Indo-Greek Bilingual Coins
docs.text: The Greek kings who ruled parts of Afghanistan, Gandhāra and the Panjab from the early second century BCE to around the turn of the era brought the Hellenistic die-struck coin, with a royal portrait and a deity. In India they adapted it in three ways. First, they added a second legend, usually in Prakrit written in Kharoṣṭhī, on the reverse, so that the coins became bilingual. Second, they struck square as well as round coins. Third, they struck silver on a lighter “Indian” standard: a drachm of about 2.4 g and a tetradrachm of about 9.7 g, against roughly 4.3 g and 17 g on the Attic standard used in Bactria. Some early issues went further. Square silver coins of Agathocles found at Ai Khanoum carry a Brāhmī legend and figures usually identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa. Menander (c. 165/155–130 BCE), remembered in the Pali Milindapañha as King Milinda, issued a very large bilingual coinage in silver and bronze (Bopearachchi 1991); one of his drachms is shown in Figure 5.2(a). The Indo-Scythian (Śaka) and Indo-Parthian rulers who followed in the first century BCE and first century CE kept the bilingual format, which helps to reconstruct their sequence of rulers.

docs.title: 5.4.2 Kuṣāṇa Gold and Copper
docs.text:
The Kuṣāṇas took the north-west and much of the Gangetic plain in the first and second centuries CE, and they changed the monetary system. Kujula Kadphises issued mainly copper. His successor, Wima Kadphises, introduced a regular gold coinage of about 8 g together with a large copper coinage. Under Kaniṣka I (accession now usually placed c. 127 CE) the legends were changed from Greek to Bactrian, written in Greek script. The reverses carry a remarkable range of deities: Iranian (Mao, Miiro, Athsho, Nana), Greek-derived, and Indian, including Oesho (usually identified with Śiva) and, rarely, the Buddha (Boddo) (Gupta 1969). A gold coin of Kaniṣka is shown in Figure 5.2(b).

The weight of Kuṣāṇa gold is close to that of the Roman aureus, and Roman gold reached the Kuṣāṇa world through trade. Some scholars think Roman coins were melted down and restruck. Others think the closeness of weight reflects a common bullion standard. The question is not settled. The Latin denarius gave Indian languages the word dīnāra, which Gupta inscriptions later use for gold coins. Kuṣāṇa copper was issued in great quantity, and it is found in excavations across north India. That suggests coin use deep into urban society (Gupta 1969).

Figure 5.2. Coins of the north-west. (a) Silver drachm of Menander (c. 165/155–130 BCE) on the lighter “Indian” standard: a Greek legend round the king’s bust on the obverse (left) and a Prakrit legend in Kharoṣṭhī round a standing Athena on the reverse (right). (b) Gold coin of Kaniṣka I: the king sacrificing at an altar, with a Bactrian legend in Greek script (left), and on the reverse a deity with the Kuṣāṇa dynastic emblem (right); Musée Guimet, Paris. Photo: ancientcointraders.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.4.3 The Western Kṣatrapas: Dated Silver
docs.text: In Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa, the Śaka Western Kṣatrapas (c. 1st–4th centuries CE) issued small silver drachms. The obverse carries the ruler’s bust and a degenerate Greek legend. The reverse shows a three-arched hill with a crescent and a Brāhmī legend naming both the ruler and his father. From the later second century CE many of these coins also carry a date behind the head, in the Śaka era (beginning 78 CE). The Western Kṣatrapa series is therefore one of the few ancient Indian coinages from which a dynasty’s succession can be reconstructed year by year. After the Gupta conquest of the region under Candragupta II (c. 400 CE), the Guptas issued silver coins of the same general type for western India (Gupta 1969; Sircar 1968).

docs.title: 5.5 The Deccan and the Far South in the Early Historic Period
5.5.1 Sātavāhana Lead, Potin and Silver
docs.text: The Sātavāhanas, who ruled in the Deccan from about the first century BCE to the early third century CE, issued coins mostly in lead, potin (a copper alloy rich in lead and tin) and copper. Lead was an unusual choice for coinage, and it gives the Sātavāhana series its particular character. The common types show an elephant, a lion, a horse or a ship (the ship coins are discussed in Chapter 13), with the “Ujjain symbol” on the reverse. A few later kings, such as Vāsiṣṭhīputra Śātakarṇi, issued silver coins with royal portraits. These carry a Prakrit legend on one side and a legend in a Dravidian language, in a Tamil-Brāhmī-type script, on the other. The conflict with the Western Kṣatrapas left its mark on the coins. A hoard of more than thirteen thousand silver coins of Nahapāna found at Jogalthembi near Nashik contained many coins restruck by Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi (Ray 1986; Sircar 1968).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Coins of the Tamil Chiefdoms
docs.text: In the far south, copper and some silver coins bear the emblems of the three Tamil royal lineages: the fish of the Pāṇḍyas, the bow of the Cēras and the tiger of the Cholas. A few carry names in Tamil-Brāhmī. Most can be dated only broadly, to the early centuries CE, and their attribution is debated. Early Tamil poetry and Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions mention gold (poṉ) and the kāṇam and kāśu as money terms. These terms do not show how far everyday exchange was monetised (Mahadevan 2003; Champakalakshmi 1996).

docs.title: 5.5.3 Roman Coins in South India
docs.text:
Roman gold and silver coins have been found in large numbers in peninsular India, especially in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra, both in hoards and as single finds. Most of the silver is denarii of Augustus and Tiberius. Gold aurei run from the Julio-Claudian emperors into the second century CE. Many coins bear a deliberate cut or gash across the emperor’s portrait (Figure 5.3). This has been read in two ways. It may have cancelled the coins as Roman currency, or it may have been a test of the metal. The hoards appear to have been valued by weight and fineness, not by the face value of Roman money. Most scholars therefore think the coins circulated mainly as bullion, or were hoarded as wealth, and were not used as everyday currency (Tomber 2008; Begley and De Puma 1991).

Figure 5.3. Gold aureus of Augustus from the Pudukottai hoard in Tamil Nadu, with a deep cut across the emperor’s portrait; British Museum. Photo: PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Pliny the Elder’s complaint that India drained the empire of fifty million sesterces a year confirms that money flowed eastwards, though his figures are a moralist’s round numbers, not accounts (Section 11.7). Late Roman bronze coins of the fourth and fifth centuries, and local imitations of them, are found in Sri Lanka and in the far south of India. Chapter 11 discusses the Indo-Roman trade itself.

docs.title: 5.6 Gupta Gold and Silver
docs.text:
The Gupta kings (c. 320–550 CE) issued mainly gold coins, which their inscriptions call dīnāra or suvarṇa. The early issues follow the Kuṣāṇa weight of about 7.5–8 g. Under Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE) a heavier coin of about 9.2 g appears, often interpreted as a return to a suvarṇa standard of 80 ratis (Gupta 1969). Numismatists classify the coins by the scene on the obverse. The reverse usually shows a goddess, generally identified as Lakṣmī. The principal types are:

  • the king-and-queen type, naming Candragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī;

  • under Samudragupta, the standard (king at an altar), archer, battle-axe, tiger-slayer, lyrist (the king playing the vīṇā) and aśvamedha types. The aśvamedha coins show the sacrificial horse before a sacrificial post, and they announce the performance of the Vedic horse sacrifice;

  • under Candragupta II, the archer (Figure 5.4), lion-slayer, horseman and chhatra (parasol) types;

  • under Kumāragupta I, a wide range including the horseman, peacock (with Kārttikeya on the reverse), elephant-rider, rhinoceros-slayer and a second aśvamedha type.

The legends are in Sanskrit, and several are composed in verse. They praise the king as unconquered and as a conqueror of a hundred battles who wins heaven. These are some of the earliest examples of Sanskrit political poetry addressed to a wide public, and the iconography links royal power with martial skill, learning and Vedic ritual (Gupta 1969). Large hoards show how much gold there was. The Bayana hoard of 1946 (Rajasthan) contained about 1,800 Gupta gold coins.

Figure 5.4. Gold coin of Candragupta II of the archer type: the king holding a bow, with his name in Brāhmī (obverse, left), and a goddess, generally identified as Lakṣmī, seated on a lotus (reverse, right); Cleveland Museum of Art. Photo: Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0 1.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The later Gupta coinage shows marked debasement. The coins of the late fifth and sixth centuries contain visibly less gold, and some late issues are of pale, alloyed metal. Metallurgical analyses of individual coins confirm the general trend, though precise percentages for the whole series should be treated with caution. In western India the Guptas issued silver coins of Western Kṣatrapa type after about 400 CE, and silver coins with Garuḍa or a peacock also circulated in the Gangetic plain. Gupta copper is comparatively scarce. This fact has been used in arguments about how far coins reached everyday transactions under the Guptas (Gupta 1969). Table 5.1 summarises the main coin series of the early historic period.

Table 5.1. Main coin series of early historic India (approximate dates and weights) Series Date (approx.) Metal Remarks Punch-marked (regional and “imperial”) c. 5th/4th–2nd c. BCE Silver; later copper Nominal 32 ratis; surviving coins commonly c. 3.3–3.5 g; issuers debated City, local and gaṇa coins c. 3rd c. BCE–4th c. CE Copper, some silver Cast and die-struck; legends in Brāhmī or Kharoṣṭhī Indo-Greek c. 2nd–1st c. BCE Silver, bronze Bilingual Greek/Kharoṣṭhī; “Indian” drachm c. 2.4 g Kuṣāṇa c. 1st–3rd c. CE Gold, copper Gold c. 8 g from Wima Kadphises; Bactrian legends from Kaniṣka Western Kṣatrapa c. 1st–4th c. CE Silver Small drachms, many dated in the Śaka era Sātavāhana c. 1st c. BCE–3rd c. CE Lead, potin, copper; some silver Silver portrait coins with Prakrit and Dravidian legends Gupta c. 320–550 CE Gold; silver in the west c. 7.5–8 g, heavier c. 9.2 g under Skandagupta; later debasement

docs.title: 5.7 The Early Medieval “Coin Shortage” Debate
docs.text:
Between about 600 and 1000 CE, much of northern India has yielded far fewer coins than the preceding centuries, and many inscriptions record grants and payments in kind. R. S. Sharma took this paucity of coins as one sign of a wider decline in trade and towns. In his view this decline accompanied the growth of land grants and of what he called Indian feudalism (Sharma 1987).

Debate: Was there an early medieval coin shortage?

Sharma argued that, from the late Gupta period onward, a scarcity of coins in excavations and a shift to payment in land and kind show de-urbanisation and a contraction of commerce (Sharma 1987). Critics have replied on several grounds. John S. Deyell’s study of north Indian coinage, Living without Silver, showed that coins did not disappear. A range of currencies continued in use. In the north-west and Rajasthan there were the Indo-Sasanian silver and billon coins and the later “Gadhaiya” pieces. There were the drammas named in inscriptions (the word derives ultimately from the Greek drachm). The Pratihāra king Bhoja I issued his “Ādivarāha” drammas. The Hindu Śāhis of Kabul and Gandhāra issued bull-and-horseman coins, which were widely copied. In the east, cowries were used. What changed, Deyell argued, was the supply of silver: the system adapted by debasing coins, using billon and relying on cowries for small change, not by giving up money (Deyell 1990). B. D. Chattopadhyaya and others have also pointed to new regional markets, temple centres and trading networks in this period (Chattopadhyaya 1994). The debate has become a question about regional variation and about the forms money took. Most scholars no longer accept a simple story of uniform decline.

In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, the Gāhaḍavālas of Kanauj and some of their neighbours issued gold coins with a seated goddess and the king’s name in Nāgarī (Gopal 1965).

docs.title: 5.8 Gold in the South: From the Cholas to Vijayanagara
docs.text:
In peninsular India, Tamil and Kannada inscriptions of the ninth to thirteenth centuries record endowments, interest and prices in gold units. The most common are the kaḻañcu (a gold weight, used also for coins), the smaller mañjāḍi, and the kāśu. In the Deccan, inscriptions use the gadyāṇa and the paṇa. The relations between these units changed over time, and the identification of named units with surviving coins is often uncertain. The Kadambas of Goa and the Western Cāḷukyas issued small cup-shaped gold coins, known from inscriptions as padmaṭaṅkas from the lotus punched on them. The Cholas issued gold, silver and very many copper coins. The Chola copper coins of the “Rājarāja” type show a standing and a seated figure and the legend śrī rājarāja in Nāgarī. They are found widely in south India and Sri Lanka, and they were imitated in Sri Lanka (Nilakanta Sastri 1955b; Hall 1980). Tamil merchant guilds used these currencies in the trade of the Chola period (Chapter 4).

The Vijayanagara kingdom (c. 1336–1565, with successor states after that) established the gold varāha of about 3.4 g as the dominant coin of the south. Its name comes from the boar emblem of earlier dynasties, though Vijayanagara coins mostly show deities such as Hanumān, Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, Śiva and Pārvatī, Bālakṛṣṇa or Veṅkaṭeśvara. Persian writers called it the hun, and the Portuguese and other Europeans called it the pagoda. Smaller gold paṇam (European “fanam”) and copper kāśu (“cash”) served lesser payments. The European companies kept their south Indian accounts in pagodas, and the English Company minted its own pagodas at Madras. The southern gold standard thus outlived Vijayanagara by more than two centuries (Subrahmanyam 1990; Nilakanta Sastri 1955a).

docs.title: 5.9.1 The Tanka and the Jital
docs.text:
The Ghurid conquerors of north India at first adopted local coin types. Muʿizz al-Dīn Muḥammad bin Sām struck gold coins at Kanauj of Gāhaḍavāla type, with the seated goddess and his own name in Nāgarī. Billon “bull-and-horseman” coins of the Śāhi type also continued, with Nāgarī legends such as śrī hamīra (from Arabic amīr). Under Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236), the Delhi Sultanate established a new pair of coins. The first was the silver tanka of about 11 g, carrying only Arabic legends. The second was the billon or copper jital, a small coin of which several dozen went to the tanka; the reckonings of 48 or 50 jitals found in different sources need care. Gold tankas were also struck. The tanka–jital system served the Sultanate for two centuries and was copied by the regional sultanates of Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa and the Deccan (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

The most famous monetary episode of the Sultanate is the token currency of Muḥammad bin Tughluq (c. 1329–1332). He ordered brass or copper tokens to pass at the value of silver tankas. According to the chronicler Ḍiyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī, the tokens were forged on a large scale, and the sultan finally redeemed them from the treasury. Historians have explained the experiment in different ways: as a response to a silver shortage, as an attempt to finance campaigns, or as an imitation of Chinese and Mongol paper money. Baranī’s hostile account shapes what we know of it.

docs.title: 5.9.2 A Mint Official’s Handbook: The Dravyaparīkṣā
docs.text: The most technical Indian text on the coinage of this period was written by a man who worked in the Sultanate’s mint. Ṭhakkura Pheru, a Jain official who served in the treasury and mint at Delhi under ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī and his successors, wrote a series of short Prakrit works on technical subjects, among them gems, metals, arithmetic and architecture. His Dravyaparīkṣā (“examination of coin”), completed around 1318, lists the coins current in north India in his time, the issues of earlier Indian dynasties as well as those of the sultans, and gives for each its weight and its content of silver and copper; it also describes how a mint refined and tested metal. John Deyell made the work a cornerstone of his study of north Indian money, because it allows the debasement of the billon coinage of the preceding centuries to be followed in a contemporary assay rather than only in modern analyses (Deyell 1990). The Dravyaparīkṣā shows that the expertise in assay that the Arthaśāstra had assigned to its examiner of coin (Section 5.10) was a living professional knowledge, and that in the Sultanate it was held by Jain and Hindu specialists working for a Muslim court.

docs.title: 5.9.3 The Rupee, the Dam and the Mohur
docs.text:
Sher Shāh Sūr (r. 1540–1545) gave north India the coin that has lasted longest. This was the silver rupiya of about 178 grains (c. 11.5 g), struck in fine silver and paired with a heavy copper dām. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) and his successors kept the rupee standard and added the gold mohur of about 11 g (Figure 5.5). The Āʾīn-i Akbarī of Abū al-Faḍl describes the imperial mints and gives the rate of 40 dāms to the rupee, which was used in revenue accounting. The Mughals ran a system of what is sometimes called “free coinage”. Anyone could bring bullion to an imperial mint and have it struck into coin on payment of a charge. Older rupees passed at a discount (baṭṭā) against new ones, and money-changers (sarrāfs) made their living from these differences (Chapter 6). India produced little silver, so the rupee depended on imports. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, very large quantities of silver arrived. Much of it was New World silver brought by European traders, and some came overland and from Persia and Japan. Irfan Habib and others have linked these imports to a rise in prices and to a growing monetisation of the land revenue. The extent and timing of a Mughal “price revolution” remain debated (Habib 1999; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Richards 1993; Moosvi 1987).

Figure 5.5. (a) Silver rupiya of Sher Shāh Sūr (r. 1540–1545), with legends in Arabic script naming the king (left) and giving the Islamic profession of faith (right). (b) Square gold mohur of Akbar (r. 1556–1605), c. 1578–1580; Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Photo: N. Sreedhar (Drnsreedhar), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Mughal rupee became the model for the coins of the successor states and of the East India Company. The Company’s uniform rupee of 1835, of 180 grains, continued the Mughal standard in all but name. Chapter 19 takes up the colonial monetary system.

docs.title: 5.10 The State Mint in the Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The fullest ancient Indian text on the making and control of coin is in Book 2 of the Arthaśāstra, a composite and normative text (Chapter 2). It describes how its authors thought a well-run kingdom should manage money. It is not an account of the Mauryan mint, and no surviving coin series has been shown to follow its rules exactly.

docs.title: 5.10.1 The Lakṣaṇādhyakṣa and the Rūpadarśaka
docs.text:
In Arthaśāstra 2.12, two officers are responsible for coinage. The lakṣaṇādhyakṣa, the “superintendent of marks” (often translated as “master of the mint”), is to have silver coins made of silver with one quarter copper and a small proportion (a māṣa) of one of the hard metals. The denominations are the paṇa, half-paṇa, quarter and eighth. Copper coins, likewise alloyed, come in the māṣaka, half-māṣaka, kākaṇī and half-kākaṇī. The rūpadarśaka, the “examiner of coin”, is to establish which coins are current for trade and which are acceptable at the treasury. The same passage lists charges on coin: a rūpika of eight per cent, a vyājī of five per cent and an examination fee of one-eighth paṇa. It also sets a fine for anyone else who makes, sells, buys or tests coin. The exact meaning of these charges is uncertain. Kangle and Olivelle discuss them, and they may refer to a premium on coin paid into the treasury, a mint charge and a testing fee (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013). The text does not divide these charges further.

Other chapters of Book 2 deal with the same field. They describe the goldsmith’s workshop (akṣaśālā) under the superintendent of gold (2.13). They describe the state goldsmith (sauvarṇika), who works precious metals for townspeople under controls against fraud (2.14). They also describe the testing of gold on the touchstone and the purification and alloying of gold and silver. In Book 4, makers of false coin (kūṭarūpakāraka) are among the “thorns” that secret agents are to detect and punish (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). Weights and the superintendent of weights (pautavādhyakṣa, AŚ 2.19) are treated in Chapter 7.

Note: What the Arthaśāstra rules imply

Read carefully, the rules show a state that wanted coins of fixed alloy and denomination. It wanted coin tested before the treasury accepted it, and it wanted fees for doing so. They do not show a monopoly of coinage in practice. The many non-royal issues of the period, the money-changers of the Pali texts and the city and gaṇa coins all suggest a more plural reality. Nor do they describe anything like a modern central bank: the concern is with the quality of coin and the treasury’s revenue, not with the quantity of money.

docs.title: 5.11 Money in the Texts
docs.text:
Indian thinkers did not write a separate treatise on money. What they thought about it must be gathered from works on statecraft, law and religion. For the Arthaśāstra, the treasury (kośa) is one of the seven constituents (prakṛti) of the state, and the text states plainly that “all undertakings depend on the treasury” (kośapūrvāḥ sarvārambhāḥ, AŚ 2.8.1). Money matters to the Arthaśāstra because it pays for soldiers, officials, works and gifts (Olivelle 2013).

The Dharmaśāstras treat money in the context of law. They set weights and fines (Manu 8.131–137 and the fines that follow), regulate debt and interest, and require the king to fix prices. They rate interest by varṇa and by security, which Chapter 6 discusses (Olivelle 2004; Kane 1930). Buddhist and Jain texts take a moral view of wealth. They also show how ordinary coin had become. The Pali Vinaya sets the threshold of serious theft for a monk at goods worth a pāda, a quarter of a kahāpaṇa (five māsakas), and the Jātaka stories reckon prices, wages and debts in kahāpaṇas as a matter of course (Chakravarti 2002). The texts know that debased and full-weight coins circulate together, and that copper coin depends on official acceptance, but they do not generalise these observations into a theory of money.

The most important monetary institutions of later centuries were not those of the state. They were those of the money-changers and bankers (śreṣṭhin, sarrāf, mahājan). These men tested and exchanged coin, kept deposits and drew hundīs on one another across the subcontinent. Their history belongs to Chapter 6.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the early coins, Allan (1936) remains the standard catalogue, and Gupta (1969) is a concise survey of the whole of Indian coinage. Kosambi (1981) collects Kosambi’s numismatic papers. Bopearachchi (1991) is the reference work for the Indo-Greek series. On the early medieval debate, read Sharma (1987) against Deyell (1990). For the Mughal currency and the silver question, see Habib (1999) and the chapters in Raychaudhuri and Habib (1982). Tomber (2008) and Begley and De Puma (1991) discuss the Roman coins in their archaeological context.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Credit, Banking and Commercial Law
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Lending at interest is attested in India from the later Vedic texts, and the law of debt is the first of the eighteen titles of law in the Manusmṛti. This chapter describes what the Arthaśāstra and the dharmaśāstra actually say about interest, pledges, sureties, deposits and partnership, including the rates graded by varṇa. It then turns to the institutions that handled credit — guilds, temples and monasteries, and professional bankers — and to the hundī, the sarrāf, and the great banking houses of the Mughal and colonial periods: the Jagat Seths, the Marwaris and the Nattukottai Chettiars, their role in revenue farming and state finance, and the colonial banks that grew up beside them. Throughout, it marks where modern categories such as insurance, the joint-stock firm or the central bank fit the evidence and where they do not.

docs.title: 6.1 Debt in Early Texts
docs.text:
The word for debt, ṛṇa, carries a heavy moral load in Indian thought. A well-known passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (6.3.10.5) says that a brāhmaṇa is born owing three debts: study to the seers, sacrifice to the gods and offspring to the ancestors. The doctrine of the “three debts” became a commonplace of later dharmaśāstra and was used to argue for the householder’s life against renunciation (Kane 1930). It is a religious metaphor, not a theory of credit, but it shows how familiar the relation of creditor and debtor was.

Commercial debt appears in the Ṛgveda itself: the gambler’s hymn (Ṛgveda 10.34) describes the indebted gambler who wanders in fear. Later Vedic texts use kusīda for a loan at interest, and the Dharmasūtras (3rd–1st c. BCE on Olivelle’s dating) regulate interest and list moneylending (kusīda) among the livelihoods of the vaiśya (Olivelle 1999). The Manusmṛti (c. 2nd c. CE) includes moneylending in the vaiśya’s occupations (1.90) and forbids brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas to lend at interest except, in distress, at a low rate (10.117) (Olivelle 2004).

Buddhist texts take a practical view of wealth, as the Sigālovāda Sutta’s advice on dividing a householder’s income shows (Section 2.11.1). Gregory Schopen has shown that the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya expects monasteries to lend their permanent endowments at interest, using written contracts with witnesses and pledges (Schopen 2004). Jain merchant communities, whose religion restricts occupations involving violence, were prominent in trade and moneylending from the medieval period onwards (Jaini 1979; Laidlaw 1995).

docs.title: 6.2 The Law of Debt
docs.text: In the Manusmṛti the non-payment of debts (ṛṇādāna) heads the list of eighteen titles of law (8.4), which also includes deposits (nikṣepa), partnership (saṃbhūya-samutthāna), sale by a non-owner, breach of compact and the rescission of sale and purchase. The later smṛtis of Yājñavalkya (c. 4th–5th c. CE), Nārada (c. 5th–6th c. CE), Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana elaborate these titles, and medieval commentaries and digests systematise them (Kane 1930). This is a body of normative law written by brāhmaṇa jurists. How far it governed actual lending is hard to know; the texts themselves repeatedly defer to local and group custom.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Interest Rates
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) opens its chapter on debts (AŚ 3.11) with a scale of monthly interest per hundred paṇas: one and a quarter is “just” (dharmya); five is the commercial rate (vyāvahārika); ten is for those who travel through wild country (kāntāraga); and twenty is for sea-traders (sāmudra). Taking more is punished by a fine, as are the witnesses to the transaction (Olivelle 2013, AŚ 3.11.1–3). The scale is explicitly a scale of risk: the further and more dangerous the journey, the higher the rate.

The Manusmṛti gives a different structure. A lender may take one-eightieth of the principal a month (one and a quarter per cent), a rate it ascribes to Vasiṣṭha; or two per cent, “remembering the conduct of good men”; or a rate graded by the borrower’s varṇa (8.140–142):

Manusmṛti 8.142

dvikaṃ trikaṃ catuṣkaṃ ca pañcakaṃ ca śataṃ samam māsasya vṛddhiṃ gṛhṇīyād varṇānām anupūrvaśaḥ

“He may take two, three, four and five per cent a month, in the order of the varṇas” (Olivelle 2004).

Yājñavalkyasmṛti 2.37–38 combines the two systems. When a pledge is given, interest is one-eightieth a month; otherwise it is two, three, four or five per cent according to varṇa; those who travel through forests pay ten and those who go by sea twenty per cent a month; or borrowers of any caste may pay the interest they have agreed to (Kane 1930). Table 6.1 sets the rates side by side.

Table 6.1. Monthly interest rates in the Arthaśāstra, Manusmṛti and Yājñavalkyasmṛti (per cent of the principal per month) Category AŚ 3.11.1 Manu 8.140–142 Yājñ. 2.37–38 “Just” rate; loan with pledge 1.25 (dharmya) 1.25 (“rule of Vasiṣṭha”) 1.25 (with pledge) “Practice of the good” — 2 — Commercial loans 5 — — Unsecured loans, by varṇa of borrower (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra) — 2, 3, 4, 5 2, 3, 4, 5 Traders through wild country 10 — 10 Sea traders 20 rate fixed by experts (8.157) 20 Rate agreed by the parties — — permitted

A monthly rate of 1.25 per cent is 15 per cent a year; 5 per cent a month is 60 per cent a year. Sources: Olivelle (2013); Olivelle (2004); Kane (1930).

Two features deserve comment. First, the varṇa-graded scale charges higher rates to borrowers of lower rank. Commentators explain it as a matter of risk and trustworthiness; whatever its rationale, it wrote into law a hierarchy in which the śūdra borrower paid two and a half times as much as the brāhmaṇa. Second, the very high rates for sea and forest trade are a recognition of risk, but the texts do not say whether the lender lost his claim if the ship or caravan was lost, as he did in the Greek and Roman maritime loan. For sea voyages Manu (8.157) leaves the rate to those expert in voyages, place and time — in effect to merchant custom. The best-documented loan connected with the India trade is in fact Greek: the second-century Muziris papyrus preserves part of a loan agreement and the valuation of a cargo shipped from Muziris on the Malabar coast to Egypt (De Romanis 2020). Sea loans and the law of the sea are discussed further in Chapters 11 and 15.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Limits on Accumulation and Kinds of Interest
docs.text:
The texts limit the total that can be recovered. Manu (8.151) rules that interest on money received at one time may not exceed the principal (so that the total due is at most double, the dvaiguṇya rule), and that for grain, fruit, wool and draught animals the total may not exceed five times the principal. Yājñavalkya (2.39) sets different maximum multiples for gold, grain, cloth and liquids, and includes the offspring of animals and of slave women among things that could be claimed as increase — a reminder of how far property in persons was part of this law (Olivelle 2004; Kane 1930).

Later jurists, especially Nārada and Bṛhaspati, classify interest. As summarised by Kane, the main kinds are periodic interest (kālikā); “bodily” interest (kāyikā), paid in labour or through the use of a pledged animal; compound interest (cakravṛddhi), interest on interest; interest stipulated by the debtor himself (kāritā), often in an emergency; and, in Bṛhaspati, a daily interest that “grows like a tuft” (śikhāvṛddhi) and the use of a pledge in lieu of interest (bhogalābha). Manu (8.153) disapproves of some of these, and the commentators differ on the exact meaning of each term (Kane 1930). Compound interest was thus disapproved of and limited rather than simply forbidden.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Pledges, Sureties and Written Contracts
docs.text:
Security for a loan took the form of a pledge (ādhi) or a surety (pratibhū). The smṛtis distinguish a pledge to be kept (gopya), which the creditor must not use, from a pledge to be enjoyed (bhogya), such as land or a house whose produce or rent stands in place of interest; they also regulate the loss or damage of a pledge. Yājñavalkya (2.53) distinguishes sureties for appearance, for good faith and for payment, and specifies when each surety, or his sons, must make good the debt (Kane 1930).

Written documents (lekhya) are treated at length in Yājñavalkya and Nārada as one of the three means of proof, alongside witnesses and possession.
