A debt document was to state the names of the parties, the amount, the interest, the date and the witnesses, and to be written by the debtor or by a scribe in his presence (Kane 1930). Buddhist Vinaya texts and later inscriptions confirm that written loan contracts were used in practice (Schopen 2004).

docs.title: 6.2.4 Model Documents: The Lekhapaddhati
docs.text: The fullest evidence for how such documents were actually drawn up comes from western India. The Lekhapaddhati (“method of writing documents”) is a Gujarati formulary: a collection of model documents in Sanskrit, with many Old Gujarati words, compiled for the use of scribes. Most of its dated specimens belong to the Caulukya and Vāghelā kingdoms of the thirteenth century. Alongside forms for royal grants, appointments and treaties, it gives models of private documents: deeds of sale and mortgage of land and houses, loan bonds, receipts, deposits, agreements between partners, and deeds for the sale of slave women (Section 18.13). The deeds name the parties, the sum, the rate of interest, the security, the guarantors and the witnesses, and they distinguish pledges whose produce the creditor enjoys from those he must merely keep, the distinction the smṛtis draw between bhogya and gopya pledges. The formulary was first edited in the Gaekwad’s Oriental Series in 1925, and Pushpa Prasad has edited and translated it with a full commentary (Prasad 2007). It shows that the categories of the law books were the working vocabulary of local scribes and merchants, and it is one of the very few bodies of evidence for ordinary commercial contracts in India before the Mughal period.

docs.title: 6.2.5 Recovery and its Harshness
docs.text: The law of recovery was severe. Manu (8.49) allows a creditor to recover his money by persuasion, by legal suit, by stratagem, by customary pressure and by force. A debtor of the same or lower caste who could not pay might be made to work off the debt, while a debtor of higher caste was to pay by instalments (8.177). Nārada’s list of the kinds of slave includes a person whose debts a master had paid. The smṛtis also make sons and grandsons liable for an ancestor’s debts — the “pious obligation”, which became an important doctrine of Anglo-Hindu law under colonial rule (Kane 1930; Olivelle 2004). These rules show the lending relationship as one of power as well as contract, and they should be read alongside the ceilings on interest.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Deposits
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra chapter on deposits (AŚ 3.12) deals with the open deposit (upanidhi), the pledge, and related transactions such as the ādeśa, an order to deliver something to a third person, and the anvādhi, a thing sent through an intermediary (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). The depositee was liable for loss caused by his own fault but not, in general, for loss by fire, flood, theft by others or the king’s action. The smṛtis treat the sealed or closed deposit (nikṣepa) and the open deposit similarly (Kane 1930).

The ādeśa resembles an order to pay, but the texts are too brief to treat it as a negotiable instrument: these are rules about bailment and agency between private persons, and the Arthaśāstra does not describe a deposit bank.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Partnership
docs.text:
“Undertaking together” (saṃbhūya-samutthāna) is the dharmaśāstra title for partnership. Manu’s section under this title is chiefly about how priests who perform a sacrifice jointly should share the fee (8.206–211). Yājñavalkya (2.259–265) and Nārada give general rules for merchants who trade jointly: profit and loss are shared in proportion to each partner’s contribution or as agreed; a partner who acts against the others’ instructions or through negligence bears the loss he causes; and one who saves the common property from a calamity caused by fate or the king receives a tenth of what he saves. The same rules are extended to farmers, artisans and others who work together (Kane 1930). The Arthaśāstra similarly provides that guild workers and partners divide their earnings as agreed or equally (AŚ 3.14) (Olivelle 2013).

These are rules for partnerships of persons who share profit and loss; the texts know no partner of limited liability and nothing resembling a joint-stock company. For the organisation of maritime ventures, the best documentary evidence comes from outside the Sanskrit tradition: the Cairo Geniza letters show Jewish merchants trading with India in the eleventh and twelfth centuries through formal partnerships and commenda-type agreements, often with Indian associates (Goitein and Friedman 2008).

docs.title: 6.4.1 Guilds as Trustees
docs.text: The earliest institutional lenders and borrowers we can document are the guilds that received permanent endowments, of which Uṣavadāta’s deposits with the weavers of Govardhana at Nasik are the best known (Section 4.5.1). The guilds evidently used the capital in their business; the inscriptions do not show them lending to the public.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Monasteries and Temples
docs.text:
Buddhist monasteries held permanent endowments and, according to the Vinaya evidence, lent them at interest (Schopen 2004; Ray 1986). In south India, temple inscriptions of the Pallava, Chola and later periods record a great many endowments in money, land and livestock. A typical endowment for a perpetual lamp (Tamil nantā viḷakku) gave a flock of sheep or a herd of cows to shepherds, who supplied ghee to the temple. Money endowments were often lent to village assemblies (sabhā, ūr), which paid interest in paddy or coin to the temple. Inscriptions of the great temple at Thanjavur under Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014) record such investments with many villages. The temple thus acted as a channel through which royal and private wealth was lent into the agrarian economy (Hall 1980; Nilakanta Sastri 1955). The temple and other religious institutions as economic actors are examined more fully in Chapter 9.

These arrangements were real and widespread, but they were endowment management rather than banking in the modern sense; the temple did not take deposits from the public or issue instruments.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Sarrāfs and Mahājans
docs.text:
From the Sultanate period onward the sources describe a professional class of bankers and money-changers, called sarrāf (from Arabic ṣarrāf, anglicised as “shroff”), mahājan, sāhūkār or seṭh. Their basic function arose from the monetary system: in Mughal India coins of different mints, years and weights circulated together, and the sarrāf assayed coins and charged a discount on worn or older ones. On this base they built deposit-taking, lending to merchants, nobles and the state, the remittance of revenue and trade payments by hundī, and the discounting of bills (Habib 1964; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

Banking was concentrated in particular communities: Gujarati vāṇiyās (Hindu and Jain), Marwaris, Khatris, the Multanis and Shikarpuris of the north-west, and in the south the Chettiars and Komatis. Indian bankers were also active abroad: Multani and Khatri moneylenders worked across Iran and Central Asia as far as Astrakhan in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Dale 1994; Levi 2002). In the ports, the sarrāfs of Surat lent to Indian merchants and to the English and Dutch companies (Das Gupta 1979; Subramanian 1996). Habib’s study of usury in Mughal India also shows the harsher side of the same system, the indebtedness of peasants to rural moneylenders (Habib 1964).

docs.title: 6.5.2 The Hundī
docs.text:
The hundī was a written order, usually in a regional mercantile script, by which one banker or merchant directed another to pay a sum to a third party. It served three purposes: to remit money between places without moving coin, to give credit (a hundī payable after a period could be sold at a discount), and to settle accounts between correspondents. The Mughal treasury used hundīs to remit revenue from the provinces, and the European companies used them for their inland payments (Habib 1964; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

Table 6.2. Common kinds of hundī as described in the early twentieth century Kind Description Darśanī Payable on sight (on presentation) Muddatī Payable after a stated period; could be discounted Śāh-jog Payable to a śāh, a respectable person known in the market, which gave some assurance about the holder Dhanī-jog Payable to the named payee Firmān-jog Payable to order Jokhamī Drawn against goods in transit and payable only if the goods arrived safely

Source: Jain (1929). Names and forms varied by region.

A merchant in one city paid cash to a local banker, who drew a hundī on his correspondent in another city; the payee presented it there and was paid, and the two bankers settled between themselves periodically (Figure 6.1). The cost of the hundī — its rate of exchange or discount — varied with distance, season and the supply of money at each place, and the rates themselves were an index of commercial conditions. The system rested on correspondent relations within communities and on reputation: a banker who dishonoured a hundī risked exclusion from the network (Jain 1929; Habib 1964).

Figure 6.1. How a hundī remitted money between two cities without moving coin (schematic). Blue arrows carry cash, orange arrows the written order; the two bankers settled between themselves periodically.

The jokhamī hundī combined remittance with a contingency: if the goods were lost, the bill was not paid. In the seventeenth century the Mughal sources and European observers also describe bīma, the underwriting of goods and ships against loss for a premium, by bankers in the major commercial centres (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). This is genuine evidence of insurance practice, and it belongs to early modern India.

Debate: How old is the hundī?

Whether the hundī is older than the European bill of exchange (the Italian lettera di cambio) cannot be shown. The instrument is well documented only from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, through Mughal-period Persian and European records (Habib 1964); attempts to trace it to the ādeśa of the Arthaśāstra or to early medieval texts rest on uncertain interpretations. Instruments for transferring money by written order existed in several societies: the suftaja of the Abbasid world, the Chinese “flying money” (feiqian) of the Tang period, and the bills of exchange of Italian merchants from the thirteenth century. The hundī belongs to this wider family; questions of priority cannot be settled and are not very illuminating.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Remittance, Revenue and the Shroff
docs.text:
The two basic kinds of hundī in Table 6.2 served different purposes. A darśanī or sight bill was chiefly an instrument of remittance: it moved purchasing power from one city to another, and its price expressed the cost of that movement. A muddatī or usance bill, payable after a stated number of days, was also an instrument of credit. A merchant who bought goods could pay with a bill falling due after the goods had been sold, and the seller could obtain cash at once by selling the bill to a shroff at a discount. The discount combined interest for the term of the bill with the cost of remittance, so that the hundī market joined the market for short-term credit to the market for exchange between places (Jain 1929).

Habib’s study of the Mughal evidence shows how far the state depended on this system. Revenue collected in the provinces was remitted to the imperial treasury by bill, and jāgīrdārs whose assignments lay far from where they served had their revenue sent to them in the same way. Nobles and officials kept deposits with sarrāfs and borrowed from them against expected revenue; the European companies raised money for their inland purchases by selling bills drawn on their coastal factories. Because bullion entered India mainly at the ports and moved inland with trade, the rates for bills between the ports and the interior moved with the seasons of trade and the arrival of the treasure ships (Habib 1964; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). Remittance by bill was, in normal times, cheaper and safer than carrying coin over long distances.

L. C. Jain’s survey, written when the system was still in full use, shows the shroff of the early twentieth century performing the same functions within the colonial economy. Indigenous bankers remitted funds for trade, financed the movement of crops from the villages to the markets and ports, and dealt in bills whose rates rose in the busy season after the harvest and fell in the slack season. Their rates were generally above those of the joint-stock banks, and the two markets were connected mainly through the rediscounting of hundīs (Jain 1929).

docs.title: 6.6.1 The Jagat Seths of Murshidabad
docs.text:
The most powerful banking house of eighteenth-century India was that of the Jagat Seths of Murshidabad. The firm was founded by Hiranand Sahu, an Oswal Jain from Marwar, who settled at Patna in the later seventeenth century. His son Manikchand followed the Mughal dīwān Murshid Quli Khan to Murshidabad, and Manikchand’s successor Fatehchand received the title Jagat Seṭh (“banker of the world”) from the emperor Muhammad Shah in the early 1720s. The house handled the remittance of Bengal’s revenue to Delhi, dominated the Murshidabad mint, lent to the Nawabs and to the English, Dutch and French companies, and had branches in many cities (Leonard 1979; Chaudhuri 1978; Prakash 1985). Figure 6.2 shows the family’s house near Murshidabad.

Figure 6.2. The house of the Jagat Seths at Mahimapur, near Murshidabad, now a museum. Photo: Gautam Tarafder, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Jagat Seth Mahtab Rai and his cousin Swarup Chand were among the Bengal notables who supported the English against Siraj-ud-Daula in 1757. The alliance did not protect them: both were put to death in 1763 on the orders of Mir Qasim, and the house declined as the East India Company took over the revenue and its remittance.

Debate: The “great firm” theory

Karen Leonard proposed that the great Indian banking firms, by shifting their credit and support from the Mughal centre to regional rulers and to the European companies between about 1650 and 1750, contributed decisively to the collapse of the Mughal empire (Leonard 1979). The thesis drew attention to the political importance of bankers, but it has been criticised: J. F. Richards argued that the Mughal fiscal system did not depend on bankers’ credit to the extent the theory requires (Richards 1981), and other historians see the bankers as adapting to political change rather than causing it. Bayly’s study of north Indian merchants and bankers shows them as resilient intermediaries in the transition to British rule (Bayly 1983). The theory is best treated as a debated interpretation.

docs.title: 6.6.2 Bankers, Revenue Farming and “Portfolio Capitalists”
docs.text:
The bankers’ most profitable business with the state was the revenue itself. In the eighteenth century the successor states of the Mughal empire and the Marathas relied increasingly on revenue farming (ijāra): the right to collect the land revenue of a district was granted for a term to a contractor who promised a fixed sum. Bankers advanced that sum to the treasury, stood surety for the farmers, or took up farms themselves, recovering their money with interest from the collections. Bayly’s study of north India shows bankers in Banaras, Lucknow and other towns financing the revenue of regional rulers, remitting tribute to the East India Company, and supplying the armies of both, so that commercial credit and state finance became closely interlocked (Bayly 1983).

Sanjay Subrahmanyam and C. A. Bayly have called the men who combined these roles “portfolio capitalists”: entrepreneurs who spread their capital across revenue farming, trade, money-lending, military supply and, in some cases, overseas shipping, and who moved between them as opportunity and political risk dictated. They trace the type from the south Indian magnates of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (Chapter 18) to the eighteenth century, and suggest that the East India Company itself rose to power by drawing on the same combination of trade, revenue and armed force, and on the same Indian creditors (Subrahmanyam and Bayly 1988). The concept widens Leonard’s argument: bankers were not a separate class that chose between rulers from outside, but part of a broader group of intermediaries whose investments in revenue gave them a direct stake in state formation. The price of this involvement was exposure to political violence, as the fate of the Jagat Seths in 1763 showed.

docs.title: 6.6.3 The Marwaris
docs.text: The Marwaris — trading and banking castes, mostly Agarwal, Maheshwari and Oswal, from western Rajasthan — spread across northern and eastern India from the seventeenth century as bankers to courts and armies and as traders. Under British rule they became the leading indigenous financiers of Calcutta’s trade, acting as brokers and baniyās to European firms and speculating in commodities, and in the twentieth century some families moved into industry. Timberg’s study traces this movement from trade to industry and emphasises the role of family firms, caste networks and credit among community members (Timberg 1978).

docs.title: 6.6.4 The Nattukottai Chettiars
docs.text:
The Nattukottai Chettiars (Nakarattār) of Chettinad in Tamil Nadu were a banking caste whose firms, organised through a system of agents and of deposits among caste members, financed trade and agriculture across southern India, Ceylon, Burma, Malaya and French Indochina in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In Lower Burma their loans financed the expansion of rice cultivation; when the depression of the 1930s caused widespread default, large areas of land passed into Chettiar hands, provoking hostility that culminated in post-independence Burmese legislation against them. Their caste institutions, including temple organisations, served to pool capital and enforce obligations (Rudner 1994; Ray 1995).

The Chettiars’ expansion followed the British empire across the Bay of Bengal. They were lending in Ceylon in the first half of the nineteenth century; after the annexation of Lower Burma in 1852 and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, which together turned the Irrawaddy delta into one of the world’s great rice-exporting regions, Burma became their largest field. Branches followed in Penang, Singapore and the Malay states, in Saigon and in Sumatra. Typically a firm’s capital and its partners remained in Chettinad, while its overseas branches were run by agents, often young men of the community, who served for a fixed term of a few years on a salary and a share of the profits before returning home (Rudner 1994).

David Rudner’s study explains how the system was held together. A firm worked with its partners’ own capital, with deposits from other Nakarattār firms and from members of the community, including funds held for women and minors, and with endowments managed for temples. Firms lent to one another, kept running accounts with one another across the network, and settled disputes within the caste rather than in the courts. Kinship, marriage and membership of the community’s clan temples defined who could be trusted and who could be excluded. Rudner argues that caste here was not an obstacle to capitalism but the form in which a sophisticated banking system was organised: its rules of membership and reputation did the work that, in European banking, was done by corporate law and regulation (Rudner 1994).

The Chettiars also stood between the colonial banks and Asian borrowers. In Rangoon, Colombo and Singapore they borrowed from the exchange banks and the presidency banks, usually on hundīs, and lent onward to cultivators, shopkeepers, rice millers and landlords whom the European banks would not serve. Their capital was therefore partly European capital, and when the depression of the 1930s cut off credit at the top, the pressure passed down to the debtor in the village (Ray 1995; Rudner 1994). The political consequences in Burma, and the later history of the community, are discussed in Chapters 19 and 21.

docs.title: 6.7 Account Books and Commercial Arithmetic
docs.text:
Indian merchants and bankers kept accounts in bound ledgers known as bahī-khātā, written in mercantile scripts such as Mahājanī. A firm kept a day book of all transactions, a cash book and a ledger with an account for each customer, in which receipts were entered on the credit side (jamā) and payments on the debit side (nāme or udhār). In many communities new account books are still ceremonially opened at Dīvālī with worship of Lakṣmī. The system allowed bankers to trace large numbers of hundīs and current accounts across correspondent networks (Jain 1929; Timberg 1978).

The books themselves had a characteristic form. They were long, narrow volumes of unruled paper, folded lengthwise, bound in red cloth and tied with string, and they opened with an invocation — śrī, the name of Gaṇeśa or Lakṣmī, a svastika or the words śubh lābh (“auspicious profit”). Entries were written in columns with the sums in a separate column to the right, and the accounts were balanced and carried forward at the end of the commercial year. In western India the new books are opened at Dīvālī with a worship of the account books (Gujarati copḍā pūjan); in Bengal the traders’ new year, on the first day of Baiśākh, is marked by the opening of a new ledger (hāl khātā), at which customers are invited to settle their dues and are offered sweets. The scripts in which the books were kept, Mahājanī, Laṇḍā and their relatives, wrote vowels sparingly or not at all, which made them quick to write and difficult for outsiders to read; the scripts of commerce are described in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā. A large firm employed a head clerk or manager (munīm), who kept the books, conducted correspondence and often managed a branch on the proprietor’s behalf; the munīm was frequently of the same community as his employer and might later set up on his own.

Village and state accounts formed a parallel tradition. In most regions each village had a hereditary accountant — the paṭvārī of north India, the kulkarṇī of Maharashtra, the karṇam of the Telugu and Tamil country — who kept the records of holdings, crops and revenue, and above him the district registrars (qānūngos in the Mughal system, deshpāṇḍes in the Deccan). Revenue accounts at the higher levels of the Mughal and successor administrations were kept in Persian, using a special numerical notation (siyāq) described in Volume 11, Gaṇita; the Maratha administration kept its own very large archive in Marathi (Chapter 18). The colonial state took over these village officers and their records, standardised them, and made the paṭvārī’s papers the basis of the record of rights in land.

Whether bahī-khātā constitutes double-entry bookkeeping, and whether it is older than the Italian system described by Luca Pacioli in 1494, has been debated. Most descriptions come from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and few dated early account books have been studied, so claims of priority cannot be tested. B. M. Lall Nigam has argued that bahī-khātā is a complete double-entry system and older than Pacioli (Lall Nigam 1986), a claim that drew a critical comment from C. W. Nobes (Nobes 1987); the first part of the claim concerns the logic of the books and can be examined, the second cannot be demonstrated without dated early account books. It is safer to say that India had a well-developed indigenous system of mercantile accounting whose history remains to be written.

Indian mathematical texts include many commercial problems. Mahāvīra’s Gaṇita­sāra­saṃgraha (c. 850 CE) and Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī (1150 CE) contain problems on simple and compound interest, partnership shares, mixtures and the price of goods, which reflect the arithmetic merchants needed. The mathematics is treated in Volume 11, Gaṇita.

docs.title: 6.8 Colonial Change
docs.text: Colonial rule changed the setting of Indian finance without abolishing indigenous banking. The Company’s assumption of the revenue of Bengal after 1765 removed the bankers’ most profitable business there, and the Company’s own treasuries took over much of the remittance of public funds that the great houses had handled.

docs.title: 6.8.1 The Colonial Banking Framework
docs.text:
The first European-style banks in India were founded by the agency houses of Calcutta in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and most of them failed with their parent houses in the commercial crisis of the early 1830s. More durable were the presidency banks — the Bank of Calcutta (1806, renamed the Bank of Bengal in 1809), the Bank of Bombay (1840) and the Bank of Madras (1843) — in which the government held shares and appointed directors. They kept the government’s balances and lent mainly to European firms and against government securities; their right to issue notes ended when the government took over the paper currency under the Act of 1861. The three were merged in 1921 as the Imperial Bank of India. Foreign trade was financed by exchange banks with headquarters in London or the East, such as the Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China (1853) and the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (1865) (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

Indian joint-stock banking grew later. The Punjab National Bank, founded at Lahore in 1894 by Indian promoters, was followed in the swadeshi years by several others (Chapter 19, Section 19.14), but many small banks failed in a wave of crises from 1913, which made depositors cautious for a generation. For the countryside the government turned to co-operation: the Co-operative Credit Societies Act of 1904 provided for village credit societies, intended to free cultivators from the moneylender. The Reserve Bank of India, recommended by the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance of 1926, began work in 1935 as the central bank, issuing the currency and holding the reserves of the banking system. Statute law replaced the dharmaśāstra and custom in commercial matters (Roy and Swamy 2016): the Indian Contract Act (1872) and the Negotiable Instruments Act (1881), the latter saving local usage for instruments in an Indian language, such as the hundī.

docs.title: 6.8.2 The Bazaar and the Banks
docs.text:
Rajat Kanta Ray has argued that the result was a two-tier structure, in which European banks and firms controlled the upper levels of finance while an Indian “bazaar” economy of sarrāfs, Marwaris and Chettiars, linked to it through the discounting of hundīs, continued to finance internal trade and agriculture until well into the twentieth century (Ray 1995). The link was concrete: the presidency banks, and later the Imperial Bank, discounted hundīs bearing the names of shroffs whom they accepted as creditworthy, and the shroffs re-lent the funds in the bazaar at higher rates (Ray 1995; Jain 1929). Rural indebtedness to moneylenders became a major colonial concern, leading to legislation such as the Deccan Agriculturists’ Relief Act of 1879 and to the banking enquiry committees of 1929–31. After 1935 the Reserve Bank tried to bring indigenous bankers into a regulated system, but most were unwilling to give up their trading business or to submit their accounts to inspection, and the attempt had little success (Chapter 21). These developments, and the wider debate on the colonial economy, are discussed in Chapter 19.

Cross-Reference: Related chapters

For coinage and money-changing see Chapter 5; for market regulation, weights and prices see Chapter 7; for sea loans, port law and the law of the sea see Chapter 15; for merchant communities in the Mughal period see Chapter 18.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the law of debt, deposits and partnership in the dharmaśāstra, Kane (1930) remains the standard survey; the primary texts are available in Olivelle (2004) and Olivelle (2013). Schopen (2004) studies Buddhist monastic lending. For the medieval and Mughal periods see Habib (1964) and Raychaudhuri and Habib (1982); for indigenous banking in the colonial period Jain (1929), Timberg (1978), Rudner (1994) and Ray (1995); and for the debate on bankers and the Mughal state Leonard (1979), Bayly (1983) and Subrahmanyam and Bayly (1988).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Markets, Prices, Weights and Regulation
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter examines how markets were described and regulated in early and early medieval South Asia. It begins with the evidence for markets in Pali, Sanskrit and Tamil literature, in Greek accounts and in inscriptions. It then turns to the market officials of the Arthaśāstra: the superintendent of trade (paṇyādhyakṣa), the superintendent of markets (saṃsthādhyakṣa), the superintendent of weights and measures (pautavādhyakṣa) and the superintendent of customs (śulkādhyakṣa). It discusses price fixing and permitted profit margins, standard weights and measures, rules against fraud and adulteration, tolls and customs, measures against scarcity and famine, and the settlement of market disputes, and ends by placing Indian ideas of a regulated price in a comparative historical frame.

Markets appear in South Asian sources in two very different lights. In poetry, narrative and travellers’ accounts they are crowded, noisy places full of goods from distant lands. In the normative literature, above all the Arthaśāstra and the dharmaśāstras, they are objects of supervision: places where prices must be fixed, weights checked, goods taxed and cheats punished. Both pictures are partial. The poets idealise abundance; the treatises describe what a king’s officials ought to do, not what they did. Used together, and with the evidence of inscriptions and archaeology, they show a long tradition in which rulers claimed the right to regulate exchange and merchants and their associations largely governed it in practice. The Arthaśāstra itself, its date and its revenue system are introduced in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 7.1.1 Vocabulary
docs.text: Sanskrit and Pali have a rich vocabulary for places of exchange. An āpaṇa is a shop or stall; a vīthi a street, often a street of shops; paṇya means goods for sale, and the Arthaśāstra calls the market paṇyasaṃsthā, the place where goods are set out. The Pali texts speak of the antarāpaṇa, the market street or bazaar inside a town. A nigama (Pali nigama) is a market town and, in some contexts, a body of merchants: copper coins of early Taxila bear the legend negama, probably referring to such a body (Allan 1936). A paṭṭana is a port or trading town. In the inscriptions of the early medieval period two further terms become common: the haṭṭa, a market, often periodic, and the maṇḍapikā, a market centre where tolls were collected (Gopal 1965; Chattopadhyaya 1994). These words do not form a fixed hierarchy; their meanings shifted between regions and periods.

docs.title: 7.1.2 Pali, Sanskrit and Tamil Literature
docs.text:
The Pali canon and the Jātaka stories are full of merchants, caravan leaders and market scenes. The Bāveru Jātaka, for example, tells of merchants who took a crow and then a peacock to the land of Bāveru, usually identified with Babylon, and sold them there for high prices. Such stories are valuable for the social world they reflect, but they must be dated with care: the verses of the Jātakas are older than the prose stories, which reached their present form in the commentary of about the fifth century CE (Chakravarti 2002). The Sanskrit epics and later kāvya describe the markets of royal cities in conventional images of plenty, with shops of jewels, perfumes and cloth.

The most vivid early descriptions of markets come from Tamil poetry of the early centuries CE. The Maturaikkāñci, one of the long poems of the Pattuppāṭṭu anthology, describes Madurai with two markets, a day market (nāḷaṅkāṭi) and an evening or night market (allaṅkāṭi), crowded with traders and goods. The Paṭṭiṉappālai’s picture of the Chola port of Pūmpuhār, with its customs officers stamping goods with the tiger emblem, is described in Section 15.2.5. These are poems, not inventories, and their catalogues of goods serve the praise of a king; but they show markets and customs procedures that the poets expected their audiences to recognise.

docs.title: 7.1.3 Greek Accounts and Archaeology
docs.text:
Megasthenes, who visited the Maurya court around 300 BCE, described the administration of the capital, Pāṭaliputra, in a passage preserved in Strabo’s Geography (15.1.50–51). According to this account, the city officials were organised in six boards of five members. One board supervised the crafts, one looked after foreigners, one registered births and deaths, one had charge of trade and commerce, including measures and the sale of produce by public notice, one supervised the sale of manufactured goods, keeping new goods separate from old, and the sixth collected a tenth of the price of goods sold, fraud in this tax being punished with death (McCrindle 1877). Megasthenes’ work survives only in fragments quoted by later authors, and parts of it are unreliable; but the passage shows that a foreign observer saw the city’s markets as closely supervised.

Archaeology shows the physical setting of urban trade. At Sirkap, the Indo-Greek and later city at Taxila, the main street was lined with shops and small buildings, a layout that recalls later bazaar streets. Excavations at early historic cities of the Ganga valley and the Deccan have produced workshops, storage jars and coin moulds that testify to urban production and exchange (Thapar 2002). Archaeology rarely allows a market as such to be identified, however, and claims that particular excavated buildings were customs houses or regulated market halls go beyond the evidence.

docs.title: 7.2 The Market Officials of the Arthaśāstra
7.2.1 The Superintendent of Trade
docs.text:
The paṇyādhyakṣa, the superintendent of trade (AŚ 2.16), is above all a manager of the state’s own goods. He must know the differences in price between goods of high and low value and whether they are in demand; whether goods are produced on land or in water and brought by land or water routes; and the right time to disperse or concentrate stocks, to buy and to sell. Goods produced on the king’s own land are to be sold through a single channel (ekamukha), and goods from foreign lands through many. Both are to be sold in a way that benefits the subjects, and he is to forbid even a large profit if it would harm them. He should not impose time restrictions on goods in constant demand or cause a glut. State goods may also be sold by private traders at fixed prices, the traders making good any loss (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013).

The same chapter encourages foreign trade. Ship captains and caravan leaders who bring foreign goods are to be granted exemptions that will encourage them to return, and, as the passage is usually read, foreign merchants are to be protected from lawsuits over money except where they are members of local associations or partners. For ventures abroad, the superintendent is to calculate the value of the goods sent out and of those brought back, deducting customs, road cess, escort charges, dues at pickets and ferries, food and fodder, and the share due to the foreign ruler, to see whether a profit remains; if not, he should consider whether the trade would bring some other advantage (AŚ 2.16). This is the closest the text comes to an analysis of the profitability of trade, and it is notable for its attention to transaction costs. It is not a theory of comparative advantage.

docs.title: 7.2.2 The Superintendent of Markets
docs.text:
Private trade in the market is the concern of a different official, the saṃsthādhyakṣa or superintendent of markets, who appears in Book 4 in the chapter on protection against traders (AŚ 4.2). His first duty is to ensure that old goods are sold or pledged in the market only by those who can show good title to them, a rule aimed at the sale of stolen goods. He inspects weights and measures, fixes prices and margins (Section 7.3), and punishes collusion, adulteration and deception (Section 7.5). The heading of the chapter is revealing: traders are listed among the “thorns” from whom the people must be protected, alongside fraudulent artisans and other wrongdoers. The Arthaśāstra values trade, but it regards traders with suspicion: a verse in the preceding chapter groups traders with artisans, actors, mendicants and tricksters as “thieves not called thieves” from whom the country must be protected (AŚ 4.1).

The city superintendent (nāgarika, AŚ 2.36) and the superintendents of weights and of customs completed the market administration. How far these offices existed in any actual kingdom is unknown. The chapter’s value lies in showing what problems an administrator expected to face in a market: theft, false measures, collusion, adulteration and the evasion of tolls.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Price Fixing in the Arthaśāstra and the Law Books
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on traders sets out a procedure for fixing prices. The superintendent of markets is to set the price of goods after calculating the outlay on them, the customs paid, interest, hire and other expenses. Over the permitted purchase price, traders are allowed a margin of five per cent on local goods and ten per cent on foreign goods; those who raise the price beyond this, or buy or sell at improper rates, are fined. Traders who combine to hold back goods or to sell or buy at improper prices are fined 1,000 paṇas. When there is a glut of a commodity, the superintendent may sell it through a single channel until the stock is cleared, other traders selling it under his control (AŚ 4.2) (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013). Table 7.1 summarises these and related provisions.

Table 7.1. Provisions on prices and supply in the Arthaśāstra and Manu (references to chapter level; numbers as generally read) Provision Source Substance Management of state goods AŚ 2.16 State goods sold through one channel, foreign goods through many; no profit harmful to subjects; no glut or artificial restriction Calculation of trade ventures AŚ 2.16 Profit assessed after customs, cess, escort and other costs Fixing of price AŚ 4.2 Price set after accounting for outlay, customs, interest, hire and expenses Permitted margin AŚ 4.2 5 per cent on local, 10 per cent on foreign goods, over the permitted purchase price Collusion among traders AŚ 4.2 Fine of 1,000 paṇas for jointly holding back goods or trading at improper prices Glut AŚ 4.2 Sale through a single channel under the superintendent Grain reserve AŚ 2.15 Half of the stock in the granary kept for times of distress Royal price fixing Manu 8.401–402 King fixes prices every five nights or every fortnight, considering import, export, storage, profit and loss

The Mānava Dharmaśāstra prescribes a similar royal role. After considering the cost of bringing goods in and sending them out, the time they have been stored, and the likely profit and loss, the king is to fix the prices at which all goods are bought and sold, doing so in the presence of experts every five nights or every fortnight (Manu 8.401–402) (Olivelle 2004). Neither text describes a free market in which prices are left to bargaining; both assume that a legitimate price can be determined by authority from costs, and that profit beyond a customary margin is suspect. How often such price fixing took place, and how it could have been enforced in the many markets of a large kingdom, the texts do not say. In practice, as later evidence shows, prices in South Asian markets were set by bargaining, by merchant associations and by local custom far more often than by royal officials.

docs.title: 7.3.2 “Just Price” in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s rules are sometimes described as a doctrine of the “just price”, a phrase borrowed from medieval European thought. Sanskrit texts speak of argha, the price or value of a commodity, and of the fixing of prices (arghasaṃsthāpana); they do not develop a theory of a just price as such.

Administered prices and limits on profit were, moreover, common in pre-modern states, and no priority can be claimed for any one tradition. Classical Athens appointed market officials (agoranomoi) to supervise sales, and grain wardens to control the price of grain. The Roman emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for hundreds of goods and services in 301 CE. Medieval Christian scholastics, including Thomas Aquinas, discussed whether it was lawful to sell a thing for more than it was worth, and later scholastics often identified the just price with the common estimate of the market. Islamic law developed the institution of ḥisba, the supervision of markets by the muḥtasib, who checked weights and measures and punished fraud, while jurists debated whether rulers might fix prices at all. Indian rules belong in this comparative company: they share the common concern with scarcity, hoarding and fraud, and they are distinctive mainly in the precision of the Arthaśāstra’s cost-based calculation.

The best documented attempt at price control in South Asian history comes much later: the market regulations that the Delhi sultan ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (r. 1296–1316) imposed from about 1303, known from Ẓiyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī’s partisan account, whose aims were military and fiscal (Section 18.2.2).

docs.title: 7.4.1 Harappan Weights
docs.text:
Standard weights are among the oldest evidence for regulated exchange in South Asia. The cities of the mature Harappan civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) used carefully made cubical weights, mostly of chert (Figure 7.1), in a series that doubles from the smallest unit (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) and then continues in decimal multiples; the most common weight, of about 13.7 grams, corresponds to sixteen units (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The uniformity of these weights across a very large area suggests some common authority or convention, though who maintained it is unknown. Similarities with later Indian weight systems exist, notably in the use of sixteen-fold divisions, but continuity across the long interval between them has not been demonstrated. The Harappan evidence is discussed further in Chapter 11.

Figure 7.1. Three cubical chert weights from Mohenjo-daro, mature Harappan period (c. 2600–1900 BCE); Ashmolean Museum, Oxford. Photo: Zunkir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.4.2 The Pautavādhyakṣa
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra gives the superintendent of weights and measures (pautavādhyakṣa) a workshop for making standard weights and measures (AŚ 2.19). Weights were to be made of iron, or of stone from Magadha or Mekala, or of other materials that do not swell with moisture or shrink with heat. Balances of various sizes are described. Weights and measures in use were to be stamped by the superintendent every four months, traders paying a small daily fee for the service; using an unstamped weight incurred a fine, generally read as 27¼ paṇas.

Two features of the system deserve notice. First, the text distinguishes between measures used for different purposes: the measure for receiving revenue, the measure for trade, and progressively smaller measures for paying out rations to servants and to the palace. The arrangement favoured the treasury, which received by a larger measure than it paid out. Second, separate scales were used for gold, silver and diamonds, reflecting the needs of the treasury, the goldsmiths and the mint. Table 7.2 gives the main units. Their modern equivalents are uncertain, since they depend on the weight assumed for the seeds that formed the base units; figures in modern writings vary and are not given here. The coinage standards that rest on these units are discussed in Chapter 5.

Table 7.2. Principal units of weight, capacity and length in the Arthaśāstra (AŚ 2.19–20; ratios after Kangle; modern equivalents uncertain) Scale Units Gold 10 māṣa beans or 5 guñjā seeds = 1 suvarṇa-māṣaka; 16 māṣaka = 1 suvarṇa or karṣa; 4 karṣa = 1 pala Silver 88 white mustard seeds = 1 silver māṣaka; 16 māṣaka (or 20 śaibya seeds) = 1 dharaṇa Diamonds 20 rice grains = 1 diamond dharaṇa Capacity 4 kuḍuba = 1 prastha; 4 prastha = 1 āḍhaka; 4 āḍhaka = 1 droṇa; 16 droṇa = 1 khārī; 20 droṇa = 1 kumbha; 10 kumbha = 1 vaha Length Units rising by eights from the smallest particle to the aṅgula (finger-breadth); 12 aṅgula = 1 vitasti; 2 vitasti = 1 aratni or hasta (cubit); 4 aratni = 1 daṇḍa

The dharmaśāstras also require the king to supervise weights and measures. Manu directs that all balances, weights and measures be properly marked and re-examined every six months (Manu 8.403) (Olivelle 2004). In practice South Asia never had a single system. Local measures varied from region to region and even from market to market, and the units of the Sultanate and Mughal periods (the tola, sīr and man) themselves varied over time and place. Their later history is traced in the next subsection.

docs.title: 7.4.3 From the Sīr and Man to the Metric System
docs.text:
The weights of medieval and early modern north India were built on the same small units as the coin standards: the rati (Chapter 5), eight of which made a māshā and twelve māshās a tolā. Goods in bulk were weighed by the sīr (seer) and the man (maund) of forty sīrs. Neither had a fixed value. Under the Mughals the sīr was defined by the weight of a number of copper dāms: the Āʾīn-i Akbarī records that Akbar raised it to 30 dāms in weight, and later emperors raised it again, so that the man of Shāh Jahān was a third heavier than Akbar’s. Irfan Habib and Shireen Moosvi, who needed these units to convert the Āʾīn’s figures for yields and prices, estimate Akbar’s man at a little over 25 kilograms (Habib 1999; Moosvi 1987). Outside the imperial administration every region, and often every market, kept its own man. The tables compiled by colonial officials list maunds of very different weights at Bombay, Madras, Surat and the Bengal factories, and even within a single town different measures might be used for different goods (Yule and Burnell 1903).

Length and area followed the same pattern. The Mughal revenue survey used the gaz-i Ilāhī, Akbar’s standard yard, and a measuring chain (jarīb); the standard bīghā was a square of sixty gaz a side, and the survey itself is described in Volume 21, Bhūgola, and the arithmetic of revenue in Volume 11, Gaṇita. Local bīghās, however, varied greatly, and in colonial Bengal the term came to denote a third of an acre. In the Tamil country the medieval inscriptions measure grain by the kalam, divided into smaller units such as the marakkāl and nāḻi, and land by the vēli and its fractions. Measures were named after their authority: a Chola grain measure might be called after the king, or, at Thanjavur, after the god of the great temple (Āḍavallāṉ, “the skilled dancer”), and a land survey would name the measuring rod used (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). Naming the measure in the document was itself a guarantee, since a measure tied to a king or a god could be checked against a standard kept at the palace or the temple.

This diversity was not mere disorder. Witold Kula, writing on pre-industrial Europe, showed that local measures embodied social bargains — a heaped or a struck measure, a larger measure for rents than for sales — and that their unification was a political act (Kula 1986). The Arthaśāstra’s different measures for receiving revenue and for paying out rations (Section 7.4.2) are an early example of the same logic. In India, as in Europe, standardisation came with the modern state.

The East India Company began the process with its coinage. A Bengal regulation of 1833 fixed the tolā at 180 grains troy, the weight of the Company’s rupee, and defined the standard sīr as 80 tolās and the man as 40 sīrs; this “Indian” or “railway” maund of 82 \(\tfrac{2}{7}\) pounds became the official unit of the railways and of government statistics. Acts of 1870 and 1871 that would have tied the Indian units to the metric standards (the Act of 1870 defined the standard sīr as the kilogram) were never brought into force, and the Standards of Weights Act of 1939 confirmed the old units on the 1833 basis (Table 7.3). Local measures nevertheless remained in daily use in markets and villages until independent India adopted the metric system. The Standards of Weights and Measures Act of 1956 provided for the change; decimal coinage was introduced on 1 April 1957 and metric weights from 1 October 1958, and the old units were withdrawn from official use over the following years. Jewellers’ weights in tolās and ratis, and the bīghā in land transactions, have survived informally to the present.

docs.title: 7.5 Fraud, Adulteration and Quality
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on traders (AŚ 4.2) lists the offences that the superintendent of markets must punish. Traders who use false weights or measures are fined according to the size of the discrepancy. Those who mix grain, oil, alkalis, salt, perfumes or medicines with substances of similar colour, or who sell inferior goods as superior, are fined. Goods of poor quality must not be passed off by trickery, and goods sold must correspond to what was shown. The chapter on artisans that precedes it (AŚ 4.1) imposes comparable rules on washermen, weavers, goldsmiths and other craftsmen who handle customers’ materials, fining them for loss, substitution and delay. The penalties increase with the gravity of the offence, a principle common to the text’s whole penal system.

The law books also allow a transaction to be undone. The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the rescission of sale and purchase (AŚ 3.15) permits a party to withdraw within a short period that, as the text is usually read, varies with occupation: a single day for traders and longer periods for cultivators and herdsmen. The dharmaśāstras treat “rescission of purchase” and “non-delivery of goods sold” as titles of law, and Nārada gives periods within which a buyer may inspect and return various kinds of goods (Kane 1930). These rules protected both parties, and especially the seller’s right to receive payment and the buyer’s right to receive what was agreed.

Religious ethics reinforced the law. The moral precepts in the opening suttas of the Dīgha Nikāya include abstaining from cheating with scales, with metal and with measures, and Jain teaching counts the use of false weights among the transgressions of the vow of non-stealing (Jaini 1979). The dharmaśāstras impose fines for false weights and adulteration (Kane 1930).

It is tempting to describe all this as “consumer protection”, and the phrase can serve as an analogy. But the ancient rules did not recognise consumers as a class with rights against sellers; they protected the king’s revenue, the order of the market and the parties to particular transactions. Many of the fines went to the treasury rather than to the injured party, and the same texts expected the king’s agents to deceive and entrap, so the likeness to modern consumer law is limited.

docs.title: 7.6.1 The Śulkādhyakṣa
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra devotes two chapters to customs (AŚ 2.21–22). The superintendent of customs (śulkādhyakṣa) sets up a customs house with a flag near the main gate of the city. When merchants arrive, his officials record who they are, where they come from, what goods they bring and where these were first sealed. Goods without a seal, or with a forged seal, incur heavy penalties. Merchants declare the quantity and price of their goods, and these are then offered for sale; if buyers bid the price up, the increase goes to the king, a device to discourage under-declaration. Concealed goods are confiscated.

The text sets a general duty on imports of one-fifth of the value, followed by a detailed schedule for particular goods: one-sixth on flowers, fruit, vegetables, roots and seeds and on dried fish and meat; rates fixed by experts on conch shells, diamonds, gems, pearls and coral; and lower fractions, from a tenth to a twenty-fifth, on textiles, metals, cattle, spices and other goods (AŚ 2.22). The text also forbids the sale of goods at the places where they are produced, so that they pass through the customs house. Goods intended for weddings, sacrifices, births, religious ceremonies and gifts are exempt. The export of weapons, armour, metals, chariots, gems, grain and cattle is prohibited, with confiscation and a fine for offenders, while these goods may be imported and sold outside the gate free of duty (AŚ 2.21). On the roads, the frontier officer (antapāla) collects a road cess (vartanī) and is required to make good goods stolen from merchants within his territory.

These are the norms of a single treatise. They show what an administrator thought customs should achieve: revenue, control of strategic goods, and the channelling of trade through supervised places. The rates are prescriptions, not records of what any state actually charged.

docs.title: 7.6.2 Other Evidence
docs.text: Manu prescribes that experts at toll stations should fix the value of goods and that the king should take one-twentieth as duty; that the export of goods reserved to the king or prohibited should be punished by confiscation of all the offender’s property; and that a trader who avoids the toll station, buys or sells at improper times or misstates the quantity of his goods should be fined eight times the duty evaded (Manu 8.398–400) (Olivelle 2004). The Paṭṭiṉappālai’s picture of goods stamped with the Chola tiger at Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam (Section 7.1.2) suggests a comparable practice of sealing goods. On the other side of the Indo-Roman trade, Roman Egypt levied a duty of one-quarter on goods imported from India, as the papyrus recording a loan for a voyage to Muziris shows (Chapter 11) (De Romanis 2020). In the early medieval period, inscriptions from northern and western India record tolls levied at market centres (maṇḍapikā) on goods such as grain, salt, oil, cloth and horses, often assigned by kings to temples (Gopal 1965; Chattopadhyaya 1994). Port duties and the administration of later ports are treated in Chapter 15.

docs.title: 7.7 Granaries, Scarcity and Famine
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra expects the state to hold reserves. The superintendent of the storehouse is to keep half of the grain in store for times of distress among the people, using the other half, and to replace old stock with new (AŚ 2.15). Among the remedies for calamities (AŚ 4.3), the text lists the measures a king should take in famine: he should distribute seed and food; employ people on building forts or irrigation works, paying them in food; share out provisions; move the population to a region with a good harvest, or to the vicinity of rivers, lakes or the sea, where people can grow grain and vegetables and catch fish and game; seek help from allies; and draw on the wealth of the rich, by levies or forced contributions. In the wider context of the text, the export of grain was prohibited in any case (Section 7.6), and hoarding by traders was punished (AŚ 4.2).

These measures are practical and recognisably sensible: food for work, the movement of people to food, and the use of stored grain. They fall well short of a famine code. The text does not say how large reserves should be in relation to population, gives no evidence that such measures were applied, and treats famine as one of several calamities alongside fire, flood and epidemic. The dharmaśāstras add the general duty of the king to protect his subjects, and Buddhist and Jain texts praise rulers and merchants who feed the hungry. Famine relief under the Delhi sultans and the Mughals, and the catastrophic famines of the colonial period, are discussed in Chapters 18 and 19. Modern analysis of famine, notably Amartya Sen’s argument that famines arise from a collapse of people’s entitlement to food rather than simply from a fall in its supply (Sen 1981), offers a useful lens for reading the older texts, which also link famine to loss of livelihood, but it is not anticipated by them.

docs.title: 7.8 Settling Market Disputes
docs.text:
Disputes arising from trade were settled at several levels. The Arthaśāstra assigns civil cases, including disputes over sales, deposits, debts and partnerships, to courts of three judges (dharmastha) and three ministers placed at the frontier posts and at the administrative centres of groups of ten, four hundred and eight hundred villages (AŚ 3.1). Offences by traders and artisans, such as fraud, adulteration and collusion, fall instead under the “eradication of thorns” and are tried by commissioners (pradeṣṭṛ) (AŚ 4.1). The distinction is roughly that between private disputes and public offences.

The dharmaśāstras recognise that most disputes never reached a royal court. Yājñavalkya lists a hierarchy of tribunals in which the family, the guild (śreṇī) and the association (pūga) decide cases before the judges appointed by the king, each higher body able to review the decision of the one below (Yājñavalkya 2.30); Nārada and Bṛhaspati describe similar arrangements and direct the king to uphold the conventions (saṃvid) of guilds and other corporate bodies (Kane 1930). Among the titles of law listed by Manu are non-delivery of goods sold, rescission of purchase and breach of convention, all of which concern commerce (Manu 8.4–7). Guild inscriptions and the records of merchant associations in south India show such bodies regulating their members and acting collectively in disputes (Chapter 4) (Thaplyal 1996; Champakalakshmi 1996). The evidence suggests that, in practice, merchants’ own associations and local custom carried most of the burden of regulating markets, and that the royal regulation described in the treatises was exercised, where it was exercised at all, alongside them.

docs.title: 7.9 Assessment
docs.text: The treatises were shrewd about the market’s weak points, collusion, false measures and adulteration, but they looked at it from the treasury: even the king’s measures were larger for receiving than for paying out. What they reveal is a view of the market as a source of wealth to be protected, taxed and watched, while in practice merchants’ own associations and custom did most of the governing.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Arthaśāstra’s chapters on trade, customs, weights and traders, read Olivelle (2013) and Kangle (1960). Chakravarti (2002) is the best general study of traders and trade in early India, and Thapar (2002) provides the historical setting. For the early medieval period, see Gopal (1965) and Chattopadhyaya (1994); for south India, Champakalakshmi (1996) and Hall (1980). On Harappan weights, see Kenoyer (1998). The dharmaśāstra rules are surveyed in Kane (1930).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Craft Production and Industry
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter is about how production was organised, not about how things were made. The agrarian base on which all craft and trade rested, including the early medieval land grants and the debate over “Indian feudalism”, is the subject of Chapter 3. This chapter looks at the main settings in which goods were made: the household, the craft village and caste, the guild, the workshop of the state or the court, the temple, and the merchant who advanced money to producers. It then follows the leading sectors as parts of the economy: textiles, which were for most of recorded history India’s chief manufactured export; metals; gems and beads; and pottery. Caste, unfree and coerced labour, and the work of women are treated as part of the subject, not as asides. Techniques are covered in depth in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru (crafts and textiles), and Volume 14, Rasāyana (chemistry and metallurgy). Shipbuilding is treated in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 8.1 Beginnings: Harappan Craft Production
docs.text:
The cities of the mature Harappan period (c. 2600–1900 BCE) supported a great deal of specialised craft work. Excavations at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Chanhu-daro, Lothal and Dholavira have found workshops for stone beads, above all long barrel beads of carnelian drilled with specially made stone drills, for shell bangles and inlay, for steatite seals, for copper and bronze objects, and for glazed faience ornaments. Indus faience is a glazed, sintered quartz paste, not glass; glass appears in South Asia only in the first millennium BCE. Harappan carnelian beads, including etched beads, reached Mesopotamia, where they were found in the royal graves at Ur. Long-distance trade was therefore already one of the outlets for specialised craft (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002; Ratnagar 2004).

The textile evidence is equally early. Mineralised cotton fibres preserved inside a copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh (6th millennium BCE) are among the earliest known evidence for the use of cotton (Moulherat et al. 2002). Fragments of cotton cloth survive at Mohenjo-daro, attached to metal objects. Silk has also been identified at Harappa and Chanhu-daro. These are fibres of wild, not domesticated, silk moths, dated to the later third millennium BCE (Good et al. 2009). Chinese silk was certainly imported later, but India had its own wild silks long before it.

How Harappan production was controlled is debated. The uniform weights, bricks and seal styles suggest strong common standards. Workshops were spread through residential quarters, though, and not concentrated in a palace, and Kenoyer and others see a network of specialist households and lineages rather than a single state-run industry (Kenoyer 1998).

docs.title: 8.2 Forms of Organisation
docs.text: From the early historic period onward, four broad forms of organising production existed side by side. Their weight changed from period to period and from craft to craft.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Household, Village and Quarter
docs.text: Most craft production in Indian history took place in households. A potter’s or weaver’s family worked as a unit, with women and children doing much of the preparatory work: cleaning and spinning cotton, preparing clay, winding yarn. Spinning in particular was done by women in peasant households across the subcontinent. The Pali Jātaka stories describe villages of smiths (kammāra-gāma) and of carpenters (vaḍḍhaki-gāma), and streets or quarters of particular crafts in towns. The concentration of one craft in one place allowed shared access to raw materials and buyers (Chakravarti 2002; Sharma 1983). Ananda Coomaraswamy’s The Indian Craftsman (1909), written under the influence of the Arts and Crafts movement, made this hereditary village and guild craftsman the ideal of a society not yet divided by industrial labour; his book is better read as a critique of industrialism than as a description of how crafts were organised (Coomaraswamy 1909).

docs.title: 8.2.2 Guilds
docs.text: Artisans in many towns were organised in śreṇīs (guilds) from at least the last centuries BCE. The inscriptions that record them, above all the Nasik endowments with weavers’ guilds and the Mandasor record of the silk-weavers from Lāṭa, show guilds trusted to hold capital, building temples and keeping a common identity even when some members changed occupation. They are discussed in Chapter 4 (Thaplyal 1996; Ray 1986).

docs.title: 8.2.3 State, Court and Temple
docs.text: States and courts ran their own workshops for goods they needed in quantity or wanted to control: arms, cloth for the court and the army, coin, and luxury goods for display and gift (Sections 8.4 and 8.5). In south India from about the tenth century, the great temples were also economic centres. They owned land, employed artisans and settled weavers around them, and endowments to temples were often managed by artisan and merchant bodies (Ramaswamy 1985; Champakalakshmi 1996).

docs.title: 8.2.4 Merchants and Advances
docs.text:
Finally, merchants organised production by advancing money or raw material to artisans against future delivery. This system, best documented for textiles in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, is discussed in Section 8.7. Table 8.1 summarises these forms of organisation.

Merchants or brokers advance cash to weavers against delivery

docs.title: 8.3 Caste, Status and Labour
docs.text:
Craft skills in India were very often hereditary, and crafts were often linked to particular jātis (endogamous birth groups). Marriage within the group and training within the family helped to keep technical knowledge within a group, and so did a reluctance to teach outsiders. But the link between caste and occupation was neither fixed nor universal. Pali texts show people changing occupation. Guild inscriptions show weavers turning to other work. Groups rose and fell in status over the centuries (Chakravarti 1987).

Status mattered, and it was unequal. The Pali texts list “low crafts” (hīna-sippa) such as basket-making, pottery, weaving, leather-work and barbering. The Brahmanical law books place most artisans among the Śūdras or among the “mixed castes”. The tenth chapter of the Manusmṛti ascribes a whole range of occupations to castes it explains as the offspring of mixed unions. This is a theory of social order, not a census, but it expressed and justified real hierarchies (Olivelle 2004). Workers in leather, and others whose work was held to be polluting, were treated as untouchable. Some artisan groups contested their place. In the Tamil country, the five metal-, wood- and stone-working crafts grouped as the Kammāḷar claimed descent from Viśvakarman and a status equal to that of Brahmins. Artisan and merchant groups there were also aligned in the medieval “right-hand” and “left-hand” caste divisions (valaṅkai, iṭaṅkai), whose disputes are recorded in inscriptions (Champakalakshmi 1996).

Not all labour was free. The Arthaśāstra has separate rules for slaves (dāsa) and hired labourers (karmakara) (AŚ 3.13–14). In its own state workshops it used convict labour and the labour of women in dependent positions (Section 8.4). The Nāradasmṛti (c. 5th–6th century CE) distinguishes five kinds of dependent worker: the student, the apprentice, the hired servant, the overseer and the slave, and it lists fifteen kinds of slave (Kane 1930). In early modern Bengal and elsewhere, weavers tied by advances could become dependent on those who advanced them, and the line between contract and coercion was not always clear (Section 8.7).

docs.title: 8.3.1 Apprenticeship
docs.text: Most artisans learned in the family. Where a boy learned from a master outside his family, the law books regulated the relationship. The Nāradasmṛti, in its title on breach of contract of service, describes the apprentice (antevāsin). With the consent of his kin, a youth who wishes to learn a craft lives with a master for an agreed period. The master teaches him, feeds him in his own house, does not set him to other work, and treats him like a son. An apprentice who leaves a blameless master before the end of the term may be forced back and punished, and one who has learned the craft early must still serve out the term, the master keeping the fruits of his work (paraphrased after (Kane 1930)). These rules show apprenticeship as a contract, enforced by law, that gave the master a period of bound labour in return for training. The sources do not describe formal grades of novice, journeyman and master of the European kind.

docs.title: 8.4 State Workshops in the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) describes a state that produces as well as taxes. Book 2 assigns superintendents (adhyakṣa) to mines and metals (2.12), to gold and the goldsmiths’ workshop (2.13–14), to forest produce (2.17), to the armoury (2.18), and to yarn and textiles (the sūtrādhyakṣa, 2.23). These are prescriptions for an ideal kingdom, not records of an actual one (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960).

The chapter on the sūtrādhyakṣa is the clearest picture of state textile production. The superintendent is to have yarn spun by women who had few other means of support: widows, crippled women and unmarried girls, women who had left home as renunciants, women working off fines, the mothers of courtesans, aged female servants of the king, and temple women whose service had ended (AŚ 2.23). Wages were to be set by the quality and quantity of yarn. Women who did not leave their houses were to receive raw material and return yarn through the superintendent’s female servants. The text adds rules on how the superintendent must behave towards these women, and penalties for misappropriation on both sides. The same chapter has weaving, rope-making and the making of armour and straps done by artisans on wages, and by men working off fines (Olivelle 2013). The arrangement gave a livelihood to women without other support, and it gave the state their labour cheaply; the text sees no tension between the two, and a modern reader should keep both in view.

Book 4 opens with a chapter on “guarding against artisans” (kārukarakṣaṇa, AŚ 4.1), which shows the state as regulator. It sets penalties for weavers who return less cloth than the yarn they received, for washermen who damage or mix up clothes, and for goldsmiths who adulterate metal, and it sets rules on wages and delays (Kangle 1960). Outside the Arthaśāstra, the fragments of Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE) preserved by Strabo say that armour-makers and shipbuilders worked for the king alone and received wages and rations from him (McCrindle 1877). Neither source sets out a general code of wages or of protection for workers; the rules on hired labour are rules of contract (Section 2.6.1).

docs.title: 8.5 The Kārkhānas of the Sultanate and Mughal Courts
docs.text:
The Delhi Sultanate and its successors organised much court production in kārkhānas (Persian “workshops”). These were departments that both made and stored goods for the ruler’s household, army and gift-giving. According to the Arab writer al-ʿUmarī, Muḥammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–1351) kept some four thousand silk-weavers making robes of honour. The chronicler Shams Sirāj ʿAfīf describes about three dozen kārkhānas under Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388), each under a noble (Habib 2008; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

The Mughal kārkhānas are better documented. The Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the imperial workshops for textiles, arms, perfumes and other goods. The French physician François Bernier, writing in the 1660s, described large halls at Delhi where embroiderers, goldsmiths, painters, lacquer-workers, tailors and other artisans worked under a master. He thought the artisans poorly paid and dependent on the nobles’ favour. Large nobles kept kārkhānas of their own (Richards 1993; Habib 2008). These workshops produced some of the finest goods of the period. They served the court, though, not the market, and most manufacture for sale, including almost all export textiles, was done outside them.

docs.title: 8.6.1 Cotton Cloth from the Periplus to the Companies
docs.text:
For most of recorded history, cotton cloth was India’s most important manufactured product and its chief manufactured export. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (mid-first century CE) names cotton cloth among the exports of Barygaza (Bharuch) and of the ports of the south and east coasts, including fine muslins from the Ganges region (Casson 1989). The Arthaśāstra lists the best cotton cloth as coming from Madhurā (Madurai), Aparānta (the western coast), Kaliṅga, Kāśī, Vaṅga, Vatsa and Mahiṣa (AŚ 2.11). The same chapter lists the fine dukūla of Vaṅga, and silks, including cīnapaṭṭa from “the land of Cīna” (Olivelle 2013).

In the medieval centuries, Indian cotton cloth moved through the whole Indian Ocean. Block-printed and resist-dyed Gujarati cottons excavated at Fustat (Old Cairo) date mostly from the later medieval centuries. Indian trade cloths kept for generations as heirlooms in eastern Indonesia have yielded radiocarbon dates going back to about the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries (Guy 1998). Indian cloth also went to East Africa and, through Gujarati, Arab, Persian and Southeast Asian merchants, to almost every port of the Indian Ocean (Chapter 12).

From the seventeenth century, the Dutch, English and French East India Companies made Indian cottons a mass consumer good in Europe, West Africa and the Americas. The scale was such that England passed the Calico Acts (1700 and 1721) to protect its own woollen and silk industries from Indian printed cottons. The essays in Riello and Roy (2009) trace this “clothing of the world” between 1500 and 1850. The main export regions were Gujarat, the Coromandel coast (painted and printed chintz, and plain cloth) and Bengal (muslins and plain cottons) (Chaudhuri 1978; Prakash 1985; Arasaratnam 1986).

docs.title: 8.6.2 Producers
docs.text: Weaving was mostly done in households of hereditary weaving castes, with spinning done by women of many groups. Vijaya Ramaswamy’s study of medieval south India follows two such communities, the Kaikkōḷar and the Sāliyar. It shows their links to temples, the loom taxes they paid, their migrations in search of better conditions and their rise in status (Ramaswamy 1985). Technique changed over time too. Irfan Habib has argued that the spinning wheel and the carding bow reached India with the Sultanate and are first securely attested in the fourteenth century. Earlier spinning was done with the hand spindle (Habib 2008).

docs.title: 8.6.3 Silk
docs.text:
India’s indigenous silks came from wild moths: tasar, eri and muga. Chinese silk was imported in the early historic period. Domesticated mulberry sericulture spread later, and by the Mughal period Bengal, especially the region around Kasimbazar, was a major producer of raw silk for the Indian market and for the Dutch and English Companies (Prakash 1985). Gujarat’s double-ikat paṭolā were in demand as prestige textiles in Southeast Asia (Guy 1998). Dyes and dyeing, including the mordant chemistry of Indian chintz, are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

Historical Note: The Dhaka muslin “thumb-cutting” story

A popular story says that the East India Company cut off the thumbs of Bengal’s muslin weavers to destroy their industry. No contemporary evidence supports this as a practice or a policy. The story seems to have grown out of a report by William Bolts (1772) that some winders of raw silk had cut off their own thumbs to escape being forced to work for the Company. That report, whatever its accuracy, describes coercion of a different kind. The coercion itself is documented, especially after 1765: weavers were bound by advances to the Company’s agents and prevented from selling to others (Section 8.7). The decline of Dhaka muslin in the nineteenth century had economic causes, which are debated (Chapter 19). The thumb-cutting story is a myth.

docs.title: 8.7 Putting-Out and the Dādanī System
docs.text:
Weavers rarely had the capital to buy yarn and to wait for a distant buyer. Merchants therefore advanced money, or sometimes yarn, against the delivery of cloth of specified type, length and quality by a fixed date. In Bengal this advance was called dādanī, and the merchants who took it from the European companies were dādanī merchants. They in turn passed advances through brokers (dalāl) and local agents to weavers in the villages. Similar chains of advance operated on the Coromandel coast and in Gujarat (Chaudhuri 1978; Prakash 1985; Arasaratnam 1986).

Historians disagree about how this system shaped the weavers’ position. Prasannan Parthasarathi argues that before the mid-eighteenth century, south Indian weavers had considerable bargaining power. They could refuse advances, sell to rival buyers or move away, and they used these options in disputes (Parthasarathi 2011). Others stress the weavers’ indebtedness to merchants. After the Company gained political power in Bengal in 1757–1765, it replaced independent merchants with its own salaried agents (gumāshtas). It bound weavers to deliver only to the Company, and it used force to collect cloth. This transition from a competitive to a coercive system is a central theme of the early colonial economy (Prakash 1998). Chapter 18 places the advance system in the wider early modern economy, and Chapter 19 follows its colonial transformation.

docs.title: 8.8 Metals
docs.text: The technology of Indian metallurgy is treated in Volume 14, Rasāyana. This section notes only the forms of production and trade.

docs.title: 8.8.1 Iron and Steel
docs.text:
Iron working spread across the subcontinent during the late second and early first millennia BCE. Iron tools mattered for clearing land and for cultivation, though historians debate how far iron caused the second urbanisation. Iron was smelted by specialist communities, many of them in forest and hill regions, in small bloomery furnaces, and the iron was traded to towns and villages. The best-known monument of Indian iron is the pillar now at Mehrauli in Delhi. It was set up c. 400 CE by a king named Candra, usually identified with Candragupta II, and it stands over seven metres high. Its resistance to rust has been explained by a protective surface film formed on its phosphorus-rich iron (Biswas and Biswas 1996). Making it required the forge-welding of many blooms, so a substantial team of smiths was needed.

Crucible steel, known in English as “wootz”, was made in small closed clay crucibles in which iron and carbon-bearing material were heated together until a high-carbon steel formed. The word “wootz” comes from ukku, the word for steel in Kannada and Telugu. The production centres were in south India and Sri Lanka, not in northern India. Archaeological evidence includes crucible fragments from Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu, in contexts of the late centuries BCE and early centuries CE, sites in Sri Lanka, and in later centuries the Deccan: for example Konasamudram in Telangana and Gatihosahalli in Karnataka. Steel cakes were traded to Persia and the Arab world, where smiths forged them into the watered-pattern blades that Europeans later called “Damascus” steel. European scientists studied samples sent from India from the 1790s onward (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004; Craddock 1995). The production was small in scale, carried out by village specialists. Its importance lay in quality and in long-distance demand.

docs.title: 8.8.2 Zinc and Brass
docs.text: Zinc boils at a lower temperature than that needed to smelt it from its ore, so metallic zinc can only be produced by distillation. At Zawar in Rajasthan, lead, silver and zinc ores were mined from the later first millennium BCE. Brass with a fairly high zinc content was made in the north-west in the early centuries CE by the cementation process, which does not require metallic zinc. Distillation of zinc at Zawar, using downward-distilling clay retorts in banks of furnaces, is dated from about the ninth century CE, and it reached a large scale in the following centuries. This is the earliest known industrial production of metallic zinc; earlier dates sometimes given for zinc distillation in India, in the fourth century CE or even BCE, are not supported by the archaeological evidence. In Europe, zinc distillation on a commercial scale began with William Champion at Bristol, who patented his process in 1738. Whether he drew on Asian knowledge is uncertain (Craddock 1995; Biswas and Biswas 1996). Bidri ware, a zinc alloy inlaid with silver, is associated with Bidar in the Deccan and probably dates from the Bahmanī period. It is an example of a court-patronised metal craft.

docs.title: 8.9 Gems and Beads
docs.text:
