Until diamonds were found in Brazil in the 1720s, India was the world’s main source of diamonds. The principal mines were the alluvial workings of the Krishna valley in the Golconda kingdom, such as Kollur, and the mines of Panna in central India. The French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier visited the Golconda mines in the seventeenth century and described large numbers of labourers digging and washing gravel under contractors who leased the mines from the ruler. He also described the dealers and cutters who bought on the spot (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). Gem knowledge was codified in Sanskrit texts. The Arthaśāstra (2.11) describes how gems were to be examined for the treasury. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century CE) has chapters on gems. A genre of “examination of gems” (ratnaparīkṣā) texts also exists, though dating its members is difficult (Biswas and Biswas 1996). Pearl fishing in the Gulf of Mannar is discussed in Chapter 17.

Bead-making is one of the longest-lived Indian craft industries. After the Harappan carnelian beads, stone beads of carnelian and agate were made at many early historic sites. In western India, carnelian and agate from the Rajpipla hills have been worked at Khambhat (Cambay) for many centuries. At Arikamedu near Puducherry and at other sites of the Indo-Roman period, excavations have found evidence for the production of stone beads and of small drawn glass beads. Small monochrome glass beads of this “Indo-Pacific” type are found across the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia (Tomber 2008; Ray 2003).

docs.title: 8.10 Pottery
docs.text:
Pottery was the most widespread craft of all. It was mostly made by village potters (kumbhakāra) for local use. Two wares of the early historic period, however, show organised production for wider markets.

  • Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW). This is a fine, glossy ware made from about the sixth century BCE (its beginning is variously dated between the seventh and fifth centuries) to about the second century BCE, at its peak in the Gangetic towns of the mahājanapada and Mauryan periods. It is regarded as a luxury tableware. Its wide distribution and consistent quality imply specialist workshops, but where and by whom it was made is still being studied.

  • Rouletted Ware. This is a fine grey-black ware with bands of rouletted decoration, of about the second century BCE to the second century CE. It was once thought to be Mediterranean. It is now regarded as Indian, and laboratory analyses point to a source in lower Bengal. It was carried along the east coast of India and to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and its distribution is one of the markers of the Bay of Bengal trade (Tomber 2008; Ray 2003).

docs.title: 8.11 Women and Work
docs.text: Women’s labour ran through every sector described in this chapter, but it is hard to see in the sources. The normative texts were written by men, most of them brāhmaṇas, and describe what women ought to do rather than what they did. Inscriptions record gifts, not wages. Company records count pieces of cloth, not the hands that spun the yarn. What follows brings together the main kinds of evidence. It does not claim more than they can show, and it does not turn women’s work into either a story of hidden equality or one of simple oppression.

docs.title: 8.11.1 Spinning and the Textile Household
docs.text:
Spinning was the most widespread form of women’s work for cash or for the market. The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of yarn, discussed above (Section 8.4), drew on the labour of women without other support, and household spinning by women of peasant and artisan families is attested in every period (Section 8.2). In the great age of the export trade in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the cloth bought by the European companies depended on the yarn of very large numbers of women spinning part-time in rural households in Bengal, on the Coromandel coast and in Gujarat. The output of a single loom needed the work of several spinners.

In weaving households the division of labour was usually by gender. In most regions men worked the loom, while women and children cleaned and carded the cotton, wound bobbins and prepared and sized the warp, though practice varied. In Assam and Manipur, by contrast, weaving on the household loom was above all women’s work, and the cloth of eri and muga silk woven in the household was both for family use and for sale. Women’s work in weaver households was essential to output but was counted, and paid, as part of the household’s work under its male head.

This dependence had a harsh consequence in the nineteenth century. When machine-spun yarn from Britain, and later from Indian mills, became cheap, hand-spinning collapsed far more quickly and completely than hand-weaving, which survived by using mill yarn. The loss of earnings fell mainly on women, often the poorest, for whom spinning had been one of the few sources of independent income (Section 8.12). When Gandhi made the spinning wheel and khādī the symbol of the national movement, he was reviving above all a form of women’s work (Chapter 21).

docs.title: 8.11.2 Women as Donors
docs.text: The donative inscriptions of the early historic Buddhist sites show that some women controlled wealth in their own names. Among the many donors recorded on the railings and gateways of the stūpas at Sāñcī and Bharhut are nuns (bhikhunī) and laywomen. Some are named alone, others as the wife, mother or daughter of a householder, a merchant or a craftsman (Lüders 1912). The same is true of the rock-cut monasteries of the western Deccan, at Karle, Nasik, Kanheri, Junnar and elsewhere. Here women of merchant and artisan families gave cisterns, pillars and cells, and the queen mother Gautamī Balaśrī dedicated a cave at Nasik in the reign of Vāsiṣṭhīputra Puḷumāvi (Ray 1986). These gifts show that women could hold and dispose of property, especially in commercial families, and that public generosity was one way in which they and their families gained standing. They do not tell us how the women had acquired the wealth, or how far they could have spent it without the consent of their kin. Women appear as donors in the guild inscriptions too, but not as guild officers (Section 4.8).

docs.title: 8.11.3 Strīdhana and Women’s Property
docs.text: The dharmaśāstras recognised a category of women’s own property, strīdhana. The Manusmṛti lists six kinds: what was given before the nuptial fire, what was given at the bridal procession, what was given as a token of love, and what was received from a brother, a mother or a father (Manu 9.194). It also rules on how this property passed to the woman’s children after her death. The same text, in a much-quoted verse, declares that a wife, a son and a slave have no property of their own, and that what they earn belongs to the man to whom they belong (Manu 8.416) (Olivelle 2004). The tension between these rules is real and was never fully resolved. Later commentators extended or narrowed the category. Vijñāneśvara’s Mitākṣarā (late eleventh or early twelfth century), the most influential commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, defined strīdhana broadly to include property a woman acquired by inheritance, purchase, partition and other means, while the Bengal school of the Dāyabhāga defined it more narrowly. The Yājñavalkyasmṛti itself placed the wife first among the heirs of a man who died without a son (Kane 1930). How far these rules governed practice is uncertain. Jewellery, the most common form of strīdhana, was a store of value that a family could draw on in hard times, and it was often under the practical control of the husband’s household.

docs.title: 8.11.4 Markets, Merchant Households and Wage Work
docs.text:
Women were prominent in petty trade. The retailing of fish, vegetables, milk and other perishables was in many regions largely in women’s hands. The best-documented examples come from fishing communities, where women who did not go to sea sold the catch (Chapter 17). In Manipur the large market of Imphal, known as Ima Keithel (“mothers’ market”), has long been run by women traders. These were not marginal activities. They supplied towns with food and gave women some cash of their own, though usually in small amounts and on terms set by wholesalers and moneylenders.

In the great merchant households women were rarely traders in their own right, but their position mattered to the business. James Laidlaw’s study of Jain merchant families in Jaipur describes how women’s religious practice, above all their public fasts, was celebrated by the whole family and bore on its reputation for piety and restraint. That reputation was part of the creditworthiness on which merchant families depended (Laidlaw 1995). Women of the Mughal court sometimes invested directly in trade: the ship Raḥīmī, owned by the emperor Jahāngīr’s mother, was seized by the Portuguese in 1613, an incident that led to an open breach between the Mughals and the Portuguese.

At the bottom of the economy women did much of the heaviest work. They transplanted, weeded and harvested rice, carried earth on construction sites, worked in salt pans and processed fish (Chapter 17). Many enslaved people in Indian history were women, employed above all in domestic service and given, sold or pledged as property; the texts discuss them chiefly from the owner’s point of view (Chakravarti 1985). In the colonial period women were recruited in large numbers for the tea gardens of Assam and worked in the coal mines of eastern India until underground work by women was prohibited in the 1930s. In the Bengal jute mills, Samita Sen has shown, the share of women in the workforce fell over the early twentieth century, as employers, the state and workers’ own families came to treat the male worker as the family breadwinner (Sen 1999).

The evidence is uneven. It is rich for the law books and for a few modern ethnographies, and thin for the women who did most of the work. Its general direction is clear, however. Women’s labour was indispensable to India’s craft and commercial economy, and it was usually less well rewarded, less secure and less visible than men’s.

docs.title: 8.12 Craft Production after 1800
docs.text: What happened to Indian crafts under colonial rule is the subject of the deindustrialisation debate, whose positions, from the nationalist economists and Amiya Kumar Bagchi to Morris D. Morris and Tirthankar Roy, are set out in Section 19.3. Two parts of the picture are broadly accepted. First, India’s exports of cotton cloth collapsed in the early nineteenth century and the country became an importer of machine-made cloth. Second, the effects on employment varied greatly by region and sector. The often-quoted fall in India’s share of world manufacturing output, from about a quarter in 1750 to under 2 per cent in 1900, comes from Paul Bairoch’s long-run estimates (Bairoch 1982). Like Maddison’s estimates of output (Section 18.5.6), they are rough reconstructions, and the fall in India’s share reflects the industrialisation of Europe and North America as well as any decline in India itself.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Harappan crafts, Kenoyer (1998) is the best introduction. For early historic organisation and guilds, see Chakravarti (2002) and Thaplyal (1996). Ramaswamy (1985) is the classic study of south Indian weavers. Guy (1998) and the essays in Riello and Roy (2009) cover the textile trade, and Habib (2008) covers technology and court workshops in the Sultanate and Mughal periods. For metals, see Craddock (1995) and Srinivasan and Ranganathan (2004).

docs.title: Chapter 9: Gift, Temple and Pilgrimage: Religious Institutions in the Economy
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Religious institutions were among the largest holders of wealth in South Asia. Monasteries, temples, mosques, Sufi shrines and gurdwārās received land, money and livestock; they employed priests, cooks, musicians, accountants and craftsmen; they lent, invested and bought; and the pilgrimages and festivals they sustained moved people and goods across the subcontinent. This chapter looks at that economy. It begins with the theory of the gift (dāna) in the Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain traditions, then turns to monasteries, to the south Indian temple as an economic institution and the hazards of temple wealth, to pilgrimage and fairs, to public works financed as gifts, to Islamic, Sikh, Christian and Parsi institutions, and to the laws by which the colonial and independent states came to regulate religious endowments. Earlier chapters have noted the endowments deposited with guilds (Chapter 4) and the lending of temple funds (Chapter 6); here the institutions themselves are the subject.

docs.title: 9.1 Gift and Merit: The Theory of Dāna
docs.text:
Every Indian religious tradition made giving a central duty of the householder, and each gave it a theory. In the Brahmanical texts the gift (dāna) is one of the duties of every twice-born man and the special duty of the king and the merchant; receiving gifts is one of the lawful livelihoods of the brahmin. The dharmaśāstras and the Purāṇas describe what makes a gift fruitful: the giver’s faith, a fitting time and place, an object that is the giver’s own and lawfully acquired, and above all a worthy recipient (pātra), usually a learned and virtuous brahmin. A gift to an unworthy person, the texts warn, is wasted or harmful to both parties. From the twelfth century this teaching was collected in large digests. The “book on gifts” (Dānakāṇḍa) of Lakṣmīdhara’s Kṛtyakalpataru, compiled for the Gāhaḍavāla court at Banaras, the Dānasāgara attributed to the Sena king Ballālasena of Bengal, and the section on gifts in Hemādri’s Caturvargacintāmaṇi, written for the Yādavas of Devagiri in the thirteenth century, classify gifts by object, occasion and recipient and set out the ritual for each (Kane 1930).

The grandest gifts were the sixteen “great gifts” (mahādāna) listed in the Matsya Purāṇa and the digests. The first of them, the tulāpuruṣa, required the donor to be weighed against gold or other precious substances, which were then distributed to brahmins. Inscriptions of several dynasties record kings performing such gifts. For the economic historian their significance lies less in the ritual than in what they did: they converted the surplus a king had collected as revenue or taken in war into gifts to a priestly class, and they advertised the king’s wealth and piety at the same time.

Most giving was more modest and more lasting. The land grants recorded on copper plates from the Gupta period onward (Section 3.2) were gifts in this sense: a brahmadeya gave a village or its revenue to brahmins, a devadāna to a temple deity, and a grant to a monastery to the Buddhist or Jain community. Such grants were often made in perpetuity and protected by imprecatory verses threatening the person who resumed them with long ages in hell. Whatever their religious purpose, they transferred rights over land and revenue on a very large scale and created religious landholders who had an interest in cultivation, irrigation and the settlement of new land.

The Buddhist and Jain traditions taught the merit of giving with equal emphasis but directed it differently. For Buddhists the monastic community (saṅgha) was the “incomparable field of merit for the world”, and gifts of food, robes, lodging and medicine to monks were the foundation of lay religious life; the merit could be transferred to others, including dead relatives. For Jains, gifts to mendicants were hedged with rules that made the mendicant dependent on lay households that understood them, while gifts for temples, images, pilgrimages and the copying of texts became the main outlet for the wealth of Jain merchant families. Maria Heim has compared the three traditions’ theories of the gift and shown how each balanced the giver’s merit against the purity and freedom of the recipient (Heim 2004). James Laidlaw’s study of Jain merchants in Jaipur shows how, in the twentieth century, public giving remained bound up with credit and reputation: a family’s standing in the business community depended in part on visible religious generosity (Laidlaw 1995).

Scholarly Note: Gift and economy

Modern anthropologists, following Marcel Mauss, have used Indian material to argue that gifts create obligations and relationships rather than simply transferring goods. The Brahmanical texts complicate this: they often present the ideal gift as one that expects no return, and some recipients regarded gifts as dangerous because they carried away the giver’s sin. Historians therefore treat dāna neither as charity in the modern sense nor as disguised exchange, but as an institution with its own rules, which redistributed wealth towards religious specialists and institutions while confirming the status of donors (Heim 2004).

docs.title: 9.2.1 Buddhist Monasteries in India and Sri Lanka
docs.text:
The Buddhist monastery began as a rains retreat for wandering monks and became, within a few centuries, a permanent establishment with buildings, lands, stores and servants. Gregory Schopen’s reading of the monastic codes alongside inscriptions has shown how far the large monasteries of the early centuries CE were engaged with property and money: the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya regulates the lending of monastic funds at interest under written contracts and the management of permanent endowments (Schopen 2004). This evidence, and the debate over how far it applies to Indian Buddhism as a whole, is discussed in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā. Here three economic points matter. First, monasteries were consumers on a large scale, and the location of the rock-cut monasteries of the western Deccan near the passes and the coastal ports points to their close relation with trade (Chapter 10) (Ray 1986). Second, they were investors, placing endowments with guilds whose interest paid for robes and food (Chapter 4). Third, from the Gupta period they became landholders. The great monastery of Nālandā was supported, according to the Chinese pilgrims, by the revenue of a large number of villages granted by kings: Xuanzang’s biographer speaks of about a hundred villages and Yijing of more than two hundred. Such figures are impressions, but copper-plate grants to Nālandā and to the monasteries of Valabhī confirm that monastic income came largely from land.

Sri Lanka offers the fullest picture of a monastic economy, because its chronicles and inscriptions are unusually rich. R. A. L. H. Gunawardana’s study of the early medieval period shows the great monasteries of Anurādhapura and Polonnaruva as owners of estates and of irrigation works, receiving a share of the crop and dues for the use of water, employing tenants and labourers, and administering their property through lay officials (Gunawardana 1979). The monks themselves were forbidden to handle money or till the soil, so the management of monastic wealth required intermediaries. Gunawardana showed that the tension between the ideal of the propertyless monk and the reality of the landlord monastery was recognised within the tradition itself, and that it shaped the relations between the saṅgha and the kings, who both endowed the monasteries and tried to regulate them.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Jain Temples and the Property of the Gods
docs.text:
The Jain community has been, for most of its history, closely tied to trade, and the economics of Jain giving show it clearly. Jain doctrine treats property given to an image or a temple (devadravya, “the god’s wealth”) as inviolable: it may be spent only on the temple and its worship, and to use it for any other purpose is held to be a grave sin. Much of this fund is raised by the auction (bolī) of ritual privileges, such as the right to perform the first worship at a festival or to carry an image in procession, for which families bid publicly (Laidlaw 1995; Cort 2001). The bidding makes a family’s wealth visible and converts it into religious honour; it also places large sums under the control of the temple trustees.

Jain temple trusts became some of the largest religious institutions of western India. The Ānandjī Kalyāṇjī Peḍhī of Ahmedabad, which grew out of arrangements made by the Śvetāmbara merchant community of that city in the eighteenth century, manages the temple-city of Śatruñjaya at Pālitāṇā and many other shrines; its long dispute with the rulers of Pālitāṇā over the dues payable for the protection of pilgrims was settled only under British arbitration. Seventeenth-century Ahmedabad merchants such as Śāntidās Jhaverī, who held the office of town headman (Chapter 4), were also builders of temples, and the pattern of merchant wealth flowing into temples, rest-houses (dharmaśālās) and animal refuges (pāñjrāpoḷs) continued into the twentieth century (Cort 2001). The giving was not only religious: the trusts and endowments of the merchant communities also provided credit, employment and relief within the community, and confirmed the standing of the families that controlled them.

docs.title: 9.3 The South Indian Temple as an Economic Institution
9.3.1 The Chola Temple
docs.text:
From the tenth century the great temples of the Tamil country became economic institutions on a scale without earlier parallel in the subcontinent. Their walls carry thousands of inscriptions recording gifts, and these are among the richest sources for the economy of medieval south India. The temple built by Rājarāja I at Thanjavur, completed around 1010, is the outstanding example. Its inscriptions list the villages assigned to it across the Chola territories and in Sri Lanka, the gold, silver and jewels given by the king, his queens and officials, and the arrangements for its staff. One inscription assigns some four hundred women attached to the temple, with house-sites in two streets near it, and lists a long roll of other servants — dance-masters, singers, drummers, accountants, watchmen, potters, washermen, carpenters, goldsmiths and others — each entitled to a fixed share of paddy from the temple’s lands (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

The temple’s wealth did not lie idle. Money and gold endowments were lent to village assemblies and to individuals, and the interest, often paid in paddy, met the cost of lamps, food offerings and festivals; endowments of sheep and cattle were entrusted to shepherds, who supplied ghee for the lamps (Chapter 6, Section 6.4.2). James Heitzman’s analysis of the Chola inscriptions shows that such endowments linked the temple to a wide network of villages, landholders and officials, and that giving to the temple was one of the main ways in which kings, chiefs and local magnates built and displayed their power (Heitzman 1997). Kenneth Hall and R. Champakalakshmi have shown how temple towns such as Kāñcīpuram, Kumbakōṇam and Thanjavur grew as centres of exchange, where merchants’ associations organised markets around the temple and supplied its needs (Hall 1980; Champakalakshmi 1996). The temple was thus at once a landlord, an employer, a lender, a large consumer of goods and a focus of urban growth.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Tirupati under Vijayanagara
docs.text:
Burton Stein’s study of the inscriptions of the temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara at Tirumala–Tirupati between the mid-fifteenth and the late sixteenth century showed another side of the temple economy (Stein 1960). Donors, among them kings, nobles, officials and merchants, gave cash endowments to the temple for the performance of particular offerings. The temple invested much of this money in the irrigation works of villages it held or controlled, building and repairing tanks and channels; the increased produce paid for the food offerings, and a share of the consecrated food (prasāda) returned to the donors, who could distribute or sell it. Stein argued that the temple thereby acted as an agency for agrarian development in a dry region, channelling the wealth of the Vijayanagara elite into irrigation.

Arjun Appadurai and Carol Breckenridge drew a broader conclusion from such evidence. In their view the south Indian temple was a redistributive centre: gifts flowed to the deity, and the deity returned them in the form of consecrated food and “honours” — shares in ritual, places in procession, the right to receive prasāda in a particular order — which defined the rank of every participant (Appadurai and Breckenridge 1976). The temple’s economy was therefore also an economy of status. Disputes over honours were among the most persistent sources of litigation in the colonial courts, and Appadurai’s study of the Śrī Pārthasārathi temple at Madras traces how they changed when colonial law redefined the temple’s trustees and their powers (Appadurai 1981).

docs.title: 9.3.3 Who Was Excluded
docs.text: The temple economy had its excluded. Its lands were cultivated largely by tenants and labourers, many of them from castes that were forbidden to enter the temple they supported. The women dedicated to the temple as dancers and ritual specialists (devadāsīs) held recognised rights and property in the medieval period, but their position declined over the following centuries, and by the nineteenth century dedication was widely associated with concubinage and exploitation; the practice was prohibited in the Madras Presidency by an Act of 1947. The movements for temple entry in the twentieth century, among whose successes was the Travancore proclamation of 1936, are discussed in Volume 24, Samanvaya. The temple’s wealth was redistributed, but along lines that reproduced the hierarchy of the society around it.

docs.title: 9.4 Temple Wealth and Its Hazards
docs.text:
The wealth that temples accumulated — gold and silver vessels, jewels for the images, coin from offerings — was not only invested; much of it was stored. Temple treasuries withdrew precious metal from circulation, and in a crisis they were an obvious reserve for rulers who needed money. The Kashmiri chronicle Rājataraṅgiṇī of Kalhaṇa (1148–49) describes how King Harṣa of Kashmir (r. 1089–1101), short of funds for his wars and his court, appointed an officer to strip the temples of their metal images, and Kalhaṇa condemns him for it. Temples were also targets in war between Indian kings, who carried off the images and treasures of their rivals’ shrines as trophies.

The raids of Maḥmūd of Ghazna into north India between about 1000 and 1027, culminating in the sack of the temple of Somanātha in 1026, are the best-known example of the plunder of temple wealth; the treasure was carried to Ghazna and helped to finance Maḥmūd’s state. Romila Thapar has shown how differently the event was remembered in Persian chronicles, Sanskrit inscriptions and later nationalist writing (Thapar 2004). Richard Eaton’s survey of the evidence for the desecration of temples under Indo-Muslim states between the twelfth and the eighteenth centuries argues that most recorded cases concerned temples closely associated with the authority of enemy kings, attacked in the course of conquest or rebellion, and that the practice continued an older pattern in which Indian kings had seized the state deities of their rivals (Eaton 2000). The argument remains debated, but it is agreed that the concentration of wealth in temples made them both economic and political targets.

The risk did not end with the medieval period. The East India Company’s administration of the finances of the temple at Purī in the early nineteenth century, and the later supervision of temple funds by government boards (Section 9.10), raised the same question in a new form: who was entitled to the wealth given to a god? The treasure recorded when the vaults of the Padmanābhasvāmī temple at Thiruvananthapuram were opened under the supervision of the Supreme Court in 2011 showed how much could still be held in a single shrine; how such holdings should be valued, guarded and used is a question of law and religion that the courts have answered case by case.

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Economy of the Tīrtha
docs.text: Pilgrimage has been one of the great movers of people in South Asia, and pilgrims were also customers, carriers and traders. The geography of pilgrimage and its literature are treated in Volume 21, Bhūgola; its economic side is considered here. A pilgrimage place (tīrtha) supported a resident population of priests and pilgrims’ guides, lodging-keepers, boatmen, barbers, sellers of flowers, images and ritual goods, and makers of the souvenirs that pilgrims carried home. At Gayā, where Hindus perform the rites for the dead (śrāddha), the hereditary Gayāwāl priests held the exclusive right to officiate and lived on the fees and gifts of pilgrims; L. P. Vidyarthi’s study of the “sacred complex” of Gayā described the organisation of this priestly community and its clients (Vidyarthi 1961). At Haridvār, Prayāga, Banaras and other centres the pilgrims’ guides (paṇḍās) kept registers in which generations of a family’s visits were recorded, so that a pilgrim’s descendants returned to the same guide. At Purī the temple kitchens of Jagannātha cooked food offerings on a very large scale, and the consecrated food was sold to pilgrims in the temple’s own market.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Fairs and Trade
docs.text: Many pilgrimage festivals were also great fairs (melās). The fair held at Sonpur, at the confluence of the Gaṇḍak and the Ganges, at the full moon of Kārttika was famous for its trade in cattle, horses and elephants; the fair at Puṣkar in the same month for camels and cattle; and the bathing festivals at Haridvār drew horse-dealers from the north-west as well as pilgrims. Such fairs were, in effect, periodic markets on a regional or supra-regional scale, timed by the religious calendar and protected by the sanctity of the occasion. Rulers taxed them, and merchants used them to buy and sell, collect debts and settle accounts. The connection between festival and market was old: the Tamil poems and the Buddhist texts already describe festival crowds as occasions of trade (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 9.5.3 Taxing the Pilgrim
docs.text: Because pilgrims were numerous and their movements predictable, states taxed them. Sultanate and Mughal rulers levied dues on Hindu pilgrims at the major centres; Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax in 1563, early in the reign, as part of the measures by which he sought the support of his non-Muslim subjects, and Abū al-Faḍl presents the decision as a matter of principle. The East India Company, inheriting the practice from earlier rulers in several places, levied pilgrim taxes at Purī, Gayā and Prayāga in the early nineteenth century and for a time supervised the finances of the Jagannātha temple, until evangelical criticism of its “connection with idolatry” led to the abolition of the taxes in 1840 (Volume 21, Bhūgola). The episode shows how large the revenue of pilgrimage could be, and how difficult it was for a state to treat it as an ordinary source of income.

docs.title: 9.5.4 The Hajj
docs.text: The pilgrimage to Mecca linked India’s ports to the Red Sea. Surat, the Mughal empire’s principal port in the seventeenth century, was known as the “gate of Mecca”, and the annual pilgrim ships, some of them owned by the emperor and his family, carried goods as well as passengers; the capture of the imperial ship Ganj-i Sawāʾī in 1695 (Chapter 18) was a blow both to the Hajj and to trade. Akbar appointed an officer to lead the annual pilgrim caravan and sent large sums for distribution in Mecca and Medina, and members of the imperial family, among them his aunt Gulbadan Begam, made the pilgrimage. Pilgrims financed their journeys by carrying goods for sale, and the Hajj season shaped the shipping calendar of the western Indian Ocean alongside the monsoon (Chapter 14) (Pearson 2003; Das Gupta 1979).

docs.title: 9.6 Public Works as Gift: Iṣṭa and Pūrta
docs.text:
Much of what a modern state provides through taxation was provided in pre-modern India through gifts. The dharmaśāstra tradition distinguished two kinds of meritorious act: iṣṭa, the sacrifices and gifts offered in ritual, and pūrta, works of public benefit — the digging of wells and tanks, the building of temples and rest-houses, the planting of gardens and groves, and the distribution of food. The Purāṇas and the digests praise pūrta as open to all, including those not entitled to perform Vedic sacrifices, and the medieval digests devote sections to the merit of each kind of work (Kane 1930).

The inscriptions show the doctrine in practice. Kings, queens, ministers, merchants and village assemblies recorded the excavation of tanks and wells, the endowment of water stalls (prapā) on roads, and the foundation of feeding houses for travellers and pilgrims. In Gujarat the monumental step-wells (vāv) were among the most ambitious of these works: the Rāṇī kī Vāv at Pāṭaṇ is traditionally attributed to a Caulukya queen of the eleventh century, and the step-well at Aḍālaj near Ahmadābād bears an inscription of 1499 recording its construction by a queen, Rūḍā; a second step-well of the same year in Ahmadābād was built by a lady of the sultan’s household. In the south, rest-houses with free kitchens (chatrams) were endowed along the pilgrim routes, and the Maratha rulers of Thanjavur built a series of them on the road to Rāmeśvaram in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Muslim rulers and nobles built wells, sarāʾīs and bridges as charitable works, often endowed as waqf; the network of rest-houses on the roads is described in Chapter 10, and the architecture of wells and tanks in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa.

For the economic historian, the significance of this tradition lies in how infrastructure was financed and maintained. A tank or a well built as a gift was usually endowed with land or money for its upkeep, and its maintenance depended on the endowment being managed honestly and on the continued interest of the donor’s family or the local community. Where these held, such works lasted for centuries; where they failed, the works silted up or fell into ruin. Colonial officials who surveyed the tanks of south India in the nineteenth century found many of them in disrepair and debated whether the state or the village should restore them, a debate that continues in the management of tank irrigation today (Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna).

docs.title: 9.7 Islamic Endowments and Sufi Shrines
docs.text:
Islamic law provided its own instrument for permanent religious and charitable giving, the waqf: property, usually land, buildings or shops, made inalienable and dedicated in perpetuity to a pious or charitable purpose, such as the upkeep of a mosque, a school (madrasa), a Sufi hospice or a public fountain, with a manager (mutawallī) to administer it. A waqf could also provide for the founder’s descendants, on condition that the benefit passed ultimately to a charitable purpose. In India, as elsewhere in the Islamic world, endowed markets and shops were often attached to mosques and shrines, so that the commercial life of a town and the support of its religious institutions were bound together.

The Delhi sultans and the Mughals also supported religious men and institutions through revenue grants. Under the Mughals the madad-i maʿāsh (“aid for subsistence”) was a grant of the revenue of a small area of land to scholars, holy men, the heads of Sufi hospices and their families, and sometimes to widows; it was administered by the ṣadr, the officer in charge of religious grants. Such grants were made to Hindus as well as Muslims, and Irfan Habib noted that their holders often became petty landholders who invested in cultivation (Habib 1999).

The shrines of Sufi saints were centres of a distinctive economy. The dargāh of Muʿīn al-Dīn Chishtī at Ajmer, which Akbar visited repeatedly, received land grants and gifts from emperors, nobles and ordinary pilgrims of every faith; its hereditary attendants (khādims) lived on offerings, and the communal kitchen (laṅgar) fed visitors from the two great cauldrons that are said to have been given by Akbar and Jahangir. The annual death-anniversary festival (ʿurs) of a saint was also a fair, at which pilgrims, traders and performers gathered. P. M. Currie’s study of the Ajmer shrine traces how its endowments, its hereditary servants and the imperial patronage it received developed over the centuries (Currie 1989). As with Hindu temples, the shrine’s income was redistributed in food, hospitality and patronage, and its control was a matter of status and frequent dispute.

docs.title: 9.8 The Sikh Gurdwārā and the Langar
docs.text:
The Sikh community developed its own economic institutions from the time of the early Gurus. The communal kitchen (laṅgar), associated with Guru Nānak’s settlement at Kartārpur and organised by his successors, fed all who came, and the obligation to sit and eat in a common line regardless of caste was one of its central meanings; Sikh tradition relates that Akbar ate in the laṅgar at Goindvāl before meeting Guru Amar Dās. The upkeep of the laṅgar and of the growing community was met by offerings, and Sikhs were expected to give a tenth of their income (dasvandh). From the time of the fourth and fifth Gurus the offerings were collected by appointed representatives (masands), who brought them to the Guru at the great festivals. As the masands became powerful and, in the view of the later tradition, corrupt, Guru Gobind Singh abolished the institution, an act the tradition associates with the founding of the Khālsā, traditionally dated 1699 (Grewal 1990).

The control of gurdwārā property became a political question in the colonial period. Many shrines had passed under the management of hereditary custodians (mahants), some of whom treated them as private property. The Gurdwara Reform Movement of 1920–1925 sought to bring them under the control of the community, and after a long and sometimes violent struggle the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 placed the principal shrines of the Punjab under an elected body, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra). The laṅgar of the Golden Temple at Amritsar, which feeds very large numbers every day, is today the best-known example of a religious institution redistributing resources on a massive scale.

docs.title: 9.9 Christian and Parsi Institutions
docs.text:
The smaller religious communities built economic institutions of their own. The Syrian Christian churches of Kerala held lands and received offerings, and their trustees, drawn from the leading families of each parish, managed church property much as temple trustees managed the property of deities; the merchant privileges granted to the Christians of Kollam in the ninth century are discussed in Section 4.7. The Portuguese brought the religious orders of Catholic Europe. In Goa and the Estado’s other territories the Jesuits, Franciscans, Dominicans and Augustinians acquired villages, rice lands and coconut groves by grant and purchase, and lived on their rents. The Jesuits were among the largest of these corporate landholders, and when the Portuguese crown expelled the order from its dominions in 1759 their estates were confiscated (Subrahmanyam 1993). Protestant missions of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, beginning with the Danish mission at Tranquebar, financed schools, presses and hospitals partly from abroad and partly from local endowments.

The Parsi community of western India developed an especially rich tradition of charitable trusts. The Parsi panchāyat of Bombay, which emerged in the eighteenth century as the community’s governing body, came to administer funds for fire temples, the towers of silence, housing for poor Parsis and relief of the needy. In the nineteenth century the great Parsi merchants of the China trade (Chapter 19) turned much of their wealth into trusts: Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy, the first Indian to be made a baronet, endowed hospitals, schools and relief funds, and later the Tata family founded the trusts that financed the Indian Institute of Science at Bangalore (Palsetia 2001). Parsi philanthropy, organised through trust deeds and managed by trustees under English law, became a model for the modern charitable trusts of other Indian communities, and it shows how the old idea of meritorious giving was adapted to the legal forms of the colonial city (Birla 2009).

docs.title: 9.10.1 Colonial Regulation
docs.text:
Pre-colonial rulers had protected, endowed, taxed and occasionally plundered religious institutions, but they had rarely administered them. The East India Company at first took over the supervisory role of the rulers it replaced. Bengal Regulation XIX of 1810 and Madras Regulation VII of 1817 gave the Boards of Revenue a general superintendence over religious and charitable endowments, to prevent their misappropriation. Evangelical opinion in Britain objected to a Christian government managing Hindu and Muslim shrines, and the Religious Endowments Act of 1863 withdrew the government from direct management, transferring it to committees and trustees subject to the civil courts.

The courts then became the main arena. They had to decide who owned temple property, who could manage it and on what terms, and in doing so they recognised the installed deity as a juristic person that could own property through a human manager (Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra). Islamic endowments followed a parallel course. In 1894 the Privy Council held that a waqf whose benefit went mainly to the founder’s family, with charity only as a remote final purpose, was invalid; Muslim opinion protested, and the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act of 1913 restored the validity of family endowments (Kozlowski 1985). Colonial law on charitable trusts and income tax, as Ritu Birla has shown, drew a line between “public” charity, which received legal and fiscal privileges, and the “private” religious giving of family firms, which was treated with suspicion (Birla 2009).

From the 1920s the provincial governments, now partly under Indian ministers, returned to direct supervision. The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act of 1926–27, passed by a Justice Party ministry, created a statutory board with power to supervise temple finances, settle schemes of management and apply surplus funds to religious, educational and charitable purposes. Its successor, the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act of 1951, created a government department that still administers many thousands of temples in Tamil Nadu. Comparable laws followed in other states, and the Wakf Act of 1954 set up boards for Islamic endowments.

docs.title: 9.10.2 Debates
docs.text: State supervision of religious endowments has been controversial since its beginnings. Its defenders argued that trustees and hereditary managers misused vast properties, that temple wealth should serve the public, and that reform of temple practice, including the admission of all castes, required the authority of the state. Its critics have argued that it subjects religious institutions to political control, diverts their income, and applies to Hindu institutions a regime not applied equally to those of other religions. The constitutional and legal questions are treated in Volume 18 and the ritual ones in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. For the economic historian, the long history traced in this chapter explains why the question matters: religious institutions have been, from the Buddhist monastery to the modern temple board, among the largest holders of land and liquid wealth in South Asia, and whoever controls them controls a significant part of the economy of the places in which they stand.

docs.title: 9.11 Assessment
docs.text: Monasteries, churches and waqfs played comparable roles in medieval Europe and the Islamic world; what was unusual in South Asia was the number of religious economies working side by side. Their history cuts two ways. Temples managed endowments but were not banks (Chapter 6), and religious giving was never pure piety detached from interest: the inscriptions show that gifts to gods and monks were among the principal ways in which rulers, merchants and landholders turned wealth into authority, and that the benefits of religious wealth were distributed according to rank.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the theory of the gift, Heim (2004); on the digests, Kane (1930). For Buddhist monastic economies see Schopen (2004) and, for Sri Lanka, Gunawardana (1979); for Jain giving, Laidlaw (1995) and Cort (2001). On the south Indian temple, Stein (1960), Appadurai and Breckenridge (1976), Heitzman (1997) and Appadurai (1981); on temple towns, Champakalakshmi (1996); on temple wealth and war, Thapar (2004) and Eaton (2000). For a pilgrimage centre, Vidyarthi (1961). On colonial law and religious giving, Birla (2009).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Overland Trade: Routes, Caravans and Trans-Asian Networks
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Most of the goods exchanged in pre-modern South Asia moved by road and river, not by sea. This chapter follows the overland routes within the subcontinent, above all the northern route (Uttarāpatha) and the southern route (Dakṣiṇāpatha), and the river systems that complemented them. It then looks at the people and institutions of overland trade: the caravan (sārtha) and its leader (sārthavāha), tolls, market towns, rest-houses and, in later centuries, the banjārā bulk carriers. The second half turns to the routes beyond the Hindu Kush, the so-called Silk Roads, the role of the Kuṣāṇas and of Buddhist monasteries, and the Indian merchant communities that lived and traded in Central Asia, Iran and Russia into the eighteenth century. A further section follows the routes across the Himalaya and through the north-east to Burma and Yunnan.

The chapter draws on four kinds of evidence: normative texts such as the Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2); narrative literature, especially the Pali Jātakas; inscriptions; and archaeology, supplemented by Greek, Chinese and Persian accounts. Each has its limits. The Arthaśāstra prescribes what a king’s officers ought to do and is not a description of Mauryan practice; the Jātaka stories are moral tales whose settings are conventional (caravans of “five hundred carts” are a stock formula); and the distribution of an artefact does not by itself tell us who carried it or why. The classic synthesis remains Moti Chandra’s Trade and Trade Routes in Ancient India (Chandra 1977), now supplemented by Nayanjot Lahiri’s archaeology of the early routes and by the work of Ranabir Chakravarti and Himanshu Prabha Ray (Lahiri 1992; Chakravarti 2002; Ray 1986). Seaborne trade, including the Indo-Roman trade and the sea routes sometimes called the “maritime Silk Road”, is treated in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 10.1 The Geography of Overland Trade
docs.text:
The physical geography of the subcontinent channelled overland movement into a limited number of corridors. The alluvial plains of the Indus and the Ganga offered the easiest going, and the long corridor between them, through the Panjab and the Ganga–Yamunā Doab, carried the greatest volume of traffic in most periods. Between the northern plains and the peninsula lay a broad belt of difficult country: the Thar desert to the west, the Aravalli hills, the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, and the forested uplands of central and eastern India. Routes crossed this belt along river valleys and through a few well-known gaps, which therefore became sites of towns, forts and toll posts (Deloche 1993).

To the north-west, the mountain wall of the Hindu Kush, the Sulaiman range and the Karakoram was pierced by passes that linked the Indus plain with Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia: the Khyber route from the Peshawar valley to Kabul; the Gomal and Bolan routes leading to Ghazni, Qandahar and the Iranian plateau; and higher, more seasonal tracks through Swat, Chitral, Gilgit and the upper Indus. Through these passes came horses, lapis lazuli, dried fruit, woollens and, later, silk; in the other direction went Indian cotton cloth, spices, indigo, sugar and other goods (Liu 2010; Deloche 1993).

In the peninsula, the Narmadā and Tāptī valleys opened an east–west corridor from Mālwa to the Gujarat coast, while the passes (ghāṭs) of the Western Ghats linked the Deccan plateau to the ports of the Konkan. On the east, routes crossed the Chhotanagpur plateau and followed the Mahānadī towards the coast of Kaliṅga, and from there ran south along the coastal plain to the Kṛṣṇā–Godāvarī delta and the Kāverī country (Ray 1986; Deloche 1993).

Climate set the rhythm of travel. During the south-west monsoon (roughly June to September) rivers flooded, unmetalled roads turned to mud and long-distance land traffic largely stopped. Caravans normally set out after the rains, when the roads had dried and fodder was plentiful, and tried to complete their journeys before the heat of April and May made water scarce on the drier routes. Monks of the Buddhist and Jain orders were similarly required to stay in one place during the rains, a rule that reflects the same conditions (Deloche 1993).

docs.title: 10.2.1 The Northern Route
docs.text:
Early Buddhist and Sanskrit texts use Uttarāpatha, “the northern route”, both for a road and, by extension, for the north-west region it led to; Dakṣiṇāpatha, “the southern route”, likewise came to mean the country of the Deccan, and the modern name “Deccan” derives from it (Chandra 1977). In its fullest extent the Uttarāpatha ran from Gandhāra, with its cities of Puṣkalāvatī (Charsadda) and Takṣaśilā (Taxila), across the Panjab and the Doab to Mathurā, then down the Ganga valley through Kauśāmbī and Vārāṇasī to the cities of Magadha (Rājagṛha and, later, Pāṭaliputra), and on to the port of Tāmralipti in the Ganga delta. Branches led north into Kashmir and north-west across the passes to Kabul and Bactria (Chandra 1977; Chakravarti 2002).

This route is not the ancestor of the Grand Trunk Road in any institutional sense. The route followed by the great road built or rebuilt by Sher Shāh Sūr (r. 1540–1545) from Bengal to the Indus, sometimes called Sarak-i Aʿẓam (“the great road”) and maintained by the Mughals, ran along much the same natural corridor; the British metalled it in the nineteenth century and named it the Grand Trunk Road (Deloche 1993). The alignment persisted because the geography did, not because a single road was maintained continuously for two thousand years. Table 10.1 lists some principal stations on the two routes.

Table 10.1. Some principal stations on the Uttarāpatha and Dakṣiṇāpatha (early historic period) Ancient name Modern site Role in overland trade Takṣaśilā Taxila, Pakistan Gateway to Afghanistan and Central Asia Śākala Sialkot, Pakistan Panjab city; capital of the Indo-Greek king Menander in the Milindapañha Mathurā Mathura, Uttar Pradesh Junction of the northern route and the road to Mālwa and the west coast Kauśāmbī near Prayagraj Ganga–Yamunā city; river and road junction Vārāṇasī Varanasi Textile centre; river port Pāṭaliputra Patna Mauryan capital; river port at the Ganga–Son confluence Tāmralipti Tamluk, West Bengal Port linking the Ganga valley to the Bay of Bengal Vidiśā Besnagar, near Vidisha Junction in eastern Mālwa Ujjayinī Ujjain Capital of Avanti; crossroads of north–south and east–west routes Pratiṣṭhāna Paithan, Maharashtra Sātavāhana city on the Godāvarī Bharukaccha Bharuch, Gujarat Port at the Narmadā mouth (Greek Barygaza)

docs.title: 10.2.2 The Southern Route
docs.text:
The Dakṣiṇāpatha left the Ganga valley either from Kauśāmbī or from Pāṭaliputra and crossed into Mālwa by way of Vidiśā to Ujjayinī. From Ujjayinī one branch went west to the Narmadā mouth at Bharukaccha, and another south across the Narmadā and the Tāptī to Pratiṣṭhāna on the Godāvarī and onward through the Deccan (Figure 10.1). The Pali Sutta Nipāta, in the prologue to its Pārāyana section, describes the journey of a group of disciples from the Godāvarī country northward through Pratiṣṭhāna, Ujjayinī, Vidiśā and Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī and Magadha, a narrative that has long been used to reconstruct the stations of this route (Chandra 1977).

The Periplus Maris Erythraei (mid-first century CE) shows how the inland routes fed the western ports. It names Ozēnē (Ujjayinī) as a former royal capital from which goods were brought down to Barygaza, and describes Paithana (Pratiṣṭhāna) and Tagara (Ter) as inland markets from which goods were carried to Barygaza by wagon over difficult roads (Casson 1989). The overland and the maritime systems were thus parts of one network, a point taken up in Chapter 11.

East of the Deccan plateau, routes ran from Magadha and Kaliṅga down the coastal plain to the lower Kṛṣṇā, where the Buddhist centre of Amarāvatī and its neighbouring town of Dhānyakaṭaka stood, and on into the Tamil country. Further west, routes descended from the plateau to the Konkan ports of Sopārā and Kalyāṇa through passes such as the Nāṇeghāṭ, at the head of which the Sātavāhana inscriptions of queen Nāganikā were cut (Ray 1986).

Figure 10.1. Sketch map of the main overland routes of the early historic period, c. 300 BCE–300 CE. Places are plotted at their approximate latitude and longitude; the coastline is the simplified one used for the maps of this series, and no rivers or boundaries are shown. Puṣkalāvatī and Takṣaśilā stand for Gandhāra, Tosalī, the Mauryan provincial seat, for Kaliṅga, and Pratiṣṭhāna and Tagara for the Deccan markets that fed Barygaza. The lines show connections, not the courses of actual roads.

docs.title: 10.2.3 Choosing a Route: The Arthaśāstra’s View
docs.text: A passage in the seventh book of the Arthaśāstra (AŚ 7.12) offers a rare piece of explicit reasoning about trade routes, set out, as the text often does, as a debate between earlier teachers and “Kauṭilya”. The teachers prefer the water route to the land route because it costs less effort and expense and yields more goods; the text replies that a water route is liable to obstruction, cannot be used in all seasons, is a source of great danger and offers no remedy when things go wrong, whereas a land route has the opposite qualities. In the same passage the teachers prefer the route towards the Himālaya, which brings elephants, horses, perfumes, ivory, hides, silver and gold of high value; the text instead prefers the southern route because, blankets, hides and horses apart, it is richer in goods, above all conch shells, diamonds, precious stones, pearls and gold. It goes on to rank routes by whether they pass through mines, are well frequented and are cheap to use (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013). Whatever its date, the passage shows that the Dakṣiṇāpatha was regarded as a source of high-value goods in its own right, not merely an extension of the northern trade.

docs.title: 10.3 Rivers and Inland Waterways
docs.text:
For bulk goods, rivers were usually cheaper than roads. The Ganga and its tributaries, the Yamunā, the Ghāghra, the Gaṇḍak and the Son, formed the most important system of navigable waterways in the subcontinent, and the Indus with its Panjab tributaries a second. Jean Deloche’s survey of transport before the railway devotes a full volume to water transport, documenting the variety of river craft, the ferries and pontoon crossings, and the seasonal limits of navigation (Deloche 1993). Navigation was easiest when the rivers were high, but floods and shifting channels made the monsoon season dangerous; in the dry months the upper reaches of many rivers became too shallow for laden boats.

The Arthaśāstra assigns to a superintendent of shipping (nāvadhyakṣa, AŚ 2.28) responsibility for ferries, boat hire and charges on river traffic, and for the safety of navigation, which shows that river traffic was regarded as a source of revenue to be regulated (Olivelle 2013). Jātaka stories describe merchants travelling by boat along the Ganga and setting out from the river ports of Vārāṇasī and Campā (near Bhagalpur) for the sea; in the Mahājanaka Jātaka, for example, the hero takes ship from Campā for Suvaṇṇabhūmi (Chakravarti 2002). Several of the great early historic cities, Pāṭaliputra, Vārāṇasī, Kauśāmbī and Campā among them, stood on river banks at points where road and river traffic met.

The Narmadā, which flows west into the Gulf of Khambhat, was navigable only in parts but gave its name to a corridor along which towns such as Māhiṣmatī grew; the Godāvarī, Kṛṣṇā and Kāverī were less used for long-distance navigation than the Ganga but were followed by roads and settlements. River transport remained central in later centuries. European travellers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries describe large convoys of boats carrying salt, grain, sugar, cotton and other goods between Agra, Allahabad, Patna and Bengal, and Bengal’s rivers carried much of its rice, sugar and textiles to the ports (Deloche 1993; Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

docs.title: 10.4 Caravans: The Sārtha and the Sārthavāha
10.4.1 The Caravan in the Jātakas
docs.text:
Long-distance overland trade was conducted by caravans, called sārtha in Sanskrit (Pali sattha), led by a sārthavāha (Pali satthavāha). Merchants travelled together for security and to share the costs of guides, guards and draught animals. The Jātakas, whose prose commentary was compiled in Sri Lanka in the first millennium CE from older material, return to the caravan again and again, and in several stories the Bodhisatta himself is born as a caravan leader (Chakravarti 2002; Chandra 1977).

Two stories at the very beginning of the collection give a sense of the risks. In the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka (no. 1), two caravans set out across a waterless wilderness; the leader of the first is persuaded by demons disguised as travellers to throw away his water, and his caravan perishes, while the Bodhisatta’s caravan, which keeps its water, survives. In the Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka (no. 2), a caravan crosses a sandy desert by night, guided by a “land-pilot” who steers by the stars; when the pilot falls asleep the caravan goes in a circle, and it is saved only by digging for water. Behind the moral lessons lie realistic details: night marches in hot country, the carrying of water and fodder in carts, professional guides, and the constant danger of robbers in forest country (Chandra 1977).

The caravan was not an egalitarian body. Its leader and the principal merchants owned the goods and the capital; carters, drovers, guards and servants were hired, and the Jātakas and the law books mention slaves (dāsa) among the workers of merchant households. The Arthaśāstra and the later dharmaśāstras treat merchants who travel together as a kind of partnership, with rules for sharing profits and losses; these rules are discussed in Chapters 4 and 6.

docs.title: 10.4.2 The Sārthavāha in Inscriptions
docs.text: The sārthavāha also appears in inscriptions, which show that caravan leaders could hold a recognised civic position: the Gupta-period sealings from Vaiśālī name a joint body of bankers, caravan traders and artisans, and the Damodarpur copper plates from north Bengal place the chief caravan trader (prathama-sārthavāha) on the district council that approved land sales (Sections 4.6.1 and 4.6.3) (Chakravarti 2002; Thaplyal 1996).

docs.title: 10.4.3 Bulk Carriers: The Banjārās
docs.text: The caravans of the Jātakas carried mostly high-value goods. For the bulk trade in grain and salt in later centuries, the essential carriers were the banjārās, communities of pack-bullock owners who moved in large camps (ṭāṇḍā) with their families and herds, buying grain where it was cheap and selling it where it was dear. Irfan Habib’s study of Mughal India shows how the banjārās made possible the long-distance movement of grain on which the cities and armies depended; European travellers of the seventeenth century, such as Peter Mundy, describe meeting banjārā caravans of many thousands of oxen (Habib 1999). Because pack oxen could graze along the way and needed no roads suitable for wheeled carts, the banjārās could reach places carts could not, though their movement was slow and depended on fodder and water. They also supplied armies on campaign, a role they continued to play into the colonial period. In the colonial period the coming of the railways undermined their trade, and some banjārā groups were stigmatised by colonial legislation; their later history belongs to Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: 10.5 Tolls, Passes and Protection
docs.text:
Every state through which a caravan passed expected a share of its goods. The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of tolls (śulkādhyakṣa, AŚ 2.21–22) sets up a toll house at the city gate; merchants declare the quantity and price of their goods; goods bear a seal, and those found without the proper seal or with false declarations are penalised by a multiple of the duty. Rates are graded by class of commodity, and some goods, such as those for sacrifices or for weddings, are exempted. The frontier officer (antapāla) collects a road cess and is required to make good goods lost to robbers within his territory (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013). These rules are normative and their date is uncertain, but they reflect a recurrent pattern: a state that taxed trade also undertook, at least in principle, to protect it.

In practice, tolls multiplied wherever political authority was fragmented. Mughal emperors repeatedly forbade the road toll known as rāhdārī, yet the repetition of the orders and the complaints of merchants and European travellers suggest that local officials and chiefs continued to levy it (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). Market dues, toll administration and state regulation of exchange are treated more fully in Chapter 7.

docs.title: 10.6 Market Towns and Nodes of Exchange
docs.text:
Trade routes connected settlements of very different size and function. Early Buddhist texts call a market town a nigama, and in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta the Buddha foretells that the village of Pāṭaligāma will become a chief city and a puṭabhedana, a place where bales of goods are opened, that is, a trading centre (Chakravarti 2002). At Taxila, local copper coins carrying the word negama were probably issued by a mercantile body of the town (Allan 1936).

The Arthaśāstra (AŚ 2.1) sets out a schematic hierarchy for a planned countryside, with central places of increasing size for groups of villages. It is an administrative ideal rather than a description of any real kingdom, but it shows how the authors imagined the relation between villages, market centres and the capital (Olivelle 2013). Table 10.2 gives the terms.

Table 10.2. Settlement terms for central places in the Arthaśāstra (AŚ 2.1), a schematic scheme Term Prescribed scale Notes saṃgrahaṇa for 10 villages Lowest collection centre khārvaṭika for 200 villages Small town droṇamukha for 400 villages Often taken to mean a town at a river mouth or confluence sthānīya for 800 villages Major administrative and commercial centre

Inscriptions supply a more concrete picture. The donors recorded at the stūpas of Bharhut and Sāñcī, and at the rock-cut monasteries of the western Deccan, often name their home towns, and the spread of these places shows which centres were linked to each other (Lüders 1912; Ray 1986). Large cities such as Mathurā, Ujjayinī, Pratiṣṭhāna and Pāṭaliputra stood at junctions of routes, combined royal administration with markets and craft production, and housed the bankers and money-changers on whom long-distance trade depended. In the early medieval period, a dense network of smaller market centres (haṭṭa, maṇḍapikā) grew up in many regions; B. D. Chattopadhyaya has argued that this reflects local and regional exchange expanding, not the general decay of trade and towns that some historians proposed for c. 300–1000 CE (Chattopadhyaya 1994; Sharma 1987).

docs.title: 10.7.1 Pottery and Coins
docs.text:
The Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), a fine, glossy pottery associated with the rise of cities in the Ganga valley from about the sixth century BCE (its beginning is variously dated between the seventh and fifth centuries) to the second century BCE, is found from the north-west to Bengal and at sites in central India and the Deccan. Its wide distribution is commonly linked to the spread of urban networks along the routes described in the texts. The ware’s spread may, however, reflect local imitation and the movement of potters as well as trade in the vessels themselves, so it is evidence of connection rather than a direct measure of commerce (Allchin 1995).

Punch-marked silver coins, issued from about the fifth or fourth century BCE, are found in hoards across much of the subcontinent, and the Chaman Hazouri and Bhir Mound hoards, which contain datable Greek coins, show that coined money was circulating in the north-western trade by the late fourth century BCE (Section 5.2).

docs.title: 10.7.2 Taxila and Ujjayinī
docs.text: Taxila, excavated by John Marshall and later archaeologists, has three successive city sites: the Bhir Mound (from about the sixth or fifth century BCE), Sirkap (the Indo-Greek and Śaka–Parthian city) and Sirsukh (the Kuṣāṇa city). Finds include coins of many dynasties, glass, metalwork and objects of Mediterranean and Central Asian origin, and they show a city that drew goods from both the Ganga valley and the lands beyond the passes (Allchin 1995; Thapar 2002). Ujjayinī, the capital of Avanti, was enclosed by a massive earthen rampart early in its history and was one of the major cities of the early historic period; its role as a meeting point of routes is confirmed by the Periplus and by the many references to it in Buddhist and Jain literature (Allchin 1995; Casson 1989).

docs.title: 10.7.3 Inscriptions along the Routes
docs.text:
The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) were cut at places that were evidently accessible: on routes, near towns and at frontier zones, from Kandahar in the west to Dhauli and Jaugaḍa in Kaliṅga in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills to Karnataka. Their distribution indicates the reach of Mauryan communications, though it cannot be read as a map of roads (Thapar 2002; Salomon 1998). Later, the rock-cut monasteries of the western Deccan, at Bhājā, Kārle (Figure 10.2), Junnar, Nāsik and Kānherī, were placed near the passes linking the Konkan ports to the plateau. Their donative inscriptions record gifts by merchants (vāṇija), guild heads (śreṣṭhin), artisans and Yavanas (Greeks or westerners), as well as by Sātavāhana and Western Kṣatrapa royalty, and they show monasteries and traders sharing the same routes (Ray 1986).

Figure 10.2. Interior of the great caitya hall at Kārle, with the stūpa at the end of the nave; photograph by Georg Morgenstierne, twentieth century. The donative inscriptions of the hall, like those of the other western Deccan monasteries, record gifts by merchants, artisans and Yavanas. Image: Georg Morgenstierne (National Library of Norway), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.8 Goods on the Roads
docs.text:
The overland trade rested on the complementary resources of different regions. The Ganga plains produced grain, sugar and cotton; central and eastern India supplied iron, copper, timber, lac and forest products; Rajasthan and the Deccan yielded precious and semi-precious stones; Gujarat and the western Deccan had cotton and carnelian and agate for beads; the south-western coast produced pepper and other spices; and the coasts supplied salt, a commodity every household needed and which therefore moved inland in great quantity (Chandra 1977; Chakravarti 2002). The north-west imported horses, which India’s climate made difficult to breed in quality, and exported textiles.

The texts show a wide range of named commodities. The Arthaśāstra’s chapters on the treasury and on the superintendent of commerce list gems, fine textiles, aromatics and metals, including a silk called cīnapaṭṭa, “Chinese cloth” (Kangle 1960). The Periplus names cottons, muslins and other goods brought to Barygaza from the interior, as well as nard and costus from the mountains of the north (Casson 1989). In later centuries the range widened: indigo from Bayana and Sarkhej, cotton cloth from Gujarat and Bengal, sugar, saltpetre and opium from Bihar, all moved overland and by river to inland markets and ports (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

docs.title: 10.9.1 Texts and Edicts
docs.text:
Most pre-modern roads in South Asia were earthen tracks, cleared and levelled rather than paved, and their maintenance depended on whoever controlled them. The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on laying out the fortified city (AŚ 2.4), prescribes widths for different classes of road (Olivelle 2013); such rules tell us what the authors thought proper, not what was built.

Aśoka’s own inscriptions are more direct. In Rock Edict II the king says that he has had wells dug and trees planted along the roads for the use of animals and men, and has provided for medical treatment and medicinal plants. In Pillar Edict VII he states that he has had banyan trees planted along the roads to give shade to animals and men, mango groves planted, wells dug at regular intervals (the distance is variously interpreted), rest-houses built, and watering places made in many places for the use of animals and men; he adds that such benefits had been provided by earlier kings too, and that his purpose was that people should follow the Dhamma (Thapar 2002; Salomon 1998). The edicts present these works as acts of moral welfare rather than commercial policy, but travellers and caravans were among those who used them.

The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who visited Pāṭaliputra around 300 BCE, survives only in quotations by later authors. According to Strabo’s summary (Geography 15.1.50), Megasthenes described a class of officials who, among other duties, built roads and set up pillars at intervals of ten stadia to show the by-roads and distances (McCrindle 1877). The report is second-hand and filtered through Greek categories, and it is no evidence of a surveyed or mapped road network; no maps from Mauryan India survive.

docs.title: 10.9.2 Monasteries, Dharmaśālās and Sarāʾīs
docs.text:
Religious institutions supplied much of the lodging along the routes. Buddhist monasteries in the western Deccan and in the north-west were sited on trade routes, and monks and merchants travelled the same roads; temple towns and pilgrimage centres later offered similar facilities, and rest-houses for travellers (dharmaśālā) were a common object of pious gifts. Under the Delhi sultans and the Mughals the sarāʾī, a walled enclosure with lodgings, stabling and a market, became the characteristic roadside institution. Sher Shāh is credited by Persian historians with building sarāʾīs at regular stages along his great road, and the Mughals built more, along with bridges and the kos mīnārs (distance pillars) that still stand along parts of the Agra–Lahore road (Deloche 1993; Richards 1993). Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who reached India in 1333, describes the Tughluq relay post of horse and foot runners, by which letters and goods reached the capital from distant provinces with great speed (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958).

Ferries were a constant feature of travel on the rivers of the north and east. They were a source of revenue for states and local lords, and the Arthaśāstra lists ferry charges. Permanent bridges over the large rivers were rare before the nineteenth century, and bridges of boats served on major routes (Deloche 1993).

docs.title: 10.10 Gandhāra, the Kuṣāṇas and the Silk Roads
10.10.1 The “Silk Road” as a Modern Term
docs.text: The term “Silk Road” (German Seidenstraße) was coined by the geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. It is convenient but misleading: silk was one commodity among many, there was no single road but a shifting web of routes linking oasis towns, and most goods travelled only short stages, changing hands many times. Valerie Hansen has stressed how much of the documented traffic was local and how important religious and diplomatic exchange was alongside commerce (Hansen 2012; Liu 2010). India’s connection with this web ran through the north-western passes.

docs.title: 10.10.2 Routes beyond the Passes
docs.text:
From Gandhāra, the main route crossed the Khyber to Kabul and then the Hindu Kush to Balkh (Bactra), the great junction of Bactria. From Balkh, one road led west through Merv into Iran; another north through Sogdiana to Samarkand; and others east over the Pamirs to Kashgar at the western end of the Tarim basin. Around the Taklamakan desert, routes ran north through Kucha and Turfan and south through Khotan and Niya, meeting near Dunhuang before entering China proper (Hansen 2012; Beckwith 2009). A more direct but very difficult route led from Gandhāra up the Indus gorges through Chilas and Gilgit to the Karakoram. Thousands of rock carvings and short inscriptions in Kharoṣṭhī, Brāhmī, Sogdian, Bactrian, Chinese and other scripts along the upper Indus, left by travellers, pilgrims and traders, show that this route was used over many centuries (Salomon 1998).

The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian, sent west by the Han emperor Wu, reported on his return around 126 BCE that he had seen in Bactria bamboo and cloth from Shu (Sichuan), which he was told had been brought from Shendu, that is India. His report is often taken as evidence that an indirect trade between south-west China, eastern India and Bactria already existed (Liu 2010).

docs.title: 10.10.3 The Kuṣāṇa Empire
docs.text:
The Kuṣāṇas, a dynasty of Central Asian origin, built in the first to third centuries CE an empire that stretched from Bactria across the Hindu Kush to Gandhāra and the Ganga plain as far as Mathurā and beyond. It thus brought under one authority the junction where the routes from Central Asia met those leading to the Indian interior and to the ports of the west coast. Kaniṣka I, the best known of its rulers, probably came to the throne in the 120s CE, although his date has long been debated (Beckwith 2009; Thapar 2002).

The Kuṣāṇas issued an abundant gold coinage, begun under Vima Kadphises, on a weight standard close to that of the Roman aureus; whether its gold came largely from melted Roman coin is debated. The coins carry Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist deities; a few of Kaniṣka’s coins show the Buddha with the Greek-script legend BODDO. This religious pluralism on the coinage is often linked to the empire’s role at a crossroads of peoples and traditions (Thapar 2002; Beckwith 2009). The rich finds made in 1937–1939 at Begram, north of Kabul, include Indian ivories, Roman bronzes and glass, and Chinese lacquer, assembled in sealed rooms of a building whose purpose (royal store, merchant’s warehouse or something else) and date are still discussed. They illustrate the range of goods that reached the region in the Kuṣāṇa period (Liu 2010).

docs.title: 10.11 Buddhism, Monasteries and Trade
docs.text:
The spread of Buddhism along the trade routes is one of the best-documented links between commerce and religion in Asian history. Buddhist texts treat trade as a legitimate occupation, and merchants were among the most prominent lay supporters of the order. The donative inscriptions at Bharhut and Sāñcī name householders, merchants and bankers among the donors (Lüders 1912), and in the western Deccan, as Himanshu Prabha Ray showed in Monastery and Guild, the location of monasteries near the passes and the frequency of mercantile donors point to a close relationship between the monastic establishments and the trade of the Sātavāhana period (Ray 1986). In a later study Ray extended the argument to the links between Buddhism and the maritime networks of early South Asia (Ray 1994).

Monasteries also handled money. Inscriptions record permanent endowments (akṣaya-nīvī) deposited with guilds, the interest on which was to provide for monks; the mechanics of these deposits are discussed in Chapter 6, and monasteries as economic institutions in Chapter 9.

Xinru Liu’s Ancient India and Ancient China argued that Buddhist devotion itself generated trade. The demand of Buddhist communities in China for relics and for the “seven treasures” (precious substances such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl and coral) used in worship, and the demand of Indian and Central Asian monasteries for silk for banners and robes, sustained a trade between India and China in the first six centuries CE (Liu 1988). Monasteries in Gandhāra and along the oasis routes, at Bāmiyān, Khotan, Kucha and Dunhuang, served as halting places for pilgrims and traders alike. Translators such as Kumārajīva (c. 344–413), born in Kucha to an Indian father, moved along these same routes, and Indian texts reached China in the baggage of merchants as well as monks (Foltz 2010).

Tansen Sen’s study of Sino-Indian relations from 600 to 1400 traces a change in this relationship. In the Tang period, Buddhism, diplomacy and trade were closely bound together; from about the eleventh century, as Buddhism declined in India and the Song state encouraged maritime commerce, exchange between India and China became increasingly commercial and increasingly maritime (Sen 2003). The Chinese pilgrims who travelled to India, among them Faxian (travelled 399–412), Xuanzang (629–645) and Yijing (671–695, by sea), left accounts that are valuable for the routes and towns they passed through; they are discussed in Volume 21, Bhūgola.

Note: Ideas along the routes

The routes carried ideas as well as goods: Buddhist texts and art, Indian astronomy and astrology (Indian astronomers served at the Tang court in the eighth century), medical knowledge and, by way of Iran and the Islamic world, the Indian decimal place-value numerals. Transmission was rarely one-way; Gandhāran art drew on Hellenistic and Iranian traditions, and India in turn received techniques and motifs from Iran and Central Asia. These exchanges are treated in Volume 11, Gaṇita, Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa, and Volume 14, Rasāyana (for crucible steel) (Foltz 2010; Liu 2010).

docs.title: 10.12 Indian Merchants beyond the Hindu Kush
10.12.1 Gāndhārī Documents and Sogdian Intermediaries
docs.text:
Some of the most direct evidence for Indian influence in Central Asia comes from the hundreds of documents in Kharoṣṭhī script found by Aurel Stein and others at Niya and near Loulan, on the southern edge of the Taklamakan. Written mostly on wooden tablets in the third and fourth centuries CE, they are the administrative and legal records of the kingdom of Shanshan (Kroraina), which used a Gāndhārī Prakrit as its official language. They deal with taxes, land, disputes and the movement of people and animals, and they show silk being used as a means of payment (Hansen 2012; Salomon 1998). They attest the reach of Gandhāran language and administrative practice rather than a large community of Indian traders, but they are part of the same network.

Much of the long-distance trade between Central Asia and China in the first millennium CE was in the hands of Sogdians from Samarkand, Bukhara and neighbouring cities. Their inscriptions on the upper Indus show that they also travelled towards India. One of the “Ancient Letters” written by Sogdian merchants in the early fourth century and found near Dunhuang reports that, after the sack of Luoyang in 311, the Indians and Sogdians there had died of starvation, a glimpse of Indian traders living in a Chinese city (Hansen 2012).

docs.title: 10.12.2 Indian Merchant Diasporas, c. 1500–1800
docs.text:
Overland trade between India, Iran and Central Asia remained important long after the first millennium.
