In the Sultanate and Mughal periods the most valuable import across the north-western passes was horses. Indian rulers needed large numbers of cavalry mounts and could not breed enough of the required quality at home, so horses came every year from Central Asia and Afghanistan through Kabul and Qandahar, while Persian and Arabian horses came by sea to the western ports (Levi 2002; Wink 1990). The trade in the other direction included Indian cotton textiles, indigo, sugar, spices and enslaved people taken from India, whom Central Asian sources record among the goods reaching Kabul and Bukhara (Levi 2002).

Stephen Dale and Scott Levi have reconstructed the history of the Indian merchant communities that carried much of this trade. From the sixteenth century, merchants and moneylenders from Multan and the Panjab, many of them Khatrīs, lived in towns across Iran, Afghanistan, Central Asia and southern Russia, organised through family firms based in India. They traded in Indian cloth and lent money, often to peasants and craftsmen, and they were active in Isfahan, Bukhara, Samarkand and many smaller towns. In the seventeenth century, Indian merchants were established at Astrakhan on the Volga, where the Russian authorities allowed them a trading house of their own (Dale 1994; Levi 2002). Armenian merchants of New Julfa, Afghan and Central Asian traders, and Persian firms shared these routes with them; no single community dominated the caravan trade.

docs.title: 10.13 The Himalaya and the North-East
docs.text:
The passes of the Hindu Kush were not the only overland links. The Himalaya, often imagined as a barrier, was crossed by many routes, from Ladakh in the west to Sikkim and Bhutan in the east, and beyond the Brahmaputra the hills of Assam and Manipur connected Bengal with Burma and Yunnan. This trade was small in value beside the caravan trade of the north-west, but it was old and persistent, and for the peoples of the mountains it was a main source of livelihood.

The Arthaśāstra already knows the Himalayan route as a source of high-value goods (Section 10.2.3), and among fine woollens it names a rain-proof blanket of Nepal (AŚ 2.11). In the seventh century the Tibetan empire opened a further way between India and China: the Tang envoy Wang Xuance reached India through Tibet and Nepal, and Buddhist monks and texts went the same way to Tibet (Sen 2003). The exchange rested on contrasting environments. The Tibetan plateau produced salt from its lakes, wool and the fine under-wool of goats (pashm), yak tails, musk, gold dust and borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), which goldsmiths used as a flux; the hills and plains sent back grain, cloth, sugar and metal goods. Communities living near the passes, among them the Bhoṭiyās of Kumaon and Garhwal and the Thakalis and Sherpas of Nepal, carried this trade and lived from it, exchanging Tibetan salt for hill grain in a seasonal cycle that Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf could still observe in the mid-twentieth century (Fürer-Haimendorf 1975).

The Kathmandu valley stood on the main route between the Gangetic plain and Lhasa. From the seventeenth century Newar merchants of the valley kept trading houses in Lhasa, and the Malla kings of the valley struck silver coins for circulation in Tibet. Quarrels over debased coin and over the trade contributed to war between the Gorkha state of Nepal and Tibet in 1788–1792, which ended only when a Qing army intervened. In the west, Leh in Ladakh was the entrepôt that linked Kashmir and the Punjab with western Tibet and with Yarkand in the Tarim basin. Its most valuable traffic was pashm from the Changthang plateau, carried to Kashmir for the shawl weavers. After a war between Tibet and Ladakh, in which Ladakh was helped by the Mughal governor of Kashmir, the treaty of Tingmosgang (1684) reserved the pashm trade to Ladakh and Kashmir and regulated the official missions between Leh and Lhasa. Janet Rizvi has reconstructed the caravans of this trade, in which great merchant houses and peasant traders took part, into the twentieth century (Rizvi 1999).

The East India Company looked to the Himalaya early. Warren Hastings sent George Bogle to the Panchen Lama at Tashilhunpo in 1774 in the hope of opening a trade route to Tibet, and British pressure culminated in the armed mission of 1903–1904 led by Francis Younghusband, after which trade marts were opened in Tibet at Gyantse, Yatung and Gartok. In the first half of the twentieth century Kalimpong was the chief market for Tibetan wool brought down over the Jelep La. That trade was cut off after 1959 and the war of 1962; a small border trade through the Nathu La was reopened in 2006.

To the east, the report of Zhang Qian that goods of Sichuan reached Bactria by way of India (Section 10.10.2) is the earliest hint of a route from south-western China to eastern India. The Ahom rulers of Assam came from upper Burma across the Patkai hills in the thirteenth century. Between Yunnan, Burma, Assam and Bengal moved horses, silver, salt and cloth, and from the Indian Ocean came cowries: Bin Yang has shown that cowries, brought from the Maldives by way of Bengal and Burma, served as money in Yunnan from about the ninth century to the seventeenth (Yang 2008). These routes were carried mainly by hill peoples and Yunnanese caravan traders, and in the colonial period the sea route across the Bay of Bengal overshadowed them.

docs.title: 10.14 Did Overland Trade Decline?
docs.text:
Debate: The “decline” of the overland routes

A common narrative holds that the overland Silk Roads declined from the tenth century, revived briefly under the Mongols and were then made obsolete, first by the growth of Indian Ocean shipping and finally by the Portuguese arrival in 1498 and the European companies. The narrative contains some truth. The bulk of India’s long-distance trade in textiles, rice, sugar and pepper went by sea, and maritime trade grew strongly from the late first millennium (Chapters 12 and 18).

But “decline” is the wrong word for the land routes. Within South Asia, the great majority of goods always moved by road and river, and the inland trade grew with the cities and armies of the Sultanate and Mughal periods. Across the passes, the evidence assembled by Dale (1994) and Levi (2002) shows that the caravan trade between India, Iran, Central Asia and Russia was large and growing in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, alongside the European seaborne trade rather than in competition with it. Central Asian horses, which could only come overland, kept the passes busy, and Indian merchant communities abroad flourished into the eighteenth century. Sea and land trade were complementary parts of the same commercial system; changes in their relative weight were real but gradual, and they varied by commodity and region (Sen 2003; Dale 1994; Levi 2002).

What did change, in the long run, was the political and technological setting. The fragmentation of the Mughal and Safavid states in the eighteenth century, the closing of Central Asian markets under Russian and British imperial rivalry, and above all the railways of the later nineteenth century reshaped Indian overland trade. The railways took over the bulk traffic of the banjārās and the river boats, and tied the interior to the colonial ports; this transformation is discussed in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the early routes, Chandra (1977) remains the standard survey, and Chakravarti (2002) the best collection of essays on traders and trade in early India; Ray (1986) links the Deccan routes to Buddhist monasteries. Deloche (1993) is indispensable for roads, rivers, vehicles and boats before the railways. Lahiri (1992) examines the archaeology of the routes before c. 200 BCE, and for the Himalaya Rizvi (1999) and Fürer-Haimendorf (1975) describe the trans-Himalayan trade. On the Silk Roads, Hansen (2012) and Liu (2010) are accessible introductions, while Liu (1988) and Sen (2003) treat India–China exchange in depth. For the later caravan trade and the Indian merchant diaspora, see Dale (1994) and Levi (2002), and for the banjārās and the Mughal economy Habib (1999).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Seaborne Trade from the Harappans to the Indo-Roman Trade
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter follows seaborne trade along the coasts of South Asia from the Harappan cities to about 600 CE. It begins with the Bronze Age exchange between the Indus region, the Gulf and Mesopotamia, and sets out the debate over the brick basin at Lothal. It then turns to the thin evidence of the following millennium, to the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts that speak of the sea, and to contacts with the Achaemenid and Hellenistic worlds. The centre of the chapter is the trade between India and Roman Egypt in the first centuries CE, known from the Periplus Maris Erythraei, from Pliny and Strabo, from the Muziris papyrus and from excavations on both sides of the Arabian Sea. The last sections look at Sri Lanka, Arabia and East Africa, the Bay of Bengal and early Southeast Asia, and the place of Buddhism in maritime exchange.

docs.title: 11.1 Sources and Their Limits
docs.text:
The evidence for early seaborne trade is uneven in time and in kind. For the third millennium BCE there are objects found far from where they were made (beads, seals, weights, pottery) and a small number of Mesopotamian texts. For most of the second and first millennia BCE the evidence is very thin. From about the third century BCE the sources multiply: Buddhist and Jain narrative literature, the Arthaśāstra and the dharma texts, Tamil poetry of the Caṅkam anthologies, Greek and Latin authors, and inscriptions. Excavations at ports on both sides of the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, many of them carried out since the 1980s, have transformed the picture for the centuries around the beginning of the Common Era (Ray 2003; Tomber 2008).

Each kind of source has its bias (Table 11.1). Archaeology, in particular, preserves pottery, beads and coins far better than pepper, textiles and timber, which made up much of what was shipped. Modern writing has its own distortions: Mookerji (1912) assembled every textual reference to ships into a picture of an ancient Indian maritime empire, while older European scholarship treated the Indo-Roman trade as a Roman enterprise with Indians as passive suppliers (Warmington 1928; Wheeler 1954). Recent work stresses that the ocean was shared by many groups of sailors and merchants (Ray 2003; Tomber 2008; Pearson 2003).

Table 11.1. Main kinds of evidence for seaborne trade before c. 600 CE Kind of evidence Examples Main limits Bronze Age artefacts Indus seals, carnelian beads and weights in Mesopotamia and the Gulf; Gulf seals at Lothal Few objects; route and agents usually invisible Mesopotamian texts References to Meluhha, Dilmun and Magan Identification of Meluhha is inferred; texts mention only what reached Mesopotamia Indian religious texts Ṛgveda, Jātakas, avadānas, Jain canonical narratives Hard to date; literary and didactic aims Normative texts Arthaśāstra, Dharmasūtras, Manusmṛti Prescriptions, not descriptions of practice Tamil poetry Caṅkam anthologies, Paṭṭiṉappālai Dating debated; poetic conventions Greek and Latin texts Periplus, Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy Western viewpoint; some figures rhetorical Documents Muziris papyrus; Tamil-Brāhmī graffiti in Egypt Rare and fragmentary Port archaeology Arikamedu, Pattanam, Berenike, Myos Hormos Perishable goods seldom survive Coins Roman coin hoards in peninsular India Hoards record deposition, not the route or the volume of trade

docs.title: 11.2 The Harappans, the Gulf and Mesopotamia
11.2.1 Meluhha, Dilmun and Magan
docs.text:
Cuneiform texts of the later third millennium BCE name three lands beyond the head of the Gulf with which Mesopotamia traded by sea: Dilmun, generally identified with Bahrain and the neighbouring coast of eastern Arabia; Magan, identified with the Oman peninsula; and Meluhha, which most scholars identify with the Indus civilisation or its coastal regions (Possehl 2002; Ratnagar 2004). Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE in the conventional chronology) claimed in an inscription that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun were moored at the quay of his capital, Akkad. Texts of the Akkadian and Ur III periods mention goods from Meluhha, among them carnelian, fine woods, ivory, gold and exotic animals; a cylinder seal of the Akkadian period belonged to a man described as an interpreter of the Meluhhan language; and administrative texts of the Ur III period refer to a settlement of Meluhhans in the territory of Lagash (Possehl 2002; Ratnagar 2004). These hints suggest that people from Meluhha travelled to Mesopotamia and that some stayed there.

The identification of Meluhha with the Indus region rests on the fit between the goods named and Harappan products, on the order in which the three lands are listed, and on Indus objects found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf; it is a strong inference rather than a proof. After about 1900 BCE references to Meluhha become rare. In the Old Babylonian period merchants of Ur went to Dilmun to buy copper and other goods there, and Dilmun, not Meluhha, appears as the main partner (Ratnagar 2004).

docs.title: 11.2.2 The Material Evidence
docs.text:
Objects of Indus manufacture or style found in Mesopotamia include long carnelian beads and etched carnelian beads, several of them from the royal cemetery at Ur, and a small number of square Indus seals and Indus-style seals from sites such as Ur and Kish (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). In the Gulf, a distinctive class of round stamp seals (“Gulf” or Dilmun seals) sometimes carries signs of the Indus script, and one such Gulf-type seal was found at Lothal (Rao 1979). Weights of the Indus standard have been found in Bahrain, and Dilmun appears to have adopted that standard for some purposes. Indus-type pottery and other objects have been reported from coastal sites in Oman, including Ras al-Jinz, which suggests that Harappan seafarers or goods reached Magan directly as well as through Dilmun (Possehl 2002; Ratnagar 2004).

Boats appear on a few Indus seals and tablets, and a terracotta boat model was found at Lothal, but these are too schematic to reconstruct a sea-going hull (McGrail et al. 2003); see Chapter 13.

docs.title: 11.2.3 Coastal Settlements
docs.text: The Harappan coast ran from the Makran in the west, where Sutkagen-dor and Balakot stand near the sea, through Sindh to Kachchh and Saurashtra. In Gujarat, sites such as Lothal, Kuntasi, Nageshwar and Bagasra (Gola Dhoro) worked marine shell, especially the conch Turbinella pyrum for bangles, and semi-precious stones such as carnelian and agate from local sources (Kenoyer 1998). Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Great Rann of Kachchh, excavated by R. S. Bisht from 1989, is one of the largest Harappan cities and is known for its reservoirs and water channels, its fortified citadel and its large inscription of Indus signs. It is often called a port, on the assumption that the Rann was then navigable; that is plausible but debated, (Possehl 2002).

docs.title: 11.2.4 What Kind of Trade?
docs.text: Shereen Ratnagar has argued that the Indus–Gulf–Mesopotamia exchange was a trade in a limited range of raw materials and luxury goods, conducted partly through intermediaries, and that it mattered more to Mesopotamian palaces and temples, which had no stone, metal or hard timber of their own, than to the Indus cities (Ratnagar 2004). Possehl similarly treats the “Middle Asian Interaction Sphere” as a network of many regional partners rather than a two-way trade between great civilisations (Possehl 2002). There is no evidence for regular open-sea crossings of the Arabian Sea in this period; the route probably followed the Makran and Arabian coasts.

docs.title: 11.3 Lothal: Port Town and the Dock Debate
docs.text:
Lothal, near the head of the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat, was excavated by S. R. Rao of the Archaeological Survey of India between 1955 and 1962 (Rao 1979). Its mature Harappan occupation is dated c. 2400–1900 BCE. The settlement was small but busy: it had a bead-making workshop that worked carnelian and other stones, copper-working areas, a raised platform with a building that Rao interpreted as a warehouse (in which clay sealings with the impressions of packing materials were found), and the Gulf-type seal mentioned above. Lothal was clearly a centre of craft production and exchange with links to the Gulf.

The most famous feature of the site is a large, rectangular, brick-lined basin on its eastern side (Figure 11.1), about 214–219 metres long and 35–37 metres wide (published figures vary), with openings in its walls that Rao identified as an inlet and a spillway. Rao interpreted the basin as a tidal dock into which ships could sail from an old course of the Sabarmati or Bhogavo river at high tide (Rao 1979).

Figure 11.1. The brick-lined basin at Lothal, Gujarat. S. R. Rao interpreted it as a tidal dock; others have read it as a reservoir or tank, and its function remains debated. Photo: Sanjunath S, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Debate: Was the Lothal Basin a Dock?

The dock interpretation. S. R. Rao argued that the basin’s size, its baked-brick walls, the inlet and spillway channels, its position next to the platform and warehouse, and the evidence of foreign contacts at the site all indicate a basin for berthing ships at high tide (Rao 1979).

The reservoir interpretation. Lawrence Leshnik argued in 1968 that the basin is better explained as a tank or reservoir for fresh water, perhaps for irrigation or drinking, and that the case for a dock had not been made (Leshnik 1968). Later scholars have been divided: some accept a dock, some prefer a tank, and others note that boats could simply have been beached or moored in the river channel, so that a dock was not necessary for Lothal to function as a port (Possehl 2002; Ray 2003).

Present position. The function of the basin is debated and cannot be settled from the published evidence. What is not in doubt is that Lothal was a craft and trading settlement with contacts that reached the Gulf. Its description as the “world’s first dockyard”, often heard in public discussion, therefore states as fact what is a debated interpretation, and the mature phase at the site dates to c. 2400–1900 BCE.

docs.title: 11.4 After the Harappans: Vedic and Early Textual Evidence
docs.text:
Between the end of the Harappan cities and the early historic period (roughly 1900–500 BCE) the evidence for long-distance seaborne trade is slight. Coastal settlements in Gujarat and elsewhere continued, and fishing and short coastal voyages must have gone on, but there is no body of finds comparable to that of the third millennium BCE or the early centuries CE (Ray 2003). Local seafaring surely continued, but a continuous long-distance trade cannot be inferred from silence.

The Ṛgveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) is the earliest Indian text to speak of ships (nau) and of samudra. The meaning of samudra in the oldest hymns is debated: it may denote the sea, but it may also mean any large gathering of waters, such as the lower Indus with its tributaries, or the heavenly waters. The best-known passage is the story of Bhujyu, son of Tugra, told in several hymns to the Aśvins (for example RV 1.116.3–5): Bhujyu is left in the waters of the samudra and the Aśvins rescue him with ships, including a ship “of a hundred oars”. Elsewhere Varuṇa is said to know the track of the birds in the air and the ships of the samudra (RV 1.25.7), and the poet Vasiṣṭha imagines himself sailing with Varuṇa (RV 7.88.3–4). These passages show that the poets knew boats and imagined voyages over large waters. They do not describe trade, and Bhujyu is not presented as a merchant; the hundred-oared ship belongs to a story of divine rescue and is not evidence for real ship sizes.

By the time of the Dharmasūtras the sea voyage had become a topic of law. The Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra lists going to sea among the customs peculiar to the north, which it does not recommend to others, and later lists it among the acts that cause loss of caste (BDhS 1.2.4; 2.2.2) (Olivelle 1999). The Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) excludes a man who goes to sea from the guests at an ancestral offering (MDh 3.158), yet also says that rates of interest on sea voyages are to be fixed by people expert in such voyages (MDh 8.157) (Olivelle 2004). Brahmanical texts thus regarded the sea voyage as polluting for Brahmins while taking for granted that others undertook it. Such restrictions were real, but they were variably observed, and they did not apply to the Buddhist and Jain merchants, Tamil traders and coastal communities who carried much of the trade discussed below.

docs.title: 11.5 Merchants at Sea in Buddhist and Jain Narrative
docs.text:
The Pali Jātaka collection is the richest Indian source of stories about sea voyages. It is a layered text: the verses are older than the prose stories that frame them, which were fixed in the commentary of about the fifth century CE, though many of the tales were known much earlier, as scenes carved at Bharhut in the second or first century BCE show. The stories therefore reflect conditions over several centuries and cannot be dated precisely (Chakravarti 2002).

Several Jātakas place merchants on the open sea. In the Bāveru Jātaka merchants sail to Bāveru, generally identified with Babylon, where there are no birds; they sell a crow for a high price, and on a later voyage a trained peacock for much more. The story is a satire on credulity, but it also preserves the memory of voyages from India to Mesopotamia. In the Suppāraka Jātaka (no. 463) the Bodhisatta is a blind but skilled pilot of Bharukaccha who guides a ship of merchants through a series of strange seas and brings them home with a cargo of treasure; the story was retold in Sanskrit in Āryaśūra’s Jātakamālā. In the Saṅkha and Mahājanaka Jātakas, heroes sail for Suvaṇṇabhūmi, the “land of gold” in Southeast Asia, are shipwrecked, and are rescued by the sea goddess Maṇimekhalā; in the Valāhassa Jātaka shipwrecked merchants are trapped on an island of ogresses in Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka) (Chakravarti 2002; Ray 1994).

Other Buddhist texts add to the picture. The story of Pūrṇa in the Sanskrit Divyāvadāna tells of the son of a merchant of Sūrpāraka (Sopara) by a slave woman, who leads trading voyages, meets Buddhist merchants from Śrāvastī on one of them and becomes a monk. The Milindapañha, compiled in the early centuries CE, compares a skilled monk to a ship-owner grown rich who can sail to Vaṅga, Takkola, China, Sovīra, Suraṭṭha, Alasanda, the Coromandel coast and Suvaṇṇabhūmi, a list that sketches the maritime horizon of its time. Jain canonical narrative, notably the Jñātādharmakathā (Prakrit Nāyādhammakahāo), likewise tells of merchants of Campā who sail out in search of profit and are tested by storms and sea deities.

The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) approaches the sea from the side of the state. It provides for a Superintendent of Shipping (nāvadhyakṣa) who collects port dues and fees from boats, enforces regulations in port towns, and is to destroy pirate vessels (AŚ 2.28); and in comparing trade routes it prefers, among water routes, the coastal route with its many ports to the route across the open sea (AŚ 7.12) (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). These are prescriptions for an idealised kingdom, not descriptions of actual ports; the law of ports and shipping is treated in Chapter 15.

docs.title: 11.6 Achaemenid and Hellenistic Contacts
docs.text:
In the late sixth century BCE the Achaemenid king Darius I brought the lower Indus region (Old Persian Hindush) into his empire. Herodotus (4.44) reports that Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda to sail down the Indus to the sea and then westward, arriving after thirty months in the Red Sea. The details are uncertain. In 325–324 BCE Alexander’s admiral Nearchus took a fleet from the mouth of the Indus along the Makran coast to the head of the Gulf, a voyage known from the account preserved in Arrian’s Indica; the fleet relied on local knowledge of the coast.

The Ptolemaic kings of Egypt developed the Red Sea harbours of Berenike and Myos Hormos in the third century BCE, at first chiefly to bring African elephants for their armies. Strabo (2.3.4), drawing on Posidonius, tells how an Indian sailor, found half-dead in a ship stranded in the Red Sea and brought to the court of Ptolemy VIII, offered to guide a voyage to India; Eudoxus of Cyzicus then made two voyages, in the late second century BCE, returning with aromatics and precious stones. Indian goods had long reached the Mediterranean through Arabian and other intermediaries, but direct voyages between Egypt and India became common only after Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE. Strabo (2.5.12), who travelled up the Nile with the prefect Aelius Gallus in the 20s BCE, says he learned that as many as 120 ships were then sailing from Myos Hormos to India, whereas under the Ptolemies only a few had dared to make the voyage (Casson 1989; Cobb 2018).

Cross-Reference: The Monsoon and “Hippalus”

The long voyages between the Red Sea and India depended on the reversing monsoon winds. The Periplus (§57) credits a ship’s captain named Hippalus with first working out the open-sea route; sailors of the Indian Ocean coasts knew the monsoon long before, and what the Greek sources credit to him is the use of the wind for direct crossings away from the coast. The question, and the sailing calendar, are discussed in Chapter 14 (Section 14.3).

docs.title: 11.7 The Indo-Roman Trade
docs.text:
From the late first century BCE to the third century CE, trade between Roman Egypt and India reached a scale, and left a body of evidence, not matched in any earlier period. Excavations in India and Egypt now allow it to be seen from both ends (Tomber 2008; Cobb 2018), and Grant Parker has examined how Roman writers built an image of India out of this contact (Parker 2008). Figure 11.2 shows the routes in outline.

Figure 11.2. The sea routes of the trade between Roman Egypt and India in the first and second centuries CE, after the Periplus and Pliny (schematic, not to scale; places are not drawn in their geographical positions). Cargoes went up the Nile to Coptos, across the desert to the Red Sea ports and by sea to the mouth of the Red Sea; from there ships crossed the open sea with the south-west monsoon and returned with the north-east monsoon. The older coastal route along Arabia and the Makran remained in use.

docs.title: 11.7.1 The Periplus Maris Erythraei
docs.text:
The Periplus Maris Erythraei (“Circumnavigation of the Erythraean Sea”) is a Greek handbook written by an anonymous merchant based in Roman Egypt, most probably in the middle of the first century CE (Casson 1989). Its author describes, port by port, the coasts of the Red Sea, the Horn of Africa and the East African coast as far as Rhapta, southern Arabia, the mouth of the Gulf, and India from the Indus delta down the west coast and up the east coast towards the Ganga. For each place he records goods sold and bought, anchorages and local rulers. The standard edition with commentary is Casson (1989); Schoff (1912) is an older translation.

The Periplus names many Indian ports (Table 11.2). Barygaza (Bharukaccha, modern Bharuch) receives the fullest description. Its approach was dangerous because of tides and shoals, and pilot boats in the king’s service met incoming ships and guided them up the river (§44; Section 14.6). Old silver drachmas of the Indo-Greek kings Apollodotus and Menander were still in use there (§47). Goods came to Barygaza from the Deccan towns of Paithana (Paiṭhan) and Tagara (Ter) by wagon (§51). Further south, Muziris and Nelkynda in Limyrikē (the Malabar coast) were the great pepper ports; the author says that large ships went there because of the bulk of the pepper and malabathrum, and that a great quantity of coin was taken there (§56). On the east coast he mentions local coasting craft, large boats called sangara made of logs lashed together, and very large ships called kolandiophōnta that sailed to Chrysē (Southeast Asia) and the Ganga (§60) (Casson 1989). Indian ships and boats are discussed further in Chapter 13.

The text also shows that rulers could open or close ports: at Kalliena (Kalyan) Greek ships were no longer allowed to trade and were sent under guard to Barygaza (§52). The southern pepper ports lay in the territories of the Cēra and Pāṇḍya kings (Casson 1989; Champakalakshmi 1996).

Table 11.2. Some Indian ports named in the Periplus and their modern identifications Periplus name Identification Status of identification Barbarikon Indus delta Exact site unknown Barygaza Bharuch (Bharukaccha) on the Narmada Secure Souppara Sopara (Śūrpāraka) near Mumbai Secure Kalliena Kalyan near Mumbai Secure Muziris Tamil Muciṟi, near the mouth of the Periyar, Kerala General area secure; Pattanam proposed as the site Nelkynda Inland port in southern Kerala Exact site uncertain Kolchoi Korkai, Tamil Nadu (pearl fishery) Generally accepted Poduke Arikamedu near Puducherry Probable, widely accepted Kamara, Sopatma Coromandel coast Proposed identifications vary Gange A port near the mouth of the Ganga Uncertain

docs.title: 11.7.2 What Was Traded
docs.text:
The Periplus lists the goods exchanged at each port, and these lists can be checked against Pliny and against archaeology. Pepper from the Malabar coast was the largest single export to Egypt by bulk and value, but the trade was diverse (Table 11.3). The English word “pepper” comes through Latin piper and Greek peperi from an Indian word related to Sanskrit pippalī, which properly means long pepper; black pepper is marica in Sanskrit and miḷaku in Tamil.

Table 11.3. Main goods in the trade between Roman Egypt and India according to the Periplus (summary) Category From India to Egypt From Egypt to India Spices and aromatics Black and long pepper, malabathrum (leaf of a cinnamon-related tree), Gangetic nard, costus, bdellium Storax, some Arabian incense Textiles Cotton cloth of many grades, including fine muslins; Chinese silk and yarn re-exported Clothing and multicoloured textiles Precious goods Pearls, diamonds, sapphires and other gems, agate and onyx, ivory, tortoise shell Coral, peridot, glass Metals and minerals — Gold and silver coin, copper, tin, lead, antimony, realgar and orpiment Other Indigo, lycium Wine (Italian, Laodicean and Arabian); at Barygaza, for the king, silver vessels, slave musicians and girls for the royal household

The list for Barygaza (§49) is a reminder that the trade included people: slave musicians and young women are among the gifts brought for the king. The Periplus also notes that the pearl fishery at Kolchoi was worked by condemned criminals (§59). Both details are reminders that this was not simply a trade in luxuries between equals (Casson 1989).

docs.title: 11.7.3 Pliny’s Figures and the Question of a “Drain”
docs.text:
Pliny the Elder, writing his Natural History in the 70s CE, gives the most quoted figures for the trade. In describing the voyage to India he says that in no year did India take less than fifty million sesterces from the Roman empire, sending in return goods that sold at a hundred times their cost (NH 6.101). Elsewhere, complaining about luxury, he says that at the lowest reckoning India, the Seres (the Chinese) and the Arabian peninsula together took one hundred million sesterces a year from the empire (NH 12.84). He also describes the route: from Alexandria up the Nile to Coptos, across the desert to Berenike, by sea to Ocelis or Cane in southern Arabia, and from there with the wind he calls “hippalus” to Muziris (NH 6.101–106); the timetable of the voyage is set out in Section 14.2.2 (De Romanis 2020; Cobb 2018).

Scholarly Note: How to Read Pliny

Pliny’s figures are rhetorical. They come from passages condemning Roman extravagance, and he does not say how they were reached. Fifty million sesterces was a large sum, but a small fraction of the revenues of the Roman state. The figures probably refer to the value of goods rather than a net outflow of coin, and much of the value was captured inside the empire: the Roman state levied a duty of one quarter on imports from India at the Red Sea frontier, and the mark-up between India and Rome went to merchants, shippers and financiers in Egypt and Italy (De Romanis 2020; Cobb 2018). Roman coins did flow to India, as the hoards show, but the trade cannot be described as a “drain” in the modern sense, and Pliny’s lament is a moral complaint, not a statistic of the balance of trade.

docs.title: 11.7.4 Finance and Tax: The Muziris Papyrus
docs.text:
A Greek papyrus in Vienna (P. Vindob. G 40822), of the mid-second century CE, gives a rare glimpse of how the trade was financed. One side preserves part of a loan contract that refers to loan agreements made at Muziris and sets out how goods brought back from India were to be carried, under the lender’s control, from the Red Sea through the desert to Coptos and down the Nile to Alexandria. The other side (Figure 11.3) values part of the cargo of a ship named Hermapollon returning from Muziris, including Gangetic nard and ivory, and calculates the one-quarter duty owed to the state. The total value of the cargo ran to millions of drachmas, a scale that required large loans and that made the import duty a significant revenue for Rome. De Romanis (2020) has used the papyrus to reconstruct the organisation of the pepper trade in detail. The document shows that the voyages were financed by credit secured on the cargo, a practice comparable in function to the sea loans with high interest mentioned in Indian law books (see Chapter 6).

Figure 11.3. The verso of the Muziris papyrus (P. Vindob. G 40822, mid-second century CE), which values part of the cargo of the Hermapollon returning from Muziris and calculates the duty of one-quarter owed on it; Austrian National Library, Vienna. Image: Austrian National Library, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 11.7.5 The Evidence in India
docs.text:
Arikamedu. The site of Arikamedu, on a lagoon south of Puducherry, was excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945, by J.-M. Casal in the late 1940s, and by Vimala Begley and colleagues in 1989–1992 (Wheeler 1954; Begley and De Puma 1991). Wheeler found Italian terra sigillata (Arretine ware), wine amphorae and other Mediterranean material and interpreted the site as a Roman trading station of the first century CE. Begley’s work showed that the settlement was older, beginning by about the second century BCE; that it was an Indian town with its own craft industries, including the large-scale making of glass and stone beads; and that Mediterranean imports were one element among many (Begley and De Puma 1991). Arikamedu also yielded Indian rouletted ware, a fine grey pottery once thought to be a Mediterranean import and now regarded as Indian, which is found at sites around the Bay of Bengal. Arikamedu is generally identified with the Periplus’s Poduke.

Pattanam. Excavations since 2007 at Pattanam, near Kodungallur in Kerala, led by the Kerala Council for Historical Research, have produced Mediterranean amphora sherds, fine wares and glass, together with West Asian pottery, beads and a large body of local material spanning several centuries. The excavators have proposed that Pattanam is part of ancient Muziris. The proposal is attractive, since Muziris lay in this area, but it is not yet settled, and full publication of the excavations is awaited (Tomber 2008). Tamil poetry confirms the importance of Muciṟi: a poem in the Akanāṉūṟu (149) describes the ships of the Yavanas arriving there with gold and departing with pepper (Champakalakshmi 1996).

Coins. Roman coins have been found in peninsular India in many hoards and single finds, concentrated in Tamil Nadu (especially the Coimbatore region and around Karur and Madurai), with others in Karnataka, Andhra and Kerala (Turner 1989; Tomber 2008). Their composition, the cut marks on many of them and the question whether they circulated as currency are discussed in Section 5.5.3.

Other sites and the hinterland. Roman finds also come from Alagankulam on the Tamil coast and from Deccan towns such as Ter and Kolhapur. In the western Deccan, rock-cut Buddhist monasteries on the routes from the ports, such as Karle and Junnar, record gifts by merchants and by donors called Yavanas, a term used in India for Greeks and, more loosely, for people from the west (Ray 1986). Lead coins of the Sātavāhana king Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi (late second century CE) show a two-masted ship. Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions on pottery and in caves, from about the second century BCE, record merchants (vaṇikaṉ) and their goods (Mahadevan 2003). The Tamil poem Paṭṭiṉappālai praises the Chola port of Pūmpuhār and the goods that reached it from as far as Sri Lanka and the Malay peninsula (Section 15.2.5).

docs.title: 11.7.6 The Evidence on the Red Sea
docs.text:
Excavations at Berenike, directed by Steven Sidebotham and Willeke Wendrich from 1994, and at Quseir al-Qadim, ancient Myos Hormos, excavated in the late 1970s and again from 1999 by David Peacock and Lucy Blue, have revealed the Egyptian end of the trade (Sidebotham 2011; Tomber 2008). Indian material at Berenike includes black peppercorns, among them a large quantity found in an Indian-made storage jar in the temple of Serapis; teak timber reused in buildings; Indian cooking pots and fine wares; cotton textiles; rice and other plant remains; and beads (Sidebotham 2011). At both Berenike and Myos Hormos short graffiti in Tamil-Brāhmī script, mostly personal names, were scratched on pots, and Prakrit inscriptions in Brāhmī have also been found in Egypt (Mahadevan 2003; Tomber 2008). Tamil and other Indian merchants or sailors were evidently present in the Egyptian ports.

Further evidence of Indian seafarers comes from the island of Socotra, where a cave at Hoq contains many inscriptions and drawings left by visitors in the early centuries CE. Most of the inscriptions are in Brāhmī script and Indian languages, and many of the names suggest sailors from western India (Strauch 2012). The Periplus (§30) already describes the island’s population as a mixture of Arabs, Indians and Greeks who had come there to trade.

docs.title: 11.7.7 Ptolemy’s Geography
docs.text: Claudius Ptolemy, writing in Alexandria in the mid-second century CE, gave coordinates for hundreds of places in India in Book 7 of his Geography, drawing on Marinus of Tyre and on merchants’ reports. His list of ports and towns shows how much information reached Alexandria through trade, but his India is badly distorted: the peninsula hardly projects southward, and Taprobane (Sri Lanka) is enormously exaggerated. Ptolemy is a valuable list of names, not an accurate picture of the coast (see Volume 21, Bhūgola).

docs.title: 11.7.8 Who Carried the Trade?
docs.text: The Indo-Roman trade was not a single enterprise. Greek-speaking merchants of Roman Egypt, with financiers in Alexandria, sent ships to India; Nabataean and South Arabian merchants handled much of the Arabian end; Indian merchants and shipowners from Gujarat, the Konkan and the Tamil country sailed to Arabia, Socotra and Egypt; and Tamil kings and Deccan rulers controlled access to their ports and drew revenue from them (Tomber 2008; Ray 2003). It was one part of a wider network that also joined India to the Gulf, Sri Lanka, East Africa and Southeast Asia; the overland routes through the Kuṣāṇa territories are discussed in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 11.8 Sri Lanka, Arabia and East Africa
docs.text:
Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka lay at the meeting point of the routes of the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. Its pearls, gems and later its cinnamon were sought by traders from both directions. The port of Mantai on the north-west coast and the town of Tissamaharama in the south have produced Indian, Mediterranean and West Asian imports (Ray 2003). Pliny (NH 6.84–91) tells how a freedman collecting customs in the Red Sea was carried by winds to Taprobane, and how its king then sent an embassy to the emperor Claudius. In the sixth century Cosmas Indicopleustes described it in his Christian Topography as a centre where ships from China met ships from Persia, Ethiopia and India.

Arabia and the Gulf. South Arabian ports such as Qana (Bir Ali) and Sumhuram (Khor Rori) in Dhofar, which handled frankincense, traded with western India, and Indian pottery has been found at both (Tomber 2008). Under the Parthians and then the Sasanians (from 224 CE) the Gulf route remained an alternative to the Red Sea.

East Africa. The Periplus describes the coast of “Azania” south of the Horn of Africa as far as Rhapta, the last market town it knew, which exported ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoise shell and imported iron tools and weapons; Rhapta has not been located, though it probably lay on the coast of what is now Tanzania (§§15–16) (Casson 1989). The same text says that ships from western India brought grain, rice, ghee, sesame oil, cotton cloth and cane sugar to the ports of the Horn, and that Indian iron and steel and cotton cloth were imported at Adulis on the Red Sea coast of Africa. Archaeological evidence for direct Indian contact on the East African coast before about 600 CE is limited; the Swahili trading towns developed later, and their links with India belong mainly to the period covered in Chapter 12 (Horton and Middleton 2000).

docs.title: 11.9 The Bay of Bengal and Early Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Contacts across the Bay of Bengal are older than the Indo-Roman trade. At Ban Don Ta Phet in west-central Thailand, a cemetery of about the fourth to second centuries BCE contained beads of carnelian and agate, including a carnelian pendant in the form of a lion, and high-tin bronze bowls, objects that point to exchange with South Asia (Glover 1989). At Khao Sam Kaeo on the isthmus of the Malay peninsula, excavations have found workshops of the last centuries BCE making stone and glass beads with South Asian techniques, which suggests that Indian craftsmen worked there alongside local ones. Indian rouletted ware and related pottery have been found in Sri Lanka, Java and Bali (Ray 2003). At Oc Eo in the Mekong delta, the main port of the polity Chinese sources call Funan, excavations in 1944 found Indian-style seals with Brāhmī legends, beads, and Roman objects including a gold medallion of Antoninus Pius, evidence that goods from the Mediterranean reached mainland Southeast Asia through Indian Ocean exchange (Coedès 1968).

Inscriptions of the fifth century CE begin to name individual traders. A stone from Province Wellesley in the Malay peninsula records, in Sanskrit, the mahānāvika (“great sea captain”) Buddhagupta of Raktamṛttikā, a place probably in Bengal (Coedès 1968). The Chinese monk Faxian, returning from India in the early fifth century, sailed from Tāmralipti to Sri Lanka on a merchant ship, and from there on a large ship carrying more than two hundred people towards China. Storms drove it to Yavadvīpa (Java or Sumatra), where he waited five months before taking another large ship for Guangzhou; when that ship too met storms, Brahmin passengers blamed the misfortune on the Buddhist monk on board (Liu 1988). Chinese sources also record a sea route from southern China towards South Asia under the Han, and envoys and merchants between Funan, India and China in the third century CE (Liu 1988; Wolters 1967).

These contacts involved neither conquest nor colonisation, and Southeast Asian sailors and ships were themselves active in the Bay of Bengal (Manguin 1993). The adoption of Indian scripts, religions and political ideas in Southeast Asia, and the debate over the term “Indianisation”, are treated in Chapter 16.

docs.title: 11.10 Buddhism and Maritime Trade
docs.text:
Himanshu Prabha Ray has argued that the spread of Buddhism and the growth of maritime trade in early South Asia were closely linked (Ray 1994). Buddhist monasteries stood near ports and on the routes leading inland from them: Kanheri near Sopara and Kalyan, Karle and Junnar on the passes of the Western Ghats, and Amarāvatī, Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, Śālihuṇḍam and other sites near the river mouths and harbours of the Andhra coast. Their inscriptions record gifts by merchants, caravan leaders, guilds and seafarers, as well as by Yavanas (Ray 1986, 1994). Buddhism, which did not share Brahmanical scruples about the sea, gave merchants a religious community that valued their giving; its stories gave them a protecting sea goddess, Maṇimekhalā, who also appears in the Tamil epic Maṇimēkalai.

The relationship had limits: monasteries were not trading firms, and Jains, Brahmins and followers of many other cults also took part in commerce. But Buddhism did travel with merchants: monks went by sea to Sri Lanka, to Southeast Asia and, by the fifth century, to China, and maritime Buddhist networks shaped the routes by which texts, images and pilgrims moved (Ray 1994; Liu 1988). Guilds and merchant donors are discussed further in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 11.11 Late Antiquity and the Road to the Medieval Ocean
docs.text:
The evidence for the Indo-Roman trade thins after the early third century CE. Fewer Roman coins of the later third century reach India, and some Red Sea ports declined, though Berenike was active again in the fourth and fifth centuries (Sidebotham 2011). Trade did not stop; its pattern changed. The kingdom of Aksum, with its port of Adulis, became a major intermediary on the African side of the Red Sea; Sasanian Persia controlled the Gulf, and Persian merchants and Christian communities linked to Persia were present in Sri Lanka and on the Malabar coast; and late Roman copper coins of the fourth and fifth centuries found in Sri Lanka and south India attest to continuing links. In the sixth century Procopius (Wars 1.20) reports that the emperor Justinian asked the Aksumites to buy silk from India and resell it to the Romans so as to bypass Persia, but that Persian merchants occupied the harbours where Indian ships put in and bought up their cargoes.

In South Asia, historians disagree about the economy of the centuries after about 300 CE. R. S. Sharma argued that towns and long-distance trade declined, while others see a reorganisation of trade around new regional centres rather than a general decline (Sharma 1987; Chattopadhyaya 1994). On the east coast and across the Bay of Bengal, at least, the fifth and sixth centuries saw active voyaging, as the Buddhagupta inscription and Faxian’s journey show. By about 600 CE the actors of the next period were in place: Persian and soon Arab merchants in the west, Southeast Asian polities in the straits, reviving Chinese demand under the Sui and Tang, and regional powers on the Indian coasts. Their world is the subject of Chapter 12.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Bronze Age, Possehl (2002) and Kenoyer (1998) give general accounts of the Indus civilisation, and Ratnagar (2004) analyses its trade with the Gulf and Mesopotamia; the Lothal debate can be followed in Rao (1979) and Leshnik (1968). Ray (2003) is the best survey of the archaeology of seafaring in early South Asia, and Ray (1994) sets out the links between Buddhism and maritime trade. Casson (1989) is the standard edition and commentary of the Periplus. For the Indo-Roman trade, Tomber (2008) reviews the archaeological evidence from both sides, Cobb (2018) gives a recent synthesis, and De Romanis (2020) studies the pepper trade and the Muziris papyrus. Begley and De Puma (1991) collects important studies, including work on Arikamedu, Parker (2008) studies the Roman image of India, and Chakravarti (2002) discusses traders and trade in early Indian society.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Indian Ocean World, c. 600–1500
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Between the rise of Islam and the arrival of the Portuguese, the Indian Ocean was crossed by a dense web of trade linking East Africa, Arabia, Iran, the coasts of India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China. No single people or state controlled it. This chapter introduces its main participants in turn: Arab and Persian merchants of the Gulf, the Arab ports of Sindh, the merchants of Gujarat, the Muslim Māppiḷas of Malabar and the Kārimī merchants of Egypt, the Jewish traders known from the Cairo Geniza, the Tamil merchant associations, the island of Sri Lanka, Chinese shipping from the Song to the voyages of Zheng He, the shippers of Śrīvijaya and Java, and the towns of the Swahili coast. It then looks at the Chola expeditions of the eleventh century, at the main goods of the trade (horses, pepper, textiles, gems and cowries), and at the religions that travelled with merchants.

The earlier history of seaborne trade, from the Harappans to the Indo-Roman trade, is treated in Chapter 11. The ships themselves are the subject of Chapter 13, the monsoon and the pilots’ craft of Chapter 14, and the port cities, their officials and the customs of the sea of Chapter 15. The cultural history of India’s links with Southeast Asia is treated in Chapter 16, and the period after 1498 in Chapter 18.

The sources for these nine centuries are richer, and more varied, than for any earlier period. They include Arabic and Persian geographies and travel accounts; the letters of Jewish merchants preserved in the Cairo Geniza; Chinese dynastic histories, trade gazetteers and the reports of Zheng He’s interpreters; Tamil, Kannada, Sanskrit and Old Malay inscriptions; the accounts of Marco Polo and Ibn Baṭṭūṭa; and a growing body of archaeology, including shipwrecks and textiles excavated in Egypt. Each was written from a particular point of view. Arabic writers saw the ocean from the Gulf, Chinese officials from the customs house, and the court poets of the Cholas from the throne. Putting them together shows an ocean with many centres, not one.

docs.title: 12.1 An Ocean of Many Centres
docs.text:
The historian K. N. Chaudhuri argued that the Indian Ocean between the seventh and the eighteenth centuries can be studied as a single economic and cultural space, held together by the regular alternation of the monsoon winds, by a recurring set of goods, and by shared commercial practices among merchants of many faiths (Chaudhuri 1985, 1990). Within that space he distinguished three overlapping circuits (Figure 12.1): the Arabian Sea, linking East Africa, the Red Sea and the Gulf to western India; the Bay of Bengal, linking eastern India and Sri Lanka to Burma, the Malay peninsula and Sumatra; and the South China Sea, linking the Straits to China. India’s long coastline lay where the first two met, which is why its ports were busy. But the system had no single hub. Aden, Hormuz, Cambay, Calicut, Quilon, Nāgapaṭṭinam, Palembang, Malacca, Quanzhou and Kilwa each served as an emporium for its own region, and the balance between them shifted over time (McPherson 1993; Pearson 2003; Alpers 2014).

One important change in the structure of the trade is generally placed around the eleventh century. In the ninth century Arabic sources describe ships sailing from the Gulf all the way to southern China and back, a voyage that took the better part of two years. Later, voyages tended to be divided into segments: goods from the Gulf or the Red Sea were sold in Gujarat or Malabar, carried on from there to the Straits, and handed on again to ships bound for China. Chaudhuri linked this segmentation to the rise of emporia that could store goods between monsoons and to the rhythms of the winds themselves (Chaudhuri 1985). Janet Abu-Lughod, writing of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, similarly described a chain of linked circuits, none of which dominated the others (Abu-Lughod 1989).

Figure 12.1. Emporia and routes of the Indian Ocean, c. 1000–1500, set within the three overlapping circuits distinguished by K. N. Chaudhuri (schematic, not to scale; places are arranged only roughly from west to east). Each emporium served its own region, their importance shifted over time, and the system had no single hub (Chaudhuri 1985). The dashed arrow marks Rājendra I’s raid of 1025 (Section 12.9.2); several of the identifications in the box are debated (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

Most of the people who made this system work have left no names: the sailors, porters, caulkers, weavers, pepper growers, divers and enslaved men and women whose labour underlay the trade. The merchants and rulers who appear in the sources were a small minority, and the sections that follow should be read with that in mind. Table 12.1 gives selected dates for the period.

Table 12.1. Selected dates in the history of the Indian Ocean, c. 600–1500 Date (CE) Event 671–695 The Chinese monk Yijing travels between China and India by sea, staying at Śrīvijaya 680s Old Malay inscriptions of Śrīvijaya near Palembang and on Bangka c. 830s Approximate date of the Belitung wreck (Indonesia), a sewn-plank ship carrying Chinese ceramics 849 Copper plates of Tarisāppaḷḷi (Quilon) grant privileges to a Christian church and name the Maṇigrāmam and Añjuvaṇṇam 851 Akhbār al-Ṣīn wa-l-Hind describes the sea route from the Gulf to China c. 993 Rājarāja I’s forces take northern Sri Lanka c. 1006 Grant for the Buddhist monastery built at Nāgapaṭṭinam by the Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya (Larger Leiden plates) 1025 Rājendra I’s naval raid on Śrīvijaya and its ports 1087 Song China establishes a maritime trade office at Quanzhou 1088 Tamil inscription of the merchant association of the “Five Hundred” at Barus, Sumatra c. 1132–1149 Abraham Ben Yijū, a Jewish merchant from Tunisia, lives and trades at Mangalore 1264 Arabic–Sanskrit inscription at Somanātha records a mosque founded by a shipowner from Hormuz 1281 Tamil inscription at Quanzhou records a Śiva temple 1340s Ibn Baṭṭūṭa at Calicut and in the Maldives 1405–1433 The seven Ming voyages of Zheng He c. 1400 Foundation of Malacca 1498 Arrival of Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Chapter 18)

docs.title: 12.2 Arab and Persian Merchants of the Gulf
docs.text:
The foundation of Baṣra in the 630s and of Baghdad in 762 created a vast new market for the goods of the ocean at the head of the Persian Gulf. Through the eighth to tenth centuries the most important Gulf port for the long-distance trade was Sīrāf on the Iranian coast, with Ṣuḥār in Oman as a second centre; ships from both sailed to western India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and southern China (Hourani 1995). Merchants, captains and sailors were Arabs, Persians, Indians and others, and the language of the sea was mixed: many of the nautical terms in later Arabic pilot guides are of Persian origin (Tibbetts 1971).

Two Arabic texts give a vivid view of this world, though both must be read with care. The Akhbār al-Ṣīn wa-l-Hind (“Accounts of China and India”), compiled in 851, describes the route from the Gulf by way of Quilon (which it calls Kūlam Malī) and the Bay of Bengal to Guangzhou, the customs of Chinese and Indian rulers, and the goods traded. It was long attributed to a merchant named Sulaymān, an attribution now doubted. Around 916 Abū Zayd al-Sīrāfī added a sequel, which reports that the trade with China was disrupted when the rebel Huang Chao sacked Guangzhou in 878–79 and killed many of its foreign merchants. The ʿAjāʾib al-Hind (“Wonders of India”), associated with a ship’s captain named Buzurg ibn Shahriyār and dated to the mid-tenth century, collects sailors’ stories of storms, shipwrecks, marvels and the kings of distant coasts; its authorship and the reliability of individual tales are uncertain, and it is best read as evidence of what seafarers talked about rather than as a record of events (Hourani 1995).

Arabic geographers of the ninth and tenth centuries, including Ibn Khurradādhbih and al-Masʿūdī (who visited western India in the early tenth century), describe the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king, whom they call the Balharā (from Sanskrit vallabha-rāja), as the greatest ruler of India and a friend to Muslim merchants. They report that Muslim communities in the ports of the western coast lived under their own headmen and practised their religion freely (Wink 1990). This is an early example of a pattern that runs through the whole period: coastal rulers, whatever their religion, protected foreign merchants because their trade brought customs revenue, luxury goods and, increasingly, war-horses.

The Gulf ports themselves rose and fell. Sīrāf declined after an earthquake in the late tenth century and the shift of trade towards the island of Kish (Qays), whose rulers dominated the Gulf trade in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. From the thirteenth century the leading port was Hormuz, whose rulers moved their town from the mainland to the island of Jarun around 1300. Hormuz remained the main outlet for Iranian and Iraqi trade to India until the Portuguese took it in 1515, exporting horses, pearls, dates, silver and other goods and importing Indian textiles, spices, rice and sugar (Chaudhuri 1985; Wink 1990). The ships that carried this trade, built of planks sewn together with coir cord, are described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 12.3 Sindh: Daybul, Manṣūra and Multan
docs.text:
The lower Indus, the stretch of the Indian coast nearest to the Gulf, was the first part of South Asia to come under Muslim rule. In 711–712 an Umayyad army under Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim took the port of Daybul and went on to conquer Sindh as far as Multan. The Arabic historians give as the occasion the seizure off Daybul of ships carrying Muslim women and gifts from Sri Lanka to the governor of Iraq, al-Ḥajjāj; whatever its truth, the story is a reminder that the province’s first importance to the caliphate was maritime (Wink 1990).

Under the governors of the caliphs and then local Arab dynasties, Sindh became a frontier province whose towns the Arabic geographers of the tenth century describe: Daybul at the mouths of the Indus, the port of the province; al-Manṣūra, the capital founded near the older town of Brahmanabad; and Multan in the upper Indus valley, whose great temple of the Sun drew pilgrims and offerings and whose Muslim rulers, according to these writers, used the threat to destroy its image to deter Hindu attack. In the second half of the tenth century Multan passed to Ismāʿīlī rulers allied with the Fatimids of Egypt, until Maḥmūd of Ghazna took it in the early eleventh century. Through these towns the Indus valley, and the routes from Khurasan and Kabul that met at Multan, were linked with the Gulf ports. The site of Banbhore, on a creek east of Karachi, excavated from 1958, has revealed a fortified port town with one of the earliest known mosques of South Asia, and it is often identified with Daybul, though the identification is not certain.

Derryl MacLean’s study of Arab Sindh shows a society in which Muslims long remained a minority, Buddhist and Hindu communities and merchants persisted, and conversion was gradual and bound up with trade and with the patronage of the new rulers (MacLean 1989); André Wink treats the province as the western gateway of what the Arabic sources called al-Hind (Wink 1990). The shifting channels of the Indus later left Daybul behind. In the Mughal period the ports of the delta were Lahari Bandar and the city of Thatta, where the English Company kept a factory for a time in the seventeenth century.

docs.title: 12.4 Gujarat and the Port of Cambay
docs.text:
On the western Indian side, the coast of Gujarat was the most important commercial region for most of this period. Its ports, above all Cambay (Khambhāt, Arabic Kanbāya) at the head of its gulf, but also Bharuch, Somanātha-Pattan, Diu and Bhadreśvar in Kachchh, drew on a large and productive hinterland. Gujarat exported cotton cloth, indigo, carnelian and agate beads, and the products of the interior, and imported horses, metals, precious goods and bullion. Al-Masʿūdī already describes Cambay in the early tenth century; under the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) kings of Aṇahilapāṭaka (c. 940–1244) and their Vāghelā successors it became one of the greatest emporia of the ocean, a position it kept under the Delhi Sultanate (from 1299–1304) and the independent sultans of Gujarat (from 1407) (Chakravarti 2002; Wink 1990).

The merchants of Gujarat were of many communities. Hindu and Jain vaṇiks (banias) dominated wholesale trade, money-lending and brokerage. Jain narrative literature of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries celebrates merchant-ministers such as Vastupāla, who served as governor of Cambay under the Vāghelās, and Jagaḍū of Bhadreśvar, who is said to have traded with Hormuz and to have relieved a famine in the 1250s with grain from his own stores; these works are literary portraits rather than accounts, but they show that seaborne trade carried prestige in Jain society. Among Muslims, there were long-established communities of Arab and Persian descent, and later converted communities such as the Bohras, Ismāʿīlīs whose tradition traces their conversion to missionaries of the eleventh century, and the Khojas, followers of the Nizārī Ismāʿīlī preachers of the later medieval period (Pearson 1976).

A bilingual Arabic and Sanskrit inscription of 1264 from Somanātha-Pattan shows how these communities lived together. It records the building of a mosque by Nūr al-Dīn Fīrūz, a shipowner (nākhudā) from Hormuz, on land acquired in the town with the agreement of local notables, in the reign of the Vāghelā king Arjunadeva, and it provides an endowment from local property for the mosque’s upkeep (Thapar 2004; Chakravarti 2002). Less than three centuries after Maḥmūd of Ghazna’s raid on the Somanātha temple, a Hormuzi shipowner was endowing a mosque in the same town with Hindu cooperation. Trade did not erase conflict, but it gave rulers and merchants strong reasons to accommodate one another.

By the fifteenth century Gujarati merchants were found in every major port from Aden to Malacca. Writing in Malacca shortly after the Portuguese conquest of 1511, the Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires described Cambay as stretching out two arms, one to Aden and one to Malacca, and gave the Gujaratis a leading place among the foreign merchants of the Straits (Pires 1944). His testimony comes from just after our period, but it describes a network that had grown over the previous two centuries.

docs.title: 12.5 Malabar, Aden and the Merchants of Egypt
docs.text:
The Malabar coast of Kerala was the world’s main source of black pepper and an important source of ginger and cardamom. Its ports changed over time: Kollam (Quilon) was prominent from the ninth century, and the kingdom of the Cēra Perumāḷs of Mahōdayapuram dominated the coast until the early twelfth century. After their decline, a number of smaller kingdoms competed for trade, and from the thirteenth century Calicut (Kozhikode), under the rulers known as the Sāmūtiri (Zamorin), became the leading port. Its reputation rested on the security it offered to merchants of all origins (Prange 2018; Malekandathil 2010).

Foreign merchants were firmly established in Malabar before 1000. The Tarisāppaḷḷi copper plates of Quilon (849), witnessed in Arabic, Middle Persian and Judaeo-Persian, and the Jewish copper plates of Cochin (c. 1000), which grant the Añjuvaṇṇam to Joseph Rabban, are described in Section 4.7; they show Christian, Jewish and Muslim merchants of West Asian origin settled under Hindu kings and integrated into the local system of corporate privileges (Malekandathil 2010; Champakalakshmi 1996).

The Muslim communities of Malabar, known as Māppiḷas, grew out of such settlement and intermarriage, and from local conversion. A later tradition, recorded in the sixteenth-century Arabic chronicle Tuḥfat al-Mujāhidīn, tells of a Cēra king who converted to Islam and travelled to Arabia; it is a legend of origins rather than history. Sebastian Prange has shown how Islam in medieval Malabar was shaped by trade: Friday mosques were endowed by merchants and protected by Hindu rulers, Islamic law and Arabic learning circulated through networks linking Malabar to Yemen, Egypt and the Gulf, and Muslim merchants acted as intermediaries between the pepper-growing interior and the ships of the ocean (Prange 2018). Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who passed through Malabar several times in the 1340s, describes the mosques and Muslim merchants of its ports, the Hindu rulers who governed them, and the Chinese ships that called at Calicut and Quilon (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958).

On the other side of the Arabian Sea, Aden was the main gateway to the Red Sea and Egypt. Roxani Margariti’s study of the port under its Zurayid and Ayyubid rulers, from the late eleventh to the early thirteenth century, shows a well-regulated harbour with officials, brokers and merchants’ representatives serving several communities, and a customs house that taxed and recorded ships from India, East Africa and Egypt (Margariti 2007). Aden kept this role under the Rasulid sultans of Yemen (1229–1454). From Aden goods went up the Red Sea to Egypt. In Egypt from the twelfth to the fifteenth century a group of wholesale merchants known as the Kārimīs specialised in the trade in pepper and spices between Aden and Cairo and Alexandria, where Venetians and Genoese bought for Europe. The Kārimīs became wealthy and influential under the Mamluk sultans, but declined after Sultan Barsbāy imposed state control over the pepper trade in the 1420s and 1430s (Chaudhuri 1985; Margariti 2007).

docs.title: 12.6 Jewish Merchants and the Cairo Geniza
docs.text:
The richest documentary evidence for the medieval India trade comes from an unexpected place. The Jewish community of Fusṭāṭ (Old Cairo) did not destroy written documents bearing the name of God but deposited them in a storeroom, the geniza, of the Ben Ezra synagogue. Over centuries, letters, accounts, contracts and legal records accumulated there, most from the eleventh to the thirteenth century. When scholars recovered them in the 1890s, they found among them hundreds of documents concerning trade with India. The historian S. D. Goitein spent decades collecting and translating this “India Book”, which was completed and published by Mordechai Friedman (Goitein and Friedman 2008).

The Geniza letters show Jewish merchants from Egypt, Tunisia, Spain and Yemen travelling to India, generally by way of Aden, and working with Muslim, Hindu and Jain partners and shipowners. They traded in pepper, cardamom, ginger and other spices, in iron and steel, in brass and bronze vessels, in textiles, timber, lac, indigo and medicinal plants, and sent to India gold, silver, copper, coral, glass, paper, textiles and household goods. Their commercial arrangements included partnerships, commenda-type agreements in which one party supplied capital and another travelled with the goods, bills of credit, and an informal system of mutual services between merchants that Goitein called “formal friendship” (Goitein and Friedman 2008). These practices were common to Jewish and Muslim merchants of the time; they are discussed further in Chapter 6.

Historical Note: Abraham Ben Yijū at Mangalore

The best-documented merchant in the India Book is Abraham Ben Yijū, a Jew from al-Mahdiyya in Ifrīqiya (modern Tunisia). He travelled by way of Egypt and Aden to India, where he lived from the early 1130s until about 1149, mostly at Mangalore on the Kanara coast. There he ran a workshop producing bronze vessels, exported pepper and other goods to Aden, and corresponded with his partner and patron in Aden, Maḍmūn ibn Ḥasan, a leading merchant and head of the Jewish community there. In India he freed and married a local woman named Ashū, who had been his slave, and had children with her; his business agent was a slave named Bomma, apparently from the Tulu-speaking coast. After leaving India Ben Yijū lived in Aden and later in Egypt (Goitein and Friedman 2008). The writer Amitav Ghosh used Ben Yijū’s papers, and the fragmentary traces of Bomma, as the framework for In an Antique Land, a book that is both history and memoir (Ghosh 1992). Elizabeth Lambourn has reconstructed the household goods he took with him when he left India, from a list among his papers (Lambourn 2018). Ben Yijū’s life shows how close the commercial and personal ties across the ocean could be, and how they could rest on slavery.

The Geniza merchants were not the only Jewish traders in the Indian Ocean. Ibn Khurradādhbih, in the ninth century, describes Jewish merchants called Rādhānites who traded between the Mediterranean and China by land and sea, and the Jewish community of Malabar is attested by the copper plates of around 1000 noted above. Later, after our period, Armenian merchants built networks that reached from Iran to India and Southeast Asia (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 12.7 Tamil Merchant Associations Abroad
docs.text:
In south India, long-distance trade was organised through merchant associations that are known mainly from inscriptions. The two most important were the Maṇigrāmam, attested from the ninth century, and the association that called itself the “Five Hundred” (Tamil Ainnūṟṟuvar) of Ayyāvoḷe (Aihoḷe in Karnataka), whose records begin in the ninth and tenth centuries and become very numerous in the eleventh to thirteenth (Abraham 1988; Champakalakshmi 1996). The Five Hundred described themselves in a long formulaic eulogy as followers of a merchant code (vīra-baḷañja-dharma), worshippers of the goddess Bhagavatī, and travellers through many lands. Their inscriptions mention allied bodies of itinerant merchants (nānādeśi), local merchant groups (nagaram), and armed men who protected caravans and markets. They were not guilds in the European sense with fixed membership and monopolies, but loose, overlapping associations that guaranteed trust, settled disputes and negotiated with rulers. Their organisation within India is treated in Chapter 4; here we follow them overseas.

Their inscriptions have been found across the Bay of Bengal. At Takuapa on the west coast of the Thai–Malay peninsula a Tamil inscription of the ninth century records the digging of a tank placed under the protection of the Maṇigrāmam and of a military camp. In Sri Lanka, especially during and after the Chola occupation, many inscriptions of the Five Hundred record their settlements and donations. At Lobu Tua near Barus on the west coast of Sumatra, a port famous for camphor, a Tamil inscription dated Śaka 1010 (1088 CE) records a decision of an assembly of the “Five Hundred of the thousand directions” in the town. In Pagan (Burma) a Tamil inscription of the thirteenth century records a Viṣṇu temple associated with the Nānādeśi merchants (Hall 1980; Abraham 1988; Kulke et al. 2009).

The most distant evidence comes from China. At Quanzhou, the great port of Song and Yuan China, a Tamil inscription dated 1281 records the consecration of a Śiva temple under the authority of the Mongol emperor, and a large number of carved stone fragments from Hindu temples, including images of Viṣṇu and Śiva and scenes from Kṛṣṇa legends, have been found in the city, some reused in the Kaiyuan Buddhist monastery (Sen 2003). Tamil merchants thus maintained a community with its own shrine at the far end of the maritime route in the thirteenth century, alongside the Arab, Persian and other foreign communities whose mosques and tombstones survive in the same city.

The inscriptions record what associations chose to commemorate, usually gifts and agreements; they rarely tell us about the goods, the ships or the profits, and they do not show that the associations controlled any territory. Kenneth Hall and Meera Abraham have shown how closely the activity of these associations was tied to the temple-centred economy of the Chola country and to Chola royal policy, but also that they operated in kingdoms well beyond Chola control (Hall 1980; Abraham 1988).

docs.title: 12.8 Sri Lanka between Two Seas
docs.text:
Sri Lanka lies just off the southern tip of the peninsula, where the routes of the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal meet. The shallow Palk Strait and the shoals of Adam’s Bridge could be crossed only by small craft, so that larger ships passing between the western and eastern coasts of India had to round the island, and its harbours — Mantai opposite the island of Mannar in the north-west, Puttalam and Colombo on the west coast, and Galle in the south — were natural places to wait for the monsoon and to exchange cargoes. The island’s own products, gems, pearls from the Gulf of Mannar, elephants, and later cinnamon, added to its attraction. Its earlier history as a meeting point of Roman, Indian and other traders is outlined in Chapter 11.

Cosmas Indicopleustes.

The fullest early description of the island’s place in the trade comes from the Christian Topography of Cosmas, a Greek-speaking merchant of Alexandria turned monk, written around the middle of the sixth century. In its eleventh book Cosmas describes Taprobane as a great mart that received silk, aloeswood, cloves and sandalwood from China and the lands to the east, and sent them on to Male (Malabar, “where the pepper grows”), to Kalliana (Kalyāṇa, near modern Mumbai), to Sindh, Persia, Yemen and the Red Sea port of Adulis, while itself receiving goods from all these places. He reports a church of Persian Christians on the island, with a priest and a deacon appointed from Persia, and says that the island had two kings, one of whom held the region of the gems and the other the part with the harbour and the mart. He also tells the story of a Roman merchant, Sopatros, who at the court of a Sinhala king set a Roman gold coin beside a Persian silver one and persuaded the king that the Romans were the greater power (Cosmas Indicopleustes 1897). Whether Cosmas himself visited the island is uncertain, and the Sopatros story is an edifying anecdote rather than a record; but his account of the island as a meeting place for ships from east and west fits the archaeological evidence.

Mantai.

The most important port of the Anurādhapura kingdom was Mantai, called Mahātittha in the Pali chronicles and Mātoṭṭam in Tamil, on the mainland of Sri Lanka opposite Mannar. Occupied from the late centuries BCE, it served as the port of the capital, Anurādhapura. Excavations at the site have produced Chinese ceramics, glazed pottery from Iraq and Iran, and glass, evidence of trade with both ends of the ocean in the later first millennium CE (Ray 2003). Nearby stood the Śiva temple of Tirukkētīśvaram, celebrated in the Tamil Śaiva hymns of the seventh and eighth centuries, a sign of the Tamil presence in the port. Mantai declined in the eleventh century, after the Chola conquest of the north and the move of the Sinhala capital to Polonnaruva (Section 12.9.1), and the island’s trade shifted to its western and southern harbours.

Sinhala kings and the sea.

The Sinhala chronicles, the Mahāvaṃsa and its continuation the Cūḷavaṃsa, were written by Buddhist monks and say little about trade, but the kings evidently drew revenue from ports and from the pearl fishery, and maintained relations across the Bay of Bengal. The Cūḷavaṃsa records that Parākramabāhu I (r. 1153–1186) sent an expedition against Rāmañña in Lower Burma, explaining it by the Burmese king’s ill-treatment of Sinhala envoys and his interference with the island’s trade, including a trade in elephants (Geiger 1929). The account is one-sided and its details cannot be checked, but it shows a Sinhala court concerned with commerce and diplomacy across the Bay. The religious ties between Sri Lanka and Pagan are discussed in Chapter 16 (Hall 2011).

Muslims, Tamils and Chinese.

Arabic writers called the island Sarandīb, and Muslim merchants settled in its western ports. A mountain in the interior, known in English as Adam’s Peak, was a place of pilgrimage for several religions: Buddhists venerated a footprint on its summit as the Buddha’s, Hindus as Śiva’s, and Muslims as Adam’s. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who landed on the west coast in 1344, describes the cinnamon gathered there, which merchants from Malabar and Maʿbar took away in return for gifts of cloth to the ruler; he was received by the Tamil ruler of the north, whom he calls Ayrī Shakarwatī (Āriya Cakravarti, of the kingdom of Jaffna), a man rich in pearls with ships of his own, before climbing Adam’s Peak and travelling to Galle and Colombo (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958). Tamil merchant associations had been active on the island since the Chola period (Section 12.7), and Tamil-speaking Muslims of the Coromandel coast traded to its ports (Chapter 17). At the end of our period the island was drawn into Ming diplomacy: besides the trilingual inscription at Galle (Section 12.10), Zheng He’s fleet fought the Sinhala ruler Alagakkonāra in 1411, took him captive and carried him to China, where the emperor later released him (Dreyer 2007). Sri Lanka thus remained, as Cosmas had described it, a place where the ships and merchants of many nations met, and where control of ports and harbours mattered to every ruler who claimed the island.

docs.title: 12.9 The Chola Expeditions
docs.text: The Chola kings of the Kāverī delta (from the mid-ninth century to 1279) are the only south Indian dynasty known to have sent armed expeditions across the Bay of Bengal. Their naval activity has often been described as a maritime empire or as “Indian Ocean dominance”. The evidence supports a narrower and more interesting picture: a series of conquests in Sri Lanka and the islands, one major raid across the Bay in 1025 and perhaps a second in the 1060s, and a long diplomatic and commercial relationship with Śrīvijaya and China, in which war was the exception rather than the rule.

docs.title: 12.9.1 Sri Lanka and the Islands
docs.text: Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014) conquered northern Sri Lanka around 993, sacked Anurādhapura and made Polonnaruva the seat of a Chola province. His Tamil praise-preface (meykkīrtti) also claims the conquest of the “twelve thousand ancient islands” of the sea, usually taken to mean the Maldives and perhaps the Lakshadweep islands. His son Rājendra I (r. 1012/14–1044) completed the conquest of Sri Lanka around 1017–18 and captured its king. Chola rule in the island lasted until about 1070, when Vijayabāhu I drove the Cholas out (Nilakanta Sastri 1955; Spencer 1983). The Sri Lankan campaigns were wars of conquest across a narrow strait, with long occupation; they gave the Cholas control of ports such as Mantai (Mātoṭṭam) and of the pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar.

docs.title: 12.9.2 Śrīvijaya: Friendship and Raid
docs.text:
Relations with Śrīvijaya, the Malay kingdom based in southeast Sumatra that controlled much of the trade of the Straits, began peacefully. The Larger Leiden plates record a grant of revenue from the village of Āṉaimaṅgalam made by Rājarāja I in about 1006, and confirmed by Rājendra I, to a Buddhist monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam built in the name of Cūḷāmaṇivarman by his son Māravijayottuṅgavarman, the Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya and Kaṭāha (Kedah). A Sumatran king was thus building a Buddhist monastery in the principal Chola port, with Chola endowment, presumably for the use of his subjects who traded there (Nilakanta Sastri 1955; Kulke et al. 2009).

In 1025 this relationship broke down. The main evidence is Rājendra I’s Tamil meykkīrtti, which appears in his inscriptions from about 1025/26 onward.
