It states that he sent ships across the sea, seized the king of Kaḍāram (Kedah), Saṅgrāmavijayottuṅgavarman, with his elephants and treasure, and took a jewelled gateway (the vidyādhara-toraṇa) and a series of named places: Śrīvijaya, Paṇṇai, Malaiyūr, Māyiruḍiṅgam, Ilaṅgāśokam (Laṅkāsuka), Māppappāḷam, Mēviḷimbaṅgam, Valaippandūru, Talaittakkōlam, Mādamāliṅgam, Ilāmuridēśam (Lamuri in north Sumatra), Mānakkavāram (the Nicobars) and Kaḍāram itself. Most of these places have been identified with ports in Sumatra, the Malay peninsula and the islands of the Bay (Nilakanta Sastri 1955; Kulke et al. 2009). The great Sanskrit and Tamil copper-plate charters of Rājendra’s reign, the Tiruvālaṅgāḍu and Karandai plates, set out the dynasty’s official genealogy and its account of its wars. No Southeast Asian source describes the raid, and there is no archaeological evidence of Chola occupation in the region.

The list of ports reads as a single sweep along the trade routes of the Straits, striking at the entrepôts through which Śrīvijaya controlled the trade, and the expedition seems to have been a raid rather than a conquest. Śrīvijaya continued to send missions to China, and Chola inscriptions do not show any administration overseas. A later Chola king, Vīrarājendra (r. 1063–1070), claims in an inscription to have conquered Kaḍāram and restored it to a king who had sought his protection, which suggests intervention in a local dispute in the 1060s (Nilakanta Sastri 1955; Spencer 1983).

Debate: Why did Rājendra raid Śrīvijaya?

Historians have proposed several motives, which are not mutually exclusive.

  • Commercial. K. A. Nilakanta Sastri suggested that Śrīvijaya was obstructing Chola trade with China, perhaps through heavy tolls in the Straits, and that the raid aimed to remove the obstruction (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). Kenneth Hall linked it to the interests of the Tamil merchant associations (Hall 1980). No source, however, records tolls or a quarrel over trade.

  • Plunder and prestige. George Spencer argued that Chola expansion in general was driven by the search for booty and glory, which kings redistributed through temples and to their followers, and that the Śrīvijaya raid fits the pattern of Chola raiding in the Deccan and on the Ganga (Spencer 1983).

  • Diplomacy and the China trade. Tansen Sen and Hermann Kulke have pointed to competition for access to the Song court, where the status of a “tributary” mission brought trading privileges. Song records at one point describe the Chola kingdom as subordinate to Śrīvijaya, apparently reflecting what Śrīvijayan envoys told the court, and the raid may have been a response to rivalry of this kind (Sen 2003; Kulke et al. 2009).

Most recent writers agree that the expedition was a single, spectacular raid with no lasting territorial result; of its scale and logistics the inscriptions say nothing specific. The places they name are shown in Figure 12.1.

docs.title: 12.9.3 Chola Missions to China
docs.text: Chinese sources record several Chola missions to the Song court between 1015 and 1077. These missions brought pearls, ivory, rhinoceros horn, textiles and aromatics, received gifts in return, and gave the merchants who accompanied them the right to trade. Tansen Sen has argued that they should be read mainly as commercial ventures in diplomatic form, organised by or with merchants, rather than as evidence of a close political relationship (Sen 2003). The trade through Nāgapaṭṭinam and other Coromandel ports continued after the end of Chola power; in the thirteenth century the Pāṇḍya coast, which Arabic and Persian writers called Maʿbar, was the main destination of the Gulf horse trade discussed below.

docs.title: 12.10 Chinese Shipping: From the Song to Zheng He
docs.text:
Until about the tenth century most of the long-distance shipping between China and the Indian Ocean was in the hands of West Asian and Southeast Asian merchants and their ships. Chinese officials taxed and regulated foreign trade at Guangzhou, where the Tang had appointed a commissioner for maritime trade, but Chinese ships rarely sailed beyond Southeast Asia. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) this changed. The Song government, which depended increasingly on customs revenue, set up maritime trade offices at several ports, including Quanzhou in 1087, and Chinese merchants began to build large ocean-going junks with multiple masts, stern-post rudders and hulls divided by bulkheads (Sen 2003; Manguin 1993). Zhao Rugua, an official at Quanzhou, compiled in 1225 a description of foreign countries and their products, the Zhufan zhi, which includes notices of Gujarat, Malabar and the Coromandel coast based on what merchants told him (Zhao 1911).

Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) Quanzhou, known to Arabic and European writers as Zaitun, was one of the largest ports in the world. Yuan envoys visited Quilon and the Pāṇḍya coast, and Chinese ships sailed regularly to the ports of south India. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, at Calicut in the 1340s, saw Chinese junks in the harbour and describes them as very large ships with several decks, private cabins for merchants, and crews who grew vegetables and herbs in wooden tubs; he planned to sail to China on one of them, but was left stranded when the junk carrying the embassy he accompanied was wrecked in a storm and the smaller vessel with his belongings sailed without him (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958).

The early Ming emperors restricted private overseas trade but sponsored official expeditions. Between 1405 and 1433 the eunuch admiral Zheng He commanded seven voyages of large fleets into the Indian Ocean. Calicut was the main destination of the first three voyages; later voyages went on to Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast, including Mogadishu and Malindi. The fleets carried tens of thousands of men, according to Ming sources, but the dimensions of the largest “treasure ships” given in later texts are disputed, and Edward Dreyer regards them as exaggerated (Dreyer 2007). The purpose of the voyages was to display Ming power, to bring foreign rulers into the tributary system and to obtain exotic goods, not to establish colonies or to dominate trade. They ended after 1433, when the court lost interest.

The interpreter Ma Huan, a Chinese Muslim who sailed on three of the voyages, describes Calicut in his Yingya shenglan: its Hindu king, its Muslim officials and merchants, its pepper trade, and the brokers who negotiated the prices of cargoes (Ma 1970). A trilingual stone inscription in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, dated 1409 and set up by the Ming envoys at Galle in Sri Lanka, records offerings made to the Buddha, to a Hindu deity and to Allah respectively (Dreyer 2007). Like the Quanzhou finds, it shows a world in which merchants and envoys moved routinely between religious communities.

docs.title: 12.11 Śrīvijaya, Java and the Straits
docs.text:
Southeast Asian sailors and merchants were not passive recipients of Indian or Chinese trade. Ships of the Malay world, built of planks edge-joined with wooden dowels and steered with paired quarter rudders, were carrying goods across the South China Sea and into the Bay of Bengal long before 600; Chinese sources call them kunlun bo. Pierre-Yves Manguin has shown that this distinct shipbuilding tradition continued into the large Javanese jong of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries (Manguin 1993).

The kingdom of Śrīvijaya, centred near Palembang in southeast Sumatra, is first known from Old Malay inscriptions of the 680s and from the account of the Chinese monk Yijing, who stayed there in 671 and again between 687 and 695 to study and copy Buddhist texts. O. W. Wolters argued that Śrīvijaya grew rich by making itself the main entrepôt between the Indian Ocean and China, attracting ships to its ports, supplying Chinese markets with Sumatran resins and forest products as substitutes for West Asian aromatics, and using its fleets to suppress rival ports (Wolters 1967). Its rulers also patronised Buddhism in India, at Nālandā in the ninth century and at Nāgapaṭṭinam in the eleventh (Section 12.9.2; Chapter 16) (Coedès 1968).

After the Chola raid of 1025, power in the Straits shifted between Jambi (Malayu), the Javanese kingdoms of Singhasari and Majapahit (from 1293), and the ports of northern Sumatra such as Samudra-Pasai, whose rulers adopted Islam by the late thirteenth century. Around 1400 a prince from Sumatra founded Malacca on the Malay peninsula. Within a few decades its rulers, who adopted Islam, had made it the principal entrepôt of the Straits, where Gujarati, Tamil (known locally as Keling), Bengali, Javanese, Chinese and Ryukyuan merchants met under the protection of the sultan and his harbour-masters (Pires 1944; Wolters 1999). The cultural and religious history of these kingdoms is treated in Chapter 16.

docs.title: 12.12 The Swahili Coast
docs.text:
The western end of the ocean was the East African coast from Somalia to Mozambique. From the eighth century small trading towns developed there, and from the eleventh and twelfth centuries some, such as Mogadishu, Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Pate and Manda, were building in coral stone, with mosques, palaces and merchants’ houses. The people of these towns were Swahili, an African society speaking a Bantu language, Muslim from an early date, with close ties to Arabia, the Gulf and India. Mark Horton and John Middleton stress that Swahili towns were African creations, not Arab colonies, despite later origin legends claiming descent from settlers from Shiraz (Horton and Middleton 2000).

The coast exported ivory, gold, ambergris, tortoiseshell, rock crystal, timber and mangrove poles, and enslaved people; it imported cotton cloth, glass beads, ceramics and metal goods. Kilwa, on an island off southern Tanzania, flourished from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century by controlling the export of gold mined on the Zimbabwe plateau and shipped through Sofala. It minted its own copper coins, and its Great Mosque and the palace of Husuni Kubwa are among the most impressive medieval buildings of the coast. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa visited Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa around 1331 and admired Kilwa as a beautiful and well-built town (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958; Horton and Middleton 2000). Indian cloth and beads, and Chinese porcelain, are common finds in Swahili towns; Indian merchants, mainly from Gujarat and the Konkan, traded on the coast, though permanent Indian settlement there is better documented after 1500.

The ocean’s trade included people. East Africans were enslaved and carried to Arabia, Iraq, Iran and India throughout this period; in ninth-century Iraq enslaved East Africans (the Zanj) rose in a long revolt (869–883). In India, Africans known as Habshīs served as soldiers and officials in several sultanates, and in Bengal Habshī commanders briefly ruled in the 1480s and 1490s. Slavery in the Indian Ocean took many forms, from domestic service to military careers, but it was everywhere a form of coercion (Alpers 2014; Pearson 2003).

docs.title: 12.13.1 Horses
docs.text: The climate and pasture of most of peninsular India were unsuitable for breeding large cavalry horses, and Indian armies depended on imports. Horses came overland from Central Asia and Afghanistan to the north (Chapter 10) and by sea from Arabia and the Gulf to the ports of western and southern India. Marco Polo, who passed along the coast of Maʿbar in the 1290s, reports that its kings bought large numbers of horses each year from merchants of Hormuz, Kish, Dhofar, Shihr and Aden, because the horses did not breed well and died quickly in south India (Polo 1903). The Persian historian Waṣṣāf, writing in the early fourteenth century, describes the horse trade from Kish to Maʿbar and the wealth it brought to Gulf merchant families, one of whose members held high office at the Pāṇḍya court. Both writers give large figures for the number and price of horses, but these cannot be checked and should be treated as impressions rather than data (Wink 1990; Digby 1971). The demand continued under the Bahmanī sultans and Vijayanagara in the fifteenth century, and horse imports were one of the main sources of the customs revenue of west-coast ports.

docs.title: 12.13.2 Pepper and Spices
docs.text: Pepper from Malabar was the most important spice of the trade, sold westward to Egypt, Venice and the rest of Europe, and eastward to China, where demand grew strongly under the Song and Yuan. Ginger, cardamom and cinnamon (from Sri Lanka) came from South Asia; cloves, nutmeg and mace came from the Maluku islands of eastern Indonesia and reached India by way of Java and the Straits. Spices were valuable but were only part of a much larger trade in bulk goods. Rice from Kanara and the Coromandel coast fed Malabar, Aden and the Maldives; sugar, cotton, timber, iron and salt moved along the coasts; and much of the shipping consisted of coastal craft carrying everyday goods between neighbouring ports (Chaudhuri 1985; Chakravarti 2002).

docs.title: 12.13.3 Textiles
docs.text:
Indian cotton cloth was the most widely traded manufactured good of the ocean. Gujarat, the Coromandel coast and Bengal each produced cloth in many qualities, from coarse cloth for everyday wear to fine muslins and printed and painted fabrics, for markets from East Africa to Indonesia. The most direct evidence comes from archaeology. Excavations at Fusṭāṭ in Egypt have yielded large numbers of fragments of block-printed and resist-dyed cotton made in Gujarat, with radiocarbon dates spread across roughly the tenth to the fifteenth century; the collection in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, catalogued by Ruth Barnes, is the best known (Barnes 1997). Figure 12.2 shows a fragment of this kind. At the other end of the ocean, Indian textiles preserved as heirlooms in eastern Indonesia include pieces radiocarbon-dated to the fourteenth century and later, with designs that match the Fusṭāṭ finds (Guy 1998). Cloth was often used in place of money: on the Swahili coast and in parts of Southeast Asia, prices were reckoned in pieces of Indian cloth. Weaving and dyeing are treated in Chapter 8 and in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

Figure 12.2. Fragment of cotton cloth from Gujarat, block-printed with a resist and dyed in indigo, probably thirteenth–fourteenth century; Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Fragments of this kind have been found in large numbers at Fusṭāṭ. Image: Los Angeles County Museum of Art, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 12.13.4 Gems, Pearls and Cowries
docs.text:
Sri Lanka was famous for its gems, especially sapphires and rubies from the gravels of the south-west, and the Gulf of Mannar between Sri Lanka and India for its pearls; Marco Polo describes the pearl fishery off the coast of Maʿbar, the divers, and the share of the catch taken by the king (Polo 1903). Diamonds came from the Deccan, and Indian lapidaries cut and polished stones from many sources. The Maldives exported coir rope, dried fish and, above all, cowry shells, which served as small change in Bengal and other parts of eastern India and, by way of Egypt and the Sahara, in West Africa. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who lived in the Maldives in the 1340s and served there as a judge, describes the gathering of cowries and their export to Bengal (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958). The use of cowries as currency is discussed in Chapter 5. Table 12.2 summarises the principal goods of the trade.

Table 12.2. Principal goods of the Indian Ocean trade, c. 600–1500 (selective) Region Main exports East Africa Ivory, gold, ambergris, tortoiseshell, mangrove timber, enslaved people Red Sea, Yemen Coral, frankincense and myrrh; transit of Egyptian and Mediterranean goods Gulf and Iran Horses, pearls, dates, silver, rose water Gujarat Cotton cloth (including block-printed cloth), indigo, beads of carnelian and agate Malabar and Kanara Pepper, ginger, cardamom, rice, teak Coromandel Cotton cloth, rice Sri Lanka and Gulf of Mannar Cinnamon, gems, pearls, elephants Maldives Cowries, coir, dried fish Bengal Fine cotton cloth, rice, sugar Southeast Asia Camphor, benzoin and other resins, aromatic woods, tin, gold; cloves and nutmeg from Maluku China Silk, porcelain, copper coins, iron goods

docs.title: 12.14 Religion Travels with Trade
docs.text:
The ocean carried beliefs as well as goods. In the first part of our period Buddhist monks travelled on merchant ships between India, Sri Lanka, Śrīvijaya and China, and Buddhist monasteries in ports, such as the one at Nāgapaṭṭinam, served merchants as well as monks (Sen 2003; Ray 1994). Hindu temples followed Tamil merchants to Pagan and Quanzhou. Islam spread along the trade routes, carried by merchants, scholars and Sufis, and found protection under non-Muslim rulers in Malabar, Gujarat and Sri Lanka long before Muslim states arose on the coasts. In the Maldives the conversion of the ruler is traditionally dated to 1153, and in northern Sumatra the first Muslim ruler of Samudra-Pasai died in 1297; carved gravestones of this period in Sumatra and Java appear to have been made in Cambay and shipped across the ocean, a small but telling sign of Gujarat’s role (Coedès 1968; Prange 2018). The cultural transmission to Southeast Asia, including the use of Sanskrit and Indian scripts, is treated in Chapter 16.

The Brahmanical law books discouraged sea voyages for members of the higher varṇas (Section 19.12.3), but Hindu and Jain merchants of Gujarat and the south crossed the sea routinely, and the restriction seems to have been applied unevenly, by caste and region, rather than as a universal rule.

docs.title: 12.15 Conclusion
docs.text: India’s place in this world rested less on its ships than on its products, cotton cloth and pepper above all, and on the readiness of its coastal rulers to protect merchants of every faith. Violence was present, from the Chola raid of 1025 to piracy and slavery, but no state before 1500 tried to control the sea lanes as a whole; that attempt came with the Portuguese (Chapter 18).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Chaudhuri (1985) remains the classic interpretation of the ocean as a single historical space, and Pearson (2003) the most readable general history. Prange (2018) is the best study of a single coast, Malabar, and its Muslim merchants. The Geniza letters are translated in Goitein and Friedman (2008). For the Chola expeditions and the Tamil merchant associations see the essays in Kulke et al. (2009); for India and China, Sen (2003); for the Ming voyages, Dreyer (2007); and for the Swahili coast, Horton and Middleton (2000).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Ships and Shipbuilding
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Very few ancient or medieval ships from Indian waters have been excavated. What we know of them comes from scattered images, from the remarks of Greek, Arab, Chinese and European observers, from a small number of Sanskrit and Tamil texts, and from the boats that are still built on the coasts of South Asia. This chapter sets out that evidence and its limits. It describes the sewn-plank tradition of the western Indian Ocean and the few shipwrecks that now document it, contrasts it with the lashed-lug ships of Southeast Asia and the Chinese junk, surveys the regional craft of the subcontinent, and explains why the ship lore of the Yuktikalpataru should be read as a textual typology rather than as a record of engineering. It ends with the shipyards of the early modern period, from Surat and the Konkan forts to the Bombay Dockyard of the Wadia master builders, and with the wooden-ship builders who still work at Beypore and Mandvi.

Writing on Indian ships has long been shaped by two opposite distortions. Radhakumud Mookerji’s Indian Shipping (Mookerji 1912), written in the years of the Swadeshi movement, gathered every textual reference to ships it could find into a picture of a great Indian maritime tradition, and its claims are still widely repeated. Older European scholarship, on the other hand, tended to treat the Indian Ocean as a sea sailed mainly by Greeks, Arabs and later Europeans. The evidence supports neither view. It shows a shared ocean in which shipbuilders on many coasts, Indian, Arab, Persian, East African, Southeast Asian and Chinese, worked within a few broad technical traditions and borrowed from each other over many centuries (McGrail et al. 2003; Ray 2003; Hourani 1995).

docs.title: 13.1 The Evidence and Its Limits
docs.text:
Five kinds of evidence are available, and each has its own weakness (Table 13.1).

Table 13.1. Sources for the history of ships in South Asian waters Kind of source Examples Limits Excavated hulls Very few in Indian waters; the ninth-century Belitung wreck in Indonesia is the best-known sewn ship of the western Indian Ocean type Wood rarely survives in warm seas; most finds are cargoes, anchors and fittings Images Indus seals and a terracotta model from Lothal; early Buddhist reliefs; Sātavāhana ship coins; the Ajanta paintings; temple reliefs; the Borobudur reliefs in Java Artistic conventions, small scale; not technical drawings Texts Periplus; Arthaśāstra; Jātakas; Tamil Caṅkam poems; the Yuktikalpataru Literary or normative; technical terms often obscure Travellers and merchants Marco Polo, Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, Chinese officials, Portuguese and later European writers Outsiders’ views; prone to generalisation Ethnography Boats recorded on the coasts of South Asia in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Shows recent practice; continuity with the past must be argued, not assumed

The most systematic modern work is ethnographic and archaeological. Seán McGrail and his colleagues recorded the traditional boats of the coasts of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka in the 1990s, and their survey remains the basis for any discussion of South Asian boatbuilding (McGrail et al. 2003); McGrail’s world survey places these boats in a comparative frame (McGrail 2001). Jean Deloche’s volume on water transport collects the textual and iconographic evidence for river and sea craft (Deloche 1993), and Himanshu Prabha Ray discusses the archaeology of seafaring, including the images of ships (Ray 2003). Arab ships are treated by George Hourani (Hourani 1995), and Southeast Asian and Chinese ships by Pierre-Yves Manguin (Manguin 1993).

docs.title: 13.2 Early Representations and Early Texts
docs.text:
The earliest images of boats in South Asia come from the Harappan cities. A few seals and moulded tablets show craft with a high bow and stern and a cabin amidships, and a terracotta model from Lothal has been read as a boat with a socket for a mast. These images are too schematic to reconstruct a sea-going hull (McGrail et al. 2003); the debate over the basin at Lothal is set out in Section 11.3.

For the early historic period, the most precise descriptions are those of the Periplus Maris Erythraei (mid-first century CE). Its author names several kinds of local craft. At Barygaza (Bharuch), fishermen in the king’s service went out in boats called trappaga and kotymba to meet incoming ships and tow or pilot them up the river (§44). On the Tamil coast he distinguishes local coasting craft, large vessels called sangara made of single logs fastened together, and very large ships called kolandiophōnta that sailed to Chrysē (Southeast Asia) and the Ganga (§60). He also mentions ships from Barygaza and Ariakē that carried grain, rice, cloth and other goods to the Horn of Africa (§14), so Indian-owned vessels were plainly at sea in the western Indian Ocean (Casson 1989). The words are Greek renderings of local names, and their exact meaning is uncertain; sangara may be related to Tamil and Malayalam words for a raft or double canoe.

The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) assigns to a superintendent of shipping (nāvadhyakṣa, AŚ 2.28) the supervision of ferries, boat hire, tolls in port towns, the treatment of ships damaged by storms, and the destruction of pirate ships. It is concerned with administration and revenue, not with how ships were built (Olivelle 2013); port administration is discussed in Chapter 15. The Pali Jātakas describe voyages from Bharukaccha, Campā and other ports in ships that carry merchants by the hundred. Such numbers are stock formulas of the story-tellers and cannot be used to estimate the size of real ships.

Three groups of images deserve mention. First, lead coins showing a ship with two masts (Figure 13.1a), found mainly in the coastal districts of Andhra and on the Coromandel coast, are commonly attributed to the Sātavāhana king Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi (late second century CE); the attribution of some specimens is debated, but the coins show that a coastal kingdom thought a sea-going ship a suitable emblem (see also Chapter 5) (Ray 2003). Second, a painting at Ajanta (Figure 13.1b), usually placed in Cave 2 and dated to the late fifth century CE, shows a sea-going ship with several masts in a narrative scene; it has been reproduced since Mookerji’s time as a picture of an “Indian ship”, but like the reliefs at Sanchi and Bharhut it follows the conventions of narrative art rather than recording the details of a real hull. Third, the reliefs of Borobudur in Central Java (c. 800 CE; Figure 16.1) show large ships with outriggers and tilted rectangular sails. They are Javanese ships, built in the Southeast Asian tradition described below, and are discussed in Chapter 16; they are not evidence for Indian shipbuilding.

Figure 13.1. Early images of ships. (a) Lead coins of the Sātavāhana period showing a two-masted ship, as reproduced in The Modern Review (1910) under the title “Andhra ship-coins of the 2nd century A.D.” (b) The ship painting at Ajanta, usually placed in Cave 2 (late fifth century CE). Image: The Modern Review, vol. 8 (1910), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.3 Sewn Boats of the Western Indian Ocean
docs.text:
The characteristic ship of the Arabian Sea from antiquity to the early modern period was the sewn-plank boat. Its hull planks were laid edge to edge and fastened by cords passed through holes drilled near the plank edges, usually in a continuous pattern of stitches along each seam. The cord was normally of coir, the fibre of the coconut husk, which resists seawater well. Wadding of fibre and a luting of resin, oil or other compounds sealed the seams, and frames were inserted after the planking had been raised, so that the shape of the hull was set by the planks rather than by a pre-erected skeleton (“plank-first” or “shell-first” construction) (McGrail et al. 2003; Hourani 1995).

The technique is old and widespread. The Periplus says that the port of Rhapta on the East African coast took its name from the sewn boats used there (§16) and that sewn boats called madarate were exported from Omana in the Gulf to Arabia (§36) (Casson 1989). Medieval Arabic writers describe the ships of the Gulf, Arabia and India as sewn with coconut cord, and the materials of the trade moved across the ocean: Indian teak (Arabic sāj) was shipped to the Gulf for shipbuilding, and coir came from the Maldives and the Lakshadweep islands as well as from the Malabar coast (Hourani 1995; Chaudhuri 1985). The ninth-century ship wrecked off Belitung in Indonesia, which was carrying Chinese ceramics westwards, was a sewn ship of this western type, a reminder that sewn ships sailed as far as China.

Outside observers often disparaged the method. Marco Polo, at Hormuz in the late thirteenth century, judged the local ships unsafe because they were sewn with cord made from coconut husk rather than fastened with iron nails. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, describing the coir trade of the Maldives in the fourteenth century, explains that the ships of India and the Yemen were sewn with this cord, and reports the sailors’ view that a sewn hull gave a little when it struck rocks where a nailed one would break (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958). A different explanation circulated widely in Greek, Arabic and later Indian writing: that magnetic rocks in the sea would pull the nails out of a ship. Ptolemy’s Geography already places such islands in the eastern ocean, and the story recurs in Arabic wonder-tales. It is a legend, not a reason, and the more practical explanations are the scarcity and cost of iron, the ease of repair with materials available in any port, and the flexibility of a sewn hull in surf and on beaches (McGrail et al. 2003; Hourani 1995).

Sewn construction was gradually displaced by nailed planking, although the chronology is uneven. Iron fastening was used in the Indian Ocean by the later Middle Ages, and Portuguese, and later other European, influence accelerated the change in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Sewn boats nevertheless survived into the twentieth century in several places: the masula surf boats of the Coromandel coast, which were sewn without frames so that they could flex as they were driven through the surf onto the beach; sewn fishing boats in parts of Kerala and Sri Lanka; and sewn craft on the coasts of Arabia and East Africa (McGrail et al. 2003; Deloche 1993). Figure 13.2 contrasts the two ways of fastening planks, and Figure 13.3 shows masula boats being built and mended on the beach at Madras in the 1820s.

Figure 13.2. Two ways of fastening hull planks (schematic, not to scale; sections through the hull). (a) In the sewn plank-first tradition of the western Indian Ocean, planks were laid edge to edge and sewn with coir cord passed through holes near the edges, over a roll of fibre wadding laid along the inside of the seam; the seam was sealed with a luting, and frames were inserted after the planking had been raised. (b) In nailed construction the planks are fixed with iron nails, here to a frame, and the seams are caulked. Nailed hulls in the Indian Ocean were not necessarily built frame-first: the uru of Beypore is nailed but still shaped plank-first, by eye (Section 13.8). Figure 13.3. “Building and mending Masula boats” on the beach at Madras: hand-coloured lithograph by John Gantz, from The Indian Microcosm (1827). The planks of the frameless hulls are sewn together; the accompanying text explains that the fire is used to bend planks for the bows. Image: John Gantz, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.3.1 Shipwrecks
docs.text: Wood rarely survives in warm seas, and until recently no hull of the western Indian Ocean type had been excavated. Three finds have changed this. The wreck found in 1998 off Belitung island in Indonesia carried a cargo of Chinese ceramics of the ninth century, one bowl inscribed with a date corresponding to 826; its hull was sewn, in the manner of the western Indian Ocean, and its excavator suggested that it was an Arab or Indian ship (Flecker 2000). A full-sized reconstruction, the Jewel of Muscat, was built in Oman and sailed to Singapore in 2010. At Phanom Surin in central Thailand a sewn-plank ship of about the eighth or ninth century was found in 2013 in land reclaimed from the sea; a storage jar from it carries a short inscription in Pahlavi (Middle Persian) script, and its construction is still being studied (Guy 2017). Off Godawaya on the southern coast of Sri Lanka, divers have recorded an early historic wreck whose cargo included glass ingots and stone querns; little of the hull survives, but the site is among the earliest wrecks yet known in South Asian waters (Muthucumarana et al. 2014). None of these ships can yet be said with certainty to have been built in India, but together they confirm what the texts and travellers report about sewn hulls and show ships of the western type at the far end of the Bay of Bengal and beyond.

docs.title: 13.4 Other Traditions: Southeast Asia and China
docs.text:
The eastern Indian Ocean and the South China Sea had their own shipbuilding traditions, and ships from these traditions regularly reached the ports of India.

Manguin has defined a Southeast Asian tradition of large plank-built ships whose planks were joined edge to edge with wooden dowels and whose frames were lashed with fibre cord to lugs carved on the inner face of the planks. These “lashed-lug” ships used no iron, had two quarter rudders, and often carried several masts with tilted rectangular sails. Chinese sources from the third century CE onward describe large ships of the “Kunlun” people (a Chinese term for the peoples of maritime Southeast Asia) carrying hundreds of passengers, and Manguin identifies them with this tradition (Manguin 1993). The ships of Śrīvijaya, and the ships shown at Borobudur, belong here (Chapter 16).

The Chinese junk was built on different principles. Its hull was divided by transverse bulkheads into watertight compartments, its planks were fastened with iron nails, and it was steered with a single axial rudder hung on the stern; its sails were stiffened with battens of bamboo. Large ocean-going junks were built from the Song period onward, and Ibn Baṭṭūṭa describes them at Calicut in the 1340s (Chapter 12). From about the fourteenth century Manguin identifies hybrid “South China Sea” ships that combined features of the Chinese and Southeast Asian traditions (Manguin 1993; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958).

The comparison shows that there was no single “Indian ship”. Indian shipbuilders worked chiefly in the sewn-plank tradition of the west and, on the east coast, in close contact with Southeast Asian practice, and ships of all three traditions met in the ports of the subcontinent.

docs.title: 13.5 Regional Craft of the Subcontinent
docs.text:
The coasts and rivers of South Asia supported a great variety of craft, adapted to local conditions of beach, surf, river and lagoon. Table 13.2 lists some of the types recorded in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. They are recent forms, but several of them preserve techniques that are clearly old.

Table 13.2. Some traditional craft of the South Asian coasts (recorded in modern times) Type Region Construction and use Kaṭṭumaram (log raft) Coromandel coast, Sri Lanka Several logs lashed together (Tamil kaṭṭu, “to tie”, maram, “wood”); a raft, not a twin-hulled boat; the source of English “catamaran” Masula Coromandel coast Sewn, frameless surf boat for landing goods and passengers through surf Dugouts and extended dugouts Many coasts and rivers Hollowed logs, sometimes with sewn or nailed washstrakes added Vaḷḷam and snake boats Kerala backwaters Long plank-built boats; the large snake boats (cuṇṭaṉ vaḷḷam) are now used in ceremonial races Uru Malabar coast Large carvel-planked sailing vessel; built today mainly for Gulf owners Pattamar Konkan and Malabar Coasting sailing vessel of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Koṭiyā and related dhows Kutch and Saurashtra Plank-built sailing vessels for the Gulf and East African trade River boats Ganga delta, Indus Many types, including large cargo boats and flat-bottomed delta craft

Most of the planked boats recorded by McGrail and his colleagues were built plank-first, and their shape was set by eye and by rules of proportion held in the builder’s memory, not by drawings (McGrail et al. 2003). This is the practice of a craft tradition, learnt by apprenticeship and transmitted within families and communities of carpenters, and it explains why so little was written down. Rigging followed broad Indian Ocean patterns: square sails were used on early ships, and the lateen sail, a triangular or near-triangular sail set on a long yard, became the characteristic rig of the Arabian Sea in the medieval period, though its date of introduction there is uncertain. Large ships were steered with quarter rudders or steering oars before the stern-post rudder became general (Hourani 1995; McGrail 2001). Figure 13.4 shows the difference between the two rigs.

Figure 13.4. Square and lateen rigs (schematic sail plans, not to scale). (a) A square sail hangs from a yard set across the hull and draws best with the wind from astern or on the quarter. (b) A lateen sail is a triangular sail on a long yard slung obliquely from the mast, its forward end low near the bow; set fore and aft, it lets a ship sail closer to the wind. The dhows of the Arabian Sea commonly carried the related “settee” form, with a short forward edge. When the lateen rig was introduced in the Indian Ocean is uncertain (Section 13.5).

Timber choices were governed by local supply. Teak (Tectona grandis) from the forests of the Western Ghats and Gujarat was valued throughout the Arabian Sea for its strength and its resistance to rot and to shipworm, while other woods, including jackwood and various local hardwoods, were used for particular parts or for smaller boats.

docs.title: 13.6 The Yuktikalpataru: A Textual Typology
docs.text:
The one Sanskrit text that classifies ships at some length is the Yuktikalpataru, a compilatory work attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā (r. c. 1010–1055). It was edited at Calcutta in 1917 (Bhoja 1917), but its ship material had already been made famous by Mookerji, who summarised it in Indian Shipping (Mookerji 1912). Most later accounts depend on Mookerji’s summary rather than on the text. The attribution to Bhoja is uncertain: many works were ascribed to that celebrated royal patron, and the date and authorship of the Yuktikalpataru have not been established. The work is a compendium of “devices” (yukti) concerning the things a king should know, of which ships are one topic among many, alongside such subjects as gems, weapons, horses and furniture.

According to Mookerji’s summary, the text divides vessels into two broad classes: sāmānya, “ordinary” vessels for river use, and viśeṣa, “special” vessels for the sea. The ordinary class is subdivided into named types by size, and the sea-going class into two groups, dīrghā (“long”) and unnatā (“high”), each again with named subtypes. The text gives schematic dimensions for these types in rājahastas (“royal cubits”), together with remarks on their qualities: some types are said to be unsteady or unlucky, others to bring prosperity. A further classification sorts vessels by the position of their cabins, along the whole length, amidships or towards the bow, and associates each with a use, such as carrying the royal treasury or horses, pleasure trips in the rains, or long voyages and war. The text also prescribes ornament: colours and metals for the prow according to the number of masts, and figures of animals for the bow.

Timber is classified on the model of the four varṇas. Wood that is light and soft and joins easily to other wood is called “brāhmaṇa”; light and hard wood that does not join well is “kṣatriya”; soft and heavy wood is “vaiśya”; hard and heavy wood is “śūdra”. The text is also reported to warn against fastening the bottom of a ship with iron, lest magnetic rocks in the sea draw the vessel to destruction, which is the same legend found in Greek and Arabic writing (Section 13.3).

Scholarly Note: How to Read the Yuktikalpataru

The Yuktikalpataru is evidence for how a learned compiler, probably in the early second millennium CE, organised knowledge about ships: by classes and sub-classes, by auspicious and inauspicious qualities, and by analogy with the social order. It is not a shipwright’s manual. It says nothing about how planks were joined, how a hull was shaped, or how a ship was rigged and steered, and its dimensions are schematic numbers of the kind found in other śāstras. Mookerji’s summary, and many later accounts that cite it at second hand, also differ among themselves in the sizes they give for particular classes, which is a further reason not to use them as data; any figure or verse attributed to the text should be checked against the 1917 edition. Whether the classes of the Yuktikalpataru correspond to any real vessels is an open question; answering it would require a critical study of the text, which has not yet been made.

docs.title: 13.7 Ships and Shipyards in the Early Modern Period
docs.text: From the sixteenth century the evidence becomes much richer, thanks to Portuguese, Dutch and English records and to the documents of Indian merchants and states.

docs.title: 13.7.1 Gujarat and the Mughal Ports
docs.text: The ports of Gujarat, above all Surat in the seventeenth century, owned and built large ocean-going ships for the trade to the Red Sea and the Gulf. Merchants, officials and members of the Mughal court invested in shipping. The largest Surat shipowner around 1700, Mullā ʿAbd al-Ghafūr, operated a substantial fleet, and his career has been reconstructed by Ashin Das Gupta (Das Gupta 1979). The imperial ship Ganj-i Sawāʾī (Section 18.9.3) was among the largest of them. Gujarati and other Indian shipwrights also built ships for Europeans, and Indian crews (lascars, from Persian lashkar, “army”; khalāsī, sailor) and officers (the nākhudā or ship’s master, the muʿallim or pilot, the tindal or boatswain) manned much of the European “country trade” in Asia (Arasaratnam 1994). The Portuguese system of passes (cartaz) and its effects on Indian shipping are discussed in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 13.7.2 The Maratha Navy
docs.text: On the Konkan coast, Śivājī began to build a fleet in the second half of the seventeenth century, and under Kānhojī Āṅgre (d. 1729) and his successors the Maratha fleet, based at sea forts such as Vijaydurg and Kolaba, challenged the English, the Portuguese and the Siddis of Janjira. The two principal warship types were the gurāb (from Arabic ghurāb), a heavier sailing vessel carrying guns, and the galbat (English “gallivat”), a lighter vessel driven by both sail and oars; they were built in Konkan yards by local carpenters (Apte 1973). The political history of the Āṅgres is outlined in Section 18.12, and naval warfare is treated in Volume 20, Yuddha and Dhanurveda.

docs.title: 13.7.3 The Bombay Dockyard and the Wadia Master Builders
docs.text:
The best-documented Indian shipbuilders of the colonial period are the Wadia family of Parsi master builders. In 1736 the English East India Company brought Lowjee Nusserwanjee Wadia, a shipwright from Surat, to Bombay to build ships for the Company, and members of the family directed the Bombay Dockyard for more than a century. The yard built merchant ships, Company warships and, from the early nineteenth century, ships for the Royal Navy, all of teak. The frigate HMS Trincomalee, launched at Bombay in 1817, survives at Hartlepool in England (Figure 13.5) and is the oldest British warship still afloat; the Cornwallis, a ship of the line launched at Bombay in 1813, was the vessel on which the Treaty of Nanking was signed in 1842; and HMS Asia (1824) was the British flagship at the battle of Navarino in 1827 (Wadia 1955). These ships show that Indian builders could meet the specifications of a European navy, using European designs, while the durability of their teak hulls was widely admired. The Bombay Dockyard is today the Naval Dockyard, Mumbai; it is distinct from the Mazagon Dock.

Figure 13.5. HMS Trincomalee, the teak frigate launched at the Bombay Dockyard in 1817, at Hartlepool in 2010. Photo: HDTurner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.7.4 Bengal
docs.text: Bengal had a long tradition of river and coastal shipbuilding, and in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries private shipyards on the Hugli at and near Calcutta built many ocean-going ships for the country trade and for the voyage to Europe. Indrajit Ray has traced the growth of this industry and its decline in the following decades, and relates the decline to British shipping policy and to changes in markets and technology (Ray 2011). The wider story of the decline of Indian shipping under colonial rule, and the debate about its causes, is told in Chapter 19.

docs.title: 13.8 Living Traditions: Beypore and Mandvi
docs.text:
Large wooden sailing ships are still built by hand at two places on the west coast of India, and they are the closest we can come to observing the older tradition at work.

Beypore. At Beypore, at the mouth of the Chaliyar river near Kozhikode in Kerala, builders construct the large wooden vessel called uru (Figure 13.6), related in form to the dhows of the Arabian Sea. The hull is of teak, carvel-planked (with the planks laid edge to edge) and, in present practice, fastened with iron rather than sewn. The work is directed by a master carpenter (mēstri) who carries the design in his memory and guides the crew without drawings; the proportions are those of the master’s training and experience. The launching of a finished hull, by hand-operated tackle, rollers and levers, is a separate skill, long associated with the Māppiḷa Muslim khalāsīs of the area. A large uru takes a long time to build, often more than a year. For most of the twentieth century the main customers were merchants of the Gulf, and orders from Oman, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates continue, though many recent vessels are built as pleasure or heritage ships rather than as cargo carriers. The supply of good timber, the cost of labour and the decline of apprenticeship threaten the craft, and its future is uncertain.

Figure 13.6. An uru under construction at Beypore, Kerala, in January 2018. Photo: Vicharam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Mandvi. At Mandvi in Kutch, on the estuary of the Rukmavati, carpenters build wooden dhows on the river bank for owners in Gujarat and the Gulf. The Kutch and Saurashtra coasts had a long tradition of seafaring to the Gulf, Arabia and East Africa, carried on by Hindu and Muslim sailing communities, and the Kachchhi navigators and their written pilot books are discussed in Chapter 14. Many vessels now built at Mandvi are fitted with engines, but the hull is still built by eye, plank-first, in teak and other hardwoods. The communities who build and sail these ships are described in Chapter 17.

Neither place preserves ancient shipbuilding unchanged: the modern uru and Kutch dhow are nailed carvel hulls, and their forms owe much to Arab, Portuguese and later influences. What they preserve is a way of working: building by eye and memory within a family and community tradition, with hand tools and teak, for a market across the Arabian Sea. That way of working is itself a valuable historical witness.

docs.title: 13.9 Conclusion
docs.text: The strongest evidence for Indian shipbuilding comes not from Sanskrit texts but from the sewn hulls of the western ocean, the craft still built on the coasts and, from the seventeenth century, the records of Indian shipowners and of yards such as Bombay’s. That evidence shows builders working by eye and memory within traditions shared across the Arabian Sea, and capable, when asked, of meeting European specifications; the decline of their yards belongs to the history of the colonial economy (Chapter 19).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The essential works are McGrail et al. (2003) on the traditional boats of South Asia and McGrail (2001) for a comparative view. Hourani (1995) remains the standard account of Arab ships and the sewn-boat tradition, and Manguin (1993) defines the Southeast Asian and Chinese traditions. Deloche (1993) gathers the Indian textual and iconographic evidence, and Ray (2003) sets it in its archaeological context. Mookerji (1912) is of historiographical interest and should be read with caution. For the early modern period see Das Gupta (1979), Apte (1973), Wadia (1955) and Ray (2011).

docs.title: Chapter 14: The Monsoon and Navigation
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

The monsoon, the seasonal reversal of the winds over the northern Indian Ocean, set the calendar of every voyage in these waters until the age of steam. This chapter first describes the monsoon system in simple physical terms and the sailing seasons it imposed, from the Roman voyages to India to the trade of the medieval and early modern ports. It then examines the much-debated story of Hippalus, the weather lore of Sanskrit texts such as Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, and the picture of seafaring in Tamil poetry and Buddhist stories. The second half turns to the pilot’s craft: coastal pilotage, the star compass and the measurement of star altitudes, the uncertain history of the magnetic compass in the Indian Ocean, and the written pilot books of later centuries. Throughout, the knowledge described was shared by sailors of many coasts and faiths; it was neither invented by nor confined to any one people.

The navigational knowledge of the Indian Ocean was mostly practical and oral. It was learnt at sea, held in memory and passed from master to apprentice, and very little of it was written down before the fifteenth century, when Arab pilots began to compose systematic treatises. The evidence for earlier periods is therefore indirect: Greek and Latin accounts of the voyage to India, Buddhist and Tamil literature, the weather lore of Sanskrit texts, and the observations of travellers. These sources are thin, and they have often been over-read. What they show is impressive enough: generations of sailors, Indian, Arab, Persian, East African, Southeast Asian and Chinese, who learnt to use a powerful seasonal wind system to cross open sea on a regular timetable (Chaudhuri 1985; Tibbetts 1971; Pearson 2003). Astronomy as a science is treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa, and geography, maps and travellers’ accounts in Volume 21, Bhūgola.

docs.title: 14.1.1 Physical Basics
docs.text:
The word “monsoon” comes from Arabic mawsim, “season”, the term used by Arab sailors for the sailing season of a particular route; it passed into Portuguese as monção and from there into Dutch and English. It refers in the first place to a wind regime, and only secondarily to the rains that the summer winds bring.

In simple terms, the monsoon results from the different rates at which land and sea heat up and cool down over the year, together with the seasonal movement of the zone where the trade winds of the two hemispheres converge. In the northern summer the land mass of South and Central Asia becomes much hotter than the ocean, a broad area of low pressure develops over the north of the subcontinent, and moist air is drawn in from the ocean. Over the Arabian Sea this produces a strong and steady wind from the south-west, roughly from June to September, which is strongest off the coasts of Somalia and Arabia. In the northern winter the pattern reverses: the land cools, pressure rises over Asia, and dry winds blow from the north-east over the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, roughly from November or December to March. Between the two lie transitional periods of variable and lighter winds. The surface currents of the northern Indian Ocean reverse with the winds (Pearson 2003; Chaudhuri 1985).

The first scientific explanation of the monsoon as a thermally driven circulation was offered by the English astronomer Edmond Halley in 1686, and systematic observation in India began under the colonial government; the India Meteorological Department was founded in 1875. Modern meteorology has refined the picture considerably. For the history of seafaring, however, what matters is not the physical explanation but the practical regularity of the winds, which sailors of the region had understood from very early times.

docs.title: 14.1.2 Regional Differences and Cyclones
docs.text:
The monsoon did not affect all coasts alike. On the west coast of India the south-west monsoon blows straight onto the shore, with heavy seas and torrential rain. Most west-coast ports were open roadsteads or river mouths with bars, and from about the end of May to August or September they were effectively closed to shipping: ships were laid up, beached or sheltered in rivers, and long-distance arrivals and departures were timed to avoid the height of the monsoon. The east coast, on the lee side during the south-west monsoon, was more exposed during the north-east monsoon and the stormy weeks of October to December. Its ports were mostly open beaches where goods were landed through surf, which is why the frameless masula boat was developed there (Chapter 13).

Tropical cyclones occur in both seas but are more frequent and more dangerous in the Bay of Bengal, especially in the transitional seasons of April–May and October–December. The low, densely populated coasts at the head of the Bay are particularly vulnerable to storm surges. Sailors therefore avoided the transitional months where they could, and ports such as Nāgapaṭṭinam, Masulipatnam and those of the delta had their own seasonal rhythms (Arasaratnam 1994). Cyclones and storms appear in many accounts of shipwreck, from the Jātakas to the letters of medieval merchants, but there is no evidence that any pre-modern tradition, in India or elsewhere, understood their structure or could forecast them beyond the observation of local signs such as a long swell, a falling sky or a sudden change of wind.

docs.title: 14.2.1 The General Pattern
docs.text:
The monsoon divided the year into fixed windows for each route. In outline, ships sailed from India westwards to Arabia, the Red Sea and East Africa on the north-east monsoon, between about November and March, and came east to India on the south-west monsoon, either at its beginning (April–May), before the west coast closed, or at its end (late August–September). In the Bay of Bengal, ships from India to Southeast Asia sailed with the south-west monsoon or at its end, and returned with the north-east monsoon. Voyages that crossed both seas had to be divided into stages, with long waits for the wind to change. Table 14.1 and Figure 14.1 summarise the pattern; the exact dates varied with the route, the type of ship and the period.

Table 14.1. The general pattern of sailing seasons in the northern Indian Ocean (simplified) Route Usual season Wind and remarks West coast of India to Arabia, Red Sea, East Africa About November to March North-east monsoon Red Sea, Arabia to west coast of India April–May, or late August–September South-west monsoon, avoiding its height, when west-coast ports were closed East coast of India to Southeast Asia With or at the end of the south-west monsoon Return with the north-east monsoon Southeast Asia to India About December to February North-east monsoon Coastal voyages Fair-weather months Many coasts closed at the height of the monsoon

The consequences went far beyond navigation. Because a ship could make only one return voyage on a given route in a year, merchants had to wait months in foreign ports for the wind to change. They needed lodgings, warehouses, credit and agents, and over time this produced resident communities of foreign merchants in almost every port of the ocean, and the institutions that served them (Chapters 12 and 15). The monsoon also made ports at the junctions of wind systems especially valuable. Melaka in the fifteenth century, for example, lay where ships from the Indian Ocean and from the South China Sea could meet and exchange cargoes before the wind turned, a point made by the Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires (Pires 1944; Chaudhuri 1985).

docs.title: 14.2.2 The Roman Voyage to India
docs.text:
The earliest detailed timetable comes from Roman Egypt. The Periplus Maris Erythraei (mid-first century CE) advises merchants bound for the mouth of the Indus, for Barygaza and for the pepper ports of the Malabar coast to leave Egypt around July (the Egyptian month Epeiph) (§§39, 49, 56). Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, describes the voyage in more detail: ships left the Red Sea port of Berenike in midsummer, reached Ocelis near the mouth of the Red Sea in about thirty days, and from there crossed to Muziris in about forty days with the favourable wind; they began the return voyage in the Egyptian month Tybi (December) or early in Mechir (January), with the north-east monsoon (NH 6.100–106) (Casson 1989; De Romanis 2020). A round trip thus took about a year, which fits what is known of the financing of these voyages from the Muziris papyrus (Chapter 11).

Figure 14.1. The monsoon calendar of the northern Indian Ocean (schematic): the winds, the sea conditions and the usual sailing windows described in Sections 14.1–14.2 and in Table 14.1. Pale segments mark approximate or variable limits; the exact dates varied with the route, the type of ship and the period.

docs.title: 14.2.3 The Medieval and Early Modern Pattern
docs.text: The letters of the Jewish merchants of the Cairo Geniza, written in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, show the same rhythm on the route between Aden and the Malabar coast. Ships left Aden for India towards the end of the summer monsoon and returned in the early months of the year, and merchants who missed a sailing had to wait a year for the next one (Goitein and Friedman 2008; Margariti 2007). The Chinese fleets of Zheng He in the early fifteenth century likewise sailed from China in the winter with the north-east monsoon, waited in Southeast Asian ports, crossed to Calicut, and returned with the south-west monsoon (Dreyer 2007). When Vasco da Gama’s ships reached Calicut in May 1498, just before the closing of the coast, and then tried to leave in the late summer against the wind, the crossing back to Africa took about three months and cost many lives from scurvy; the Portuguese learnt the timetable the hard way (Subrahmanyam 1997).

docs.title: 14.3 Who “Discovered” the Monsoon? The Hippalus Question
docs.text:
The Greek and Latin sources name a single discoverer of the route to India across the open sea. The Periplus (§57) says that earlier sailors had made the voyage in smaller ships following the coasts, and that the ship’s captain (kybernētēs) Hippalus, by working out the location of the ports and the shape of the sea, first discovered the route across open water; a further sentence, which may be a later gloss, adds that the south-west wind of the region is called “hippalus” after him. Pliny (NH 6.100–106) uses “hippalus” as the name of the south-west wind that carried ships to India, without describing a discoverer (Casson 1989).

The story has been read in two opposite ways. Older European scholarship often treated Hippalus as the discoverer of the monsoon itself, as though the winds had been unknown before a Greek noticed them. The opposite reading, that the story was an attempt to take from Indian sailors the credit for a discovery that was theirs, is equally one-sided.

Debate: The Hippalus Question

What is certain. The people who lived on the coasts of the Arabian Sea knew the seasonal winds from the earliest times, as farmers and fishermen as well as sailors. Seaborne trade between the Indus region and the Gulf in the third millennium BCE, and the later trade of Arabian, Indian and East African ports, depended on that knowledge, although much of it may have been coastal (Chapter 11). The Periplus itself records ships from Barygaza and Ariakē sailing to the Horn of Africa (§14), and Strabo (2.3.4) tells how an Indian sailor guided the first voyage of Eudoxus of Cyzicus to India in the late second century BCE (Casson 1989).

What the Greek sources claim. The Periplus does not say that Hippalus discovered the winds, but that he discovered the open-sea route, which Greek-speaking sailors from Egypt then adopted, first from the mouth of the Red Sea and later more boldly. That is a claim about a change in the practice of Egyptian Greek sailors, and it may well be true in that sense.

What is debated. Some scholars have argued, from the wording of Pliny, that “hippalus” was first the name of the wind and that the pilot Hippalus was invented later to explain it; others accept him as a historical figure of the late second or first century BCE. The question remains open (Casson 1989; De Romanis 2020).

Conclusion. Neither name can claim the monsoon for one people. Indian, Arab and other sailors of the region did not need to be taught the winds, and Greek-speaking sailors from Egypt learnt to use them for direct crossings; both statements can be true at once.

docs.title: 14.4 Weather Lore in Sanskrit Texts
docs.text:
Sanskrit literature has much to say about rain and weather, but almost all of it concerns agriculture, not the sea. The Arthaśāstra (AŚ 2.24) states the amount of rain to be expected in different regions, measured in a standard vessel, and relates the success of crops to its distribution through the rainy season (Olivelle 2013). The fullest treatment is in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (sixth century CE), an encyclopaedia of divination (saṃhitā) that devotes a group of chapters to the prediction of rain. It describes how clouds “conceive” (garbha) in the cool season, to be “delivered” as rain some six and a half months later; how rainfall is to be measured; how the conjunctions of the moon with the asterisms Rohiṇī, Svāti and Āṣāḍhā, and the direction of the wind on certain days, foretell the rains of the coming season; and which signs, including the behaviour of animals and the colour of the sky, announce immediate rain.

These chapters preserve careful observation of the sky and of nature within a framework of omens and astral correspondences. They are evidence of a long tradition of weather lore, closely tied to the farming year, that was shared with village almanacs and proverbs; similar traditions survive in regional agricultural calendars, such as the Malayalam calendar of ñāṭṭuvēla periods named after the asterism in which the sun stands. They are a divinatory tradition rather than a meteorology in the modern sense, and they are not a manual for sailors: nothing in them refers specifically to navigation. The astronomical background of the nakṣatra system is described in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa, and agricultural weather lore in Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna.

docs.title: 14.5 Seafaring in Tamil and Buddhist Literature
14.5.1 Tamil Caṅkam Poetry
docs.text:
The Tamil poems of the Caṅkam anthologies, composed in the early centuries CE, are among the few early Indian texts that speak of the sea from the coast. In the poetic grammar of akam (love) poetry, the coastal landscape, neytal, is the setting of separation and anxious waiting, and many poems evoke the waves, the boats of fishermen and the absence of a lover gone to sea. Other poems name ships and ports directly. A poem of the Akanāṉūṟu (149) describes the well-made ships of the Yavanas (here, traders from the Roman world) arriving at Muciri on the Periyar with gold and leaving with pepper. A poem of the Puṟanāṉūṟu (66), addressed to the Chola king Karikāl, praises him as a descendant of a hero who sailed ships on the wide ocean and made the wind serve him; the line is often quoted as evidence of royal interest in seafaring, though its exact sense is debated. The Paṭṭiṉappālai’s port of Pukār, where horses arrived by ship, is described in Section 15.2.5.

These poems are conventional literature, not ships’ logs. They show that seafaring was a familiar part of the life and imagination of the Tamil coast, that the arrival and departure of ships followed the seasons, and that foreign traders were a visible presence in the ports. They do not describe navigational techniques.

docs.title: 14.5.2 Jātakas and Other Buddhist Texts
docs.text:
The sea stories of the Pali Jātakas, among them the Suppāraka, Mahājanaka and Bāveru Jātakas, are described in Section 11.5. For the history of navigation the most telling is the Suppāraka Jātaka, with its blind master mariner of Bharukaccha. Its seas are fantastic and the numbers of passengers in such tales are formulaic, but the stories show that the pilot was a respected figure and that a voyage was understood as a venture of great risk and great profit (Chakravarti 2002; Ray 1994).

One practical technique appears clearly. In the Kevaddha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya (DN 11), the Buddha uses the image of sea-going merchants who release a “land-sighting bird” from their ship when they cannot see land: the bird flies in each direction, and if it finds no shore it returns to the ship, while if it sees land it does not come back. Pliny says the same of the sailors of Taprobane (Sri Lanka), who, he writes, did not steer by the stars but carried birds which they released to find the direction of land (NH 6.83). The practice is known from other ancient seafaring cultures as well, and it is a reminder of how much early navigation depended on reading nature rather than instruments.

docs.title: 14.6 Pilotage and Coastal Knowledge
docs.text:
Most voyages, even long ones, involved long stretches of coastal sailing, and the most dangerous moments were usually the approach to land. The Periplus gives a vivid account of the difficulties at Barygaza: a narrow and shoal-ridden gulf, rocks and banks at the entrance, and very strong tides with a tidal bore in the river. Fishermen in the service of the king went out in the boats called trappaga and kotymba as far as the coast of Saurashtra to meet incoming ships and pilot them up the river (§§43–46). These were local pilot and towing boats, not ocean-going ships, and they show that local pilotage was an organised service under royal control. The same text notes that sailors approaching the coast near the mouth of the Indus knew they were close to land when they saw sea snakes coming up from the deep (§38) (Casson 1989).

The signs that pilots used to know their position near land are familiar from all pre-modern seafaring: the colour of the water and its change from blue to green over shallower ground; floating vegetation near river mouths; the flight of seabirds; the character of the swell; clouds standing over islands and high coasts; and, above all, soundings. A lead line, with a cavity filled with tallow to bring up a sample of the bottom, told the pilot both the depth and the kind of seabed, sand, mud or shell, which an experienced pilot could match to known stretches of coast. Knowledge of local tides and currents, of the landmarks visible from the sea, and of the seasons when particular harbours were safe was the pilot’s stock in trade. Little of this was written down before the fifteenth century, but it is implied by the regularity of the trade in every period and described in detail in the later pilot books (Tibbetts 1971; Hourani 1995).

docs.title: 14.7.1 Steering by the Stars
docs.text:
For crossing open water, pilots relied on the stars. The most fully documented system is that of the Arab pilots, set out in the treatises of Aḥmad ibn Mājid of Julfar, whose Kitāb al-Fawāʾid fī uṣūl ʿilm al-baḥr wa-l-qawāʿid was completed around 1490, and of Sulaymān al-Mahrī in the early sixteenth century. These works were translated and analysed by G. R. Tibbetts (Tibbetts 1971). They describe a “star compass” in which the horizon is divided into thirty-two points named after the rising and setting points of fifteen prominent stars, together with the Pole Star and the opposite pole. A course was given as the rising or setting point of a particular star. Distances were reckoned in units of sailing time, and positions north and south by the height of stars above the horizon.

Star altitudes were measured in “fingers” (Arabic iṣbaʿ), a unit of a little over one and a half degrees, originally the width of a finger held at arm’s length against the sky. The height of the Pole Star, or of other stars when it was low or invisible, gave a measure of latitude, and a pilot who knew the star height at his destination could sail north or south until he reached it and then run along that parallel, east or west, to make his landfall. South of the equator, where the Pole Star cannot be seen, other stars were used, among them Canopus, known in Sanskrit as Agastya and in Arabic as Suhayl.

Ibn Mājid regarded the knowledge he set down as the inheritance of earlier pilots, whom he names, and of practice on many coasts. The system was shared by the pilots of the western Indian Ocean whatever their origin, and Gujarati, Malabari and other Indian pilots will have used the same or similar methods. No early text, however, describes a separate Indian star-compass system. The nakṣatras of Indian astronomy are divisions of the ecliptic used for the calendar and for astrology (Volume 12); sailors doubtless knew and named stars in their own languages, but no early text describes how Indian sailors used them at sea.

docs.title: 14.7.2 The Kamal
docs.text:
The instrument known in English as the kamal was a small rectangular board with a cord attached to its centre (Figure 14.2). Holding the cord in his teeth and the board at arm’s length, the pilot set the lower edge on the horizon and the upper edge on the star; knots on the cord, set at known distances, corresponded to known star heights, for example those of particular ports. It was used by Arab, Indian and other pilots of the western Indian Ocean, and examples were still in use in the nineteenth century. Its origin and date are uncertain; it probably developed from the older practice of measuring star heights with the fingers, and its early history cannot be traced in detail (Tibbetts 1971).

Figure 14.2. A simple modern wooden kamal: a small board with a knotted cord passed through its centre. Photo: Bordwall, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 14.7.3 The Magnetic Compass and the “Matsya-yantra”
docs.text:
The magnetic compass was first used for navigation in China. The military compendium Wujing zongyao (1044) describes a “south-pointing fish” of thin iron, magnetised by heating and cooling, floated on water. A work written in the early twelfth century by Zhu Yu, describing the port of Guangzhou around 1100, says that pilots steered by the stars at night and the sun by day, and in overcast weather consulted the south-pointing needle. In the Islamic world the floating needle is described in the thirteenth century, and Arabic and Persian writers of that century speak of a magnetised iron leaf or hollow iron fish floated in water; one of them, Baylak al-Qibjāqī, writing in 1282, says that this fish form was used by the captains of the Indian Ocean. By the fifteenth century the compass was a standard part of the Arab pilots’ equipment, alongside the star compass whose names it took over (Tibbetts 1971).

Scholarly Note: The “matsya-yantra”

Radhakumud Mookerji’s Indian Shipping stated that Indian sailors used a magnetic compass called the matsya-yantra (“fish machine”), an iron fish floating in oil (Mookerji 1912), and the statement has been widely repeated since. No securely dated Sanskrit text describing such a navigational instrument has been identified. It is quite possible that floating iron fish of the kind described by Chinese and Arabic writers were used on ships sailing to and from India in the thirteenth and later centuries, but nothing shows that the device was invented in India, and the term matsya-yantra itself is not attested in any early source known to us. The claim remains unproven.

docs.title: 14.8.1 The Pilot and his Knowledge
docs.text:
On the ships of the western Indian Ocean the pilot (Arabic muʿallim, “master”, which passed into Indian languages as mālim or mālmī) was a specialist distinct from the ship’s master (nākhudā). Pilots were hired for particular routes, and their knowledge of a coast, its seasons and its dangers was valuable and often guarded. Gujarati pilots were well known in the trade between India, Arabia and East Africa, and pilots from the Malabar coast, the Konkan, the Maldives and the Lakshadweep islands worked on their own regional routes. In many cases navigation was a family occupation, and the communities of Kutch, Lakshadweep and other coasts that preserved it into the twentieth century are described in Chapter 17.

Ibn Mājid’s and Sulaymān al-Mahrī’s treatises, written in Arabic verse and prose, were partly composed in verse so that they could be memorised. They give sailing directions for the whole western Indian Ocean, from East Africa to the coasts of India and on to Southeast Asia, including detailed instructions for the Indian coasts. Some of their content was later incorporated in the Ottoman admiral Seydi ʿAlī Reʾīs’s work on the navigation of the Indian Ocean, written in Gujarat in the 1550s (Tibbetts 1971). Ibn Mājid’s works are the best guide we have to the practice of the pilots of his time.

docs.title: 14.8.2 The Rahmānī of Gujarat and Kutch
docs.text: The navigators of Kutch and Saurashtra kept written pilot books, known as rahmānī (from Persian rāhnāma, “book of the road”; the Arabic pilots used the related term rahmānaj). The surviving examples are manuscripts in Gujarati or Kachchhi, mostly from the eighteenth to the early twentieth century, kept in navigators’ families. They are reported to contain sailing directions for routes to the Gulf, Arabia, East Africa and along the Indian coasts, with courses expressed by the points of the star compass, star altitudes, soundings and descriptions of landmarks. They are thus late representatives of the same tradition as the Arab treatises, adapted to the needs of the Kutch sailors and written in their own language. They are valuable historical documents, but they have been little studied and few have been published, and nothing yet shows the genre to be older than the Arab pilot books from which it borrowed its name.

docs.title: 14.8.3 Vasco da Gama’s Pilot
docs.text: The best-known pilot in the history of the Indian Ocean is the one who guided Vasco da Gama from Malindi on the East African coast to Calicut in 1498, a crossing of about four weeks in April and May. The Portuguese sources describe him only briefly. Later Portuguese chroniclers call him a Gujarati, and one gives his name as “Malemo Caná”, in which malemo is the Arabic muʿallim, “pilot”. In the sixteenth century the Arabic chronicler Quṭb al-Dīn al-Nahrawālī claimed that the Portuguese had been guided by Aḥmad ibn Mājid, whom he blamed for opening the ocean to them; this identification was popularised in the twentieth century by the French orientalist Gabriel Ferrand and is still often repeated. Modern historians reject it: Ibn Mājid would have been an old man by 1498, nothing in his own writings or in the Portuguese sources supports the story, and it belongs to the legend that grew up around the voyage (Subrahmanyam 1997). The pilot is best described as a Muslim pilot of the western Indian Ocean, probably from Gujarat, provided by the ruler of Malindi. The episode illustrates the point of this chapter: the route the Portuguese “discovered” was one that Asian pilots sailed every year.

docs.title: 14.9 Charts and Maps
docs.text: No pre-modern Indian sea chart survives, and there is no evidence that Indian pilots used charts before contact with Europeans. Arab pilots before the sixteenth century relied above all on their written directions and their star compass; no Arab sea chart of this period survives, and how far pilots used drawn charts at all is uncertain (Tibbetts 1971). Portuguese sources of the early sixteenth century do mention maps in the hands of Asian pilots, most famously a large Javanese map that Afonso de Albuquerque had copied in 1512 and that was later lost at sea, but none has survived from the Indian coasts. Indian cartography, including the regional maps of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, is discussed in Volume 21, Bhūgola.

docs.title: 14.10 Conclusion
docs.text: The monsoon made the Indian Ocean one of the great highways of the pre-modern world, but it also bound every voyage to a strict calendar. Sailors of all its coasts learnt to use the seasonal winds, to read the signs of land and weather, to steer by the stars and to measure their height, and in time to use the magnetic compass. The knowledge was practical, oral and shared; Indian sailors contributed to it and drew on it, as did Arab, Persian, East African, Southeast Asian and Chinese sailors. The surviving texts, from the Periplus and the Jātakas to Ibn Mājid and the Kutch rahmānīs, reveal a world of skilled specialists whose knowledge, built up over many generations, made long-distance trade possible.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Chaudhuri (1985) and Pearson (2003) explain the place of the monsoon in the economic history of the Indian Ocean. Tibbetts (1971) is the essential study of Arab navigation and includes a translation of Ibn Mājid’s Kitāb al-Fawāʾid; Hourani (1995) covers the earlier period. For the Roman voyage see Casson (1989) and De Romanis (2020); for the Geniza merchants and their sailing seasons, Goitein and Friedman (2008) and Margariti (2007). Subrahmanyam (1997) discusses the voyage of Vasco da Gama and the legend of his pilot.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Port Cities, Port Administration and the Law of the Sea
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

This chapter surveys the principal ports of the subcontinent in chronological order, from Bharukaccha and the Indo-Roman ports through the medieval emporia and the ports of the Bengal sultanate to Surat, Masulipatnam and Hughli in the Mughal period, and asks how ports were governed: by the Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of boats, by Tamil and Chola customs officers, by the shāhbandar of the Indian Ocean emporia and by Mughal port officials. It then sets out what the legal sources actually say about ships, ferries, sea loans, shipwreck and piracy. No Sanskrit code of maritime law exists; the relevant rules are scattered, brief and mostly concerned with revenue, interest and the liability of boatmen, and much of the law that governed sea trade in practice was the law of merchants’ own communities.

docs.title: 15.1 Ports and Their Settings
docs.text:
Few South Asian ports had natural deep-water harbours. Most stood on river estuaries (Bharuch on the Narmada, Surat on the Tapti, Tāmralipti and Hughli on the distributaries of the Ganga), on lagoons and backwaters (Arikamedu, Kollam, Cochin), or on open beaches and roadsteads where ships anchored offshore and goods were landed by boat (Calicut and Masulipatnam). Estuarine ports had to contend with tides, shoals and silting; open roadsteads closed when the south-west monsoon made the west coast dangerous between about June and August. Rivers changed course and gulfs silted, and so the leading port of a region shifted over time: Bharukaccha gave way to Cambay and Cambay to Surat, while Tāmralipti gave way to Saptagrāma (Satgaon) and Saptagrāma to Hughli. A port’s fortune depended as much on its hinterland, the roads and rivers that brought cotton, pepper or grain to the coast, as on its anchorage (Chapter 10).

Sanskrit texts and inscriptions use several words for a port or trading town. Paṭṭana (Tamil paṭṭiṉam) is a trading town, often on the coast; velākula, literally “shore”, is used for ports in inscriptions of western India; Persian and Arabic sources use bandar. None of these words implies a particular kind of installation (Chakravarti 2002).

The earliest site often called a port is Lothal in Gujarat, a Harappan craft and trading town whose brick basin may or may not have been a dock (Section 11.3).

docs.title: 15.2 Ports of the Early Historic Period
docs.text: The Periplus Maris Erythraei (mid-1st c. CE) names many ports of the west coast and some of the east, and Tamil poetry, Buddhist narrative, inscriptions and archaeology add to its picture. The trade that passed through these ports is discussed in Chapter 11; here the emphasis is on the ports themselves.

docs.title: 15.2.1 Bharukaccha (Barygaza)
docs.text: Bharukaccha (Prakrit Bharukaccha, Greek Barygaza, modern Bharuch) stood on the north bank of the Narmada, upstream from its estuary. The Periplus gives it more space than any other Indian port (§§41–49), describing its dangerous approach, the royal pilot boats that guided ships up the river (Section 14.6) and the goods it imported and exported, which included slave musicians and young women for the king (Section 11.7) (Casson 1989).
