Bharukaccha drew on a large hinterland reaching to Ujjayinī and the Deccan towns of Paiṭhan and Ter. It remained a port into the medieval period, when Arabic geographers knew it as Barūṣ, but from about the tenth century it was overshadowed by Cambay. Buddhist narrative remembers it as the home port of the blind pilot of the Suppāraka Jātaka (Section 11.5).

docs.title: 15.2.2 Śūrpāraka (Sopārā) and Kalyāṇ
docs.text:
Śūrpāraka (Pali Suppāraka, Greek Souppara, modern Nala Sopara) lies on the coast of the northern Konkan, in Palghar district of Maharashtra, north of Mumbai. A fragment of Aśoka’s Rock Edicts (part of the eighth edict) was found there, and in 1882 Bhagvanlal Indraji excavated a Buddhist stūpa that contained a relic deposit with a silver coin of the Sātavāhana king Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi. In Buddhist tradition Śūrpāraka is the home of Pūrṇa, a merchant who made sea voyages before becoming a monk (the Pūrṇāvadāna of the Divyāvadāna). The Periplus lists Souppara among the local markets south of Barygaza (§52) (Ray 1986, 2003).

Kalyāṇ (Greek Kalliena), on the Ulhas creek inland from Mumbai, was a port of the Sātavāhana period. The Periplus (§52) says that it had been a lawful port of trade under an earlier king, but that since it had passed into the hands of a ruler called Sandanes its trade was obstructed, and Greek ships that put in there were sent under guard to Barygaza (Casson 1989). The passage shows a ruler directing foreign trade to a particular port, presumably to control it and tax it. Inscriptions in the Buddhist caves of Kanheri, close to both Sopārā and Kalyāṇ, record gifts by merchants and residents of Kalyāṇ (Ray 1986). In the sixth century the Alexandrian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes still knew Kalliana as a market with a Christian bishop appointed from Persia.

docs.title: 15.2.3 Muziris (Muciṟi)
docs.text: Muziris (Tamil Muciṟi) was the chief pepper port of the Cēra kings on the Malabar coast. The Periplus places it on a river some distance from the sea and says it was full of ships from Arabia and from Roman Egypt (§§53–56) (Casson 1989). Its exact location is not known. It is traditionally placed near Kodungallur, at the old mouth of the Periyar, and the excavators of Pattanam, a few kilometres to the south, identify that site as part of Muziris, a plausible but unproved identification. The Tamil poems, the Pattanam finds and the Muziris papyrus are discussed in Section 11.7.

docs.title: 15.2.4 Arikamedu
docs.text: Arikamedu, on a lagoon just south of Puducherry and usually identified with the Periplus’s Poduke, is the best-excavated early port of the east coast. Once taken for a Roman trading station, it is now known to have been an Indian settlement older than Roman contact, with its own bead and pottery industries, in which Mediterranean imports were one element among many (Section 11.7) (Begley and De Puma 1991).

docs.title: 15.2.5 Kāveripaṭṭinam (Pūmpuhār)
docs.text:
Kāveripaṭṭinam, also called Pukār or Pūmpuhār, at the mouth of the Kaveri, was the port of the early Chola kings. Two Tamil works describe it at length. The Paṭṭiṉappālai, one of the Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) of the Caṅkam corpus, praises the city of the Chola king Karikāl. It describes goods arriving from many directions: horses by sea, pepper by land, gems and gold from the northern mountains, sandalwood from the western hills, pearls from the southern sea and coral from the eastern, the produce of the Ganga and the Kaveri, food from Īḻam (Sri Lanka) and goods from Kāḻakam (probably Kedah). It also describes customs officers who stamped the tiger emblem of the Cholas on goods once the duty had been paid, and piled the goods in open yards (Champakalakshmi 1996).

The Cilappatikāram, a Tamil narrative poem of the post-Caṅkam period (probably 5th–6th c. CE), opens in Pukār. It describes the city as divided into a quarter by the sea, Maruvūrppākkam, where the houses of Yavana and other foreign merchants stood near the warehouses and the shops of artisans, and an inland quarter, Paṭṭiṉappākkam, of the king, the nobles and the great merchants. The heroine’s father bears the title Mānāykaṉ, “great captain”, which marks him as a shipowning merchant. Both poems are idealising works and their numbers and splendours cannot be taken literally, but they show how a Tamil port was imagined: a city of two halves, foreign and native, organised around the exchange of goods (Champakalakshmi 1996). The Maṇimēkalai tells that Pukār was swallowed by the sea, a legend that may preserve a memory of coastal erosion.

Excavations since the 1960s at Kāveripaṭṭinam and nearby villages have found brick structures interpreted as a wharf, a Buddhist monastery and other remains, and underwater surveys offshore have reported submerged structures whose date and function are still uncertain (Ray 2003).

docs.title: 15.2.6 Tāmralipti
docs.text: Tāmralipti (modern Tamluk in Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal), on the Rupnarayan near its junction with the Hugli estuary, was the main port of the lower Ganga region from the late centuries BCE to the end of the first millennium CE. It linked the river trade of the Gangetic plain to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian stayed there for two years in the early fifth century, copying scriptures and images, before sailing on a merchant ship to Sri Lanka; Xuanzang described it in the seventh century as a port near the sea with Buddhist monasteries; and Yijing landed there in 673 and studied Sanskrit at a monastery in the town before going on to Nālandā (Ray 1994; Sen 2003). As the river silted, trade moved to Saptagrāma (Satgaon), and in the sixteenth century to Hughli.

docs.title: 15.2.7 The Kaliṅga and Andhra Coasts
docs.text:
Between Tāmralipti and the Tamil country lay the coasts of Kaliṅga, roughly modern Odisha, and Andhra. They linked the Ganga delta with the south and faced Southeast Asia across the Bay of Bengal. Their place in that trade left a trace in language: in Malay and neighbouring languages, people from India, especially from the south, came to be called Keling, a word generally derived from Kaliṅga.

Ptolemy’s Geography (7.1) names a place called Paloura on this coast and, near it, a “point of departure” (aphetērion) for ships sailing to Chrysē, which suggests that vessels bound across the Bay set out from here; Paloura is often identified with Palur in Ganjam district, though the identification is not certain. The fortified town of Sisupalgarh near Bhubaneswar, excavated by B. B. Lal in 1948, yielded Rouletted Ware of the kind found at Arikamedu and around the Bay, and at Manikpatna on the Chilika lagoon finds of Rouletted Ware and, from later contexts, Chinese and West Asian glazed ceramics have been reported; no full excavation report has been published, but the finds suggest a harbour used over many centuries (Ray 2003). On the Andhra coast the deltas of the Kṛṣṇā and Godāvarī supported Buddhist centres such as Amarāvatī, Nāgārjunakoṇḍa and Śālihuṇḍam, whose inscriptions record merchant donors (Section 11.10). Ghaṇṭaśālā near the mouth of the Kṛṣṇā is often identified with Ptolemy’s Kontakossyla and with the Kaṇṭakasela named in an inscription at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, and the lead ship coins attributed to Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi come mainly from this coast (Section 13.2) (Ray 1986; Chakravarti 2002). In later centuries Motupalli (Section 15.6.4) and Masulipatnam carried the Andhra coast’s trade.

In Odisha the memory of seafaring survives in festival. Bali Jātrā, held at Cuttack on Kārttika Pūrṇimā, and the household rite of floating small boats on the same day (boita bandāṇa) are popularly understood to commemorate the voyages of Kaliṅga merchants (sādhaba) to Bali, Java and Sumatra. These are living traditions. The voyages they recall are real in general terms, but the particular memories attached to them cannot be dated, and talk of Kaliṅga “colonies” overseas belongs to the “Greater India” writing discussed in Chapter 16.

docs.title: 15.3 Ports of the Early Medieval and Medieval Periods
15.3.1 Mamallapuram
docs.text: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), south of Chennai, takes its name from the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla (r. c. 630–668). Its rock-cut shrines, monolithic rathas and great relief are among the masterpieces of early South Indian art, and the structural Shore Temple was built under Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha (c. 700). Mamallapuram was a Pallava port, but direct archaeological evidence of its harbour is slight, and its commercial importance is usually inferred from its setting and from the Pallava kingdom’s contacts with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. The architecture is treated in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; the links with Southeast Asia are discussed in Chapter 16 (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

docs.title: 15.3.2 Nāgapaṭṭinam
docs.text: Nāgapaṭṭinam, south of the Kaveri delta, was the principal port of the imperial Cholas, where a Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya built a Buddhist monastery endowed by Rājarāja I and Rājendra I (Section 12.9.2) (Kulke et al. 2009). Large numbers of Buddhist bronzes have since been found in the town, and a brick tower known to Europeans as the “China pagoda” stood there until it was demolished in 1867. The port continued after the Cholas, became a Portuguese settlement in the sixteenth century and was taken by the Dutch in 1658. The Chola expeditions launched from the Coromandel coast are discussed in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 15.3.3 Kollam (Quilon)
docs.text: Kollam, on the backwaters of southern Kerala, was prominent from the ninth century; the Kollam era, still used in Kerala, begins in 825 CE. The Tarisāppaḷḷi copper plates of 849, issued there, record privileges granted to a Christian church under the protection of two merchant bodies (Section 4.7). The ninth-century Arabic account of the route to China names Kūlam Malī as the port where ships from the Gulf took on water before crossing the Bay of Bengal, and Chinese writers of the Song period describe it as a place where large ships transferred cargo. Marco Polo describes it, and Ibn Baṭṭūṭa visited it (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958; Polo 1903). In the later middle ages it was eclipsed by Calicut and then by Cochin.

docs.title: 15.3.4 Calicut
docs.text:
Calicut (Kozhikode) became the leading port of Malabar in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries under the rulers known as the Sāmūtiri (Zamorin). It had no sheltered harbour (Figure 15.1): ships anchored in the open roadstead and goods were landed by boat, and the port was all but closed during the south-west monsoon. Its success rested on the security it offered to merchants of every origin and on its access to the pepper of the interior (Prange 2018).

Figure 15.1. Calicut in Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg’s Civitates orbis terrarum (1572), under the title “Calechut, the most celebrated emporium of India”. The European engraving shows ships in the open roadstead, boats plying to the shore and ships being built on the beach. Image: Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who was in Calicut several times in the 1340s, calls it one of the great ports of Malabar, visited by merchants from China, Java, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Yemen and Fārs. He names the shāhbandar, the official in charge of the port and its foreign merchants, as a merchant from Bahrain, describes the Muslim community with its own judge (qāḍī) under a Hindu ruler, and saw Chinese junks in the roadstead waiting for the season (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958). Ma Huan, the Muslim interpreter on Zheng He’s voyages, describes Calicut in the early fifteenth century as the great country of the western ocean, ruled by a Hindu king who employed Muslim officials. He describes how, when the Chinese ships arrived, the king’s officials, a Muslim chief and the local brokers met the Chinese commanders to agree the prices of the goods; the bargain was sealed by clasping hands, and after that it could not be changed (Ma 1970). The office of shāhbandar was later held by the leading Muslim merchant of the town, known locally as the Shāhbandar Koya.

After Vasco da Gama’s arrival in 1498, the Zamorins’ refusal to exclude the Muslim merchants of the port led to long conflict with the Portuguese (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 15.3.5 Cambay
docs.text: Cambay (Khambhāt), at the head of the gulf of the same name, was the chief port of Gujarat from about the tenth to the sixteenth century, and its merchants were found from Aden to Melaka (Chapter 12). Silting and dangerous shoals made it increasingly difficult for large ships, and Portuguese control of Diu (from 1535) and of the sea lanes reduced its independence; by the late sixteenth century Surat had begun to take its place (Pearson 1976).

docs.title: 15.3.6 Chittagong, Sonargaon and Satgaon: Bengal under the Sultans
docs.text:
At the head of the Bay, Bengal was ruled by independent sultans from the mid-fourteenth century, when Ilyās Shāh united the province in the 1350s, until the Afghan and Mughal conquests of the sixteenth (Eaton 1993). Three ports served it: Chittagong on the Karnaphuli, close to the open sea in the east; Sonargaon, the old eastern capital near modern Dhaka, reached by river; and Satgaon (Saptagrāma) on the Hugli in the west, the successor of Tāmralipti. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa landed in 1346 at a port he calls Sudkāwān, usually identified with Chittagong, and later sailed from Sonargaon for Southeast Asia; he remarks on the abundance and cheapness of Bengal’s rice (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1958).

In the early fifteenth century Bengal entered Ming diplomacy. Its sultans sent missions to the Yongle emperor, among them one of 1414 that brought a giraffe, which had itself come from the African coast and was greeted at the Chinese court as an auspicious creature, and squadrons of Zheng He’s fleets and Ming envoys called at Chittagong (Dreyer 2007). Ma Huan describes how ships arriving at Chittagong sent their goods up river by smaller boats to Sonargaon and the capital, and he notes that the kingdom used a silver coin, the tanka, with cowries for small purchases, and produced many kinds of fine cotton cloth (Ma 1970). Bengal’s rice, sugar, cotton cloth and silk went to Southeast Asia and the west coast: writing at Melaka soon after 1511, Tomé Pires counted Bengali merchants among the traders of the city (Pires 1944). Portuguese private traders settled at Chittagong and at Satgaon, which they called the great and the little port, from the 1530s; as the river at Satgaon silted, its trade passed to Hughli.

docs.title: 15.4 Ports of the Early Modern Period
15.4.1 Surat
docs.text:
Surat, on the Tapti upstream from its mouth (large ships anchored at Swally, Suvālī, in the estuary), came under Mughal rule when Akbar conquered Gujarat in 1572–73. In the seventeenth century it was the main port of the Mughal empire and one of the busiest in Asia (Figure 15.2). Its ships sailed to the Red Sea, the Gulf, the Malabar coast and Southeast Asia, and it was the principal port of embarkation for pilgrims to Mecca. The port was governed by a Mughal official, the mutasaddī, with a customs house and a separate commander of the fort. Its merchants included Hindu and Jain vāṇiyās such as the great financier Vīrjī Vorā, Muslim shipowners such as Mullā ʿAbd al-Ghafūr, Bohras, Armenians and Parsis, and from the second decade of the seventeenth century the English and Dutch companies maintained factories there. The Maratha raids of 1664 and 1670 under Śivājī showed the city’s vulnerability. Das Gupta (1979) has shown how Surat’s trade declined in the first half of the eighteenth century, as the Mughal, Safavid and Ottoman markets on which it depended were disrupted, its shipowners lost their ships and their capital, and Indian merchants increasingly moved under the protection of the English at Bombay (Subramanian 1996).

Figure 15.2. The port of Surat during a fight between English and Dutch ships: anonymous Dutch painting, c. 1670. The walled city and its castle lie across the water; Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Photo: Anonymous Dutch painter (Rijksmuseum), CC0 1.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 15.4.2 Masulipatnam
docs.text: Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam), on the Krishna delta, was the port of the Qutb Shāhī sultanate of Golconda in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Its ships sailed to Pegu, Arakan, Tenasserim and Aceh in the east and to the Gulf in the west. Persian merchants and officials, some of them great shipowners, were prominent in its trade alongside Telugu merchant groups such as the Komaṭis (a trading caste, not weavers) and Balijas. The Dutch established a factory there in 1606 and the English in 1611, and both bought the painted and printed cottons of the hinterland, which were in demand in Southeast Asia and later in Europe (Arasaratnam 1986; Subrahmanyam 1990). The companies depended on Indian merchants and brokers to advance money to weavers and to deliver cloth, a system Arasaratnam (1994) and others have analysed in detail.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Hughli
docs.text:
Hughli, on the river of the same name above modern Kolkata, began as a Portuguese settlement in about 1579–80, with Mughal permission. In 1632 a Mughal army took the town and expelled the Portuguese, and Hughli became the main Mughal port of Bengal and the seat of a faujdār. The Dutch at Chinsurah, the English at Hughli and later at Calcutta (from 1690), the French at Chandernagore and the Danes at Serampore all settled along the same stretch of river to buy the silk, cotton cloth, saltpetre and sugar of Bengal (Prakash 1985; Chaudhuri 1978). The rise of Calcutta in the eighteenth century belongs to Chapters 18 and 19. Table 15.1 summarises the principal ports discussed in this chapter, and Figure 15.3 shows where they lay.

The coastline is simplified and shows the present shore, not the shores of the periods concerned; islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no political boundaries are shown. Several ports were important in more than one period (Table 15.1). docs.title: 15.5.1 The Arthaśāstra’s Superintendent of Boats
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (Chapter 2) devotes one short chapter (AŚ 2.28) to the nāvadhyakṣa, the superintendent of boats or of shipping. Read in Olivelle’s and Kangle’s translations, it is a revenue and security chapter, not a law code (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1960). Its main provisions can be paraphrased as follows:

  • The superintendent keeps the accounts of voyages on the sea and at river mouths, and of ferries on lakes, reservoirs and rivers near the royal fortified towns.

  • Villages on the coast and on the banks of rivers and lakes pay a fixed tax; fishermen give a sixth of their catch as boat hire; merchants pay the share of duty customary in port towns; passengers on the king’s boats pay a fare; and those who fish for conch and pearl pay boat hire or use their own boats.

  • He is to observe the established customs of port towns. A ship that arrives damaged by storm is to be treated with fatherly kindness, and goods damaged by water may be exempted from duty or charged half.

  • Pirate ships (hiṃsrikā) are to be destroyed, as are ships bound for enemy territory and those that violate the customs of the port.

  • On large rivers the king’s boats are to carry a commander, a steersman, men to handle the ropes and a bailer. People may cross only at the official ferries and at the proper times; a schedule of fares, graded by load and by the size of the river, is given, and certain persons (among them brāhmaṇas, renunciants, children, the aged, the sick, royal messengers and pregnant women) cross free.

  • If a boat is lost through the fault of the ferry service, for example through lack of crew or equipment or failure to repair it, the superintendent must make good the loss.

The customs house and the customs duties on imported goods, which are treated in a separate pair of chapters (AŚ 2.21–22), are discussed in Chapter 7; they apply to goods entering the capital by any route, not specifically by sea. Like the rest of the Arthaśāstra, these provisions describe an ideal kingdom; we do not know that any state applied them.

docs.title: 15.5.2 Tamil and Chola Ports
docs.text: The Paṭṭiṉappālai’s officers stamping the tiger seal on goods at Pukār are the earliest description of customs collection at a Tamil port (Section 15.2.5). Chola inscriptions speak of tolls and customs (suṅkam) and of merchant bodies with privileges in particular towns, and Kulottuṅga I (r. 1070–1122) bore the title “the Chola who abolished tolls”, which probably refers to the remission of certain transit dues rather than to free trade in any modern sense (Hall 1980). Much of the day-to-day regulation of merchants was left to their own associations, discussed in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 15.5.3 The Shāhbandar and the Emporia of the Ocean
docs.text: From the later medieval period many ports of the Indian Ocean had an official called the shāhbandar (Persian, “king of the port”). He received foreign ships, assigned warehouses, assessed duties, and represented the merchants of his community before the ruler. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa met one at Calicut. Tomé Pires, writing just after the Portuguese conquest of Melaka in 1511, describes four shāhbandars there, each responsible for a group of nations: one for the Gujaratis alone; one for the merchants of the Coromandel coast, Bengal, Pegu and Pasai; one for those of Java, the Moluccas and the nearer islands; and one for the Chinese and the people of the Ryukyus and Champa. He reports that merchants from the west paid a duty of six per cent of the value of their cargoes, while those from the east gave presents instead (Pires 1944). The arrangement shows how a port could govern a cosmopolitan population by community, with each group represented by its own officer.

docs.title: 15.5.4 Mughal Ports
docs.text: At Surat the mutasaddī was responsible for the port, the customs house and the city, while a separate commander held the fort. Customs were levied on the value of goods. In 1665 Aurangzeb fixed the rate at two and a half per cent for Muslim merchants and five per cent for Hindus; two years later he abolished duties for Muslims altogether, an exemption that was later withdrawn (Richards 1993). Merchants complained frequently of the exactions of particular governors, and Das Gupta’s study of Surat shows how much the fortunes of the port depended on the relations between its merchants and the officials sent from the court (Das Gupta 1979).

docs.title: 15.6 The Law of the Sea: What the Sources Say
docs.text: There is no Sanskrit treatise or chapter on maritime law. The Yuktikalpataru, a late compilation of uncertain date, classifies ships but contains no law (Chapter 13). What the texts offer is a small number of scattered rules, set out below.

docs.title: 15.6.1 Ferries, Boats and the Liability of Boatmen
docs.text: Besides the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the superintendent of boats, the main passage is near the end of the eighth chapter of the Manusmṛti (c. 2nd c. CE) (Olivelle 2004). Manu 8.404–409 sets ferry fares: a cart pays one paṇa, a man with a load half a paṇa, an animal or a woman a quarter, and a man without a load an eighth. Carts carrying goods pay according to the value of the goods, and empty vessels and people without property pay a small amount. On long journeys by water the fare is to be fixed according to place and time; this, the text says, applies to rivers, for on the sea there is no fixed standard. Pregnant women, ascetics, hermits and brāhmaṇa students are not to be charged. If anything is damaged in a boat through the fault of the boatmen, the boatmen are to make it good together, each paying his share; for damage caused by fate (daiva) there is no penalty. This last rule is a genuine distinction between loss by negligence and loss by accident, but it concerns ferry boats on rivers and is very brief.

docs.title: 15.6.2 Sea Loans and Interest
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra (AŚ 3.11.1) and the Yājñavalkyasmṛti (c. 4th–5th c. CE; 2.38) both allow monthly interest of twenty per cent for those who trade by sea, against ten for those who travel through wild country. Manu (8.156–157) treats contracts tied to a journey: a party who has agreed to a return for carriage over a stated distance and time and fails to keep to them loses the agreed return, and for sea voyages the rate fixed by men expert in sea voyages, who know place, time and goods, is to be accepted (Olivelle 2004; Kane 1930). These rules recognise that sea trade was risky and that its terms were set by merchant custom, but they do not say whether the lender lost his claim if the ship was lost, the defining feature of the Greek and Roman maritime loan. The rates are discussed in Chapter 6; the only surviving loan document connected with the India trade, the Muziris papyrus, is Greek (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 15.6.3 Partnership and Shared Loss
docs.text:
The dharmaśāstra title on partnership (saṃbhūya-samutthāna) rules that partners share profit and loss in proportion to their contributions or as they have agreed, and Yājñavalkya and Nārada (c. 5th–6th c. CE) add that a partner who saves the common goods from a calamity caused by fate, by the king or by thieves is entitled to a tenth of what he saves (Kane 1930). These rules apply to any joint enterprise, by land or by sea. Nārada treats debt, deposits, partnership and wages in detail but has no title on sea trade. Table 15.2 summarises the relevant rules.

Table 15.2. Rules bearing on ships and sea trade in the Arthaśāstra and dharmaśāstra (paraphrased) Passage Content AŚ 2.28 Superintendent of boats: revenue from boats, fishermen and ports; storm-damaged ships and goods; destruction of pirate ships; ferries, fares and exemptions; liability for boats lost through the service’s fault AŚ 3.11.1 Monthly interest of 20 per cent for sea traders Manu 8.156–157 Contracts tied to a journey; rate for sea voyages to be fixed by experts Manu 8.404–409 Ferry fares; no fixed fare on the sea; exemptions; boatmen jointly liable for damage through their fault, not for damage by fate Yājñavalkya 2.38 Monthly interest of 20 per cent for sea traders Yājñavalkya, Nārada (partnership) Profit and loss shared by contribution; a tenth to a partner who saves the common goods

Debate: Did Indian law know “general average”?

General average is the rule that when cargo is thrown overboard to save a ship, the loss is shared by all whose goods were saved. No passage on jettison has been found in the Arthaśāstra or the smṛtis surveyed here. The partnership rule on proportional sharing of loss is a different principle: it applies to partners in a single enterprise, not to unrelated shippers on one vessel. The question whether Indian merchants followed a custom of contribution for jettison is open; the law books do not tell us.

docs.title: 15.6.4 Shipwreck and the Right of Wreck
docs.text: In many parts of the world rulers claimed wrecked ships and their cargoes. Marco Polo reports that in the kingdom of Eli, on the Malabar coast north of Calicut, a ship that entered the river mouth by accident, instead of by intention, was seized with all its goods (Polo 1903). The Persian envoy ʿAbd al-Razzāq, who was at Calicut in 1442–43, contrasts the practice of other ports, where a ship driven in by the wind was plundered, with that of Calicut, where every ship, whatever its origin or destination, was treated like any other (Major 1857). The clearest Indian legal document on the subject is the inscription set up at Motupalli on the Andhra coast in 1244–45 by the Kākatīya king Gaṇapatideva. It declares that former kings had seized the entire cargo of ships wrecked by storms and driven ashore, and that he, for the sake of merchants who brave the sea, renounces this right and will take only the fixed duty (Chakravarti 2002). Gaṇapatideva’s promise was an invitation to merchants: a port that guaranteed their goods could hope to attract their trade.

docs.title: 15.7 Merchants’ Law: Associations, Communities and Islamic Law
docs.text:
Much of the law that governed sea trade in practice was not royal law at all. The dharmaśāstras themselves tell the king to respect the customs (dharma) of regions, castes, guilds and associations of merchants. In south India the merchant bodies known as the Five Hundred (Ayyāvoḷe), the Maṇigrāmam and the Añjuvaṇṇam held privileges from kings, settled disputes among their members and appear in inscriptions from Sri Lanka to Sumatra, the Kollam plates of 849 being the classic example (Section 4.7) (Abraham 1988; Malekandathil 2010).

Muslim merchants, who dominated much of the trade of the western ocean from the ninth century, lived by Islamic law and settled their disputes before their own qāḍīs, even in ports ruled by Hindu kings. In Malabar the Muslim communities, mostly of the Shāfiʿī school, had Friday mosques endowed by merchants and protected by the rulers, and their legal and religious scholars were linked to Yemen, the Hijaz and Egypt (Prange 2018). The letters of the Cairo Geniza show Jewish merchants trading between Egypt, Aden and Malabar in the eleventh and twelfth centuries through partnerships, commenda-type investments and informal relations of mutual service, and resolving disputes before rabbinical courts or merchant representatives (Goitein and Friedman 2008); Aden, the entrepôt between India and Egypt, had a customs regime that recalls what Ibn Baṭṭūṭa and Pires describe in India and Melaka (Margariti 2007). The Indian Ocean was thus a space of plural law, in which each community kept its own law for its internal affairs while rulers and port officials regulated duties, security and the treatment of strangers.

docs.title: 15.8 Comparisons: Rhodian Sea Law and the Maritime Laws of Melaka
docs.text:
The Mediterranean had a longer tradition of written maritime law. The Roman jurists preserved, in a title of Justinian’s Digest (533 CE) on the “Rhodian law of jettison” (Digest 14.2), the rule that cargo thrown overboard to lighten a ship in danger is to be made good by the contribution of all who benefited. A separate Byzantine compilation, the Rhodian Sea Law (Nomos Rhodiōn Nautikos), probably of the seventh or eighth century, sets out rules on the shares of shipowners, merchants and crew, on loans, jettison and wreck (Ashburner 1909).

A closer parallel in the Indian Ocean is the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka, the Maritime Laws of Melaka, compiled in the fifteenth century, by tradition from the customs of ship captains (nakhoda), and presented to the sultan. It describes the captain as a ruler at sea, sets out the duties and ranks of the crew, the position of merchants travelling on board, the allotment of cargo space, discipline and punishments, and procedure in danger, combining Malay custom (adat) with Islamic law (Winstedt and Josselin de Jong 1956). Gujarati and Tamil merchants traded at Melaka and would have sailed under such rules. Nothing comparable survives from an Indian port, which does not mean that Indian captains and merchants had no customs, only that they were not written down or have not survived.

docs.title: 15.9 Piracy
docs.text:
Piracy is a constant in the sources. The Arthaśāstra orders the destruction of pirate ships (Section 15.5.1). The Periplus mentions islands south of Kalliena inhabited by pirates (§53) (Casson 1989), and Pliny the Elder writes that ships sailing to India carried companies of archers because of pirates (Natural History 6.101), and that Muziris was not a desirable place to call because pirates occupied a place nearby (6.104). Marco Polo describes pirate fleets from Gujarat and Malabar that cruised in line abreast to catch merchant ships in the sailing season (Polo 1903).

“Pirate” was also a political label. The Portuguese called the fleets of the Kuñjāli Marakkārs, hereditary Muslim admirals of the Zamorin who fought them for most of the sixteenth century, pirates; the last Kuñjāli was executed by the Portuguese at Goa in 1600 (Malekandathil 2010). The English applied the same word to Kānhojī Āṅgre, admiral of the Maratha fleet in the early eighteenth century, who taxed and seized shipping off the Konkan as the Portuguese and the English themselves did (Apte 1973). European pirates were in turn a danger to Indian shipping, as the capture of the Ganj-i Sawāʾī in 1695 showed (Section 18.9.3). Lakshmi Subramanian has shown how the label “pirate” served states on India’s western coast, Indian and British, as an instrument for ordering the maritime communities they sought to control (Subramanian 2016).

docs.title: 15.10 The Portuguese Cartaz and the End of the Open Sea
docs.text:
Before 1500 no power tried to control navigation on the high seas of the Indian Ocean. Rulers taxed and protected the ports they held, and sometimes, like Sandanes at Kalyāṇ, closed them to particular traders, but the sea itself was open. The Portuguese changed this. From the first decade of the sixteenth century they claimed the right to license all Asian shipping in the waters they sought to control. An Asian ship was required to carry a cartaz, a pass issued by a Portuguese official, naming its captain and stating its cargo and destination; it had to call at a Portuguese fort, such as Goa, Diu, Hormuz or Melaka, to pay customs; and it was forbidden to carry certain goods, such as pepper and other spices reserved for the Portuguese crown, horses, arms and munitions, or to trade with the crown’s enemies. Ships without a cartaz could be seized, and their crews were liable to be killed or enslaved (Pearson 1987).

The fee for a cartaz was small; its purpose was to channel trade through Portuguese customs houses and to exclude rivals. It was a form of protection sold under threat of force. Many Gujarati and other merchants complied, Mughal ships took passes, and Asian trade continued on a large scale, but the system made the Portuguese, and later the Dutch and English who adopted similar passes, the arbiters of who could sail where. The contrast between this Portuguese claim to a closed sea and the earlier practice of Asian ports has been used, notably by Alexandrowicz (1967), to argue that Asian practice informed Hugo Grotius’s defence of the freedom of the seas in Mare Liberum (1609); the thesis is debated. The Portuguese and later European systems are discussed in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 15.11 Conclusion
docs.text: The coexistence of many communities in these ports was pragmatic: it rested on revenue, it accommodated slavery and coercion, and it could break down in violence. Their law was plural, and the Sanskrit texts contribute only a handful of rules to it, on ferry fares, the liability of boatmen, sea loans and partnership; the rest lay with merchants’ associations, Islamic and Jewish law and local custom.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the early ports see Ray (2003) and Chakravarti (2002), with Casson (1989) for the Periplus. Prange (2018) is the best study of Malabar and its ports, and Das Gupta (1979) the classic account of Surat. For the Coromandel coast see Arasaratnam (1986), and for the ocean as a whole Pearson (2003). Olivelle (2013) and Olivelle (2004) provide reliable translations of the legal texts, and Pearson (1987) explains the cartaz system.

docs.title: Chapter 16: India and Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

From the early centuries CE, rulers across mainland and island Southeast Asia took up Sanskrit, Indic scripts, Hindu and Buddhist cults, Indian ideas of kingship and Indian literary forms, and used them for their own purposes. This chapter looks at how that happened: through traders, Brahmins and Buddhist monks, and above all through the choices of Southeast Asian elites. It surveys the evidence from Funan and Champa, Borneo and Java, Śrīvijaya, Angkor and Pagan, the Rāmāyaṇa traditions of the region and the Hindu culture of Bali. It treats “Indianisation” as a debated concept and stresses that the traffic ran both ways: Southeast Asian ships, sailors, spices and Buddhist patrons were as much a part of the story as Indian merchants.

Indian texts called the lands beyond the Bay of Bengal Suvarṇabhūmi (“land of gold”) and Suvarṇadvīpa (“island of gold”). Merchants in the Jātaka stories sail there to make their fortunes, and the Rāmāyaṇa’s survey of the eastern quarter names Yavadvīpa, probably Java. Ptolemy’s Geography (2nd c. CE) knows a “Golden Chersonese” (the Malay peninsula) and an island called Iabadiou, a Greek rendering of the same name (Coedès 1968; Wolters 1967). The names tell us what Indian merchants hoped to find, not how the inhabitants saw themselves, and the lands they referred to are hard to pin down.

The earliest contacts across the Bay, attested by beads, pottery and bronzes from the last centuries BCE, are treated in Chapter 11; the trade of the Straits between 600 and 1500, including Śrīvijaya’s commercial history and the Chola raid of 1025, in Chapter 12. This chapter is concerned with the cultural side of the relationship. Temple architecture is treated in more depth in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa, and scripts in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā.

docs.title: 16.1 “Indianisation”: A Debated Concept
docs.text:
The word “Indianisation” was made familiar by the French epigraphist George Coedès, whose survey of the early kingdoms of the region, first published in French in the 1940s, appeared in English in 1968 as The Indianized States of Southeast Asia. Coedès defined Indianisation as the spread of an organised culture founded on the Indian conception of kingship, marked by Hindu or Buddhist cults, the mythology of the Purāṇas and the norms of the Dharmaśāstras, and expressed in Sanskrit (Coedès 1968). He stressed that this did not involve Indian conquest. But he pictured it largely as a transfer from a more advanced culture to less developed ones, carried by Indian settlers, merchants and priests.

Earlier Indian nationalist writers had gone further. In the 1920s the Greater India Society in Calcutta, and historians such as R. C. Majumdar, wrote of “Indian colonies” in the Far East, by analogy with the colonies of the European powers. That picture has been abandoned. No Indian state ruled any part of Southeast Asia, there is no evidence of large-scale Indian settlement, and the Southeast Asian kingdoms were founded and governed by local people.

Debate: How should the Indic culture of Southeast Asia be described?

  • “Indianized states” (Coedès). Indian culture was carried by Indian merchants, Brahmins and settlers and adopted by local rulers, who thereby created states of a new type. The model emphasises the Indian source and the completeness of the transfer (Coedès 1968).

  • Localisation (Wolters). O. W. Wolters argued that the starting point must be the Southeast Asian societies themselves. Their leaders were “men of prowess” whose authority rested on personal achievement and spiritual power, and their polities were shifting circles of allegiance (maṇḍalas) rather than bounded states. Such leaders selected Indian materials that fitted ideas they already held, especially about divinely charged kingship, and reworked them so thoroughly that the result was local. Wolters called this process “localisation” (Wolters 1999).

  • The Sanskrit cosmopolis (Pollock). Sheldon Pollock described a “Sanskrit cosmopolis” extending from Afghanistan to Java between about 300 and 1300 CE. Within it, rulers who had no political link with one another used the same literary language and the same forms of royal praise poetry to express power. The cosmopolis spread without conquest, mass migration or a church; its participants joined it by choice. Pollock also noted that Sanskrit was used in Southeast Asia, as in India, for poetic and political expression, while practical records were written in local languages such as Old Khmer and Old Malay (Pollock 2006).

Most historians now treat the process as the selective adoption and adaptation of Indic forms by Southeast Asian elites, who often had their own reasons for wanting them. “Indianisation” is still used as a convenient label, but with these qualifications.

The debate matters for how the evidence is read. A Sanskrit inscription of a Javanese king is evidence that the king, or his court, valued Sanskrit and could find someone to compose in it. It is not evidence that the king, his subjects or the poet were Indians, or that the society around him resembled Indian society.

docs.title: 16.2.1 Merchants
docs.text:
Trade created the contacts. Ships crossing the Bay of Bengal had to wait in port for the change of the monsoon, and merchants stayed for months at a time in Southeast Asian harbours (Chapter 14). From the ninth century onward Tamil merchant associations left inscriptions in the region, at Takuapa on the Thai–Malay peninsula, at Barus in Sumatra and at Pagan in Burma, and in some ports they maintained temples of their own (Chapter 12). Merchants carried images, ritual objects and textiles, and connected Southeast Asian rulers with the ports and sanctuaries of India (Hall 1980; Ray 1994).

Merchants alone, however, could not have produced Sanskrit court poetry, temple consecration rituals or the specialised vocabulary of kingship. The Dutch historian J. C. van Leur argued in the 1930s that the decisive actors were Brahmins invited by Southeast Asian rulers, not traders, and most later historians have agreed that the impetus came from the courts (Wolters 1999).

docs.title: 16.2.2 Brahmins and Buddhist Monks
docs.text:
Chinese accounts of Funan preserve a foundation legend in which a man from overseas, called Hun Tian in the Chinese records, marries a local queen called Liuye (“Willow Leaf”) and founds the royal line. A later Chinese history adds a second founder figure, Kauṇḍinya, a Brahmin who came from India in the fifth century and reorganised the kingdom according to Indian customs; and a seventh-century Sanskrit inscription from My Son in Champa tells of the Brahmin Kauṇḍinya marrying Somā, daughter of a serpent (nāga) king. These are dynastic myths, not historical records. They are nevertheless revealing: rulers chose to trace their legitimacy to a union between a foreign Brahmin and a local ruler or spirit of the land (Coedès 1968).

Inscriptions confirm that Brahmins received gifts and served as priests and advisers at Southeast Asian courts, though some of those named in later inscriptions appear to have been local families who had acquired Brahmin learning and status. Buddhist monks moved along the same sea routes. The Kashmiri monk Guṇavarman preached in Java in the early fifth century before going on to China; Chinese pilgrims such as Yijing sailed by way of Śrīvijaya; and in the early eleventh century the Bengali monk Atiśa spent years studying in Suvarṇadvīpa under a Sumatran teacher, Dharmakīrti, before going on to Tibet (Sen 2003; Ray 1994). The last case is a reminder that learning flowed in both directions.

docs.title: 16.2.3 Southeast Asian Agency
docs.text: Southeast Asians did not wait for Indians to come to them. Their ships carried much of the trade of the Bay (Chapter 13), their pilgrims and envoys travelled to India, and their kings endowed monasteries at Nālandā and Nāgapaṭṭinam. Inscriptions show rulers choosing among Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist cults and adapting them to local spirits, ancestors and sacred mountains. The Indic forms that took root were those that served the ambitions of local elites, and they were transformed in the process (Wolters 1999; Pollock 2006).

docs.title: 16.3.1 Funan and the Mekong Delta
docs.text: Chinese envoys who visited the Mekong delta in the mid-third century CE described a polity they called Funan, with walled settlements, a king, taxes paid in gold, silver and pearls, and books and archives written in a script resembling that of the “Hu” (Central Asians or Indians). Its main port was probably Oc Eo, whose finds are described in Chapter 11; it lay on the route between the Bay of Bengal and southern China. The few Sanskrit inscriptions attributed to Funan date from the fifth and sixth centuries and name rulers with Sanskrit names ending in -varman (Coedès 1968; Hall 2011).

docs.title: 16.3.2 The Vo Canh Inscription
docs.text: A Sanskrit inscription found at Vo Canh, near Nha Trang on the south-central coast of Vietnam, is often described as the oldest Sanskrit inscription in Southeast Asia. Dated on the basis of its script to about the third or fourth century CE, it records a donation by a ruler of the family of a king called Śrī Māra. Whether this ruler belonged to an early Cham polity or was a dependent of Funan is debated (Coedès 1968; Salomon 1998). An inscription of about the fourth century from Dong Yen Chau in central Vietnam was written in Old Cham; it is often regarded as the earliest surviving text in any Austronesian language, and it shows that the local language was being written in an Indic script almost as soon as Sanskrit was.

docs.title: 16.3.3 Mūlavarman at Kutai
docs.text: At Muara Kaman on the Mahakam river in East Kalimantan (Borneo), seven stone pillars carry Sanskrit inscriptions in verse. They call themselves yūpas, the sacrificial posts of Vedic ritual, and record the gifts of a king named Mūlavarman to Brahmins. On palaeographic grounds they are dated to about 400 CE, the earliest inscriptions from the islands. Their genealogy is instructive. Mūlavarman was the son of Aśvavarman, described as the founder of the dynasty, and the grandson of Kuṇḍuṅga, a name that is not Sanskrit. The family appears to have been a local one that adopted Sanskrit names and Brahmanical ritual within two generations (Coedès 1968; Salomon 1998).

docs.title: 16.3.4 Pūrṇavarman in West Java
docs.text:
A group of Sanskrit inscriptions in West Java, near modern Bogor and Jakarta, names a king Pūrṇavarman of Tārumānagara. They are dated on palaeographic grounds to the fifth century. The Ciaruteun stone carries a pair of carved footprints that the inscription compares to the footprints of Viṣṇu; the Tugu inscription records the digging of a canal and a gift of cattle to Brahmins. Pūrṇavarman thus presented himself in the idiom of an Indian king: a patron of Brahmins, a builder of waterworks and a ruler whose power was likened to a god’s (Coedès 1968). Table 16.1 lists selected early inscriptions from the region.

docs.title: 16.4 Śrīvijaya
docs.text:
The kingdom known as Śrīvijaya, centred near Palembang in southeast Sumatra, is known from a small group of inscriptions of the 680s and from Chinese sources. The earliest, the Kedukan Bukit inscription found at Palembang, is dated in the Śaka year 604, equivalent to 682 CE. It is written in Old Malay, in a southern Indic script, with Sanskrit loanwords, and records that the ruler, called the dapunta hiyaṃ, set out on a sacred expedition (siddhayātrā) with an army and founded a settlement. Other inscriptions of the following years, at Palembang, on the island of Bangka and in the Sumatran interior, threaten those who betray the ruler with terrible curses, and one, at Talang Tuo (684), records the foundation of a park for the benefit of all beings in Buddhist terms (Coedès 1968; Wolters 1967). Their language is significant. Śrīvijaya’s rulers were Buddhists who patronised Sanskrit learning, but they addressed their subjects in Malay, which became the language of trade and diplomacy throughout the archipelago.

The Chinese monk Yijing gives the best contemporary picture of the place. He sailed from Guangzhou in 671, stayed some months at Śrīvijaya studying Sanskrit grammar, went on to India and studied for about ten years at Nālandā, and returned to Śrīvijaya, where he lived from the late 680s to 695 copying and translating texts. He reported that more than a thousand Buddhist monks lived in the walled city, studying and practising much as in India, and he advised Chinese monks bound for India to spend a year or two there first to learn the rules and the language (Yijing 1896; Sen 2003). Śrīvijaya was thus not a distant outpost of Indian learning but one of its centres.

O. W. Wolters explained the kingdom’s wealth by its role as the main entrepôt between the Indian Ocean and China, which is discussed in Chapter 12 (Wolters 1967). Its kings were also patrons of Buddhism in India. In the ninth century a ruler of Suvarṇadvīpa, Bālaputradeva, had a monastery built at Nālandā; the Nālandā copper plate of the Pāla king Devapāla records that, at the request of Bālaputradeva’s envoys, Devapāla granted villages for its upkeep. The plate describes Bālaputradeva as the grandson of a Śailendra king of Yavabhūmi (Java) (Coedès 1968; Sen 2003). In the early eleventh century a later Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya and Kaṭāha (Kedah) built a monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam, endowed by the Chola kings.

Relations with the Cholas then broke down. In 1025 Rājendra I sent a naval expedition that raided Kaḍāram and the ports of Śrīvijaya, an episode known mainly from his Tamil meykkīrtti; it was a raid with debated motives, not a conquest, and it is discussed fully in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 16.5.1 The Śailendras and Borobudur
docs.text:
In the second half of the eighth century a dynasty calling itself Śailendra (“lords of the mountain”) rose to power in Central Java. Its Sanskrit inscriptions reveal close links with eastern India. The Kalasan inscription of 778 records the foundation of a temple to the Buddhist goddess Tārā, and the Kelurak inscription of 782 records the installation of an image of Mañjuśrī by a teacher from Gauḍa (Bengal), Kumāraghoṣa. Both are written in a north Indian script of the kind then used in Bengal and Bihar, unlike the southern scripts of earlier inscriptions (Coedès 1968; Salomon 1998).

Borobudur, built in Central Java around 800 (construction probably spanned several decades from the late eighth century), is the largest Buddhist monument in Southeast Asia. It is a stepped structure built over a natural hill: square terraces lined with galleries of relief panels, rising to three circular terraces carrying perforated stūpas, each enclosing a seated Buddha, and a single large stūpa at the summit. A pilgrim circling upward passes reliefs illustrating the workings of karma, the life of the Buddha according to the Lalitavistara, jātaka and avadāna stories, and the pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana in the Gaṇḍavyūha. The texts are Indian; the selection, the architectural conception and the carving are Javanese, and nothing quite like Borobudur was built in India.

Among the reliefs are several ships, some fitted with outriggers (Figure 16.1). They are among the best visual evidence for the ships of the region in this period, and they show features of the Austronesian shipbuilding tradition, such as outriggers, that were not used on Indian ships (Manguin 1993). A modern replica based on the reliefs, the Samudra Raksa, sailed from Indonesia across the Indian Ocean to Africa in 2003–04. Its voyage shows what such a design could do, not what route ancient ships took (Chapter 13).

Figure 16.1. A ship with an outrigger in a relief at Borobudur, Central Java (c. 800 CE), from the series illustrating the Divyāvadāna (the landing of Hiru). Photo: Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 16.5.2 Prambanan
docs.text:
A few kilometres away stands the Śaiva temple complex of Prambanan (Loro Jonggrang), built in the mid-ninth century. Its three principal shrines are dedicated to Śiva, at the centre, and to Brahmā and Viṣṇu; facing them are shrines for their mounts. Reliefs on the balustrades of the Śiva and Brahmā temples narrate the Rāmāyaṇa, and those of the Viṣṇu temple the story of Kṛṣṇa. The Old Javanese Śivagṛha inscription of 856 describes the dedication of a great Śiva sanctuary, generally identified with Prambanan (Coedès 1968).

Older accounts attributed Borobudur and Prambanan to two rival dynasties, the Buddhist Śailendras and the Śaiva house of Sañjaya; many scholars now see one royal line whose members patronised different religions. Either way, ninth-century Central Java supported monumental Buddhist and Śaiva building side by side.

docs.title: 16.5.3 Later Java
docs.text: After the tenth century the centre of Javanese power moved to East Java, where Old Javanese court poetry (kakawin), written in Indian metres on themes from the epics and Purāṇas, flourished. The Deśavarṇana (better known as the Nāgarakṛtāgama), completed by the poet Prapañca in 1365, describes the court of Majapahit (1293–c. 1527). The coastal rulers of Java adopted Islam in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, but the shadow theatre (wayang) with its epic repertoire survived the conversion.

docs.title: 16.6 The Mainland: Angkor, Champa and Pagan
16.6.1 Angkor
docs.text:
The Khmer kingdom of Angkor dates its foundation to 802, when, according to an inscription written about 250 years later (the Sdok Kak Thom inscription of 1052), Jayavarman II had himself consecrated as universal ruler (cakravartin) on the Kulen hills in a ritual performed by a Brahmin. The same inscription speaks of a cult of the devarāja. Coedès understood this as a cult of the divine king; others, notably Hermann Kulke, have argued that it was the cult of a protective deity of the kingdom, and the question remains open (Coedès 1968).

Angkor’s inscriptions illustrate Pollock’s distinction. Sanskrit inscriptions, often long and accomplished poems, praise kings and record religious foundations. Old Khmer inscriptions, frequently on the same stones, list the lands, rice fields, livestock and labourers assigned to temples. Among these were many knum, temple dependants whose status ranged from servants to people who were effectively slaves, a reminder that the temple economy rested on bound labour (Pollock 2006; Coedès 1968).

Angkor Wat, built for Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), is a temple dedicated to Viṣṇu. Its plan represents the cosmos, with the central tower as Mount Meru and the enclosing walls and moat as the mountain ranges and oceans around it. Its galleries carry long reliefs of the churning of the ocean of milk, the battle of Kurukṣetra and the battle of Laṅkā, together with a procession of Sūryavarman’s own army, identified by short Old Khmer labels. The iconography draws on Indian texts; the architecture, the planning and the sculptural style are Khmer. Later Angkorian kings turned to Mahāyāna Buddhism, notably Jayavarman VII (r. 1181–c. 1218), and by the fourteenth century Theravāda Buddhism, which reached the mainland through Sri Lanka and Burma, had become the religion of the Khmer and Thai kingdoms (Coedès 1968).

docs.title: 16.6.2 Champa
docs.text: “Champa”, a name taken from Indian usage, covers a series of polities of Cham-speaking people on the central and southern coast of Vietnam, from the early centuries CE until the last was absorbed by the Vietnamese state in the nineteenth century; their ports lay on the route between the Straits and China. The religious centre of My Son, in a valley inland from Da Nang, began as a sanctuary of Śiva under the name Bhadreśvara, founded by a king Bhadravarman around 400; it holds the remains of brick temples built between the seventh and thirteenth centuries, with inscriptions in Sanskrit and Old Cham (Coedès 1968). At Nha Trang the temple of Po Nagar honours a local goddess, “lady of the realm”, identified in Sanskrit inscriptions with Bhagavatī, a clear case of an indigenous deity given an Indic identity. Most Cham today are Muslims, but a Cham community that follows a Hindu-derived religion survives in southern Vietnam.

docs.title: 16.6.3 Pagan
docs.text: In Burma, the Pyu cities of the first millennium CE have yielded Buddhist texts in Pali and Sanskrit inscribed on gold and silver leaves. From the mid-eleventh century the kingdom of Pagan (Bagan), founded on the middle Irrawaddy by Anawrahta (r. 1044–1077), became a major Buddhist power. Its kings favoured Theravāda Buddhism in close contact with Sri Lanka, and its thousands of brick temples and stūpas, built between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, combine forms known from eastern India with local developments. The Myazedi inscription of about 1113 is written in four languages, Pali, Mon, Pyu and Burmese, a fitting symbol of the kingdom’s mix of traditions. Burmese kings also sent missions to repair the Mahābodhi temple at Bodh Gayā, and a Tamil inscription at Pagan records a Vaiṣṇava temple of the Nānādeśi merchants (Coedès 1968; Hall 2011).

docs.title: 16.7 Languages, Scripts and Calendars
docs.text:
The scripts used in Southeast Asia from the earliest inscriptions onward derive from the Brāhmī scripts of southern India. They are often called “Pallava” scripts, but the label is misleading, since they were not confined to the Pallava kingdom and scholars now prefer to speak of late southern Brāhmī. From these early forms developed, over many centuries and with much local innovation, the scripts used today for Khmer, Thai, Lao, Burmese, Javanese, Balinese and several other languages. In the eighth and ninth centuries north Indian scripts were used for some Sanskrit inscriptions in Java and Sumatra, reflecting the links with Bengal and Bihar noted above (Salomon 1998).

Writing in an Indic script did not mean writing in an Indian language. Old Cham, Old Malay, Old Khmer, Old Javanese, Mon and Burmese were all written in Indic scripts within a few centuries of the first Sanskrit inscriptions, and they absorbed many Sanskrit and Pali words; Malay still uses bahasa (language), negara (state) and raja (king).

Indic systems of time-reckoning travelled with the scripts. Inscriptions of Champa, Cambodia, Sumatra and Java are dated in the Śaka era, which begins in 78 CE, using Indian month names, lunar days and, in many cases, astronomical details. In Java the Śaka era remained in use until 1633, when Sultan Agung of Mataram introduced a lunar calendar of Islamic type that continued its year count; in Bali the Śaka year is still used, and the Balinese new year, Nyepi, is observed as a day of silence. The mainland Buddhist kingdoms used an era beginning in 638 CE as well as Buddhist eras counted from the Buddha’s death. These systems sat alongside indigenous calendars, such as the 210-day pawukon cycle of Java and Bali, which is not of Indian origin. Indian astronomy in Southeast Asia is treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa.

docs.title: 16.8 The Rāmāyaṇa in Southeast Asia
docs.text:
No Indian work was more widely adapted in Southeast Asia than the story of Rāma. It appears in temple reliefs at Prambanan (ninth century) and Angkor Wat (twelfth century), in court poetry, in dance and shadow theatre, and in oral tradition. The Southeast Asian versions do not derive simply from Vālmīki. The Old Javanese kakawin follows a later Sanskrit poem, Bhaṭṭi’s Rāvaṇavadha (the Bhaṭṭikāvya), closely in its earlier cantos; other versions draw on Tamil, Jain or popular retellings, and each tradition has added episodes and characters of its own (Richman 1991). Table 16.2 lists some of the main written versions.

Table 16.2. Some Southeast Asian versions of the Rāma story (dates are approximate and in several cases debated) Work Language and region Approximate date Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa Old Javanese; Java 9th–10th c. Reamker (Rāmakerti) Khmer; Cambodia earliest parts c. 16th–17th c. Hikayat Seri Rama Malay; Malay world known from manuscripts of the 17th c. onward Ramakien Thai; Thailand standard version composed under King Rama I, 1797 Phra Lak Phra Lam Lao; Laos date uncertain

The variety is the point. In the Thai Ramakien Hanumān is a worldly and amorous hero; in the Malay Hikayat Seri Rama, written for a Muslim audience, Rāvaṇa receives his kingdom by the favour of Allah. The Rāma story was not a fixed Indian text received intact but a narrative that every court and community retold in its own way.

docs.title: 16.9 Bali
docs.text:
Bali is the one region of island Southeast Asia where a religion of Indic origin remained the faith of the majority after the spread of Islam. Balinese religion combines the worship of Śiva, Buddhist elements, and the veneration of ancestors, local deities and the sacred mountain Gunung Agung. Brahmin high priests (pedanda) recite Sanskrit hymns and formulas in their rituals, many of them preserved in Bali in forms not known in India; the island’s literature was long written in Old Javanese and Balinese on palm leaf. Bali’s links were above all with Java, whose courtly culture it absorbed over many centuries, rather than directly with India (Geertz 1980).

Balinese society has a hereditary hierarchy that borrows the vocabulary of varṇa (brahmana, satria, wesia and the commoner sudra), but it differs greatly from Indian caste in its rules; Clifford Geertz’s study of the nineteenth-century Balinese state shows how titles of this kind were bound up with temple ritual and royal display (Geertz 1980). In the twentieth century Balinese reformers, seeking recognition from the Indonesian state, reshaped their tradition as a form of Hinduism and drew more directly on Indian texts. Bali is not a “living museum” of ancient India but a tradition with its own long history, in which Indian elements have been repeatedly reinterpreted.

docs.title: 16.10 Flows in Both Directions
docs.text:
The story told so far could be read as a one-way transfer from India to Southeast Asia. It was not. Southeast Asian ships, built with planks edge-joined by wooden dowels and fitted with lashed internal frames, were sailing the South China Sea and the Bay of Bengal by the early centuries CE; Chinese texts describe large ships of the kunlun (southern) peoples carrying hundreds of passengers (Manguin 1993). Austronesian-speaking seafarers from the islands crossed the whole Indian Ocean to settle Madagascar, probably in the second half of the first millennium CE; the Malagasy language is most closely related to languages of southern Borneo (McPherson 1993).

Some of the most valued goods of the Indian Ocean came from Southeast Asia. Cloves grew only in a few islands of northern Maluku, and nutmeg and mace only in the tiny Banda islands, in eastern Indonesia. Indonesian traders carried them westward to Java and the Straits, where they entered the networks that took them to India, the Middle East and eventually Europe. Camphor from Barus in Sumatra, benzoin and other resins, sandalwood from Timor, tin from the Malay peninsula, gold and aromatic woods went the same way (Chapter 12). In return Indian cotton cloth became an essential good in Southeast Asian exchange and ceremony: Gujarati and Coromandel textiles were traded for spices, and some, kept as heirlooms in eastern Indonesia, have been dated to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries (Guy 1998).

The traffic in ideas was also two-way. Southeast Asian rulers built and endowed monasteries in India, Indian monks studied in Sumatra, and the Buddhist art of Java and Burma influenced that of eastern India as well as drawing on it. From the thirteenth century Islam reached the region along the same sea routes, carried in part by Gujarati, Tamil and Bengali Muslim merchants alongside Arabs and Persians, and Malacca and the ports of the archipelago became Muslim centres in their own right (Chapter 12).

The links between India and Southeast Asia thus show how culture could move in the pre-modern world without empire. What resulted was not a copy of India but a range of distinctive civilisations, Khmer, Javanese, Cham, Burmese, Malay and Balinese, each of which made the borrowed forms its own.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Coedès (1968) remains the standard narrative of the early kingdoms and their inscriptions, though its framework is now questioned. Wolters (1999) sets out the localisation approach, and Pollock (2006) the idea of the Sanskrit cosmopolis. On Śrīvijaya and early trade, see Wolters (1967) and Hall (2011); on Buddhist networks, Ray (1994) and Sen (2003). Manguin (1993) is the key study of Southeast Asian ships, Salomon (1998) surveys the inscriptions and scripts, and Richman (1991) introduces the many tellings of the Rāma story.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Coastal Communities: Fishers, Sailors and Maritime Knowledge
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Ships, ports and merchants depended on people who are seldom named in the sources: fishers, boatmen, sailors, divers, salt-makers and shipwrights. This chapter introduces the principal coastal and seafaring communities of the subcontinent, Hindu, Muslim and Christian, and is frank about their often low place in caste hierarchies. It describes their boats, their working knowledge of tides, winds and fish, and some well-attested forms of their religious life. It follows the curing and trade of fish, in which women’s work was central, and the island economies of Lakshadweep and the Maldives, and then turns to three other coastal industries (pearl and chank diving, salt-making, with the colonial salt monopoly, and the use of mangrove forests) and to the changes of the last seventy years.

docs.title: 17.1 Who Lived by the Sea
docs.text:
The coasts of the subcontinent were home to many communities whose livelihood depended on the sea: fishers who worked from the beach or from small craft, boatmen who carried goods and passengers through the surf and along the coast, deep-sea sailors and pilots, divers for pearls and chank, salt-makers, and the carpenters who built boats. These communities were usually organised as castes (jāti) or as distinct religious groups, each with its own dialect, customs and territory along the shore. Their knowledge was transmitted by practice within families and was rarely written down, and so most of what we know of them comes from the last two centuries: colonial ethnographies and gazetteers, the work of anthropologists and historians, and the communities’ own testimony.

Their social position was generally low. Brahmanical norms treated the killing of fish as polluting, and the Manusmṛti places the Mārgava, also called Dāsa or Kaivarta, who lives by work on boats, among the mixed castes born of irregular unions (Manu 10.34) (Olivelle 2004). In many regions fishing castes were ranked low and excluded from temples and from landholding, though the hierarchy varied a great deal from coast to coast, and some seafaring and trading groups held considerable wealth and local power. Conversion to Christianity and Islam was common on the coasts, and was often a collective decision by a community in search of protection or of status (Bayly 1989). Today many fishing communities are classified as Other Backward Classes, and a few as Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.

docs.title: 17.2 Communities of the West Coast
docs.text:
Gujarat and Kutch. The Kolis are a large and varied cluster of castes in Gujarat and Maharashtra, many of them cultivators; on the coast Koli groups fished and sailed. The Khārvās of Saurashtra and Kutch, in ports such as Porbandar, Veraval and Mandvi, were the hereditary sailors of Gujarat’s sailing ships (Gujarati vahāṇ), which traded to the Gulf, Arabia and East Africa until the mid-twentieth century and in some cases still do. Among Muslims, the Bhaḍālās of the Kutch and Saurashtra coast were shipowners and sailors in the same trade. The Vāghers of Okhamandal, around Dwarka, Hindu and Muslim, combined fishing, sailing and, in British eyes, piracy; British naval actions against “pirates” of the Kathiawar coast in the early nineteenth century were directed partly at them, and they rose against British and Gaekwad authority in 1857–59. Lakshmi Subramanian has traced how the states of the western littoral used the category of piracy to bring such maritime groups under control (Subramanian 2016). As with the Kuñjāli Marakkārs and Kānhojī Āṅgre (Chapter 15), the label “pirate” tells us as much about who held power at sea as about the people it described.

The Konkan. Around Mumbai the Koli fishing villages (koḷīvāḍā) are among the oldest settlements of the islands, and Koli women have long dominated the retail sale of fish in the city. The Gābits of the southern Konkan, the Kharvis of the Goa and Karnataka coast and other groups fished and served as sailors, including in the Maratha fleets of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Apte 1973).

Malabar and Travancore. In Kerala the principal Hindu fishing castes are the Mukkuvar, mainly in Malabar, and the Arayar (Araya) of central Kerala. The Mukkuvar of the far south, in present-day Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari districts, became Catholic in the sixteenth century, when Francis Xavier baptised fishing villages on the Travancore coast in the 1540s, and remain so; in Malabar some fishing groups became Muslim. Kalpana Ram’s study of Catholic Mukkuvar women in Kanyakumari describes a community in which women carried much of the work of marketing and the household economy, while being excluded from the boats and the sea (Ram 1991). The Māppiḷas, the Muslims of Malabar, emerged from the settlement of Arab and Persian merchants, intermarriage and local conversion; they included wealthy merchants and shipowners as well as boatmen, fishers and labourers (Prange 2018). Chapter 12 discusses their history.

Lakshadweep. The people of the Lakshadweep (Laccadive) islands, Muslim and Malayalam-speaking except on Minicoy, where a language close to Dhivehi of the Maldives is spoken, lived by coconut cultivation, coir-making and fishing. Their sailing vessels (oḍam) carried coir, copra and dried fish to the Malabar coast in the fair-weather season and brought back rice and other goods. The islands were under the Ali Rājās of Kannur and later under the British, and the rulers’ monopoly of the coir trade was a long-standing grievance of the islanders. Minicoy men were known in the twentieth century as sailors on merchant ships.

docs.title: 17.3 Communities of the East Coast and Sri Lanka
docs.text:
The Paravar. The Paravar (Bharathar) of the Gulf of Mannar coast, between Kanyakumari and Rameswaram, were fishers and divers for pearls and chank. In the 1530s, in conflict with Muslim merchants over the pearl fishery and its revenues, the Paravar converted collectively to Catholicism to obtain Portuguese protection, and Francis Xavier worked among them in the 1540s. Their headman (jāti talaivaṉ) at Tuticorin (Thoothukudi) was both a caste chief and a lay leader of the church, and the community kept its own hierarchy and institutions within Catholicism (Bayly 1989; Subrahmanyam 1990).

The Marakkāyar. The Marakkāyar were Tamil-speaking Muslims of the Coromandel and Gulf of Mannar ports, such as Kāyalpaṭṭiṉam, Kīḻakkarai, Nāgūr and Nāgapaṭṭinam. They were shipowners and merchants trading to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and the Malabar coast, and dominant in the pearl and chank trade before the Portuguese arrived. Other Tamil Muslim groups, such as the Labbais, included fishers, divers and weavers (Bayly 1989; Arasaratnam 1994).

Other Tamil and Sri Lankan communities. The Paṭṭiṉavar fished from the beaches of the northern Tamil coast, around Chennai and Puducherry, using log rafts and nets. The Karaiyar, a Tamil fishing and seafaring caste of northern Sri Lanka and parts of the Tamil coast, and the Sinhala Karāva of the west coast of Sri Lanka, were also sailors and traders. Further north, Telugu-speaking fishing communities such as the Jālāris of the north Andhra coast and the Noliyās of southern Odisha worked the surf beaches, and in Bengal fishing castes such as the Kaibarttas and Mālos worked the rivers, estuaries and the sea.

Sailors for hire. Khalāsī, a word of Arabic origin for a seaman or labourer, was used across western India for ship’s hands and dock workers; at Beypore it denotes a Māppiḷa group known for launching and hauling heavy hulls (Chapter 13). From the sixteenth century European ships hired Asian seamen, whom the English called lascars (from Persian lashkar). By the nineteenth century large numbers of men from Ratnagiri, Gujarat, Bengal and Sylhet served on British merchant ships and steamers, on separate contracts and at lower wages than European sailors, a labour history that belongs to Chapter 19.

docs.title: 17.4 Boats and the Work of Fishing
docs.text:
The construction of traditional craft is treated in Chapter 13; here the focus is on how they were used. The standard survey is McGrail et al. (2003), based on fieldwork in the 1990s.

On the surf beaches of the Coromandel coast the kaṭṭumaram (Tamil, “tied logs”), a raft of shaped logs lashed together (Figure 17.1), could be launched through breaking waves, would not sink if swamped, and could be taken apart and carried up the beach. It carried a small crew, with a sail and paddles, and was used for hook-and-line and net fishing offshore. The English word “catamaran” derives from it, although the English word now denotes a twin-hulled boat. The masula of the Coromandel coast was a large, frameless boat of planks sewn together with coir, flexible enough to survive the surf. Until harbours were built in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, masula crews carried all passengers and cargo between ships anchored in the roads and the beaches of Madras and Masulipatnam, and they formed a recognised occupational group whose services European travellers often described.

Figure 17.1. A kaṭṭumaram drawn up on the beach at Chennai: shaped logs lashed together with rope. Photo: vivek, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

On the Kerala and Tamil coasts plank-built boats called vaḷḷam and tōṇi were used with large shore-seines and boat-seines, nets hauled by teams of men. The Lakshadweep islanders, especially on Minicoy, fished for tuna with pole and line, using live bait, from rowing and sailing boats. In Kutch and Saurashtra the sailing koṭiyā and similar vessels carried cargo to the Gulf and East Africa, while smaller craft fished inshore (McGrail et al. 2003).

Fishing was organised by community and by family. Crews were often kin, and the catch was divided by shares between boat owners, net owners and crew according to local custom. Women’s work was essential, if less visible: on most coasts women did not go to sea, but they mended and made nets, dried and salted fish, processed prawns and sold the catch, often travelling long distances to inland markets (Ram 1991). Merchants and moneylenders who advanced money for boats and nets in return for the right to buy the catch were a constant presence.

docs.title: 17.5 Fish as a Commodity
docs.text:
Fresh fish spoils within hours in a tropical climate, and before ice and refrigeration only a small part of the catch could be eaten fresh, on the coast itself or in towns close to it. The rest had to be preserved. Fish curing turned a perishable catch into a commodity that could be stored, carried inland and shipped overseas, and it linked fishing villages to markets far from the sea.

Methods. The simplest and commonest method was drying in the sun. Small fish such as anchovies and sardines were spread on the sand or on mats; larger fish were split, gutted and salted before drying. Fish could also be salted in pits or vats, packed in layers of salt, or dried on racks. On the Konkan coast the Kolis dried the bombil (Harpadon nehereus, the “Bombay duck” of Anglo-Indian cookery) on bamboo frames along the shore. On the Bengal coast and in the estuaries of the delta, dried fish (Bengali śuṭki) was made in large seasonal camps. Fermented fish and fish pastes were made around the Bay of Bengal, above all in Burma and the north-east of the subcontinent. In years of great sardine landings on the Malabar coast, much of the catch was boiled for oil or dried and sold as manure.

Markets. Dried and salted fish was cheap protein for people who could rarely afford meat or fresh fish. It was carried inland by pack animals, carts and boats, and later by rail, to the markets of the interior: from the Malabar and Kanara coasts to the plateau of Mysore, from the Coromandel coast to the Tamil interior, and from the Bengal coast up the rivers. Dried fish was sold at the weekly markets of the countryside alongside salt, which was traded inland along the same routes. Overseas, Sri Lanka was a major market for dried and salted fish from the south Indian coast, as it was for south Indian rice. In the Bay of Bengal the trade in dried and fermented fish connected the coasts of Bengal, Arakan and Burma. The curing and trade of fish were often in the hands of people other than the fishers: merchants who advanced money against the catch, curers who bought the fish on the beach, and traders who carried the dried product inland.

Salt and curing under British rule. Curing needed salt, and the British salt tax (Section 17.10) made salt dear. Because curers could not afford to salt their fish properly, much of the fish sent inland was poorly cured. From the late nineteenth century the Madras government opened fish-curing yards on the Malabar and Kanara coasts and elsewhere, enclosed sites where licensed curers could buy salt at a reduced price under official supervision, so that the duty would not be evaded. In the early twentieth century the Madras Fisheries Department, set up under Sir Frederick Nicholson, tried to improve curing methods and promoted the fish-oil industry. These measures were the beginning of state involvement in the fisheries that would grow greatly after independence (Section 17.13).

docs.title: 17.5.1 Women in Processing and Selling
docs.text:
The division of labour on most Indian coasts kept men at sea and women on land, and the processing and sale of fish were largely women’s work (Section 17.4). Women met the boats on the beach, bought or received fish, and carried it in baskets on their heads to nearby villages and markets, or to the bus and railway for longer journeys. They dried and salted fish, sold it in local markets, and handled much of the household’s cash and credit. The Koli women of Mumbai, who dominate the city’s retail fish trade, are one well-known example; women fish sellers in the markets of Goa and Kerala are another.

Kalpana Ram’s study of the Catholic Mukkuvar of Kanyakumari is the fullest account of this work. Mukkuvar women were kept from the boats and the sea by custom and belief, and were excluded from authority in the church and community. Yet they carried much of the economic weight of the household: they sold fish, managed the household’s borrowing and lending, and held it together through the months of poor catches. Ram also traces how the capitalist transformation of the fishery changed women’s position, in many respects for the worse (Ram 1991). Her account is a warning against seeing women’s market role as a sign of independence: they handled money, but on terms set by others.

The export trade in frozen prawns from the 1960s created new kinds of women’s work. The peeling and grading of prawns in sheds and processing plants was done mainly by women, many of them young migrants working on contract far from home, in conditions that fishworkers’ organisations have campaigned against. Women vendors were also among those most affected when mechanised boats and merchants with lorries and ice reorganised the marketing of fish.

docs.title: 17.6 The Islands: Lakshadweep, the Maldives and Cowries
docs.text:
The coral islands off the west coast, the Lakshadweep group and, further south, the Maldives, formed a distinctive maritime world. Their people had little land and few resources except the coconut palm, the reef and the sea. They lived by exporting coconut products, dried fish and cowries, and they imported rice, cloth and other necessities from the mainland. The economy of Lakshadweep is described above (Section 17.2).
