Indrani Chatterjee has shown how much of the slavery that these laws touched was female and domestic, and how colonial courts, by treating household slaves as servants or dependants, left many of them in the same condition under another name (Chatterjee 1999). The end of legal slavery did not end unfree labour; it changed its forms, towards debt bondage and contract labour, both of which recur in the chapters that follow.

docs.title: 18.14 Conclusion
docs.text:
The economy of the five and a half centuries surveyed here was large, monetised and unequal. The Sultanate and the Mughal empire built revenue systems that drew a large share of the agricultural surplus to a ruling class, paid it out to soldiers, nobles and workshops, and in doing so pushed money and markets deep into the countryside. Indian manufactures, above all cotton cloth, supplied the Indian Ocean and, from the seventeenth century, Europe, West Africa and the Americas, and India absorbed a large part of the world’s silver in return. Indian merchants and bankers were numerous, wealthy and sophisticated, though they worked within states that taxed them and did not share power with them.

The Europeans who arrived after 1498 changed the conditions of maritime trade by introducing armed shipping and the licensing of navigation, but for two and a half centuries they remained one group of traders among many, dependent on Indian producers, merchants and rulers. The transformation came after 1757, when the English Company acquired the revenues of Bengal and with them the power to reorganise the economy for its own ends. That story is told in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Raychaudhuri and Habib (1982) is the standard survey of the period. For the Mughal agrarian system see Habib (1999b) and Moosvi (1987); for the empire as a whole, Richards (1993). Subrahmanyam (1990) covers southern India and the Portuguese impact, Richards (1975) Mughal Golconda, and Pearson (1987) and Subrahmanyam (1997) the Estado da Índia and Vasco da Gama, with Subrahmanyam (1993) for the Portuguese empire as a whole. For Indian merchants and the European companies see Das Gupta (1979), Arasaratnam (1986), Chaudhuri (1978) and Prakash (1998); for the textile trade, Riello and Roy (2009). Bayly (1983) is the classic statement of eighteenth-century regional dynamism; for Bengal see Marshall (1987), for the Marathas Gordon (1993), and for the Armenian networks Aslanian (2011). On the crisis of the empire compare Chandra (1959), Alam (1986) and the essays in Alam and Subrahmanyam (1998) and Marshall (2003); on slavery, Chatterjee and Eaton (2006), Eaton (2005), Vink (2003) and Allen (2015); on wages, Moosvi (1987), Parthasarathi (1998) and Broadberry and Gupta (2006).

docs.title: Chapter 19: The Colonial Economy and Maritime Decline, 1757–1947
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

In 1757 the English East India Company was one trading company among several; by the mid-nineteenth century it, and then the British Crown, ruled the subcontinent. This chapter follows the economic consequences: the Company’s use of Bengal’s revenue to finance its trade, the decline of India’s textile exports, the land revenue settlements, the commercialisation of agriculture, the opium trade with China, the railways, the famines, the growth of Indian-owned industry, the decline of Indian shipbuilding and shipping, and the migration of Indian labour and merchants across the Indian Ocean. Almost every one of these subjects is the object of a historiographical debate, between the nationalist critique of Dadabhai Naoroji and R. C. Dutt and its successors on one side, and revisionist economic historians such as Morris D. Morris and Tirthankar Roy on the other. The chapter sets out the evidence and the main positions, and uses only figures whose source can be given.

docs.title: 19.1 Approaching the Colonial Economy
docs.text:
The first systematic analysis of the economics of British rule was written by Indians. Dadabhai Naoroji’s papers on the poverty of India, from the 1870s, collected in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), and R. C. Dutt’s Economic History of India (1902–1904) argued that British rule had impoverished India through the “drain” of resources to Britain, the ruin of its manufactures and a heavy land tax (Naoroji 1901; Dutt 1902). Their arguments became the economic programme of the early Indian National Congress, whose development Bipan Chandra traced (Chandra 1966).

After independence, this nationalist view was elaborated by Marxist and dependency historians, notably Amiya Kumar Bagchi on deindustrialisation (Bagchi 1976). It was challenged by Morris D. Morris, who argued in 1963 that the evidence for nineteenth-century impoverishment was weak and that the period may have seen modest growth (Morris 1963); Morris’s essay provoked sharp replies from Bipan Chandra and others. Later surveys by B. R. Tomlinson and Tirthankar Roy have stressed the limits of colonial state power, regional variation, and the role of geography, technology and world markets alongside policy (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000, 2012). The second volume of the Cambridge Economic History of India gives contributions from several points of view (Kumar 1983). Polemical works such as Shashi Tharoor’s Inglorious Empire (Tharoor 2017) have brought the nationalist critique to a wide modern readership; they are a part of the public debate, but their figures should be checked against the scholarly sources before they are used.

Angus Maddison’s estimates, whose nature and limits are discussed in Section 18.5.6, carry India’s share of world output down from about 24 per cent in 1700 to 16 per cent in 1820 and about 4 per cent in 1950 (Maddison 2001). A falling share does not by itself show that India’s output fell, since the shares of every pre-industrial economy fell as western Europe and North America industrialised; China’s fell even more steeply after 1820. The telling evidence is income per head, which on Maddison’s own estimates was little higher in 1950 than in 1820, while income per head in Britain rose several times over. That long stagnation is the central fact that any account of the colonial economy must explain.

docs.title: 19.2.1 Plassey and the Dīwānī
docs.text: Conflict between the English Company and the nawāb of Bengal, Sirāj al-Dawla, over the fortification of Calcutta and the abuse of the Company’s duty-free passes (Chapter 18), led to the battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757. The Company’s victory owed much to the defection of the nawāb’s commander Mīr Jaʿfar and to the support of Bengal’s bankers, the Jagat Seths (Chapter 6). Mīr Jaʿfar was made nawāb and paid the Company and its officers very large sums as “presents” and compensation. After the defeat of Mīr Qāsim, the nawāb of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shāh ʿĀlam II at Buxar in 1764, the emperor granted the Company the dīwānī — the right to collect the revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in August 1765 (Kumar 1983; Prakash 1998).

docs.title: 19.2.2 The “Investment” and Private Trade
docs.text:
The dīwānī changed the economics of the Company’s trade. Before 1757 it had paid for Bengal cloth and silk largely with imported silver. After 1765 it could use the surplus of Bengal’s land revenue to buy the goods it exported, a purchase known in the Company’s books as the “investment”. The import of bullion into Bengal fell away, and part of the province’s revenue was in effect exported as goods for which no return flowed back (Prakash 1998; Dutt 1902). The Company’s servants also traded privately on a large scale. They used the Company’s passes to avoid customs, forced goods on local merchants, and, through Indian agents (gumāshtas), bound weavers by advances to deliver cloth only to them at prices they set (Chapter 8). The abuses were notorious in Britain itself and led Parliament to regulate the Company by the Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt’s India Act of 1784.

The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company’s monopoly of trade with India (though not with China), opening the Indian market to private British merchants and manufacturers; the Act of 1833 ended its commercial activities altogether; and after the rebellion of 1857 the Crown took over its government in 1858.

Historical Note: The Bengal famine of 1770 and two later famines

The famine of 1769–1770 in Bengal and Bihar, which followed the failure of the rains, was the first great famine in a territory under Company administration. Company officials, among them Warren Hastings, estimated that about a third of the inhabitants had perished; modern historians regard this as an impression rather than a count, and the true toll is unknown. The Company did not substantially reduce its revenue demand, and its servants were accused of profiting from the grain trade. The famine has rightly become a symbol of the human costs of early Company rule (Dutt 1902; Kumar 1983).

Two other great famines of the period struck regions mostly outside the Company’s rule. The Chalisa famine of 1783–1784 struck the Delhi region, the Punjab, Rajputana and the upper Doab, and the Doji Bara or “skull” famine of 1791–1792 struck mainly the Deccan, Hyderabad and western India. The regions affected were ruled, in the main, by the Mughal emperor, the Marathas, the Sikh chiefs, the Nizam and other Indian rulers, not by the Company; no reliable count of their dead exists.

docs.title: 19.3.1 What Is Agreed
docs.text:
Some facts are not in dispute. In the eighteenth century, cotton textiles were India’s chief export to Europe (Chapter 18). In the early nineteenth century, mechanised spinning and weaving made British cloth cheaper than Indian cloth in most grades, and India’s exports of cotton piece-goods collapsed. From the 1820s British cotton yarn and cloth flowed into India in rising quantities, and by the later nineteenth century India was one of the largest markets for Lancashire. Cities whose prosperity rested on export textiles, such as Dhaka, declined. India exported raw cotton, indigo, opium, jute and grain instead (Roy 2000; Tomlinson 1993; Riello and Roy 2009).

Policy contributed. R. C. Dutt cited the historian H. H. Wilson’s statement that, in the early nineteenth century, Indian cotton and silk goods could have undersold British goods in Britain and were kept out by duties of 70 to 80 per cent or by prohibition, while British goods entered India on low duties (Dutt 1902). Later, when the government of India imposed import duties on cotton goods for revenue in the 1890s, Lancashire’s pressure led to a countervailing excise on Indian mill-made cloth, fixed in 1896 at 3.5 per cent, equal to the import duty. The excise, which was abolished only in 1926, became a standing grievance of Indian nationalists (Chandra 1966).

docs.title: 19.3.2 What Is Disputed
docs.text:
The disagreement concerns the scale of the loss, its causes, and its effects on employment and incomes. Amiya Kumar Bagchi used Francis Buchanan-Hamilton’s surveys of 1809–1813 and the census of 1901 to estimate the proportion of the population of Gangetic Bihar dependent on secondary industry. He found that it fell from about 18.6 per cent to about 8.5 per cent, and he interpreted this as deindustrialisation caused by British competition and policy (Bagchi 1976). These figures refer to one region, Gangetic Bihar, and to the share of the population dependent on industry; they are not estimates for India as a whole.

Morris D. Morris and, later, Tirthankar Roy argued that the evidence for an all-India collapse of industrial employment is weak. Handloom weaving survived on a large scale into the twentieth century by specialising in goods machines did not make well and by using cheap mill yarn; and the decline of some crafts was offset by the growth of others and of modern industry. In their view, the main cause of the decline of hand manufactures was a change in technology and in world markets that would have affected India under any government (Morris 1963; Roy 2000). Indrajit Ray, studying Bengal between 1757 and 1857, argues that the Company’s political power, its monopolies and its commercial policies did more damage to Bengal’s cotton, silk, salt, sugar and shipbuilding industries than competition alone would have done (Ray 2011). Prasannan Parthasarathi places India’s loss of its textile markets in a global account in which British industrialisation was itself a response to Indian competition (Parthasarathi 2011). Revisionists also point to the growth of modern factory industry from the 1850s, which partly offset the decline of hand manufactures; its history is traced in Section 19.11.

docs.title: 19.4 The Drain of Wealth: A Historiographical Debate
19.4.1 The Nationalist Case
docs.text: Naoroji’s central argument was that India paid large sums every year to Britain for which it received no economic return. He identified as channels the “Home Charges” paid by the government of India in London (pensions, the costs of the India Office and of the army raised for India, interest on the public debt, and the purchase of stores); the remittances of savings and salaries by British officials and soldiers; and the profits of British firms, banks, shippers and insurers. India’s regular surplus of exports over imports was, he argued, the visible form of this transfer (Naoroji 1901). Dutt added a detailed account of land revenue, trade and famine policy (Dutt 1902). Bipan Chandra showed how the drain theory became the core of nationalist economic thought between 1880 and 1905 (Chandra 1966).

docs.title: 19.4.2 Counter-Arguments
docs.text:
Critics accept that India made large unrequited payments but dispute how they should be measured and what they meant. Part of the Home Charges paid interest on capital borrowed in London for railways and irrigation, or bought services and stores that India would have had to obtain somewhere; the question is therefore not whether payments were made but what India would have paid, and gained, under a different political order. Revisionist historians, notably Tirthankar Roy and B. R. Tomlinson, argue that the annual transfer was small in relation to national income, and that its effect on growth was smaller than that of low agricultural productivity and low public investment (Roy 2000, 2012; Tomlinson 1993); estimates of the transfer as a share of national income depend on which payments are counted and are themselves disputed. Defenders of the drain theory reply that payments for a government India had not chosen, for wars fought for imperial purposes, and for services in which Indians were not allowed to compete, cannot be treated as ordinary commercial exchanges. S. Ambirajan’s study of classical political economy and British policy shows how much the doctrines of the economists — free trade, Ricardian rent theory, non-intervention in markets — shaped decisions in India, often to India’s cost (Ambirajan 1978).

Scholarly Note: Utsa Patnaik’s estimate

Utsa Patnaik has argued that Britain appropriated India’s foreign exchange earnings from its export surplus with the rest of the world, paying Indian producers out of Indian taxes, and has estimated the resulting transfer for 1765–1938. Her calculation, which compounds the estimated annual transfers at an assumed rate of interest, produced a cumulative figure widely reported as about 45 trillion US dollars (Patnaik 2017). Three features of the calculation matter for its use. The result depends very heavily on the assumed rate of interest and the length of the compounding period; treating the whole export surplus as a transfer leaves aside the part of it that paid for capital and services, which is exactly what the revisionists dispute (above); and a compounded cumulative sum cannot be compared with annual measures of national income. The figure is therefore best treated as one contested estimate within the drain debate, not as an established fact.

docs.title: 19.4.3 Money and Exchange
docs.text: The monetary system added a further dimension. The Company’s uniform silver rupee of 1835 continued the Mughal standard (Chapter 5), and government paper currency was introduced under the Paper Currency Act of 1861. After 1873 the price of silver fell in terms of gold, and with it the sterling value of the rupee. Because the Home Charges were fixed in sterling, the rupee cost of meeting them rose, which strained the government’s budget. In 1893 the mints were closed to the free coinage of silver, and by 1898–1899 the rupee was fixed at 1 shilling 4 pence, under what became a gold exchange standard. Nationalists argued that the exchange rate was set to suit British creditors and exporters rather than Indian producers, a charge the government denied (Tomlinson 1993; Chandra 1966).

docs.title: 19.5 Land Revenue Settlements
docs.text:
Land revenue remained the largest source of public income. The Company inherited a Mughal vocabulary — zamīndār, jamaʿ, dīwānī — but the settlements it made were new: they defined private property rights in land, fixed who was liable for the revenue, and made land saleable for arrears. Table 19.1 summarises the three main systems (Kumar 1983; Roy 2000).

Table 19.1. The main British land revenue settlements Permanent Settlement Ryotwari Mahalwari Introduced 1793 (Cornwallis) 1790s (Read, Munro); general in Madras from 1820, in Bombay from the 1830s 1822 and 1833 in the North-Western Provinces Regions Bengal, Bihar, parts of Orissa; later Banaras Most of Madras and Bombay presidencies North-Western Provinces; later Punjab and parts of the Central Provinces Who paid Zamīndār, declared proprietor Individual holder (raiyat) Village or estate community, through headmen or co-sharers Revenue Fixed in perpetuity Revised at long intervals (often 30 years) Revised periodically

The Permanent Settlement.

Lord Cornwallis’s settlement of 1793 fixed the revenue of Bengal and Bihar for ever and recognised the zamīndārs as proprietors of their estates. The demand was set high in relation to the rental of the time, and estates in arrears were sold at auction under the so-called sunset law; in the first decades many old estates passed to new purchasers, often from Calcutta. The cultivators’ rights were left undefined. As rents and cultivation grew over the nineteenth century while the revenue stayed fixed, the burden shifted from the state to the tenants, and zamīndārs and layers of intermediate tenure-holders gained. Tenancy legislation, such as the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885, came late (Kumar 1983).

Ryotwari.

In Madras and Bombay, the revenue was settled directly with the cultivator, on the basis of surveys and assessments of the land’s productive capacity. Ricardian rent theory influenced the design of the assessments (Ambirajan 1978). The early assessments were heavy and rigid, collected in cash in bad years as well as good, and pushed cultivators into debt. The transfer of land to moneylenders led to the Deccan riots of 1875 and to legislation such as the Deccan Agriculturists’ Relief Act of 1879; in the Punjab, the Land Alienation Act of 1900 restricted sales of land to non-agricultural castes.

Mahalwari.

In the North-Western Provinces, the revenue was settled with village communities or co-sharing bodies, which were made jointly responsible for the payment of the whole.

The real burden of the land revenue fell during the later nineteenth century, as prices rose and assessments lagged behind (Roy 2000; Kumar 1983). But the settlements had created a land market and a class of rentiers and moneylenders that outlasted colonial rule, and they were a main target of land reform after independence.

docs.title: 19.6 The Commercialisation of Agriculture
docs.text:
From the early nineteenth century, a growing share of Indian agricultural output was grown for sale, much of it for export. Indigo was grown in Bengal and Bihar for European planters under coercive contracts, which provoked the indigo revolt of 1859–1860 and, in Champaran in 1917, Gandhi’s first campaign in India. The poppy was grown in Bihar and around Benares for the government’s opium monopoly, and in the princely states of Malwa, for export to China (Section 19.7). The American Civil War (1861–1865) caused a boom in Indian raw cotton and a speculative mania in Bombay that collapsed in 1865. Jute from eastern Bengal supplied the mills of Dundee and then of Calcutta; tea was grown in Assam on plantations worked by labourers recruited under penal contracts; and canal irrigation in the western Punjab from the 1880s created new wheat-growing colonies whose grain was exported (Kumar 1983; Roy 2000).

Historians disagree about how far this commercialisation benefited cultivators. Some see it as “forced”, driven by the cash demands of the revenue and of creditors, and exposing smallholders to world price movements and famine. Others see a response to new opportunities, which raised incomes where irrigation and transport made specialisation profitable, as in the canal colonies. Both effects occurred, in different regions and for different groups (Roy 2000; Tomlinson 1993).

docs.title: 19.7 Opium, Cotton and the China Trade
19.7.1 The Triangle
docs.text: The English Company’s most valuable trade in the later eighteenth century was not with India but with China, from which it bought tea for the British market. China wanted few European goods, and the tea had to be paid for largely in silver. The solution that emerged was to sell Indian goods in China. Raw cotton from Gujarat, shipped through Bombay, was the first of these exports, from the later eighteenth century; opium soon overtook it. The goods were carried by private British and Indian merchants in the “country trade” between Asian ports, licensed by the Company. At Canton they sold their cargoes for silver, which they paid into the Company’s treasury there in exchange for bills payable in London or Calcutta, and the Company used the silver to buy tea. The result was a triangle: Indian opium and cotton went to China, Chinese tea went to Britain, and British manufactures, together with the remittances of the Company and of private fortunes, connected Britain and India. The China trade thus became one of the channels through which the surplus of Bengal’s revenue, and the savings of Company servants, were transferred to Britain (Roy 2012; Trocki 1999; Kumar 1983).

docs.title: 19.7.2 Bengal and Malwa Opium
docs.text:
Opium had been grown in Bihar long before British rule, and Dutch and English merchants had traded it in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Chapter 18). In 1773, under Warren Hastings, the Company made the purchase of Bihar opium a monopoly, and from 1797 it controlled production directly through two agencies, for Bihar at Patna and for Benares. Cultivators had to be licensed, received cash advances, and were obliged to deliver their whole crop at a price fixed by the agency. The opium was processed in government factories (Figure 19.1), packed in chests and sold at auction in Calcutta to private merchants, who carried it to China. Because the Qing government prohibited the import of opium, the Company kept its own ships out of the trade, an arrangement that let it take the profit while disclaiming responsibility for the smuggling (Trocki 1999; Roy 2012). How far the monopoly price rewarded the peasants who grew the poppy has been questioned.

Figure 19.1. The stacking room of the government opium factory at Patna, with balls of opium on racks: lithograph after W. S. Sherwill, c. 1850. Image: After W. S. Sherwill (Wellcome Collection), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A second supply came from Malwa, in the princely states of central and western India, beyond the Company’s direct control. Indian merchants shipped Malwa opium to China through Karachi and the Portuguese port of Daman, in competition with the Bengal product. After attempts to buy up or suppress the Malwa crop failed, the Bombay government in the 1830s chose to tax it instead, allowing the opium to pass through Bombay on payment of a duty; after the annexation of Sind in 1843 the alternative route was closed and Bombay became the trade’s main outlet. Bengal opium thus earned revenue through monopoly sale, and Malwa opium through the pass duty (Trocki 1999). Together they made opium, for much of the nineteenth century, one of the government of India’s largest sources of revenue after the land tax, and the government’s budget was exposed to the swings of the China market (Tomlinson 1993; Kumar 1983).

docs.title: 19.7.3 Merchants of the China Trade
docs.text: The trade drew merchants of many communities. Among British firms, the agency house of Jardine, Matheson and Company, established at Canton in 1832 by William Jardine and James Matheson, became the largest; its partners worked closely with Parsi merchants of Bombay such as Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy. Parsi firms sent their own agents to Canton and later to Hong Kong. Baghdadi Jewish merchants, led by David Sassoon, who settled in Bombay in the early 1830s, entered the China trade in the following decades, and in the later nineteenth century the Sassoon firms were among the largest dealers in Malwa opium. Armenian merchants of Calcutta took part, as did other Hindu and Muslim merchants of Bombay; and Marwari merchants in Calcutta speculated heavily on the prices at the opium auctions (Timberg 1978; Ray 1995). Profits from cotton and opium financed shipping, urban property, philanthropy and, from the 1850s, cotton mills (Section 19.11); the later careers of these communities are followed in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 19.7.4 The Opium Wars and the End of the Trade
docs.text:
By the 1830s the opium trade had reversed the flow of silver: China now paid out silver to settle its trade with India. In 1839 the imperial commissioner Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed the foreign merchants’ opium at Canton. Britain went to war. The First Opium War (1839–1842), in which Indian sepoys, Indian-built ships and Indian supplies took part, ended with the Treaty of Nanking (1842), which ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five ports to British trade and imposed an indemnity. The Second Opium War (1856–1860) opened China further, and the import of opium was legalised in 1858. Bombay’s Parsi, Jewish and other merchants followed the British flag to Hong Kong and the treaty ports (Trocki 1999; Roy 2012).

In the later nineteenth century, Chinese domestic production of opium grew and Indian exports declined. In Britain an anti-opium movement attacked the trade on moral grounds; a Royal Commission on Opium (1893–1895) declined to recommend prohibition. Under an Anglo-Chinese agreement of 1907, Indian exports to China were to be reduced step by step as China reduced its own cultivation, and the export of Indian opium to China ended in 1913 (Trocki 1999). For more than a century, then, part of the public finance of British India rested on the sale of a narcotic to China, imposed by war on a government that had tried to forbid it. The episode belongs to the history of Indian commerce as much as to that of China, and Indian merchants were among its beneficiaries.

docs.title: 19.7.5 The Rise of Bombay
docs.text: The China trade transformed Bombay. In the mid-eighteenth century it was a fortified island port of secondary importance, overshadowed by Surat. Lakshmi Subramanian has shown how, in the second half of the century, the English at Bombay and the Gujarati vāṇiyā, Parsi and other merchants of Surat and Bombay formed a partnership of mutual interest: the merchants financed the Company’s needs and its wars on the west coast, and in return enjoyed its protection and a share in the growing trade in raw cotton to China. As Surat declined, capital, merchants and artisans moved to Bombay (Subramanian 1996). Opium reinforced this trajectory in the nineteenth century, and the cotton boom of the American Civil War (Section 19.6) gave the city a further burst of speculative wealth. The commercial capital accumulated in these trades, and the skills of the communities that handled it, laid the foundations of Bombay’s cotton-mill industry.

docs.title: 19.8 Railways
docs.text:
The first passenger railway in India opened between Bombay and Thane on 16 April 1853. The early lines were built by private British companies to which the government of India guaranteed a return of 5 per cent on their capital, with any shortfall met from Indian revenues; by the end of the century India had one of the largest railway networks in the world. The railways’ critics, from the nationalists onward, point to the cost of the guarantees, the purchase of rails, locomotives and expertise from Britain rather than in India, freight rates that favoured traffic to and from the ports, and the planning of lines for military and commercial rather than developmental ends (Chandra 1966; Tomlinson 1993).

Their defenders point to the fall in transport costs, the integration of grain markets, and the ability to move food to famine areas. A quantitative study by Dave Donaldson finds that the railways reduced trade costs and price differences between districts and raised real agricultural incomes (Donaldson 2018). The two views can be reconciled in part: the railways were a large and genuine improvement in transport, but they were built on terms that served British interests, and their benefits depended on what was carried on them and to whom the gains accrued. The effect on the overland and river trade they replaced is noted in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 19.9 Famines
docs.text:
Famine was not new to India (Chapter 7), but the colonial period saw a series of very destructive famines: in the North-Western Provinces in 1837–1838, in Orissa in 1866, the “great famine” of 1876–1878 in Madras, Bombay, Mysore and Hyderabad, and the famines of 1896–1897 and 1899–1900, which affected large parts of western, central and northern India. Mortality figures for these famines are estimates made by officials and later demographers, and they vary widely; but deaths were counted in millions.

Government policy in the 1870s was shaped by the doctrines of political economy. Officials were reluctant to interfere with the grain trade, feared that generous relief would demoralise the poor, and paid relief labourers low rations; grain continued to move by rail out of some distressed districts to where prices were higher (Ambirajan 1978). After the great famine, the Famine Commission of 1880 laid down principles of relief, and Famine Codes from 1883 set out procedures for declaring famine, opening relief works and suspending revenue. These measures, with railways and irrigation, are generally credited with reducing famine mortality after 1900, though their application in the late 1890s was still harsh (Roy 2000). Mike Davis has interpreted the famines of 1876–1878 and 1896–1902 as the product of El Niño droughts and of imperial policy together, in a deliberately polemical comparative study; his work is one interpretation among several (Davis 2001).

The Bengal famine of 1943 took place in wartime. The Famine Inquiry Commission of 1945 estimated about one and a half million deaths; Amartya Sen estimated about three million (Sen 1981). Sen argued that the supply of food in Bengal in 1943 was not much lower than in earlier non-famine years, and that the famine was caused by a collapse of the “entitlements” of rural labourers, artisans and fishermen, whose wages lagged far behind food prices in a war-time inflation driven by military spending and speculation. The loss of rice imports from Burma after its occupation by Japan, a “denial” policy that removed boats and rice from coastal districts, delay in declaring famine, and the War Cabinet’s refusal of several requests for larger food imports all contributed. Mark Tauger has argued that crop disease and the cyclone of October 1942 made the shortfall of the 1942 harvest much larger than Sen allowed, so that shortage and wartime policy acted together (Tauger 2003); the role of wartime policy is not in doubt.

docs.title: 19.10 Indigenous Banking under Colonial Rule
docs.text: Colonial rule changed the setting of Indian finance without destroying indigenous banking. The Company’s assumption of Bengal’s revenue removed the great bankers’ most profitable business; the presidency banks and the European exchange banks took over government and foreign business; and statute law replaced custom in commercial matters. Yet the sarrāfs, Marwaris, Multanis and Nattukottai Chettiars continued to finance internal trade and agriculture, linked to the European banks through the discounting of hundīs, and some Marwari families moved into industry in the twentieth century (Ray 1995; Timberg 1978; Jain 1929). These developments are described in Chapter 6 (Section 6.8).

docs.title: 19.11 Indian Enterprise and Industry, c. 1850–1947
docs.text: Modern factory industry began in India in the 1850s and grew slowly; on the eve of independence it still employed only a small part of the workforce and produced a modest share of national income. Its history nevertheless matters, because it shows where Indian capital and enterprise went under colonial rule, and because the industrial economy of independent India was built on it (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

docs.title: 19.11.1 Cotton: Bombay and Ahmedabad
docs.text: The cotton-mill industry was Indian from the start. Cowasjee Nanabhoy Davar, a Parsi merchant, founded one of the first Bombay mills in 1854, and others followed, financed largely by merchants who had made their money in the China trade (Section 19.7.5). The Bombay mills at first spun coarse yarn, both for India’s handloom weavers and for export to China and Japan. When Japanese mills captured the Chinese yarn market from the 1890s, Bombay turned increasingly to weaving cloth for the home market. Ahmedabad, where the first mill opened in 1861, developed differently: its mills were founded and run by local Gujarati Jain and Hindu merchant families, drew on local deposits, and concentrated on cloth for Indian consumers; between the wars the industry grew faster there than in Bombay (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000). Bombay’s mill workers came mostly from the Konkan and the Deccan and were recruited and supervised through jobbers, on whom they also depended for housing and credit; Rajnarayan Chandavarkar has shown how the mill economy was embedded in the neighbourhoods, kin networks and politics of the working-class districts (Chandavarkar 1994). Factory legislation from 1881 onward gradually limited hours and child labour.

docs.title: 19.11.2 Jute and Steel
docs.text:
Eastern India followed a different pattern. The jute mills that grew up along the Hugli from 1855 were owned and managed mainly by British, often Scottish, firms in Calcutta; they processed raw jute grown by peasants in eastern Bengal and competed with the mills of Dundee for the world market in sacking and hessian. The Calcutta firms also controlled much of the coal, tea and engineering industries of eastern India. Only after the First World War did Marwari firms, enriched by wartime trade and speculation, begin to build or buy jute mills of their own (Timberg 1978; Tomlinson 1993). The contrast between an Indian-owned industry in western India and a European-owned one in the east is one of the clearest features of the colonial industrial economy.

The Tata Iron and Steel Company, registered in 1907 to realise plans of Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata (1839–1904), was financed largely by Indian investors after London capital proved unwilling. Its works at Sakchi, renamed Jamshedpur, began producing steel in 1912, and wartime demand for rails and other materials secured its survival. The Tata group, which had begun in the China trade and cotton mills, also founded hydro-electric companies near Bombay (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

docs.title: 19.11.3 Managing Agencies and Business Communities
docs.text:
The characteristic form of large-scale enterprise was the managing agency. A firm of managing agents promoted a joint-stock company, held part of its shares, and managed it under a long-term contract in return for commission. One agency might control a group of companies in different industries, moving capital, managers and credit among them. The system economised on scarce managerial skill and gave investors confidence in known names, but it also allowed agents to profit from commissions and from dealing with their own companies at the shareholders’ expense. British agencies dominated Calcutta, while Indian ones prevailed in Bombay and Ahmedabad; the system was abolished in independent India in 1970 (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

Most Indian industrialists came from a few trading and banking communities: Parsis, Gujarati Hindus and Jains, Bhatias, Khojas and Bohras in western India, Marwaris in the north and east, Chettiars and others in the south. Thomas Timberg explains the Marwaris’ move from trade into industry by their access to capital and credit within the community, the information shared across a dispersed network of family firms, and their experience of speculative markets (Timberg 1978). Rajat Kanta Ray has described the “bazaar” from which these firms emerged, a sphere of Asian credit and trade linked to, but distinct from, the European banks and agency houses (Ray 1995). Ritu Birla has examined how colonial law — on contracts, companies, taxation, charitable trusts and gambling — redefined what counted as a legitimate market, treating the joint family firm and indigenous forms of speculation as matters of “culture” to be regulated (Birla 2009). Portraits of the main communities are given in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 19.11.4 Policy and Protection
docs.text:
Until the First World War the government of India followed free trade, with tariffs set for revenue and, in the case of cotton, balanced by the countervailing excise (Section 19.3.1). The war, which cut off imports and revealed the country’s dependence on foreign manufactures, changed official attitudes. An Indian Industrial Commission sat from 1916 to 1918, and after the Fiscal Commission of 1921–1922 recommended “discriminating protection” for industries that met certain conditions, a Tariff Board examined applications. Steel was protected from 1924, and other industries, including cotton textiles, paper, matches and sugar, received protection in the following years. Higher revenue tariffs during the depression of the 1930s also helped Indian industry, and by the 1940s Indian mills supplied most of the home market for cotton cloth (Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

Indian business organised itself politically. The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry was founded in 1927, and many leading industrialists supported the Congress while bargaining with the colonial government. In 1944 a group of them, including J. R. D. Tata and G. D. Birla, published a plan for economic development, often called the Bombay Plan, which proposed a large role for the state in investment (Chapter 20). How the growth of industry should be judged remains disputed: nationalists saw it as achieved against official indifference and imperial preference, revisionists as a response to markets that the colonial state did little either to help or to hinder until the 1920s (Chandra 1966; Tomlinson 1993; Roy 2000).

docs.title: 19.12.1 Shipbuilding: Bombay and Bengal
docs.text:
In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Indian yards built large ocean-going ships for Indian and European owners. The Bombay dockyard, directed from 1736 by the Parsi master builders of the Wadia family, built teak ships for the country trade, for the Company and, in the early nineteenth century, for the Royal Navy (Section 13.7.3). Teak was valued for its durability, and Bombay-built ships had a reputation for long service. In Bengal, private yards at Calcutta and on the Hugli, and at Chittagong, built many ships for the country trade between about 1780 and 1830 (Ray 2011; Subramanian 1996).

The decline of these yards had several causes. British shipbuilders and shipowners lobbied against India-built ships after the Company’s monopoly ended in 1813, and the regulation of the shipping trade with Britain, including the status of India-built ships and of Indian seamen, was shaped by those interests until the Navigation Acts were repealed in 1849. Indrajit Ray argues that this hostile policy, together with the Company’s withdrawal of support, explains much of the decline of Bengal shipbuilding from the 1830s (Ray 2011). From the mid-nineteenth century, the change to iron and then steel hulls and to steam propulsion transformed shipbuilding everywhere, and India, which lacked an iron and engineering industry, could not follow. The relative weight of policy and technology remains debated; no single law or policy explains the decline. The construction of the ships themselves is described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 19.12.2 Shipping, Steam and Seamen
docs.text:
In the eighteenth century, Indian merchants owned much of the shipping in the Asian “country trade”, at Surat, Bombay, Calcutta and the Coromandel ports, often in partnership with private European traders (Subramanian 1996; Das Gupta 1979). In the early nineteenth century, Bombay’s Parsi, Gujarati and other merchants, such as Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy (1783–1859), took a large part in the export of raw cotton and opium to China, often in their own ships (Section 19.7), and some of the capital they accumulated later went into Bombay’s cotton mills (Roy 2012; Tomlinson 1993). In the later nineteenth century, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 and the spread of steamships gave the advantage to large British lines with access to capital and to government mail contracts, among them P&O and the British India Steam Navigation Company, founded in Calcutta in 1856 (under that name from 1862). By the early twentieth century they dominated India’s overseas and coastal shipping, and Indian attempts to compete met rate wars and the lines’ agreements to share traffic (Tomlinson 1993).

Indian seamen did not disappear from the sea. Large numbers of Indian sailors, known as lascars, worked on British merchant ships, on separate articles of agreement and at lower wages than European crews. Sailing craft from Gujarat, Kutch and the Malabar coast continued to carry the coastal trade and the trade to the Persian Gulf and East Africa into the twentieth century. These communities are discussed in Chapter 17.

docs.title: 19.12.3 The Kālā Pānī Question
docs.text:
The idea that Hindus lose caste by crossing the sea — the kālā pānī (“black water”) taboo — had textual roots long before colonial rule. Restrictions on sea travel go back to the dharmaśāstra: the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra counts going to sea among the acts that cause loss of caste, and the Manusmṛti excludes a man who goes to sea from ancestral offerings (Section 11.4) (Olivelle 1999, 2004). Medieval digests list among the practices forbidden in the Kali age the re-admission of a twice-born man who has made a sea voyage, even after expiation (Kane 1930).

The prohibition was always variably observed. It applied in its strict form mainly to Brahmins and to the upper castes who accepted their authority; merchants of many communities, Hindu and Jain, Gujarati, Kutchi and Tamil, traded overseas for centuries (Chapters 12 and 16), and Muslim, Christian and Parsi seafarers were not bound by it at all. In the colonial period the taboo was both challenged and sharpened. Bengal army sepoys resisted service overseas, and the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856, which required recruits to accept it, was one of the grievances behind the rebellion of 1857; Gandhi was declared an outcaste by his caste in 1888 for going to study in England; and hundreds of thousands of indentured labourers crossed the ocean to Mauritius, the Caribbean, Natal and Fiji between 1834 and the end of indenture (Section 19.13). The taboo was real, of ancient textual origin and unevenly enforced; it was neither a colonial construction nor a reason for the decline of Indian shipping, which had economic and political causes.

docs.title: 19.13 Labour and Diaspora across the Indian Ocean
docs.text: While Indian shipping lost ground, Indians crossed the sea in greater numbers than ever before. Between the 1830s and the Second World War millions of labourers, traders, clerks and professionals left India, most of them by steamship and most of them for destinations within the Indian Ocean and the wider British empire. Three streams can be distinguished: indentured labour for the plantation colonies; the far larger, circulating migration of labourers to Ceylon, Burma and Malaya; and the movement of merchants and financiers, who travelled at their own expense (Tinker 1974; Amrith 2013; Markovits 2000). Sugata Bose has argued that these movements made the Indian Ocean of the imperial age an arena of its own, with ties that ran across and beneath the empires that ruled it (Bose 2006).

docs.title: 19.13.1 Indenture
docs.text:
The abolition of slavery in the British empire, which took effect in 1834, left the sugar planters of the colonies in search of labour. Indian labourers under contract were shipped to Mauritius from 1834, to British Guiana from 1838 and to Trinidad and Jamaica from 1845; later destinations included Natal (from 1860) and Fiji (from 1879), as well as the French colonies and Dutch Suriname. Recruiters working from depots at Calcutta and Madras drew migrants mainly from Bihar and the eastern districts of the North-Western Provinces, and from the Tamil and Telugu country. A labourer signed an agreement — remembered in Fiji and elsewhere as girmiṭ — to work for a fixed term, usually five years, for a set wage, with a return passage due after a longer period of residence. Breach of contract and absence from work were criminal offences. Deception in recruitment, high mortality on the early voyages and on some estates, the small proportion of women, and the planters’ control over workers’ lives led Hugh Tinker to call the system “a new system of slavery” (Tinker 1974). Other historians have stressed that many migrants chose to go, that some re-indentured or settled by choice, and that a minority prospered; neither view denies the coercion built into the contracts.

Well over a million Indians emigrated under indenture. The system became a nationalist cause. Gandhi’s campaigns in South Africa, Gopal Krishna Gokhale’s resolutions in the Imperial Legislative Council, and the reports of C. F. Andrews on Fiji turned opinion against it. Emigration to Natal was stopped in 1911, recruitment under indenture ended in 1917, and the system was formally abolished in 1920. The descendants of indentured migrants form large parts of the populations of Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana and Suriname, and a substantial community in South Africa (Tinker 1974).

docs.title: 19.13.2 Kaṅkāṇi and Maistry: Ceylon, Burma and Malaya
docs.text: Across the Bay of Bengal migration took a different form. The coffee and then tea estates of Ceylon, and later the rubber estates of Malaya, drew Tamil labourers from the southern districts of the Madras Presidency through the kaṅkāṇi system: a foreman, often from the labourers’ own village or caste, recruited a gang, advanced money for the journey, and supervised and paid them on the estate. Burma, annexed in stages between 1826 and 1886, drew Tamil and Telugu labourers to the docks and rice mills of Rangoon and to the harvest, recruited and managed by labour contractors called maistrys. This migration was overwhelmingly male and largely temporary: men went for a season or a few years and returned, many of them repeatedly. It was not indenture, but debt to the recruiter and penal labour laws limited the migrants’ freedom. Sunil Amrith has reconstructed the scale of this traffic, which made the Bay of Bengal one of the great migration corridors of the age, and its human and environmental consequences (Amrith 2013). In Burma, competition for work and land and the role of Indian moneylenders bred resentment, which broke out in anti-Indian riots in Rangoon in the 1930s; the Japanese invasion of 1942 drove hundreds of thousands of Indians to flee overland to India, with great loss of life.

docs.title: 19.13.3 Merchant Networks
docs.text:
Merchants moved along the same routes. Gujarati and Kutchi traders, Hindu and Muslim, had been established in the ports of East Africa long before British rule; in the nineteenth century they became the principal financiers and wholesalers of Zanzibar under the Omani sultans, whose world of credit and debt Fahad Bishara has reconstructed (Bishara 2017), and after the building of the Uganda Railway, on which indentured Punjabi labourers worked, Indian shopkeepers spread into the interior of East Africa (Alpers 2014; Pearson 2003). In South Africa, Gujarati Muslim merchants followed the indentured labourers to Natal; it was as legal adviser to one such firm, Dada Abdulla and Company, that Gandhi went there in 1893. In the Persian Gulf, Hindu and Muslim merchants from Kutch, Sind and Bombay were established in Muscat and the pearling ports, Bombay was the chief market for Gulf pearls, and the Indian rupee circulated as everyday currency. In Burma, Malaya and Ceylon the Nattukottai Chettiars provided much of the credit for agriculture and trade (Chapter 6, Section 6.6.4).

Claude Markovits’s study of the merchants of Sind shows how such networks worked. Shikarpuri bankers, heirs to the older Multani diaspora (Chapter 10), financed trade and lent money across Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia through hundīs and family firms. From the later nineteenth century the “Sindworkies” of Hyderabad (Sind), who began by selling the handicrafts of Sind, built a worldwide network of shops selling silks and curios in the ports of the empire and beyond, from Egypt and the Mediterranean to Japan and Panama. In both cases firms were based in Sind, where the families stayed, and men circulated abroad for a period of years before returning; credit, information and trust moved within the community (Markovits 2000). Markovits stresses that these networks used the opportunities created by empire but were not simply its creatures, and that they often extended beyond British territory.

These Indian communities overseas were a major part of the Indian Ocean world of the colonial era, alongside Chinese, Arab, Hadrami and European traders and labourers. Their position depended, however, on imperial order, and many of them proved vulnerable when that order ended: Indians left Burma in large numbers after 1942 and again in the 1960s, and the Asian population of Uganda was expelled in 1972. The coastal sailors who continued to work this ocean are discussed in Chapter 17.

docs.title: 19.14 Swadeshi and Economic Nationalism
docs.text:
The drain theory and the critique of free trade gave Indian nationalism an economic programme. Mahadev Govind Ranade argued for state support of Indian industry, as other late-developing countries had protected their infant industries (Chapter 20), and Naoroji, Dutt and Gopal Krishna Gokhale pressed for lower military spending, lower land revenue and the employment of Indians in the public services (Chandra 1966).

The partition of Bengal in 1905 turned these ideas into a mass movement. A meeting at Calcutta in August 1905 resolved to boycott British goods, and the Swadeshi movement promoted Indian-made cloth, salt, sugar and other goods. It gave new support to Indian enterprises such as Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, which the chemist Prafulla Chandra Ray had founded a few years earlier, and to new banks such as the Bank of India (1906), the Indian Bank (1907) and the Central Bank of India (1911), which joined the older Punjab National Bank (1894). The Tata Iron and Steel Company (1907) belongs to the same moment (Section 19.11.2).

The sea was part of the movement. In 1906 V. O. Chidambaram Pillai founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin to run steamers to Colombo in competition with the British India Steam Navigation Company. The company bought two steamers, the Gallia and the Lawoe, but faced a rate war and official hostility; Chidambaram Pillai was arrested in 1908 and convicted of sedition, and the company was wound up a few years later. In 1919 the Scindia Steam Navigation Company, founded by Walchand Hirachand and associates, began service when its steamer Loyalty sailed from Bombay to London on 5 April, the day now marked in India as National Maritime Day. Scindia became the largest Indian shipping company, but until independence Indian lines carried only a small part of India’s trade.

From the 1920s, Gandhi made hand-spinning and khādī the symbols of a different kind of economic nationalism, one that valued village self-sufficiency over factory industry. The tension between this vision and the industrial programme of others in the Congress carried over into the planning debates of independent India (Chapters 20 and 21).

docs.title: 19.15 Assessment
docs.text:
How should the economic record of colonial rule be judged? Several conclusions command wide agreement among historians of different schools. Income per head grew little, if at all, between the early nineteenth century and 1947, and agricultural output per head stagnated in the last decades of colonial rule. The colonial state invested little in education, health and agricultural improvement; its fiscal priorities were defence, administration and the servicing of its sterling obligations. India’s handicraft exports collapsed and its modern industry grew only slowly. Indian shipping and shipbuilding were marginalised by a combination of British commercial power, policy and technological change. Famines were frequent and severe until the early twentieth century, and the last great famine, in 1943, was the product of war and of political choices.

The disagreements are about causes and counterfactuals. The nationalist tradition, from Naoroji and Dutt to Bagchi and Patnaik, attributes India’s poverty mainly to colonial extraction and policy. Revisionists such as Morris and Roy stress the constraints of geography, climate, low productivity and world markets, and point to areas of growth: railways, irrigation in the Punjab, commercial agriculture, modern industry and the integration of markets. Each side has strong evidence for parts of its case, and much depends on what alternative is imagined. Neither the picture of a rich economy destroyed at a stroke nor that of an economic blessing survives a close look at the evidence.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Kumar (1983) remains the most comprehensive survey, and Rothermund (1993) a concise one. Roy (2000) and Tomlinson (1993) give revisionist overviews, and Roy (2012) places India in the world economy. For the nationalist case see Naoroji (1901), Dutt (1902) and Chandra (1966). On deindustrialisation compare Bagchi (1976), Morris (1963) and Ray (2011); on famine, Sen (1981) and Ambirajan (1978). On Bombay and the China trade see Subramanian (1996) and Trocki (1999); on Indian business and industry Timberg (1978) and Birla (2009); on migration and merchant networks Tinker (1974), Amrith (2013), Markovits (2000) and Bose (2006).

docs.title: Chapter 20: Economic Thought and Planning in Modern India, c. 1870–1956
docs.text:
Chapter Overview

Chapter 2 began this volume with the Arthaśāstra and the early Indian tradition of thinking about wealth, carried on in the Tirukkuṟaḷ and in the Indo-Persian writing on revenue (Section 2.9). This chapter follows the modern sequel: the economic thought that Indians developed between the 1870s and the first Five-Year Plans in response to colonial rule and to the economics of Europe. It looks at the critique of classical political economy by Ranade and his contemporaries, the founding of an Indian economics profession, the attempts to measure India’s national income, the long controversy over the rupee and the exchange rate, the economic writings of B. R. Ambedkar, the agrarian question, the development programmes of the princely states, the planning schemes of the 1930s and 1940s, socialist thought, and the strategy of the Second Five-Year Plan associated with P. C. Mahalanobis. The drain theory and the debates on deindustrialisation, which belong to the same intellectual history, are set out in Chapter 19; Gandhian economics and the cooperative movement are discussed in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 20.1 From Political Economy to Indian Economics
docs.text:
Modern economics reached India as part of the education of the colonial elite. The universities founded at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857 taught political economy from British textbooks, and the doctrines of Adam Smith, Ricardo and John Stuart Mill — free trade, the benefits of the division of labour, Ricardian rent, the self-correcting market — shaped the policies of the government of India (Chapter 19, Section 19.4.2) (Ambirajan 1978). The first generation of Indian economic writers were therefore critics from within: they had learned the classical doctrines, and they asked whether those doctrines fitted a poor, agrarian, colonial country.

Their answers formed what Bipan Chandra called the economic ideology of the early national movement (Chandra 1966). Its central claims were that India was poor and growing poorer; that the causes lay in the drain of resources to Britain, the ruin of handicrafts and a heavy and inflexible land revenue; and that the remedy lay in industrialisation promoted by the state, protection for Indian industry, lower military spending and a greater share for Indians in the services. Ajit Dasgupta’s history of Indian economic thought argues that this body of writing was more than a nationalist polemic: its authors developed recognisable positions on the theory of value, on the role of the state and on the measurement of poverty, and some of their questions anticipated those of later development economics (Dasgupta 1993). Manu Goswami has stressed a different point: in arguing about the drain and the national income, these writers helped to define “the Indian economy” as a single bounded territory with its own interests, distinct from the empire of which it was part (Goswami 2004).

docs.title: 20.2 Ranade and the Critique of Classical Economics
docs.text:
Mahadev Govind Ranade (1842–1901), a judge of the Bombay High Court and a social reformer, gave the most systematic statement of the critique. In a lecture on “Indian Political Economy” delivered at the Deccan College, Poona, in 1892, and reprinted in his Essays on Indian Economics (1898), he argued that the conclusions of English classical economics rested on assumptions — the dominance of self-interest, free competition, the mobility of labour and capital, a society organised by contract — that did not hold in India, where status, custom and caste still governed much economic life (Ranade 1898). A science built on those assumptions could not simply be applied to Indian conditions. Ranade drew on the German historical school and on the national economics of Friedrich List, which held that a late-developing country might need to protect its infant industries and that the state had a positive part to play in economic development. He pointed to the examples of the United States, Germany and Japan, which had industrialised behind tariff walls, and he urged the government of India to encourage industry, to make credit available to cultivators, and to treat the land revenue as a tax rather than a rent.

Ranade’s ideas were developed by a circle of writers in western India. Ganesh Vyankatesh Joshi wrote detailed critiques of the land revenue settlements of the Bombay Presidency and of the government’s finances, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale (1866–1915), as a member of the Imperial Legislative Council from 1902, used the annual budget debates to attack the government’s surpluses, the salt tax and the level of military expenditure, and to press for spending on education and for Indian employment in the higher services (Chandra 1966). The arguments of Dadabhai Naoroji and R. C. Dutt on the drain and on the economic history of British India, which belong to the same body of thought, are set out in Chapter 19.

These writers were not opponents of markets as such. Most of them accepted private property and commerce and admired the industrial economies of the West; what they rejected was the doctrine that the state should leave the economy alone in a country where, as they saw it, the state was foreign and the market was weighted against Indian producers. Their programme of state-assisted industrialisation became the main line of Indian economic thought until independence and beyond.

docs.title: 20.3 The Economics Profession and Its Questions
20.3.1 Universities, Journals and Institutes
docs.text: In the early twentieth century economics became an academic discipline in India. Chairs and departments were created in the universities, and in 1916 the Indian Journal of Economics began publication at Allahabad; the Indian Economic Association was founded in the following year. The Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics was founded at Poona in 1930, with D. R. Gadgil (1901–1971) as its director; the Indian Statistical Institute was founded at Calcutta by Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis (1893–1972) in 1931, and its journal Sankhyā began in 1933. The Delhi School of Economics followed in 1949, founded by V. K. R. V. Rao. These institutions trained the economists who staffed the planning agencies after independence.

docs.title: 20.3.2 The Village and the Region
docs.text:
Much of the early work was empirical and rural. Harold Mann, an agricultural chemist who directed agricultural research in the Bombay Presidency, published in 1917 a detailed survey of a single Deccan village, recording its land, crops, debts and incomes household by household (Mann 1917); it was the first of a series of village surveys that became a tradition of Indian economics. Radhakamal Mukerjee (1889–1968), later a professor at Lucknow, argued in The Foundations of Indian Economics (1916) that Indian economic life had to be understood through its own institutions — the village community, the caste, the joint family and the handicraft workshop — and that development should build on them rather than sweep them away (Mukerjee 1916). His approach, which combined economics, sociology and what would later be called ecology, ran counter both to the classical tradition and to the planners who followed.

Gadgil’s The Industrial Evolution of India in Recent Times (1924) was one of the first systematic economic histories of India under British rule written by a professional Indian economist. It described the decline of the old urban handicrafts, the survival of village industries, the growth of factory industry and the changes in agriculture and transport, with a balance and attention to evidence that made it a standard text for decades (Gadgil 1924). Its measured judgements contrast with the sharper claims on both sides of the later debate on deindustrialisation (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 20.4 Measuring the National Income
docs.text:
How poor was India, and was it becoming poorer? The question could be answered only by estimating the national income, and Indian economists made the first attempts. Dadabhai Naoroji, in the papers collected in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, estimated the income of British India in 1867–68 at about 20 rupees a head and argued that this was insufficient even for the bare necessities of life (Naoroji 1901). Officials replied with estimates of their own, generally somewhat higher, and the argument over the figures became a recurring feature of political debate. All these early estimates rested on rough assumptions about yields, prices and population, and their differences reflected method as much as reality.

The first estimate made on a systematic basis by modern methods was V. K. R. V. Rao’s study of the national income of British India for 1931–32, published in 1940, which built up the total by sectors from the best available statistics of output and income and discussed the margins of error at each step (Rao 1940). After independence a National Income Committee, chaired by Mahalanobis with Gadgil and Rao as members, was appointed in 1949 to establish official estimates; its reports laid the foundations of the national accounts of India. Modern reconstructions of the whole twentieth century, notably by S. Sivasubramonian, have used these and other sources to produce consistent series (Sivasubramonian 2000). They show that income per head grew little in the last half-century of colonial rule, a finding that underlies the assessment in Chapter 19.

The statistical tradition that Mahalanobis founded had wider consequences. The Indian Statistical Institute developed the methods of large-scale sample surveys, and in 1950 the government set up the National Sample Survey to collect data on consumption, employment and production across the country. India thus acquired, soon after independence, one of the most extensive systems of economic statistics among the poorer countries of the world. Its history is outlined in Volume 11, Gaṇita.

docs.title: 20.5.1 Keynes and the Gold Exchange Standard
docs.text: The fall in the gold price of silver after 1873, the closing of the mints to silver in 1893 and the fixing of the rupee at 1 shilling 4 pence by 1898–99 (Chapter 19, Section 19.4.3) created a currency system that had no exact parallel elsewhere. The rupee remained a silver coin, but its value was held to a fixed rate in sterling by the government’s management of reserves in London and of the supply of rupees in India. John Maynard Keynes, who had worked in the India Office, made this system the subject of his first book, Indian Currency and Finance (1913). He argued that India had arrived, without design, at a “gold exchange standard” — a currency convertible not into gold coin but into claims on a gold currency abroad — and that this was an economical and modern arrangement which other countries might adopt (Keynes 1913). Keynes served in the same year on the Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency, which broadly endorsed the system. Anand Chandavarkar’s study of Keynes’s long engagement with Indian questions shows how much his early monetary thinking owed to the Indian case (Chandavarkar 1989).

docs.title: 20.5.2 The Ratio Controversy
docs.text:
The First World War upset the arrangement. The price of silver rose above the value at which rupees could be coined, and in 1919 a committee recommended a new rate of 2 shillings in gold; the attempt to hold it collapsed in 1920. In 1925–26 the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, chaired by Edward Hilton Young, recommended that the rupee be stabilised at 1 shilling 6 pence, on a gold bullion standard, and that a central bank be created to manage the currency and credit. One of its Indian members, the Bombay merchant Sir Purshotamdas Thakurdas, dissented, arguing for the older rate of 1 shilling 4 pence. The Currency Act of 1927 adopted 1 shilling 6 pence.

The choice of rate became a nationalist grievance. Indian business and nationalist opinion held that the higher rate made imports cheaper and exports dearer, injured Indian industry and agriculture, and lightened the burden of the government’s sterling payments at the expense of Indian producers; the government and its supporters replied that it held down prices and that the rate had already been established in the market. In the depression of the 1930s, when Britain left the gold standard in 1931 and the rupee was tied to sterling, the outflow of gold from India — “distress gold” sold by hard-pressed cultivators and others — helped Britain to meet its obligations, and was criticised in India as a further drain. G. Balachandran’s study places these controversies in the setting of Britain’s own monetary difficulties between the wars (Balachandran 1996). The Reserve Bank of India, established under an Act of 1934, began operations on 1 April 1935 as a shareholders’ bank; it was nationalised on 1 January 1949.

During the Second World War the position was reversed. The government of India spent heavily on behalf of Britain and was paid in sterling credited in London, and India, which had been a debtor, ended the war as a large creditor of Britain. The use of these “sterling balances” after independence was one of the first questions of Indian economic policy.

docs.title: 20.6 Ambedkar as Economist
docs.text:
B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956) is remembered above all as the leader of the Dalit movement and the chief architect of the Constitution, and his life and social thought are treated in Volume 24, Samanvaya. But his training was in economics, at Columbia University and the London School of Economics, and much of his early published work was economic.

In “Small Holdings in India and Their Remedies” (1918) he argued that the fragmentation of holdings was not the cause of agricultural poverty but a symptom of the pressure of surplus labour on the land, and that the remedy lay in industrialisation, which would draw labour off the land and allow holdings to grow. The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India (1925), based on his Columbia dissertation, analysed the division of revenues between the central and provincial governments and criticised the centralised, revenue-driven character of colonial finance (Ambedkar 1925). The Problem of the Rupee (1923), his London thesis, entered the currency debate against Keynes. Ambedkar argued that the gold exchange standard left the issue of currency to the discretion of the government and had permitted a rise in prices that hurt the poor; he preferred a gold standard with a gold currency, under which the issue of money would be limited by rule rather than by official judgement (Ambedkar 1923). His position was a minority one, and the standard he advocated was soon to be abandoned everywhere, but the book is an informed contribution to an international argument about rules and discretion in monetary policy.

Ambedkar’s later economic writing was bound up with his politics. He argued that the village economy, far from being a model, was the foundation of caste and of the dependence of untouchable labourers on landholders (Chapter 21), and in his memorandum States and Minorities (1947), submitted to the Constituent Assembly, he proposed that key industries and agricultural land be owned by the state and that the state socialism this implied be written into the Constitution. The Assembly did not adopt the proposal, but it shows an economist for whom economic organisation and social equality were inseparable.

docs.title: 20.7 The Agrarian Question: Revenue, Debt and Land
docs.text:
Most Indians lived by agriculture, and the economists’ most persistent questions concerned the land. The first was the land revenue. In his open letters to the Viceroy, Lord Curzon, published in 1900, R. C. Dutt argued that the frequent revision and heavy level of the assessments in the temporarily settled provinces left cultivators without reserves, and that this explained the severity of the famines of the 1890s; he urged that the revenue be fixed for long periods or permanently. Curzon’s government replied in 1902 with a resolution on land revenue policy that denied the connection, pointed to the failure of the rains and to the cultivators’ indebtedness, and defended the existing settlements. The exchange is an early instance of a pattern that recurred throughout the period: Indian economists explained poverty by policy, officials by nature and by the habits of the people (Chandra 1966; Ambirajan 1978).

The second question was debt. The riots of 1875 in the Deccan, directed against moneylenders who had acquired cultivators’ land through the courts (Chapter 19, Section 19.5), made rural indebtedness a central concern of policy, and a series of laws tried to protect cultivators by restricting the transfer of land and the enforcement of debts. The most influential study came from an official, Malcolm Darling, whose The Punjab Peasant in Prosperity and Debt (1925) argued that debt in the Punjab had grown not with poverty but with prosperity: rising land values had made the peasant creditworthy, and moneylenders lent freely against the security of land. The Royal Commission on Agriculture of 1926–28 and the provincial banking enquiries of 1929–31 (Chapter 6) gathered a mass of evidence on rural credit, and in the depression of the 1930s several provinces created debt conciliation boards to scale down debts that falling prices had made unpayable.

After independence the question became one of reform. The Congress Agrarian Reforms Committee, chaired by J. C. Kumarappa, recommended in 1949 the abolition of intermediaries between the state and the cultivator, security for tenants and limits on the size of holdings. The abolition of zamīndārī followed in the early 1950s in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and other states; when the courts questioned the compensation provisions, the First Amendment to the Constitution (1951) placed these laws beyond challenge. The All-India Rural Credit Survey, whose report appeared in 1954, found that cooperatives and the government supplied only a small fraction of the credit that cultivators used and that the moneylender remained dominant. It recommended a state partnership in cooperative credit and the conversion of the Imperial Bank of India into a state-owned bank with a mandate to extend banking into the countryside; the State Bank of India was created in 1955. Tenancy reform and ceilings on holdings proved much harder to enforce, and the debate over cooperative farming, which divided the Congress at the end of the decade, showed how far the planners’ agrarian programme lagged behind their industrial one (Hanson 1966; Chakravarty 1987).

docs.title: 20.8 Development in the Princely States
docs.text:
Some of the earliest Indian-directed programmes of economic development were carried out not in British India but in the princely states, whose rulers and ministers had more freedom to spend on development than the provincial governments of British India. Two examples stand out.

In Baroda, Sayajirao Gaekwad III (r. 1875–1939) made primary education compulsory throughout the state in 1906, well before any British Indian province, encouraged industry and cooperatives, and sponsored the foundation of the Bank of Baroda in 1908. In Mysore, a succession of dīwāns used the revenue of a well-administered state to build public works and industries. Visvesvaraya, as chief engineer and then as dīwān (1912–1918), directed the building of the Krishnarajasagara dam on the Kāverī, begun in 1911, and as dīwān saw the founding of the Bank of Mysore (1913) and the University of Mysore (1916) and planned the state iron works at Bhadravati, which began production in the 1920s; the hydro-electric works at Śivasamudram, commissioned in 1902, had already made Mysore one of the first places in Asia to use electric power on a large scale. Visvesvaraya’s later writings on planning (Section 20.9.1) grew out of this experience.

These states were not models of popular government: their rulers were autocrats, and the resources they invested came from land revenue and from monopolies as in British India. But their record mattered to the debate. Nationalist economists pointed to Mysore and Baroda as evidence that an Indian government with control over its own revenue could invest in education, irrigation, power and industry, and that the failure of the government of India to do so on a comparable scale was a matter of policy rather than of Indian incapacity.

docs.title: 20.9.1 Early Proposals
docs.text:
The idea that the economy as a whole could be planned reached India in the 1930s, under the influence of the Soviet Five-Year Plans and of the depression, which discredited reliance on the market. The engineer and former dīwān of Mysore, M. Visvesvaraya (1861–1962), had long argued for industrialisation as the remedy for Indian poverty; in Planned Economy for India (1934) he proposed a ten-year plan to double the national income, to be prepared by a national economic council (Visvesvaraya 1934). The Indian National Congress, at its Karachi session in 1931, adopted a resolution on fundamental rights and economic policy that called for state ownership or control of key industries and services, relief for peasants and protection for labour.

In 1938 the Congress president, Subhas Chandra Bose, set up a National Planning Committee with Jawaharlal Nehru as chairman and the economist K. T. Shah as secretary. The Committee brought together industrialists, economists, scientists and politicians, and worked through a large number of sub-committees on agriculture, industry, finance, labour, education, health and other subjects. Its work was interrupted by the war and by the imprisonment of its members, and its reports were published only in the later 1940s, but it established planning as part of the programme of the national movement and laid down principles — a leading role for the state in heavy industry, the coordination of investment, and the protection of cottage industries — that the planners of independent India inherited (Zachariah 2005).

docs.title: 20.9.2 The Plans of 1944
docs.text:
In 1944 three very different plans were published. The first, A Plan of Economic Development for India, usually called the Bombay Plan, was signed by eight leading businessmen and economists, among them Purshotamdas Thakurdas, J. R. D. Tata, G. D. Birla, Ardeshir Dalal, Kasturbhai Lalbhai and John Matthai. It proposed a fifteen-year programme of investment, much of it in basic industries and power, financed in large part by the state and by the sterling balances, with the aim of doubling income per head. That India’s leading capitalists proposed so large a role for the state surprised contemporaries. Vivek Chibber has argued that the businessmen wanted the state to provide infrastructure, protection and finance, but not to discipline private firms, and that this ambivalence shaped the limits of planning after independence (Chibber 2003).

The second, the Gandhian Plan of Shriman Narayan Agarwal, set out an economy of self-sufficient villages, cottage industries and decentralised production, in line with the ideas of Gandhi and J. C. Kumarappa (Chapter 21). The third, the People’s Plan, issued by the Indian Federation of Labour associated with M. N. Roy, gave priority to agriculture and consumer goods and to the redistribution of land. The colonial government itself created a Planning and Development Department in 1944, with Ardeshir Dalal as its member, which asked the provinces to prepare post-war development schemes. The range of these proposals shows that by the end of the war almost every political tendency in India accepted that the state would plan the economy; the argument was about what the plan should contain (Zachariah 2005; Chakravarty 1987).

docs.title: 20.10 Socialist Thought and the “Socialistic Pattern”
docs.text:
Alongside the liberal nationalism of Ranade and the business planning of 1944, a socialist current shaped Indian economic thought from the 1920s.
